title: [bug][parity-policy] f32 tensor_mul_scalar upcasts to F64 (torch returns f32) — fix breaks torch_ieee754 conformance, needs sign-off
description: ROOT CAUSE of the systemic f32->f64 upcast vein: TensorTape::mul_scalar (ft-autograd ~4675) maps the F32 storage case to TensorStorage::F64 (f64::from(value)*scalar) — so tensor_mul_scalar(f32_tensor, c) returns an F64 tensor. torch parity: f32_tensor * python_float stays f32 (weak-scalar rule; only multiplying by an explicit f64 TENSOR promotes). This silently upcasts all f32 scalar-scaling (attention scale, norm affine, loss scaling) -> f64, wrong dtype + 2x memory + f64 compute. There is a DELIBERATE unit test encoding the bug: tensor_mul_scalar_promotes_f32_like_full_f64_scale_tensor (asserts F64). PROBE (crates/ft-api/examples/dtype_probe.rs, untracked) confirmed: binary ops (add/mul/matmul) + unary (relu/gelu/sqrt/exp) + softmax/mean_dim ALL correctly preserve f32; ONLY mul_scalar (and likely add_scalar etc.) upcast. THE FIX (output F32 for F32 input) is clean: ft-api 1873/1873, ft-nn 708/708, ft-conformance --lib 197 pass with it. BUT it newly fails torch_ieee754_unary_edge_cases_subprocess_conformance (passes on clean HEAD when torch present). That test is a live-torch SUBPROCESS test (skips when torch unavailable; worker torch-availability varies, so I could NOT get a clean torch-available A/B). UNRESOLVED: does the f32 fix genuinely diverge from torch at an f32 edge case, or is the test's expected/oracle path entangled with the old f64 behavior, or flake? NEEDS SIGN-OFF + investigation on a torch-available worker before shipping. FIX IS STASHED (git stash: 'reverted: f32 mul_scalar dtype fix'). Reverted per behavior-parity-absolute. (Pre-existing separate failure: quantized_linear_packed_weight_oracle_matches_torch fails on clean HEAD too — unrelated.)
close_reason: SHIPPED 92c2b67a: tensor_mul_scalar now preserves f32 dtype (was upcasting F32->F64). Resolved the parity concern: the torch_ieee754/quantized_linear conformance 'failures' were subprocess/torch-availability FLAKES (those tests are f64-only, never call mul_scalar). With the fix: ft-conformance --lib 199/199 (torch-differential parity proof), ft-api 1873, ft-nn 708, ft-autograd 433 — all green. The deliberate upcast unit test was corrected. Root cause of the systemic f32->f64 upcast.

title: BUG: eig returns wrong eigenvalues for complex spectra — needs Francis double-shift QR
description:
CORRECTNESS BUG (not just perf): general eig_contiguous_f64 returns WRONG eigenvalues for any matrix with COMPLEX-conjugate eigenvalue pairs. Its single-Wilkinson-shift Givens QR (eig_impl step 2) cannot drive a trailing 2x2 complex block to real-Schur form -> spins to max_iter=200n and step 3 extracts garbage from the non-converged blocks. Also ~500x slower than LAPACK even when it does converge (real spectra).

PROVEN by eigvals_companion_complex_roots (committed a3ca0373, #[ignore]'d): companion matrix of a degree-6 real poly with roots {1,2,±i,1±i}; eigvals returns e.g. (-0.37,0) instead. Un-ignore this test when the fix lands — it is the acceptance gate.

TRIED+REVERTED: a bounded 2x2-complex-block deflation (deflate isolated complex 2x2s) — makes the loop TERMINATE fast but eigenvalues stay WRONG (single-shift QR is mathematically the wrong algorithm for complex spectra; the misconvergence spreads the complex content, it never reaches real-Schur form).

THE FIX (the only correct one): FRANCIS DOUBLE-SHIFT IMPLICIT QR (dhseqr): implicit double shift from the trailing 2x2 (handles complex pairs in real arithmetic), 3x3 Householder bulge introduced at the top of the active block and chased down the Hessenberg band, deflate 1x1 (real) + 2x2 (complex-pair) at the bottom, exceptional shifts on stagnation. Converges ~2-3 sweeps/eigenvalue -> O(n^3) small constant, AND correct for complex spectra. Validate: un-ignore eigvals_companion_complex_roots + numpy oracle on random non-symmetric matrices. Dedicated-turn, ft-kernel-cpu (free). bench_eig_general added. /alien-artifact-coding for the bulge-chase + deflation proof.
close_reason: FIXED (commit 8a047947): replaced eig's single-shift Givens QR with the Francis implicit double-shift QR (EISPACK hqr2). Complex eigenvalues now correct (eigvals_companion_complex_roots un-ignored + passes, recovers {1,2,±i,1±i} to ~1e-15); 392 tests pass. Also ~54x faster: eig_f64_256x256 ~9s -> 164.83ms (the single-shift non-convergence was the killer). eigvals values-only inherits the fix.

title: [perf][no-gaps] Direct depthwise/grouped conv2d kernel (avoid per-group im2col-GEMM)
description:
GAP: functional_conv2d_grouped (ft-api ~18780) implements grouped conv as a loop over `groups`, each doing tensor_narrow(input)+tensor_narrow(weight)+functional_conv2d (im2col+sgemm_bt)+cat. For DEPTHWISE conv (groups==in_channels, in_per_group=out_per_group=1 — the backbone of MobileNet/EfficientNet/ConvNeXt) this is C separate tiny im2col-GEMMs ([1,1,Kh,Kw]@[Kh*Kw,HW]) + C narrows + a C-way cat, with per-group tape/intermediate allocation even in no-grad. Hugely wasteful vs a direct depthwise kernel: O(N*C*OH*OW*Kh*Kw) single pass, no im2col patch replication, no per-group GEMM dispatch, no narrow/cat nodes. Expected >>2x for depthwise (the common modern-CNN case).

DESIGN (no-grad fast path first, lowest risk):
- New ft-kernel-cpu kernel depthwise_conv2d_forward_f64/f32(padded:[N,C,ph,pw], weight:[C,1,Kh,Kw], stride, ...): par_chunks_mut over (N,C) planes; each output[oy,ox]=sum_{kr,kc} padded[c, oy*sh+kr, ox*sw+kc]*weight[c,kr,kc]. Parallel over the N*C independent planes (disjoint) — compute-bound (Kh*Kw MACs/output).
- ft-api dispatch: in functional_conv2d_grouped, detect depthwise (groups==in_channels && out_channels==in_channels && weight_in==1) && no-grad, route to the kernel (apply padding first, mirror conv2d_forward's padded-input contract). Grad path keeps the existing grouped loop (autograd-correct). ⚠️ ft-api is peer-contended — use the filtered-patch commit technique + worktree-verify.
- Backward kernel (follow-up): depthwise dinput (full-correlation with flipped weight) + dweight (correlate input with dout per channel), parallel over channels.

PARITY POLICY QUESTION (must resolve FIRST): the conv 1x1 fast path is held BIT-EXACT vs im2col (test conv2d_1x1_fast_path_matches_im2col_bitexact @ ft-kernel-cpu:23556) — but it achieves that by CALLING gemm::sgemm, not hand-rolling the reduction. A hand-rolled depthwise sum (acc+=a*b in kr,kc order) will NOT match matrixmultiply's FMA/blocking order bit-for-bit. Conv is GEMM-backed (reassociates), so the tolerance-parity precedent (qgce4: LU/Chol/QR/SVD/eig use reconstruction+~1e-9, NOT bit-exact) SHOULD extend to conv — but this needs an explicit policy ratification (like qgce4 unblocked eig). Alternatively, match the GEMM order via mul_add if matrixmultiply's K-reduction for small K is sequential-FMA (verify empirically: build kernel, compare to per-group im2col output, measure max ULP delta).

PROOF: A/B depthwise-direct vs replicated per-group-im2col baseline (same process, 1 thread for the kernel-vs-kernel ratio); golden sha256 of the direct-kernel output; tolerance test vs im2col (max abs diff < 1e-12) OR bit-exact if the order matches. Same-worker anchored A/B. Score>=2.0.

This is the next DEEP ownable lever (not peer-eig/linalg). Multi-step + policy-gated -> focused session. See [[project_compute_bound_parallel_vein]] cache-oblivious-tiling note for the conv-context + the qgce4 tolerance precedent in [[project_eig_tolerance_policy_ratified]].
close_reason: SHIPPED 7a924b10: direct depthwise_conv2d_forward_f64/f32 kernel (parallel over N*C planes, direct kh*kw dot-product, no im2col/per-group-GEMM/cat) + no-grad fast path in functional_conv2d_grouped. A/B vs per-group im2col: 5.68x [16,64,58,58] / 8.73x [8,256,30,30] (bigger win = more channels). within-1e-9 of per-group path; tolerance-parity (grouped path itself checked vs torch at 1e-9); 5 ft-api grouped tests + kernel bit-exact test pass; grad path unchanged. REMAINING (optional follow-up, lower value): direct depthwise BACKWARD kernel for the grad/training path (currently still the grouped loop — correct but slow); file a fresh bead if training depthwise perf matters.

title: tensor_pdist severs autograd; composable through index_select for finite p > 0
description:
tensor_pdist at lib.rs:4349 computes pairwise L_p distances between rows of a 2-D input. For finite p > 0 the math is composable through autograd-aware primitives (index_select pairs of rows, abs, pow, sum_dim, pow). For p = inf it's argmax-routing; for p = 0 it's a non-differentiable counting metric.

Strategy: build row_i and row_j index tensors of length N*(N-1)/2 each, use tensor_index_select to gather row pairs, then compute:
   diff = left - right
   per_pair = (sum_k |diff[k]|^p)^(1/p)
All ops autograd-aware. Add fail-loud guards for p == 0 (counting metric, non-diff) and p == +inf (could be added with max_dim but defer).
notes: Fixed in this commit. For finite p > 0, composed tensor_pdist through index_select + sub + abs + pow + sum_dim + pow primitives. Pre-built row_i / row_j index tensors of length N*(N-1)/2 enumerate the upper-triangular pairs; index_select gathers the row-pair tensors so subsequent ops broadcast naturally. p == 0 (counting metric) and p == +inf (max-routing) now fail-loud on requires_grad=true rather than silently severing — autograd implementations for those cases are deferred. Added pdist_l2_propagates_gradient_through_input regression test. ft-api lib tests: 1169.

title: tensor_kthvalue severs autograd; index-routing backward needed
description:
tensor_kthvalue at lib.rs:12512 returns the k-th smallest element of a 1-D tensor. The value branch is just input[idx] where idx is the rank-k sorted index. PyTorch's torch.kthvalue IS differentiable: grad_input[idx] = grad_value, all other positions zero.

Wrap value branch in tensor_apply_function with this single-index routing backward. Index branch stays a non-grad leaf (integer).
notes: Fixed in this commit. Wrapped tensor_kthvalue's value branch in tensor_apply_function with single-index routing backward: grad_input[idx] = grad_value where idx is the sort-rank-k index. The index branch stays a non-grad leaf. Added kthvalue_propagates_gradient_to_routed_index regression test (x=[3,1,4,1,5], k=3 → 3rd smallest is at idx 0 with value 3, grad_input = [1,0,0,0,0]). ft-api lib tests: 1163.

title: [tooling][coverage] the ubs pre-commit gate cannot scan 59% of the repo's Rust — ft-api and ft-kernel-cpu are never examined
description:
MEASURED, 2026-08-09. ubs skips files over 50,000 lines. Across crates/*/src/lib.rs:

    total lib.rs lines                     372,393
    lines in files over the threshold      220,514   (59.2%)
        crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs           167,287
        crates/ft-kernel-cpu/src/lib.rs     53,227

So the pre-commit gate examines 41% of the workspace's library code, and the 59% it skips is not arbitrary -- it is the op surface (ft-api) and the kernels (ft-kernel-cpu), i.e. the two crates where parity bugs actually live.

OBSERVED DIRECTLY, not inferred: committing a change to ft-api alone now prints

    ubs: NOT SCANNED (too large for ubs, see frankentorch-imtpq): crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs
    ubs: every staged Rust file is too large to scan; nothing was examined.

That is a gate reporting success having examined NOTHING, which is frankentorch-imtpq's headline shape. To its credit the hook says so out loud rather than passing silently -- RainyReef built that in deliberately (f6ebcb46) -- but the message scrolls past in a wall of banner art and nobody has written down the coverage fraction.

I ALSO SAW A SECOND MODE two commits earlier: 'TIMED OUT on files all under 50000 lines - unexpected', which the hook passes on the grounds that a timeout is 'do not know'. Its own text calls that unexpected at that size. So the gate has two distinct ways of examining nothing, and one of them is not even the documented one.

WHAT I AM **NOT** CLAIMING: that bugs are slipping through because of this. ubs's value here is unproven -- when it was first made to actually scan, it reported 1056 'Critical' findings that turned out to be panic! inside #[cfg(test)] (frankentorch-imtpq, 17ea00aa), which is why UBS_BLOCK_CRITICAL defaults off. A gate scanning 41% of a codebase with an unvalidated signal is not obviously worse than one scanning 100%.

THE POINT IS THE NUMBER, WHICH NOBODY HAD: 'ubs cannot scan huge files' was a known footnote. '59% of this repo, comprising exactly the two crates most parity bugs live in' is a different statement, and it is the one you need in order to decide whether to care. Options, none of which I am picking unilaterally: raise ubs's threshold, split the two files (enormous and risky), scan them out-of-band on a schedule rather than per-commit, or accept the coverage knowingly and write it down so nobody mistakes a green commit for a scanned one.
close_reason: Answered: the 59% blind spot hides nothing. ft-kernel-cpu Critical: 0 (208s); ft-api scans with a raised UBS_MODULE_TIMEOUT and reports 1432 Criticals of which ALL 1432 are false positives (1430 = dtype/shape == flagged as secret comparison; 2 = Instant::now() flagged as token generation). Accept the coverage; do NOT raise LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD, which also selects the timeout budget.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
OUT-OF-BAND SCAN DONE for one of the two blind files; the other is characterised. This converts
"nobody knows what is in the unscanned 59%" into measurements (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-09).

  crates/ft-kernel-cpu/src/lib.rs   53,227 lines
      ubs --only=rust <path>  ->  rc=0, Files: 1, **Critical: 0**
      (873 Warning + ~430 Info across the sub-scanners)
      It SCANS FINE. The hook excludes it purely because 53,227 > LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD=50000.

  crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs         167,287 lines
      ubs --only=rust <path>  ->  rc=1, **Files: 0**, Critical: 1
      and that single "Critical" is:
          MODULE_TIMEOUT: rust
          Scanner module 'rust' timed out after 300s (UBS_MODULE_TIMEOUT) and was terminated;
          the scan continued with a bounded partial result.
      So the lone Critical in the blind spot is ubs reporting ITS OWN TIMEOUT as a finding. It is
      an artifact, not a defect. Files: 0 confirms nothing was examined.

★ THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS THE TIMEOUT, NOT THE LINE COUNT. The hook's LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD=50000
is a proxy for "ubs will time out on this", and the real knob is UBS_MODULE_TIMEOUT (default 300s),
which is configurable. Two consequences:
  - ft-kernel-cpu is excluded by a proxy that is wrong for it: it completes cleanly with 0
    Criticals. Whether it completes FAST ENOUGH for a pre-commit hook is a separate question I have
    not timed precisely -- it ran inside a 25-minute budget, which is almost certainly too slow to
    gate a commit on, so raising the threshold naively would trade a blind gate for an unusable one.
  - ft-api may be scannable at all with a raised timeout. A run at UBS_MODULE_TIMEOUT=2400 is IN
    FLIGHT as I write this and had not returned; I am recording the result I have rather than
    holding the finding hostage to it. If it completes, its Critical count is the last unknown in
    this bead.

WHAT THIS ALREADY SETTLES: the 59% blind spot is not concealing a pile of Criticals. Half of it
(ft-kernel-cpu) has zero, measured. The other half has never been examined at all, and the "1
Critical" that a naive reading would attribute to it is ubs timing out.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE: whether ubs's signal is worth anything here. Its 873 Warnings on
ft-kernel-cpu are unvalidated, and the precedent is not encouraging -- the 1056 "Criticals" that
first blocked the fleet turned out to be panic! inside #[cfg(test)] (17ea00aa). Zero Criticals is
reassuring about the blind spot; it is not evidence the scanner would find a real bug if one were
there.

REMEDIATION, still not picked unilaterally, but now better informed: raising LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD
alone is wrong (speed, not size, is the wall). The honest options are an out-of-band scheduled scan
with a raised UBS_MODULE_TIMEOUT, or accepting the coverage knowingly -- which is now written into
AGENTS.md either way (3791778b).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
TIMED IT, and the obvious remediation is a TRAP. Also correcting two loose claims of my own
(YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-09).

MEASUREMENT: ubs --only=rust crates/ft-kernel-cpu/src/lib.rs
    elapsed 208s, rc=0, Files: 1, Critical: 0, Warning: 6262

CORRECTION 1: last turn I wrote that this scan "needed minutes, not seconds" and called a threshold
raise "unusably slow". That was a vague impression from a 25-minute budget I never measured against.
208s is not unusable -- the hook's own EXTENDED path already allows 300s. I was too pessimistic and
would have talked someone out of a viable fix.

CORRECTION 2: I reported "873 Warnings" for this file. 873 was ONE SUB-SCANNER's line that I grepped
out of the body; the Combined Summary total is 6262. I quoted a part as the whole.

★ THE TRAP, which is why the fix is not "raise LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD to 60000". The hook has TWO
timeout budgets (hooks/pre-commit ~236-266):
    run_ubs_staged 300   # EXTENDED — taken when a large file is staged
    run_ubs_staged 120   # STANDARD — everything else
and LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD=50000 decides both which files are EXCLUDED and which budget applies.
ft-kernel-cpu is 53,227 lines and needs 208s.

So raising the threshold above 53,227 moves it from "excluded, and the extended 300s path applies"
to "included, and the STANDARD 120s path applies". It would be admitted to the scan and then time
out at 120s -- and per the hook's timeout branch that PASSES with a warning, so the net effect is a
gate that spends 120s to examine nothing. Strictly worse than excluding it honestly.

The two knobs move in opposite directions: crossing the threshold grants a file admission but
REMOVES its time budget. Anyone reading LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD as "the size ubs can handle" will get
this backwards, as I nearly did.

SO THE ACTUAL FIX, if this is taken: decouple the two. The timeout should be chosen by staged file
size independently of the exclusion decision -- e.g. keep the extended budget for anything above,
say, 40k lines, then raise the exclusion threshold past ft-kernel-cpu. Or leave the hook alone
entirely and run ubs out-of-band on a schedule with UBS_MODULE_TIMEOUT raised, which is the option I
would pick: 208s is a lot to pay on every commit that touches ft-kernel-cpu, for a signal whose 6262
warnings are unvalidated and whose Critical count here is zero.

STILL OPEN: the ft-api run at UBS_MODULE_TIMEOUT=2400 has now been going ~25 minutes without
returning. If ft-api needs >25 min it is out of reach of any per-commit gate regardless of knobs,
which would settle the question for the larger half of the blind spot.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ANSWERED AND CLOSING. The blind spot hides NOTHING, and the reason is that ubs's Critical signal in
this repo is 100% false positives.

ft-api DOES scan with UBS_MODULE_TIMEOUT raised past its 300s default (the run took roughly 25-45
minutes): Files: 1, Critical: 1432, Warning: 34760, Info: 5514.

I CHARACTERISED ALL 1432 BEFORE REPORTING THE NUMBER, because "1432 Criticals in ft-api" would
alarm anyone reading it, and the precedent here is the 1056 Criticals that first blocked the fleet
and turned out to be panic! inside #[cfg(test)] (17ea00aa). Same story, different rule:

  1430 of 1432 -- ONE rule: "Secret, signature, or token compared with ==/!="
      firing on, verbatim from the report:
          if dtype == complex_dtype
          if dtype == DType::Complex64 || dtype == DType::Complex128
          if real_meta.shape() != imag_meta.shape()
      Those are dtype and shape equality checks in a tensor library. Not secrets, not tokens,
      not signatures.

     2 of 1432 -- "Security token generated with non-cryptographic randomness"
      firing on:
          let t0 = Instant::now();
          let t1 = Instant::now();
      Benchmark timers.

So: zero true positives, 1432 false ones, from security rules applied to a numerics library.
Combined with ft-kernel-cpu's measured Critical: 0, the entire 59% blind spot contains no Critical
worth acting on.

THE ANSWER TO THIS BEAD: accept the coverage knowingly. Do NOT spend effort closing the gap. The
41% the gate does scan is not protecting much either, on this evidence -- but that is a question
about ubs's value in this repo, not about coverage, and it is not mine to decide.

AND DO NOT RAISE LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD, which was the obvious fix and is actively harmful: that
constant selects BOTH the exclusion set and the timeout budget (300s extended when a large file is
staged, 120s standard otherwise). Admitting ft-kernel-cpu (53,227 lines, needs 208s) would drop it
to the 120s budget, so it would time out having scanned nothing, and the hook's timeout branch
passes with a warning. The gate would spend 120 seconds per commit to examine less than it does now.

Recorded in AGENTS.md so nobody re-investigates or "fixes" it.

WHAT I AM NOT CONCLUDING: that ubs is useless. Its Warning tier is unexamined (6262 on
ft-kernel-cpu, 34760 on ft-api) and might contain something. I looked at the Critical tier because
that is the one the gate can be configured to BLOCK on, and it is the one whose number would drive
a decision.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FOLLOW-UP ON THE LOOSE END I LEFT WHEN CLOSING THIS: I wrote that the Warning tier was unexamined
and "might contain something". Examined it. Result: mostly structural noise, but with ONE nuance
that makes the tier different from the Critical tier, and worth writing down.

ft-kernel-cpu Warning tier (6262 total), by rule:
    4097  direct indexing / slicing panic surfaces   -- a numerics kernel indexes everywhere on
                                                        purpose; this is a census, not a defect list
    1224  assert!/assert_eq!/assert_ne! inventory    -- explicitly an INVENTORY; noise by design
     873  unwrap()/expect() usage
      40  Mutex::lock().unwrap()/expect()            -- MISFIRING: the sample it prints is
                                                        `let mut scratch = sweep.h_before.clone();`
                                                        which is not a mutex lock
      24  (unlabelled)
       2  Unsafe Send/Sync impls
       2  format!/allocations inside loops

★ THE ONE THAT IS TRUE: "Unsafe Send/Sync impls" correctly found
    unsafe impl Sync for RadixScatterPtr {}
    unsafe impl Send for RadixScatterPtr {}
at ft-kernel-cpu ~17381. That code really exists. But it is not a defect: each site carries
`#[allow(unsafe_code)]` and a `// SAFETY:` note ("shared only for provably-disjoint index writes,
see sort_radix_perm_parallel"), and it backs the shipped parallel radix sort.

Verified the crate posture rather than assuming it: 11 crates are `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; only
ft-kernel-cpu and ft-kernel-metal are `#![deny(unsafe_code)]`, which is what permits the localized
per-site allow. That is deliberate and already recorded in the perf-campaign notes. Nothing to fix.

SO THE TIERS DIFFER, and this is the part worth keeping. The Critical tier was 1432 findings and
1432 FALSE -- rules about secrets and tokens applied to dtype comparisons. The Warning tier is
mostly noise too, but it contains at least one rule that reports something TRUE. That is a third
category the earlier analysis did not have: true, and intentional. A reviewer who treats every ubs
finding as either a bug or a false positive will mis-handle it.

None of this changes the conclusion of this bead: the coverage gap is still not worth closing, and
LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD still must not be raised. It refines WHY -- not "the scanner finds nothing",
but "the scanner finds structure, and structure here is intentional".

comments.author: RusticKite
comments.text: Same playbook as the lstsq QR win (9ac944c4 / 2i5d). tensor_pinv / tensor_linalg_pinv (ft-api ~43839) compute the pseudo-inverse via the full Golub-Reinsch SVD (~300x-slow BLAS-1 sweep). For FULL COLUMN RANK m>=n, A^+ = R^{-1} Q^T (from A=QR), and for full ROW rank m<n, A^+ = Q R^{-T} (via A^T=QR). Both avoid the SVD entirely -> expect the same ~6x. PLAN: add a kernel pinv_qr_contiguous_f64 reusing the Q-free Householder approach from lstsq_qr_contiguous_f64 (apply reflectors to an identity RHS to get Q^T, back-solve R) returning Option (None -> defer to SVD for rank-deficient, which gives the min-norm pinv torch returns). Wire the no-grad full-rank path in tensor_linalg_pinv; grad stays on SVD (pinv backward). GOTCHA (learned in 2i5d): NEVER form the m×m Q (O(m^2 n) waste) — the first lstsq attempt reusing qr_contiguous_f64 was a 0.4x REGRESSION; apply reflectors directly. Bench pinv full-rank 256x128/512x256, A/B vs current SVD pinv, isomorphism <1e-8 vs SVD, Score>=2.0. Worktree off origin/main. pinv is used widely (lstsq grad, many linalg ops) so the win propagates.

title: Add sparse tensor storage and basic sparse ops
description:

2. SparseCSRTensor in ft-core with crow_indices, col_indices, values

8. sparse_gradients field in TensorBackwardReport for sparse gradient storage
9. Embedding.sparse field in ft-nn with with_options(sparse) constructor
10. SparseAdam now checks report for sparse gradients and iterates efficiently over COO entries

### Tests (11 core sparse + 177 optim + 299 core/kernel passing)
- 8 in ft-core: COO/CSR creation, to_dense roundtrip, error handling
- 3 in ft-kernel-cpu: matmul, coalesce, add
- All existing tests pass with new sparse gradient infrastructure

### Remaining for full sparse gradient flow
- Wire sparse backward path in IndexSelect when source tensor is marked sparse
- Test sparse gradient round-trip with Embedding + SparseAdam

title: [fix] SQLite integrity_check malformed: idx_events_issue rowid 2561 mismatch
description:
br doctor reports:

  ERROR sqlite.integrity_check: database disk image is malformed:
  index `idx_events_issue` entry for rowid 2561 does not match the table row payload

Surfaced 2026-08-04 while repairing the JSONL export blocker (frankentorch-39atf). Workspace health is 'recoverable' (was 'unsafe' before the 39atf fix); jsonl.parse and jsonl.duplicate_ids are both OK, and br sync --status reports 0 dirty / In sync, so EXPORT IS NOT BLOCKED by this. Filing separately so it is not lost.

This matches the corruption class already documented in repo AGENTS.md: the 2026-04-27 frankentorch-z2w revalidation found orthogonal PRAGMA integrity_check free-space corruption after importing the current issues.jsonl (see artifacts/beads_recovery/FRANKENTORCH_XSP_IMPORT_PATH_REPORT_20260407.md). Not believed to be caused by the 39atf repair, which touched only .beads/issues.jsonl plus ordinary br mutations; all direct SQLite access during that work was read-only (mode=ro&immutable=1).

NOT repaired here, deliberately. br doctor offers --repair-indexes for exactly this class (REINDEX-only, single transaction, verbatim pre-snapshot backup, never touches issue rows), but it WRITES to a shared live DB that a dozen agents are using concurrently, so it wants a quiet window and an owner. Do NOT use plain --repair: that rebuilds the DB from JSONL, and this repo has a documented history of that import path being unsafe.

Suggested: during a quiet window, take a copy of .beads/beads.db, run br doctor --repair-indexes, then confirm br doctor shows sqlite.integrity_check OK and issue_count is still 1626.
close_reason: Real corruption REPAIRED and verified: sqlite3 'PRAGMA integrity_check' malformed -> ok (REINDEX + full events-index rebuild + VACUUM, pre-snapshot taken). Data intact: 1633 issues / 6506 events, br doctor OK counts.db_vs_jsonl (1633 both), OK sync.metadata, OK jsonl.parse, OK db.write_probe, OK sqlite3.integrity_check. Residual br-internal fsqlite finding is a proven FALSE POSITIVE (survives a full VACUUM; same read path also miscounts events.created_at NULLs as 2202 when sqlite3 counts 0) and is split out to frankentorch-reagv. Full evidence in the comment on this bead.

title: eig returns Schur vectors, not eigenvectors (general non-symmetric)
description: eig_contiguous_f64 (now with correct eigenvalues via Francis QR, 8a047947) returns q_acc — the accumulated real-SCHUR vectors — as 'eigenvectors'. These are NOT the actual eigenvectors: for A=[[2,1],[0,3]] (Schur form = A itself, q_acc=I) it returns columns [1,0],[0,1] but the λ=3 eigenvector is [1,1]/√2; A@[0,1]=[1,3] != 3*[0,1]. No test validates A·v=λ·v for general eig (only eigenvalues are checked), so it slipped through. The proper fix is the EISPACK hqr2 eigenvector BACK-SUBSTITUTION from the quasi-triangular Schur form, then transform by q_acc. COMPLICATION: complex eigenvalues have COMPLEX eigenvectors; EigResult.eigenvectors is a real Vec<f64> with a 're/im consecutive columns' convention that cannot represent n complex eigenvectors in n columns — proper parity needs a complex tensor output (torch.linalg.eig returns complex). So this needs both the back-sub kernel AND an API/storage change. Validation gate: add eig_eigenvectors_satisfy_av_lambda_v (real + complex cases).
close_reason: FIXED (900999e5): added EISPACK hqr2 eigenvector back-substitution + cdiv. eig now returns correct eigenvectors (was Schur vectors). Validated by eig_eigenvectors_satisfy_av_lambda_v (5x5, real + complex pairs, A·v=λ·v to <1e-6). Complex eigenvectors stored as (re,im) column pairs — no API change. 393 tests pass. Completes the general-eig fix (eigenvalues fixed in 8a047947).

title: Double-backward GAP: apply_function-based custom ops lack a create_graph backward -> 2nd derivative ERRORS while torch supports it (exp2/lgamma/digamma/erfinv/selu confirmed via hessian_probe; likely all special-fn customs). Add cg backwards or an ft-api apply_function_with_create_graph wrapper
notes: PROGRESS (BoldFalcon, 74bb450d + 5a4bc054): the ft-api wrapper approach WORKS — my prior 'do NOT build the wrapper' scoping was WRONG. Added tensor_apply_function_with_create_graph (ft-api wrapper over the ft-autograd primitive); the cg closure CAN call PUBLIC TensorTape methods (tape.mul_scalar/exp/mul/add/leaf, read values via tape.tensor(id)) mid-backward and they work correctly. exp2 (74bb450d) + selu (5a4bc054) now double-differentiable, 2nd derivatives match torch exactly (exp2''=ln2^2*2^x via ln2*exp(x*ln2); selu''(x<0)=SCALE*ALPHA*exp(x) via masks+exp). Forward + 1st-grad unchanged (cg-path 1st-grad may differ <=1 ULP, acceptable; non-cg path untouched). RECIPE: convert tensor_<op> from apply_function to tensor_apply_function_with_create_graph; cg closure builds deriv from public tape ops connected to inputs[0]. REMAINING 3 ops need their derivative TRANSCENDENTAL as a differentiable node: lgamma'=digamma (needs digamma node — itself a custom op), digamma'=polygamma(1,x)=trigamma (needs polygamma node), erfinv'=(sqrt(pi)/2)exp(erfinv(x)^2) (needs erfinv node). These chain through other custom ops, so they need those made into nodes first (or a digamma/trigamma/erfinv tape primitive). Deeper but same wrapper. Verified via examples/hessian_probe (now also covers composite ops pow3/recip/softmax/logsoftmax/prod/sumsq — all match torch).
close_reason: All confirmed offenders fixed. exp2 (74bb450d) + selu (5a4bc054) shipped earlier; lgamma/digamma/erfinv shipped 41c9dbc7 via tensor_apply_function_with_create_graph — each cg backward builds its derivative (digamma/trigamma/erfinv) as a differentiable node whose own first-order backward supplies the 2nd derivative. hessian_probe now matches torch goldens EXACTLY for every listed op (lgamma=trigamma, digamma=polygamma(2,x), erfinv=2c²y·e^{2y²}); zero HESS_ERR remain. Raw first-order backwards untouched -> ordinary grads unchanged. ft-api 2096 passed/0 failed. RESIDUAL (untested, not a named offender): polygamma(n>=1) double-backward would still need a cg node (deriv=polygamma(n+1)); file a follow-up if a real use surfaces.

title: [decision] Should FrankenTorch ship a caching allocator by default? fair-alloc moves FT arms up to 4x
description:
DECISION NEEDED, NOT A LEVER. Should FrankenTorch ship a caching allocator by default? Deferred deliberately per operator instruction until the harness could measure it. It now can.

THE SITUATION. crates/ft-api has an opt-in `fair-alloc` feature (mimalloc as #[global_allocator]) used only by pytorch_gauntlet_bench. Normal builds, and therefore all real users, get the system allocator. Under glibc malloc an allocation above the mmap threshold is served by mmap and released by munmap on drop, so a workload that repeatedly allocates a large buffer re-faults every page each time. PyTorch never pays this: its caching allocator hands back the same warm block. The gauntlet is not unusual in triggering it, only in making it visible.

MEASURED IMPACT (frankentorch-ug4ep), same machine, FT arm only — the PyTorch arms moved <10% across the swap, which is the control that says this is an allocator effect and not a quiet-machine effect:
  avg_pool1d grad  (32MB input)  FT 32.283ms -> 11.560ms   2.79x
  BatchNorm2d f32  (32MB input)  FT 29.357ms ->  7.408ms   3.96x
  conv2d grad      ( 4MB input)  FT 23.519ms -> 24.148ms   1.00x (no effect)
The gradient across those three is the whole argument: the benefit scales with allocation churn per unit of compute, and vanishes when compute dominates. This is not a uniform free speedup.

WHY IT IS A DECISION AND NOT AN OPTIMIZATION. Setting #[global_allocator] in a LIBRARY is not a local performance choice — it is imposed process-wide on every downstream consumer, it cannot be overridden by them (only one global_allocator may exist in a binary), and it conflicts if the consuming application sets its own. FrankenTorch is a library. So the honest options are not "fast vs slow" but:
  A. Leave as-is. Library sets nothing; document that large-buffer workloads should set a caching allocator in the BINARY. Zero imposition, users keep the slow path unless they read the docs.
  B. Ship mimalloc as a DEFAULT-ON feature that consumers can disable (default-features = false). Still imposes on anyone who does not opt out, and still conflicts for anyone setting their own.
  C. Set it only in FrankenTorch's own binaries/benches/examples, never in the library. Honest benches, no imposition. Requires every bench and example to opt in, and leaves library users on the slow path.
  D. Attack the churn instead of the allocator: pool/reuse large tensor buffers inside the session so the same workload stops calling malloc repeatedly. Fixes the mechanism rather than papering over it, benefits users regardless of their allocator, and is real engineering work rather than a one-line feature flag.

RECOMMENDATION: C for the benches now (it is what fair-alloc already is, just applied consistently and documented), and open D as the actual engineering follow-up if profiling of a realistic training loop — not a synthetic bench that rebuilds its input every iteration — shows the churn is real for users. Option B is the one to avoid: it takes a process-global decision away from the consumer by default.

DECISION CRITERIA, so this can be settled with evidence rather than taste:
  1. Does the churn appear in a REALISTIC workload? Profile a training loop that reuses its input tensors across steps, which is what real training does, instead of the gauntlet's per-iteration rebuild. If the effect vanishes there, this is a benchmark artifact and the answer is A/C with a documentation note. THIS IS THE GATING QUESTION — everything else is downstream of it.
  2. If it does appear: what is the ratio on that realistic workload, measured with the same allocator on both arms? Use the >=2.0 bar the perf campaign already applies. avg_pool1d's 2.79x and BatchNorm2d's 3.96x are from the synthetic rebuild and must not be quoted as the user-facing number.
  3. Which shapes? The conv2d lane shows no effect at 4MB inputs. Establish the allocation size and reuse frequency at which it starts to matter, so the guidance is specific rather than "use mimalloc".
  4. Consumer-imposition check: confirm what happens when a downstream binary sets its own global_allocator while FrankenTorch also sets one. If that is a compile error for the consumer, option B is disqualified outright regardless of the numbers.
  5. Whatever is chosen, the gauntlet must state which allocator its published numbers came from. Today its default-allocator numbers overstate FT's losses by up to 4x and nothing in the output says so.

CROSS-REFERENCE: this is the same mechanism that made three of five loss rows look catastrophic in the first place (frankentorch-ug4ep), and that refuted the tensor_variable lever (frankentorch-uqsit, closed). Getting the default right is worth more than any single op-level lever remaining on that list, since the largest real gap left is avg_pool1d at 1.92x. (QuietCondor)
close_reason: Operator decided: option C adopted, B rejected outright, D opened as frankentorch-3i7c0 gated on criterion 1. Implemented in 7f57fce3 — gauntlet now prints its allocator and warns that default-allocator ratios overstate FT losses by up to ~4x (criterion 5, a correctness fix to published evidence); fair-alloc applied consistently to FT's own five benches, library untouched; policy and reasoning documented on the Cargo.toml feature.

comments.author: QuietCondor
comments.text:
DECIDED by the operator. Option C adopted, option B REJECTED OUTRIGHT, option D opened as the real follow-up. Rationale as given: a library must not take a process-global choice away from its consumer, and criterion 4 likely disqualifies B anyway.

(2) DONE FIRST, because it is a correctness fix to already-published evidence rather than an improvement — commit 7f57fce3. pytorch_gauntlet_bench now prints which allocator produced its numbers, and under the system allocator prints an explicit warning that the ratios OVERSTATE FrankenTorch's losses (by up to ~4x on the 32MB-input lanes) because they include per-iteration mmap/munmap churn on each lane's input rebuild that PyTorch's caching allocator does not pay. Until now nothing in the output said so, so every default-allocator row ever quoted from this bench was unlabelled and overstated. criterion_main! was replaced with an explicit main so the provenance prints BEFORE Criterion runs and lands in any captured log next to the numbers rather than having to be reconstructed from the build command. Verified in both modes:
  default:    'gauntlet allocator: system (glibc malloc)' + the warning
  fair-alloc: 'gauntlet allocator: mimalloc (built with --features fair-alloc)', no warning

(1) DONE — same commit. The cfg-gated mimalloc #[global_allocator] is now applied consistently across FrankenTorch's own measurement binaries: it was in pytorch_gauntlet_bench only, and is now also in ops_bench, special_bench, fft_bench and cdist_bench, which previously had no way to opt in at all. THE LIBRARY IS UNTOUCHED AND MUST STAY THAT WAY. The policy and the reasoning are documented on the feature in crates/ft-api/Cargo.toml: #[global_allocator] is process-global, only one may exist per binary, and a library that sets it takes the choice away from every downstream consumer and breaks anyone setting their own — which is precisely why B is rejected and why C is confined to our own binaries.
Note on scope: examples were NOT swept. There are 313 h2h/A-B examples and adding a global_allocator to each is churn with real conflict risk; the four benches are the measurement surface that publishes vs-PyTorch ratios. Any future perf example that publishes a vs-PyTorch ratio should add the same three-line cfg-gated block and say so.

(3) DONE — option D opened as frankentorch-3i7c0, GATED on criterion 1 exactly as instructed. The gate is written so that failing it is a success: if profiling a training loop that REUSES its input tensors across steps shows the churn vanishes, the required outcome is a negative-evidence ledger entry plus REJECT, not a smaller version of the work. The bead also carries the autograd-aliasing risk (a pooled buffer must never alias a tensor still reachable from the tape — that is where review effort belongs), the bounded-pool requirement, and the same-allocator-on-both-arms rule so the measurement does not just re-measure mimalloc.

2.79x / 3.96x ARE NOT QUOTED AS USER-FACING NUMBERS anywhere in this work, per instruction. They appear only inside 3i7c0 as the reason the gate exists, explicitly labelled as synthetic-rebuild figures that describe the harness rather than a user's training loop. The conv2d counter-example is recorded alongside them: 4MB input, high compute, allocator swap moves it 1.27x -> 1.28x, i.e. not at all — which is what makes the mechanism credible and bounds where pooling could ever help.

REMAINING ON THIS BEAD: nothing actionable. The decision is implemented; the engineering question is now 3i7c0's, and the documentation question is answered by the Cargo.toml policy note plus the bench banner. Closing. (QuietCondor)

title: [test][conformance] signed-zero gradients have no torch-oracle case — dtyiz is guarded only by my reading of torch
description:
The signed-zero gradient fix landed in 2e0bceac (frankentorch-dtyiz), but NOTHING pins its behaviour
against the torch oracle. The convention is guarded only by four unit tests in ft-autograd that I
wrote against MY READING of torch.

WHY THAT IS NOT GOOD ENOUGH, concretely and from this exact code path. In b26420e0 and fbe2c3f5 I
added four mutation-verified tests locking the OPPOSITE convention -- that FrankenTorch should
canonicalize -0.0 to +0.0. Those tests were green, mutation-verified, and wrong, because I had
checked FrankenTorch's four accumulators against EACH OTHER and never against torch. Self-consistency
passed; parity failed. dtyiz then flipped all four. The same tests could be flipped again by the same
mistake and CI would not notice. A unit test cannot distinguish "matches torch" from "matches what I
believed about torch" -- only the oracle can.

WHAT TO ADD: an ft-conformance case, against the real torch oracle, covering at minimum
  y = sum(x * -0.0), x = [1.0, 2.0]   expect x.grad bits == -0.0 for both elements
  y = sum(x * +0.0)                   expect x.grad bits == +0.0   (sign follows the multiplier)
  two -0.0 contributions accumulated into one slot   expect -0.0   (survives accumulation)
Compare BIT PATTERNS (to_bits), not values: -0.0 == +0.0 under ==, so a value comparison passes under
either convention and would be exactly as blind as the unit tests it is meant to backstop.

Reference measurement already taken on torch 2.12.1+cpu, f64 -- recorded in dtyiz. Note the pinned
version matters: per the ledger the torch version IS part of the measurement, so the case should
record which version produced the golden.

COVERAGE NOTE: route the exercise through the accumulators that can construct an EMPTY slot (borrowed
par+serial, owned, zip_map, par_with), since that is where the canonicalization lived. A case that
only ever accumulates into an already-populated slot exercises none of the changed code.

Not blocking anything -- dtyiz is landed and workspace-green. This is the difference between the fix
being verified and the fix being believed.
close_reason: Done in 3b0954d7: 6-case torch-oracle conformance test, bit-pattern comparisons, mutation-verified against the reintroduced pre-dtyiz canonicalization. Must run locally — rch runs it on the worker where the oracle venv is absent and it silently skips.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
DONE in 3b0954d7: crates/ft-conformance/tests/pytorch_signed_zero_gradient_conformance.rs.

I re-measured the oracle BEFORE writing the test rather than trusting dtyiz's recorded numbers,
since inheriting a claim without checking it is what this bead exists to correct. torch 2.12.0+cpu
confirms all three cases this bead specified, and I added a fourth that is not in dtyiz:

  one -0.0 contribution PLUS one +0.0 contribution -> +0.0

That case changes what the suite proves. torch is not PRESERVING negative zero as a policy -- it
simply does not canonicalize, and ordinary IEEE addition supplies the rest. An implementation that
"preserved -0.0" by special-casing it would pass every obvious case and fail this one, in the
opposite direction from the original bug. Six cases total, four constructing an EMPTY slot (where
the canonicalization lived) and two accumulating into a populated one (untouched by dtyiz, must
stay plain IEEE).

ALL THREE OF THIS BEAD'S REQUIREMENTS MET: to_bits() comparisons throughout (never ==, since
-0.0 == +0.0 is true and a value comparison would be as blind as the unit tests it backstops);
coverage routed through the empty-slot constructors; the oracle's torch version printed on every
run, because per the ledger the version IS the measurement -- dtyiz recorded 2.12.1 and this box's
.venv-oracle carries 2.12.0, agreeing on behaviour, but a silent drift must not be able to rewrite
the golden unnoticed.

ONE HAZARD THIS BEAD DID NOT ANTICIPATE, now closed in the test: the JSON boundary. serde_json and
Python's json can both round-trip -0.0 to +0.0. Had that happened, every assertion would have
compared +0.0 against +0.0 and passed while proving nothing. Zeros therefore cross as "-0.0" string
tags, and a final assertion checks that at least one -0.0 actually SURVIVED the round-trip. That is
frankentorch-imtpq's headline failure -- a gate green because it executed nothing -- reachable here
by pure data-encoding rather than by shell plumbing.

MUTATION-VERIFIED, which is the difference between a test and a decoration: reintroducing the exact
pre-dtyiz canonicalization (0.0 + v on the returned gradient) makes it FAIL on
negative_zero_multiplier reporting FrankenTorch 0x0000000000000000 against torch
0x8000000000000000. Restored, re-run green. So this test would have caught the original bug.

GATES (local, redirect-captured, no pipeline): 1 passed / 0 failed with "oracle torch 2.12.0+cpu"
printed -- positive evidence it reached torch rather than skipping; fmt clean; clippy --no-deps
rc=0 (the one warning is a pre-existing nix v0.31.2 future-compat notice, not a lint on this code).

★ RUN THIS ONE LOCALLY. `rch exec -- cargo test` executes on the worker, where .venv-oracle does
not exist, so torch_available() returns false and the test SKIPS while reporting success. I started
exactly that run before catching it. Set FT_LEGACY_ORACLE_PYTHON to a torch-bearing interpreter and
run local. Worth noting on frankentorch-fl87u's ledger too: an oracle-backed conformance test is a
category that CANNOT be offloaded, and its skip path is silent by design.

dtyiz is now verified rather than believed.

title: [parity][dtype] sweep the 10 unguarded callers of tensor_apply_function_f64_borrowed_inputs for the f32 hard-error
description:
Generalises frankentorch-wp18c, where tensor_rrelu HARD-ERRORED on f32 with DenseTensor(UnsupportedDType(F32)) because it called this helper without a dtype guard. torch accepts f32 for all of these.

THE HELPER IS THE HAZARD, NOT THE OP. tensor_apply_function_f64_borrowed_inputs (ft-api ~9317 -> tape ~9037 in ft-autograd) does two things that make every unguarded caller wrong for non-f64:
  1. reads inputs via node.tensor.contiguous_values()          <- f64 accessor
  2. TensorMeta::from_shape(output_shape, DType::F64, device)  <- output dtype HARDCODED
So the defect is systematic: any caller lacking an upcast-compute-narrow guard inherits it.

CANDIDATE SITES — 22 call sites, 14 distinct enclosing fns. Guard detection below is a HEURISTIC (searched the fn body before the call for '!= DType::F64' or 'tensor_to_dtype'), so treat it as a candidate list, NOT a defect list:

  GUARDED (4):  tensor_relu6, tensor_celu, tensor_rrelu (fixed by wp18c), tensor_amax
  UNGUARDED (10):
    scaled_dot_product_attention          fn@6595
    tensor_cdist                          fn@12448
    tensor_smooth_l1_loss                 fn@14764
    tensor_cross_entropy                  fn@15650
    tensor_gaussian_nll_loss              fn@16315
    tensor_prelu                          fn@21910
    tensor_sum                            fn@25473
    tensor_scaled_dot_product_attention   fn@28529
    tensor_batch_norm2d_sum               fn@38518
    functional_batch_norm1d_sum           fn@39143

DO NOT FIX FROM THIS LIST. Probe each first — the heuristic misses guards of other shapes, and several of these almost certainly have an EARLIER f32 native fast path that returns before ever reaching the helper. tensor_sum in particular is used everywhere and would be loudly broken if it truly rejected f32, so it is the best evidence that the list over-reports. That is the a1nz2 rule and it has now cost me twice in this lineage: on jedc6 my source-read table was wrong in both directions, and on wp18c the predicted 'errors OR returns f64' turned out to be the harder failure.

DECISIVE PROBE per op (three lines, mirrors rrelu_preserves_f32_dtype):
  let x = s.tensor_variable_f32(vec![...], vec![n], false)?;
  let o = s.<op>(x, ...)?;                       // does it even return Ok?
  assert_eq!(s.tensor_dtype(o)?, DType::F32);    // and does it keep the dtype?

FIX SHAPE once confirmed, identical to relu6/selu/rrelu:
  let dt = self.tensor_dtype(input)?;
  if dt != DType::F64 {
      let in64 = self.tensor_to_dtype(input, DType::F64)?;
      let out64 = self.<op>(in64, ...)?;
      return self.tensor_to_dtype(out64, dt);
  }
The f64 path stays byte-identical because the guard is dt != F64.

Worth considering as a follow-up rather than doing here: the helper itself could take the output dtype from its input instead of hardcoding F64, which would fix the whole class at the root instead of one caller at a time. That is a bigger change and needs its own measurement of what depends on the current behaviour.
close_reason:
REFUTED. Landed as 88b06506. All ten call sites already keep f32 — rrelu (fixed by wp18c) was the only defect.

The premise was that tensor_apply_function_f64_borrowed_inputs is a systematic hazard: it reads inputs with the f64 accessor and hardcodes DType::F64 in its output meta, so any caller without an upcast-compute-narrow guard should inherit rrelu's hard UnsupportedDType(F32) failure. Mechanically true of the helper; false of its callers.

*** THE CANDIDATE LIST WAS WRONG TEN TIMES OUT OF TEN. *** It was built by grepping each enclosing fn body for '!= DType::F64' or 'tensor_to_dtype'. The real guard is usually an EARLIER f32 native fast path that returns before the helper is entered, which a grep for the guard's textual shape cannot see. I flagged this over-report risk when filing (tensor_sum being the tell — it is used everywhere and would be loudly broken if it truly rejected f32), and the probe confirmed the list was pure false positives.

PROBED DIRECTLY, all pass (Ok + F32 output dtype): scaled_dot_product_attention, tensor_scaled_dot_product_attention, tensor_cdist, tensor_smooth_l1_loss, tensor_cross_entropy, tensor_gaussian_nll_loss, tensor_prelu, tensor_sum, tensor_batch_norm2d_sum, functional_batch_norm1d_sum. Coverage is 10 of 10 — the batch-norm pair returns a tuple and scaled_dot_product_attention is a separate entry point from tensor_scaled_dot_product_attention, so those three are checked directly rather than through the closure vector.

WHAT SHIPPED: f64_borrowed_helper_callers_accept_f32_survey, kept as a LIVE gate rather than an #[ignore]d survey. It costs ~0.01s and fails the moment a new unguarded caller of the helper lands or an existing f32 fast path is removed — which is the durable value, since the helper's hardcoded F64 output meta is still there.

NOT DONE, and still worth its own bead if anyone wants it: fixing the helper itself to take the output dtype from its input rather than hardcoding F64. That would remove the hazard at the root instead of relying on every caller having a fast path, but it is a bigger change and needs its own measurement of what depends on the current behaviour.

title: Investigate persistent beads SQLite integrity warning after clean rebuild
description:
## Context
After a full non-destructive rebuild of `.beads/beads.db` from canonical `issues.jsonl`, `br doctor --json` still reports:

`sqlite.integrity_check: database disk image is malformed: page 17 is never used`

This persists even on the freshly rebuilt DB, while all operational checks are otherwise healthy (`br ready --json` is empty, sync metadata matches, blocked cache is not stale).

## Goal
Determine whether this warning reflects:
1. a genuine low-level SQLite file/layout problem,
2. expected frankensqlite behavior that `br doctor` should not flag as suspicious, or
3. a beads/br bug in the integrity-check path.

## Acceptance
- Reproduce the warning on the current canonical DB
- Compare against a freshly rebuilt temp DB
- Gather enough evidence to classify the issue as workspace-local vs tool-level
- If it is tool-level or not safely fixable from this repo, document the finding clearly and close or hand off with evidence
close_reason: Reproduced the integrity warning on canonical and rebuilt DBs, proved a plain SQLite VACUUM clears it, then observed br doctor --repair reintroduce the warning on a different page number while keeping logical metadata healthy; this classifies the issue as a tool-level beads/frankensqlite write-path problem rather than repo-local issue-data corruption

title: [tooling][rch] ft-conformance test builds are schedulable on at most 4/10 workers — 6 refuse on insufficient_total_slots
description:
Eight consecutive inline attempts at 'cargo test -p ft-conformance --test <...>' were refused with REAL_EXIT=103:

  [RCH] remote required; refusing local fallback (no admissible workers: insufficient_slots=3, insufficient_total_slots=6, active_project_exclusion=1) — retryable

READ THE BREAKDOWN, NOT THE HEADLINE. At the last attempt the fleet reported '10/10 healthy, 17/49 slots available' — not busy in the ordinary sense — and the refusal still decomposed as 3 workers short of FREE slots, 1 worker excluded for already building this project (a 13m33s frankentorch-api --tests release build), and 6 workers short of TOTAL slots. The last class is CAPACITY, not availability: six of ten workers can never serve this job at any load, because their total slot count is below what a ft-conformance test build requests. ft-conformance depends on ft-api (167k lines), so its request is large.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ONE BLOCKED TEST: '— retryable' is misleading for this class. Retrying re-rolls the 3 availability-limited workers and the 1 exclusion; it cannot change the 6 capacity-limited ones. I lost roughly ninety minutes of wall clock treating this as transient contention before reading the breakdown. Combined with active_project_exclusion removing any worker already building frankentorch, a single long peer build drops the eligible pool from 4 to 3.

WHAT TO INVESTIGATE (not yet done — this bead is the diagnosis, not the fix):
  1. What slot count does rch compute for a ft-conformance test job, and from what input? If it scales with dependency-crate size or workspace size rather than actual parallelism, it is over-requesting.
  2. Can a large-crate test opt into a smaller request (cargo test -j N already exists; peers are using 'cargo test -j2' and 'cargo test -j 1' on other projects, which suggests this is already a known workaround)?
  3. Should the refusal message distinguish capacity-limited from availability-limited workers in its retryable flag? A refusal that is only partly retryable invites exactly the backoff-and-retry loop that cannot succeed.

RELATED: frankentorch-c1ct1 ('[tooling][rch] Bound remote target-pool pressure to unblock 85cy6 example linking') is TopazGorge's and is adjacent but not the same — that one is about target-pool disk pressure, this one is about slot-count admission.

Recorded as a NEGATIVE-EVIDENCE row in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md (2026-08-16 refusal row). No ratio, no worker and no harness is banked from any of these attempts, because nothing ran.
close_reason: Answered empirically and documented in AGENTS.md (commit e766b10f, amended). Q1 (what sets the slot count): a FIXED per-command-verb request from the shared ~/.config/rch/config.toml -- build_slots=4, test_slots=8, check_slots=2 -- NOT scaled by crate or workspace size, so ft-conformance's size is not the cause. Q2 (can a large test opt into a smaller request): YES, -j N does it, and this is measured rather than folklore: at the same instant, same crate, 'cargo test --release -p frankentorch-autograd --lib' was refused EXIT=103 with insufficient_total_slots=7 while the identical command with -j2 ran to completion on hz2 (492 passed) -- and hz2 owns THREE total slots, so it could never have taken the 8-slot request. Q3 (should the message distinguish capacity from availability): the breakdown already does, in the field names; what misleads is the '-- retryable' suffix applied uniformly, and AGENTS.md now says so. Additional finding: -j2 --workspace exceeds the 1800s SSH limit (REAL_EXIT=1, zero test lines), so the working recipe is -j2 PLUS -p <crate>; ft-api gates in seconds that way (2571 passed, hz2). Also documented the build-lane + local-execution escape and its two traps (--clean-overlay breaks insta snapshot paths; a filtered pipeline reports the filter's exit code).

comments.author: QuietCondor
comments.text:
FIXED — commit a413af9c. clippy -D warnings on ft-kernel-cpu --lib is now CLEAN. That was the 4-error blocker this bead names, so direct ft-api bench clippy is unblocked.

DIAGNOSIS: all four uninit_vec findings were the SAME deliberate pattern — Vec::with_capacity + set_len + parallel fill — which exists on purpose so the fill performs the first touch rather than paying a dead serial zeroing pass first (the expand/broadcast_to first-touch work). build_uninit already encapsulated that pattern with a documented SAFETY contract; three call sites had open-coded their own copy of it instead of calling it.

FIX — removed the cause rather than suppressing the lint. NO allow() was added anywhere:
  1. build_uninit now stages through MaybeUninit. Growing a Vec<T> across uninitialized capacity is exactly what the lint flags, and it flags it for a good reason: the intermediate Vec<T> momentarily claims to hold initialized Ts that do not exist yet. MaybeUninit states the same thing in the type system, so the lint is satisfied BY CONSTRUCTION. The set_len now happens on Vec<MaybeUninit<T>>, which has no initialization requirement of its own, and the buffer is reconstituted as Vec<T> via ManuallyDrop + from_raw_parts once fill has honoured its contract.
  2. The three open-coded sites — broadcast-expand row materialization, transpose_batched_materialize_f64, transpose_batched_materialize_f32 — now call build_uninit, DELETING THREE UNSAFE BLOCKS. Each retains a comment stating how it satisfies the contract (chunk count x chunk width == numel, every chunk written in full before any read).

NET EFFECT: four unsafe blocks become one. The SAFETY reasoning now lives in exactly one place instead of being restated (and drifting) in four. That is the part worth more than the lint fix.

BEHAVIOUR IS UNCHANGED BY CONSTRUCTION: same allocation, still no zeroing, same parallel fill doing the first touch. This is a refactor of how the buffer is typed on the way out, not of what is computed — so there is no perf question to measure and no tolerance question to argue.

VERIFIED (run in full because this is unsafe code on hot materialization paths, where a mistake is silent memory corruption rather than a test failure in the changed function):

  ft-kernel-cpu --lib: 592 passed / 0 failed
  ft-api --lib:        2484 passed / 0 failed
  ft-conformance:      ALL GREEN (199 + the rest, 0 failed)

title: ft-kernel-cpu: panel-blocked parallel triangular solve for lu_solve/inv
description: lu_solve matrix-RHS triangular substitution is serial O(n^3); it dominates inv (factor is already parallel) and gated the rejected matrix_exp Pade. Naive per-column rayon parallelization REGRESSED 3x (256x256 inv 10.7ms->35.9ms) because it loses the inner-rhs-loop's L-coefficient reuse (each L loaded once, applied across all RHS cols, cache/SIMD-amortized). Correct lever = panel-block the RHS columns (transpose into contiguous panels of width ~32-64), rayon over panels, each panel running the inner-rhs-loop with L-reuse within its panel. Keeps amortization AND parallelizes. Bit-exact per panel. Baseline inv_f64: 256x256 10.7ms, 512x512 55ms. Target >=2x at 512.
notes: REJECTED: panel-blocked parallel triangular solve does NOT clear Score>=2.0. On 64 cores: pw=4 (64 panels) gave inv 256x256 1.05x / 512x512 1.25x; pw=64 (4 panels) was WORSE (noisy ~4x regression). Root cause: the triangular solve is MEMORY-BANDWIDTH-BOUND (low arithmetic intensity: 1 FMA per L-coefficient per column), so fanning across cores saturates bandwidth rather than speeding up; additionally inv is partly lu_factor-bound. Bit-exact but not worth shipping. Triangular solve is the WRONG primitive to parallelize. NEXT: pivot to compute-bound ops (conv via im2col+dgemm, or getri-style inv that inverts U then multiplies).

title: porting: add tensor_mv (matrix-vector multiply) for torch.mv parity
description: torch.mv(M, v) returns M @ v for a 2-D matrix M (shape [m, n]) and 1-D vector v (shape [n]); output is 1-D of shape [m]. PyTorch has it as a dedicated op even though matmul covers the same shape; user code calls it directly. Compose through autograd-aware primitives: reshape v to [n, 1] → tensor_matmul(M, v) → reshape to [m]. Add a few correctness and gradient regression tests.
close_reason: Added pub fn tensor_mv(M, v) at crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs — matrix-vector product M @ v matching torch.mv. Composes through tensor_reshape + tensor_matmul + tensor_reshape; autograd-aware on both inputs. Added 3 unit tests: mv_known_values (forward correctness), mv_propagates_gradient_to_matrix_and_vector (analytic gradient regression for sum(M @ v)), mv_rejects_wrong_ranks (fail-loud for 1-D M, 2-D v, mismatched n). ft-api now at 1211 lib tests (up from 1208).

title: [perf][svd] full_matrices basis completion is O(m^4): a 256x32 SVD takes 4.43 SECONDS
notes:
SHIPPED in b9bca8c1. Bit-exact cursor past consumed seeds.

MEASURED, same worker vmi1149989, same example, before vs after:
  shape   full-U before      full-U after   speedup

   64x8    6,161,683 ns      245,889 ns      25.1x
   96x8   46,107,276 ns      785,723 ns      58.7x
  128x8  254,953,269 ns    2,474,025 ns     103.0x

title: Numerical gradient check: tensor_linalg_det backward via finite differences
description: Lock the new autograd-aware tensor_linalg_det backward (added under frankentorch-pvfk) against numerical Jacobian computed by central finite differences. For each entry A[i,j], perturb ±eps, recompute det, and confirm (det(A+) - det(A-)) / (2*eps) matches the analytic backward to within finite-difference truncation tolerance. Catches any sign flip, transpose error, or scaling bug in the Jacobi-formula backward.
close_reason: Added linalg_det_backward_matches_central_finite_difference — exercises the new tensor_linalg_det backward (pvfk) on 4 well-conditioned 2x2/3x3 matrices (diag, general, rotation, perturbed-identity). Compares analytic ∂det/∂A from FrankenTorch's autograd against central FD with eps=1e-6 and abs_tol=5e-5. Locks the Jacobi-formula backward against any sign/transpose/scaling regression. ft-conformance now at 148 base lib tests, 194 with --features fuzz.

title: [perf] attribute avg_pool2d's ~11 ms backward-engine stage (34x its kernel) — sweep numel first
description:
frankentorch-uufyp localised avg_pool2d's cost to ONE stage: tensor_backward takes ~11 ms while the
backward kernel it dispatches takes 0.32 ms (~34x). This bead attributes that 11 ms. It is NOT a
licence to "optimise tensor_backward" — that is the unit, and splitting before levering is the rule
that 8obhh's post-mortem earned.

WHAT IS ALREADY RULED OUT (measured, artifacts/perf/frankentorch-uufyp/session_decomposition.md):
  - session construction: 0.000 ms, FREE
  - leaf materialisation: ~= a bare 16 MiB Vec::clone, session adds nothing on top
  - forward tape: ~1.5-1.7 ms, real but a seventh of the backward
  - the backward KERNEL: 0.32 ms
So ~11 ms is spent in the engine between "backward called" and "kernel returns".

WHAT IS ALREADY RULED OUT (code read, this session):
  - TensorBackwardStep records are METADATA ONLY (node id, incoming_grad_len, a &'static str rule),
    so the evidence/step log is not plausibly 11 ms.
  - The avg_pool2d backward CLOSURE is thin: it calls ft_kernel_cpu::avg_pool2d_backward_f64 and
    returns. crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs ~33415.

SO THE 11 ms IS IN THE MACHINERY AROUND THE CLOSURE. Candidates, none tested:
  1. tensor_apply_function_with_create_graph's backward dispatch — what does it copy per call?
  2. gradient accumulation into grads[] — full-size adds/clones per contribution?
  3. THE PAD/UNPAD PAIR. The f64 fused path operates on a PADDED input and the comment at
     crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs ~33376 says "tensor_pad's backward un-pads". With padding (0,0) — the
     probe's case — check whether a pad node is created at all; if it is, the backward pays an extra
     full-size un-pad over 16 MiB.
  4. grads[root].values = vec![1.0; numel] and similar full-size initialisations per backward.
  5. project_gmuml_tape_retention: the session tape reportedly never frees nodes.

THE DECISIVE FIRST EXPERIMENT, and it is cheap: SWEEP THE INPUT SIZE. Add avg_pool2d session lanes at
several numels (e.g. 1, 4, 16, 64 MiB) and plot backward-stage time against numel.
  - scales ~linearly with numel  -> DATA MOVEMENT; count the full-size passes and find the extra ones
  - roughly constant            -> FIXED per-backward overhead; look at node/slot machinery
  - superlinear                 -> something quadratic or an allocator cliff; that is its own finding
This distinguishes the candidate classes in one build+run and needs no torch arm.

METHOD CONSTRAINTS (zoqws / un3os / o5t00 / 8obhh):
 - condition the allocator before each timed region; carry an A/A pair at DIFFERENT positions in the
   interleave (that veto fired at 83% once when it was missing).
 - the small stages in the uufyp decomposition are at/below noise — the bare-clone control read
   164%/128%/234% of leaf_build. Do not attribute anything of that magnitude.
 - ANY lever that comes out of this must be A/B'd AT THE LANE with a negative control, not only in
   isolation. 8obhh: 4.24x in the kernel, 1.13x SLOWER at the lane.
 - autograd correctness outranks kernel speed (AGENTS.md). Anything touching the backward needs
   bit-exact gradient parity, ideally mutation-verified.
close_reason: CANDIDATE LIST EXHAUSTED; the answer is DIFFUSE PER-BACKWARD WORK (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). All five named mechanisms tested: pad/unpad pair eliminated (no pad node at padding (0,0)); full-size root init eliminated (root is the scalar sum, numel=1); tape retention eliminated (flat over 8 fwd+bwd cycles in one session, last/first 0.93x and 1.08x); create_graph dispatch eliminated (strict_default sets it FALSE so the measured path never pays it — note it costs 3.5x when enabled, 8.2 -> 29.8 ms, which is a separate double-backward fact worth its own owner); -0.0 canonicalization pass identified but unmeasured and plausibly only ~5-10%. No single sub-term dominates the conditioned ~5.6 ms. That is the honest answer and it is the one I said to be ready for when filing. Closing the avg_pool2d gap would need instruction-granularity profiling (perf/flamegraph — no probe in this tree does that) or ledgering the bound, which is defensible since k1h8g already showed FT's avg_pool2d KERNELS beat PyTorch's whole op. NEXT AGENT: do not add a sixth speculative candidate; bring a profiler or ledger it.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SWEEP RAN; IT DID NOT DISCRIMINATE — THE STAGE IS NON-MONOTONIC (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). Artifact: artifacts/perf/frankentorch-27aci/numel_sweep_nonmonotonic.md. Bead stays OPEN.

avg_pool2d [N,64,64,64] f64, 15-rep medians, two runs, bwd_stage = (through-backward minus through-sum):
   N  MiB  bwd_stage r1/r2   raw_bwd   stage/kernel  ms/MiB
   1    2   1.057 / 1.641    0.08      13-23x        0.53/0.82
   2    4   1.858 / 1.232    0.12      11-15x        0.47/0.31
   4    8   3.724 / 2.655    0.18      15-20x        0.47/0.33
   8   16  12.089 / 12.377   0.31-0.36 34-40x        0.76/0.77
  16   32   6.171 /  6.360   4.5-5.2   1.2-1.4x      0.19/0.20

THIS BEAD PREDICTED linear => data movement, flat => fixed machinery. It is NEITHER.
 1. NOT simple linear movement: if the stage were N full-size passes, 32 MiB would cost ~2x the
    16 MiB point. It costs HALF — 6.2 vs 12.1. A monotone cost model of any kind is refuted.
 2. THERE IS A SPIKE EXACTLY AT 16 MiB, the shape uufyp measured and the one this whole thread has
    reasoned about. Both runs agree to 2% (12.089/12.377) while neighbouring points scatter 30-40%,
    so it is not noise.
 3. At 32 MiB the RAW KERNEL changes regime — 0.36 -> 4.5-5.2 ms, ~14x for 2x data. That is the
    per-CCD L3 cliff un3os measured independently, arriving from a different direction. Consistency
    check on that finding, not a new one.

I AM NOT EXPLAINING THE SPIKE. I can construct a plausible story — allocator size class, THP, the
buffer plus a second live copy crossing the L3 slice — and any would read well in a commit message.
None is tested, and this session already produced one confident, well-measured, thoroughly-argued
mechanism (8obhh's buffer-size L3 predictor) that was wrong at the level that mattered. A fourth
plausible mechanism is worth less than the measurement that kills three of them.

NEXT, IN ORDER: (1) finer spacing around the spike (N=6,7,8,9,10) to confirm it is a property of the
stage and not of the harness — a single-point spike at exactly the size everything else was measured
at deserves ruling out before being explained; (2) separate allocation from work inside the stage,
pre-warmed vs not, using the condition_allocator pattern from dense_scatter_attribution (introduced
because an unconditioned probe once measured its own lane order at 83%); (3) only then a lever, A/B'd
at the lane with a negative control.

uufyp's finding is unaffected: tensor_backward really does cost ~11 ms against a 0.32 ms kernel at
16 MiB, and that is still the largest term on this lane. What changed is that the simple explanations
for it are now measured to be wrong.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
STEP 1 DONE, NEGATIVE — THE SPIKE IS A HARNESS ARTIFACT (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). Artifact: artifacts/perf/frankentorch-27aci/spike_is_a_harness_artifact.md

Ran the sweep BOTH DIRECTIONS in one invocation. If the cost were a property of the shape it must sit at the same N in both passes. It does not.
   N  MiB  ascending  descending
   5   10      2.210       3.277
   6   12      4.063       1.983
   7   14      3.909       3.523
   8   16     11.895       1.820   <- 6.5x swing on identical work
   9   18     13.893       2.379
  10   20     13.979      13.996
  12   24     16.658      17.335

WHAT PREDICTS THE COST is not the size but WHETHER THE SIZE IS AT OR ABOVE THE LARGEST ALLOCATED SO FAR IN THE PROCESS. Ascending, every N from 8 up is a new high-water mark and all are expensive. Descending, only 12 and 10 are new high-water marks and are expensive; the same N=8/N=9 that were expensive ascending are now cheap because a larger block has been faulted and can be recycled. N=10 and N=12 are expensive in BOTH passes — the control, since they are the largest either way. That is allocator/first-touch behaviour, not engine work.

It is the SAME confound that made two byte-identical lanes read 83% apart in dense_scatter_attribution.rs, which is exactly why condition_allocator() exists — AND THIS SWEEP HAS NO CONDITIONING.

CONSEQUENCE I HAVE TO OWN: uufyp's headline (tensor_backward ~11 ms, ~34x its kernel) is SUSPECT. That decomposition also has no allocator conditioning, and its backward lane is the first in the cumulative chain to allocate the 16 MiB GRADIENT buffer. An unknown and possibly dominant share of the 11 ms may be first-touch for a not-yet-seen size. I am NOT claiming uufyp is wrong — the backward may still be the largest term once conditioned — but the 34x figure is NOT currently defensible and I stated it as though it were.

BEFORE ANYTHING IS BUILT ON IT: (1) add condition_allocator() to the decomposition lanes and re-run; (2) add an A/A pair at different positions in the cumulative chain — the decomposition has NO null lane, which is the gap that let this through; (3) only then re-state where session time goes.

UNAFFECTED: uufyp's session_new-is-free and leaf_build-is-just-a-clone results, which are comparisons against a same-size baseline rather than absolute first-touch costs. And k1h8g's core claim survives independently — avg_pool2d's KERNELS are ~1.3 ms against PyTorch's ~1.7-2.7 ms whole op, which comes from the raw kernel lanes and does not depend on the decomposition.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
STEP 2 DONE — CONDITIONED BASELINE ESTABLISHED (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). See artifacts/perf/frankentorch-uufyp/conditioned_decomposition.md. With condition_allocator() before every timed rep and an A/A null lane added, the backward stage reads 5.620/6.024/5.063 ms (A/A 1.5%/13.7%/13.2%), against 10.9-11.8 unconditioned. So ~18x its 0.32 ms kernel, not 34x, and ~55-60% of a 9.5 ms session rather than 65-70% of 17 ms. uufyp re-closed on that basis.

THIS BEAD'S REMAINING QUESTION IS UNCHANGED AND NOW HAS A TRUSTWORTHY BASELINE: where do the ~5.6 ms go INSIDE the backward pass? The candidate list is untouched by the re-measure — create_graph backward dispatch, full-size gradient accumulation, the PAD/UNPAD pair (does a pad node exist at padding (0,0)?), full-size per-backward inits such as grads[root].values = vec![1.0; numel], and project_gmuml_tape_retention. Steps 1 and 2 of this bead are done; step 3 (a lever, A/B'd at the lane with a negative control) must not start until the split exists. NOTE the harness now carries condition_allocator + an A/A null — reuse them in any new lane rather than re-deriving why they are needed.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
STEP 3 PROGRESS — TWO CANDIDATES ELIMINATED BY READING, ONE CONCRETE TERM IDENTIFIED (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). No measurement in this note; code reading only, against the conditioned ~5.6 ms baseline.

ELIMINATED:
 1. THE PAD/UNPAD PAIR — does not exist at padding (0,0). crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs ~33320:
      let padded = if padding_h > 0 || padding_w > 0 { self.tensor_pad(...)? } else { input };
    The probe's lane uses (0,0), so no pad node is created and the backward pays no unpad. This was my
    most concrete suspicion from the 27aci filing and it is wrong.
 2. FULL-SIZE ROOT INIT — grads[root].values = vec![1.0; numel] is sized by the ROOT node, and the root
    here is the scalar tensor_sum. numel = 1. Not a full-size allocation.

IDENTIFIED, NOT MEASURED: a full-size -0.0 CANONICALIZATION PASS in
accumulate_tensor_gradient_owned (crates/ft-autograd/src/lib.rs ~20507). On the FIRST contribution to a
gradient slot the buffer is MOVED in with no fresh allocation — good — but before the move every
element gets , parallel above 32768 elements, purely to canonicalize -0.0 to +0.0 so the
owned path matches the borrowed path bit-for-bit. For this lane that is a full 16 MiB read-modify-write
pass over 2M elements.

WHAT I AM AND AM NOT CLAIMING: I have NOT measured it. By comparison the whole avg_pool2d backward
KERNEL, which writes the same 16 MiB, measures ~0.32 ms, so a same-shape pass is plausibly of that
order — i.e. maybe ~5-10% of the 5.6 ms, NOT the dominant term. I am flagging it because it is (a)
concrete, (b) full-size, and (c) arguably removable: it exists only for bit-exact agreement between two
paths, so a cheaper canonicalization (or making the borrowed path match the owned one instead) could
delete a full pass without touching gradient values. That is a parity question before it is a perf one.

STILL UNATTRIBUTED: the bulk of the 5.6 ms. Remaining candidates are the create_graph backward dispatch
and project_gmuml_tape_retention. The next step should MEASURE inside the backward rather than read —
e.g. time a backward on this graph with create_graph off vs on, and a second backward on the same
session to see whether retention makes it grow.
