comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
STEP 3 CONTINUED — TAPE RETENTION IS NOT THE TERM (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). Measured, negative.

project_gmuml_tape_retention records that the session tape never frees nodes. If that were what the
conditioned ~5.6 ms backward stage buys, successive forward+backward cycles IN ONE SESSION would get
progressively slower as the tape grows. Every other lane in this probe builds a fresh session, so this
is the only lane that could see it.

8 cycles in one session, allocator conditioned before each, two runs:
  run 1: 6.09 6.00 5.68 5.90 7.08 6.12 5.85 5.67   last/first 0.93x
  run 2: 5.12 5.50 8.39 6.81 5.65 6.06 5.67 5.52   last/first 1.08x

FLAT. No growth across 8 cycles in either direction; the two runs bracket 1.0 from opposite sides and
the within-run scatter (one 8.39 outlier in run 2) is larger than any trend. Retention may well still
be real as a memory-growth issue — this probe does not test that — but it does NOT make successive
backwards slower on this workload, so it is not the explanation for the 5.6 ms.

CANDIDATE LIST FOR 27aci NOW STANDS AT:
  pad/unpad pair .................. ELIMINATED (no pad node at padding (0,0))
  full-size root init ............. ELIMINATED (root is the scalar sum, numel = 1)
  tape retention .................. ELIMINATED (this comment; flat over 8 cycles)
  -0.0 canonicalization pass ...... IDENTIFIED, unmeasured; full-size but plausibly only ~5-10%
  create_graph backward dispatch .. UNTESTED, and now the last named candidate standing

SO THE NEXT STEP IS SPECIFIC: time this graph's backward with create_graph off versus on. If the gap
is small, the 5.6 ms is diffuse per-backward work and the honest answer may be that there is no single
lever — which is a legitimate outcome and should be recorded as one rather than chased.

Incidental observation, NOT a claim: a full cycle in a reused session runs ~5.5-6 ms here against a
cumulative-through-backward of ~8.5 ms in the fresh-session decomposition. That gap is unexplained and
may just be load (this ran at loadavg 2.6-14.6 against 82-143 for the decomposition). Do not difference
the two; they are different framings, which is the same trap k1h8g's artifact warns about.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
STEP 3b — CREATE_GRAPH ELIMINATED, AND THE CANDIDATE LIST IS NOW EMPTY (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08).

Interleaved off/on/off/on, conditioned, two runs, loadavg 2.4:
  create_graph=false: 8.027 / 8.434 ms   (mean 8.230)
  create_graph=true : 29.197 / 30.336 ms (mean 29.767)
  on/off = 3.4-3.6x
A/A null on the through-sum lane in the same invocations: 8.4% and 9.0%.

TWO SEPARATE CONCLUSIONS, and I nearly conflated them:

1. create_graph is ELIMINATED as an explanation for the ~5.6 ms default-path backward — but NOT
   because the arms agree. They differ by 3.5x, far outside the null. It is eliminated because
   BackwardOptions::strict_default() sets create_graph = FALSE (ft-autograd ~727), so the measured
   decomposition never pays it. My probe originally printed "within the A/A null => NOT the term",
   which reached the right verdict by reasoning that contradicts its own numbers; that line is fixed
   in this commit rather than left to mislead the next reader.
   Consistency check: the create_graph=false arm reads 8.0-8.4 ms cumulative-through-backward against
   ~8.5 ms measured independently in the conditioned decomposition. They agree, which is the sanity
   test that this lane is measuring the same thing.

2. SEPARATELY, asking for a differentiable second-order graph costs ~3.5x on this lane (8.2 -> 29.8 ms).
   That is a real double-backward fact, was not previously recorded anywhere I can find, and belongs to
   whoever owns that surface rather than to this bead.

SO 27aci's CANDIDATE LIST IS EXHAUSTED:
  pad/unpad pair ................. ELIMINATED (no pad node at padding (0,0))
  full-size root init ............ ELIMINATED (root is the scalar sum, numel = 1)
  tape retention ................. ELIMINATED (flat over 8 cycles in one session)
  create_graph dispatch .......... ELIMINATED (default is false; the path never pays it)
  -0.0 canonicalization pass ..... IDENTIFIED, unmeasured, full-size but plausibly only ~5-10%

THE HONEST ANSWER IS THE ONE I SAID TO BE READY FOR: the ~5.6 ms is DIFFUSE PER-BACKWARD WORK with no
single dominant sub-term. Every named mechanism has been tested and none of them is it. That is a
legitimate result and I am recording it as one rather than inventing a sixth candidate.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE CAMPAIGN: a lane whose cost is diffuse does not have a lever in the sense this
campaign has been hunting. Closing the avg_pool2d gap would need either (a) profiling at instruction
granularity rather than stage granularity — perf/flamegraph, which no probe in this tree does — or
(b) accepting the lane as-is and ledgering it. Option (b) is defensible: k1h8g already established
FT's avg_pool2d KERNELS beat PyTorch's whole op, so what remains is engine overhead spread thin.

NEXT AGENT: do NOT add a sixth speculative candidate. Either bring a profiler or ledger the bound.

title: [measure] TWO REPLICATED STANDINGS: max_pool3d_nopool 2.99-3.17x SLOWER and prelu_noshortcut 1.39-1.53x FASTER, both certified twice
description:
THE CAMPAIGN'S FIRST REPLICATED vs-PyTorch STANDINGS. Each lane cleared the full gate in TWO independent invocations — both A/A nulls PASS, parity match, min estimator — which is what rule 4 requires to promote a candidate to a standing.

STANDING 1 — A LOSS: max_pool3d_nopool
  run A (y4nj9)  MIN ratio 0.335 [0.313,0.350] = FT 2.99x SLOWER  PT null 0.995 PASS  FT null 0.988 PASS
  run B (here)   MIN ratio 0.315 [0.301,0.330] = FT 3.17x SLOWER  PT null 1.014 PASS  FT null 0.982 PASS
  CONSERVATIVE CLAIM: FrankenTorch is AT LEAST 2.86x SLOWER on this lane (taking 0.350, the most favourable ratio bound either run produced). Not the 3.17x headline.

STANDING 2 — A WIN: prelu_noshortcut
  run A (vhgue)  MIN ratio 1.533 [1.458,1.598] = FT 1.53x FASTER  PT null 1.009 PASS  FT null 0.994 PASS
  run B (here)   MIN ratio 1.392 [1.321,1.435] = FT 1.39x FASTER  PT null 0.982 PASS  FT null 1.016 PASS
  CONSERVATIVE CLAIM: FrankenTorch is AT LEAST 1.32x FASTER on this lane (taking 1.321, the lowest confidence bound either run produced). Not the 1.53x headline.

PROVENANCE for run B: executing_elf_sha256 = 1fa33e62b39e125e69f2d2e29a9e533bdd505e3d2f6a7dd3661561e5eee7c5a8; BUILD WORKER vmi1152480 (rch, RCH_WORKER-pinned, cargo build -j2 --release --features fair-alloc); harness crates/ft-api/examples/gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h.rs; measurement_host thinkstation1 (5975WX 32-Core, x86_64+avx2, powersave, rayon_threads=64, online_cpus=64, torch threads=8); allocator mimalloc; balanced-square ABBAABBA 32 rounds; incumbent PyTorch 2.12.1+cpu; load 14.21 -> 14.90 (+5%).

title: [perf][no-gaps] ft-autograd: eliminate per-node double-clone floor in tensor_backward
description: tensor_backward()'s main loop does TWO ~numel f64 clones per node before any contrib work: (1) apply_tensor_hooks() returns incoming.to_vec() even when the node has no hooks (common case), and (2) grads[node_id.0] = incoming.clone(). title: Add custom autograd Function API (torch.autograd.Function equivalent)
description:
Users cannot currently define custom backward functions. This is arguably the single most impactful missing feature for real-world use — without it, any layer whose backward isn't built into FrankenTorch's op set is impossible to implement.

PyTorch's torch.autograd.Function API allows users to:
1. Define a custom forward() that registers itself on the autograd tape
2. Define a custom backward() that computes gradients for the custom op
3. Save tensors for backward via ctx.save_for_backward()

Implementation plan:
1. Add a CustomFunction trait in ft-autograd with forward/backward methods
2. Add a TensorNodeOp::Custom variant to the tensor tape
3. Add session.apply_custom_function() to ft-api that invokes the user's forward, registers the op on the tape, and stores the backward closure
4. During backward traversal, call the user's backward function when encountering Custom nodes
5. Handle save_for_backward by capturing TensorNodeIds in the closure context

Key design decisions:
- The backward closure must receive upstream gradient and return downstream gradients
- Must respect no_grad context (custom forward inside no_grad should not record on tape)
- Must work with the existing deterministic backward scheduler
- Error handling: user backward functions should return Result, not panic

Tests:
- Unit test: custom ReLU equivalent (forward: max(0,x), backward: 1 if x>0 else 0)
- Unit test: custom function with multiple inputs/outputs
- Unit test: custom function inside no_grad context (should not record)
- Unit test: custom function backward produces correct gradients (numerical gradient check)
- E2E test: train a model with a custom layer and verify loss decreases
- Edge case: nested custom functions
- Edge case: custom function that saves tensors for backward
close_reason: Core functionality already exists: tensor_apply_function() with FunctionCtx (save_for_backward, needs_input_grad) + backward closure. Extensive tests in ft-autograd (lines 17484+) and used internally by ft-api for ~12 ops. The closure-based API is the Rust-idiomatic equivalent of PyTorch's class-based torch.autograd.Function. A trait wrapper could be added later for API sugar but is not blocking.

title: [measure][harness] record load drift per run and refuse QUOTABLE when the host moved under the measurement
description:
NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE item 18 found the hole: both A/A nulls PASSED in two runs of prelu_noshortcut that certified OPPOSITE directions (1.16x SLOWER and 1.15x FASTER). A null establishes that an arm was STABLE WITHIN the invocation; it cannot see that the whole invocation was unrepresentative. A run where every arm is uniformly 40% slow has immaculate nulls -- and that is precisely what happened: FrankenTorch's own arm read 23.0 ms against 14.5-18.3 ms typical.

Concretely, several runs this session started at load ~6-9 and ENDED at 28-32 because a peer build landed mid-run. The interleaved balanced square protects against a step change between ARMS, not against the host drifting under both of them together.

BUILD, in crates/ft-api/examples/gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h.rs only:
  1. Read /proc/loadavg at run start and at run end, print both in the provenance header beside cpu/governor/threads, so every banked row carries them.
  2. Compute the drift ratio (end/start of the 1-minute figure) and print it.
  3. Gate on it: a row may print QUOTABLE only if the drift is within a stated band. Outside the band, label it LOAD-DRIFTED and say so explicitly, the same way WIDE and OFFSET already work -- the harness should refuse the row rather than leave the reader to notice.

NEGATIVE CASE a naive implementation would fail: the gate must not simply reject high load. A run at a steady load of 25 is measurable; a run that goes 6 -> 30 is not, and a run that goes 30 -> 6 is equally not. The signal is DRIFT (both directions), not level. A gate keyed on absolute load would have rejected the y4nj9 certified row (steady 8.63 -> 9.25) for the wrong reason and accepted a 30->30 run that is fine.

Threshold: pick it from the runs already recorded rather than by taste -- the certified rows ran at drifts of about 1.07x (8.63->9.25) and 1.15x, while the contradicting pair ran at 1.30x and 1.41x. State the chosen number and its justification in the code.

DO NOT change the estimator, the nulls, or the balanced square. This adds one refusal condition; it must not alter any number a currently-quotable row produces.
close_reason: Landed 5b9136a2. harness_provenance gains load_average_1m(), load_drift_is_quotable() and MAX_LOAD_DRIFT=1.25; the harness reads /proc/loadavg before sampling and after the co-process exits, prints both with the verdict, and a row prints QUOTABLE only if the drift gate passes too -- otherwise it says 'LOAD-DRIFTED (nulls passed; the host did not hold still)'. Threshold taken from recorded runs rather than taste: certified rows drifted ~1.07x and ~1.15x, the item-18 contradicting pair drifted 1.30x and 1.41x, so 1.25 admits every certified row and refuses both contradictions. Negative case pinned by test: the signal is DRIFT in either direction, not level -- steady load 25 stays quotable, 30->6 is refused like 6->30, a missing reading is refused rather than read as a pass, and a near-idle host is not failed by ratio jitter (0.2->0.9 passes via a floor). Gate: frankentorch-api --lib 2572 passed/0 failed on hz2 via the -j2 lane. Estimator, nulls and balanced square untouched, so no currently-quotable row changes value.

title: [measure][harness] warmup asymmetry in gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h: FrankenTorch warms 3 iters per lane, torch warms 4
description:
Found by a read-only audit of the harness behind the campaign's ONE certified row (prelu_noshortcut, frankentorch-rled4). No rch slot was used; this is a source observation, not a measurement.

  torch arm   crates/ft-api/src/harness_interleave.rs SAMPLE_LOOP_PY: 'for _ in range(4)' per lane before PT_READY, added deliberately by frankentorch-6atx2 so no lane's first interleaved sample carries its own warmup cost.
  FT arm      crates/ft-api/examples/gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h.rs ~line 914: 'for _ in 0..3' per lane.

NOT A DEFECT TODAY, and the direction is why: under-warming the FrankenTorch arm makes FT's times SLOWER, which UNDERSTATES a FT-faster ratio. Every certified row is a FT-faster claim, so the asymmetry is currently conservative — it cannot have inflated the 1.07x standing.

WHY FIX IT ANYWAY: the sign of the bias is a property of which arm happens to be faster, not of the instrument. The moment a lane is quoted where torch is ahead, the same asymmetry inflates rather than deflates. An instrument should not have a bias whose direction depends on the answer.

FIX: make both arms warm the same number of iterations (4/4). One-line change in the example.

VERIFY: this is a timing harness, so the change must be shown not to move the certified row beyond its replication band — re-run prelu_noshortcut under BOTH estimators with nulls adjudicated per rule 3, and compare against items 14/14b (1.180x/1.113x median, 1.213x/1.175x min, conservative standing at least 1.07x). Needs an rch slot and a same_host run; NOT done here because rch refused repeatedly (no admissible workers).

AUDIT NOTE, recorded because a clean audit is evidence too: the other four hazards I checked are all handled. Leaves are built OUTSIDE the timed region on both arms; inputs are deterministic and constructed once, so there is no randn inside the timed loop; sampling is interleaved within ONE invocation; and each arm independently DECLARES its timed region (PT_TIMED_STEPS forward,loss_sum,backward) with a cross-check whose guard is itself covered by a planted-asymmetry mutation test (frankentorch-574cu). The declaration is written as an independent literal rather than generated from the Rust constant, specifically so the agreement check is not tautological.
notes:

assertion.

title: Severed-autograd loss umbrella: focal, poisson_nll, gaussian_nll
description:
Three more loss functions in ft-api that extract values, compute the per-element loss in plain f64, build a requires_grad=false leaf, then take tensor_mean — same severed-autograd pattern recently fixed for cross_entropy_with_smoothing / multilabel_soft_margin / soft_margin / multi_margin. The tensor_mean step preserves autograd from that point but the prior leaf has already severed the tape — so input never receives gradient.

Affected:
  - focal_loss (lib.rs:10324) — used in dense object detection (RetinaNet etc.)
  - poisson_nll_loss (lib.rs:10357) — count regression
  - gaussian_nll_loss (lib.rs:10398) — variational / probabilistic regression

Each has a closed-form composition through autograd-aware primitives; Stirling / 2pi correction terms are constants and can be added as scalars without affecting the tape.

Children: each loss gets its own fix bead. Surfaced during continuing /reality-check pass.

title: porting: add tensor_asinh / tensor_acosh / tensor_atanh for torch parity
description:
torch.asinh / acosh / atanh — inverse hyperbolic functions. Compose through autograd-aware primitives:
  asinh(x) = log(x + sqrt(x^2 + 1))
  acosh(x) = log(x + sqrt(x^2 - 1))   (x >= 1)
  atanh(x) = 0.5 * log((1 + x) / (1 - x))   (|x| < 1)
Gradient-correct since all sub-ops are on the autograd tape. Useful for normalizing-flow models, conformal maps, and porting numpy code.
close_reason: Added tensor_asinh / acosh / atanh in ft-api. Closed-form compositions: asinh(x) = log(x + sqrt(x² + 1)); acosh(x) = log(x + sqrt(x² - 1)) (defined for x >= 1); atanh(x) = 0.5 * log((1+x)/(1-x)) (defined for |x| < 1). All autograd-aware via existing primitives. 5 unit tests cover known values (asinh(sinh(t)) = t round-trip etc.) and analytic gradient regression for asinh and atanh (d/dx asinh = 1/sqrt(1+x²), d/dx atanh = 1/(1-x²)). ft-api now at 1250 lib tests.

title: Activation functions lack subprocess conformance: sigmoid, tanh, silu, mish
description:
Existing subprocess conformance suite covers gelu, softplus, exp/log/expm1/log1p/erf/erfc/lgamma/trig/hyperbolic, but the workhorse activations sigmoid / tanh / silu / mish have no scipy or libm reference comparison. PyTorch parity for these matters because:
- sigmoid (= 1/(1+exp(-x)) = expit) is the building block for binary classification, gating, attention
- tanh is the workhorse for RNN/LSTM
- silu/swish (= x*sigmoid(x)) is used in transformer FFN
- mish (= x*tanh(softplus(x))) is used in detection / vision

Reference: scipy.special.expit (sigmoid), numpy.tanh, numpy compositions for silu and mish. ULP-tolerant comparison; FrankenTorch composes these through libm exp/tanh which should match within ~1 ULP on smooth interior plus edge cases for ±inf / NaN / large-magnitude saturation.

Add torch_activations_libm_subprocess_conformance covering all four with ~30 inputs spanning negative / zero / positive / large / Inf / NaN. Filed during testing-conformance pass.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Added torch_activations_scipy_subprocess_conformance covering sigmoid (vs scipy.special.expit), tanh (vs numpy.tanh), silu = x*sigmoid(x), and mish = x*tanh(softplus(x)) across 30 inputs spanning negative / zero / positive / saturation (±50, ±100, ±700) / Inf / NaN. ULP-tolerant comparator: 4 ULP for sigmoid/tanh, 16 ULP for the composed silu/mish. Subprocess conformance count now 33 (was 32).

title: [parity][rrelu] verify the x>=0 branch against torch, same shape as the prelu x4cx3 defect
description:
Lead found while fixing frankentorch-x4cx3, NOT yet verified. tensor_rrelu in crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs branches on x >= 0.0 in both its forward (map |&x| if x >= 0.0 { x } else { slope * x }) and its backward (map |(&x,&go)| if x >= 0.0 { go } else { go * slope }). That is exactly the shape that turned out to be wrong for prelu, where torch uses where(input > 0, ...).

Do NOT assume rrelu shares prelu's convention — check it. torch is installable at /data/tmp/torchvenv-2121/bin/python (2.12.1+cpu, pinned; the version IS part of the measurement). The decisive probe is three lines:

  x = torch.tensor([[-1.0, 0.0, 1.0]], dtype=torch.float64).requires_grad_(True)
  torch.nn.functional.rrelu(x, 0.125, 1.0/3.0, training=False).sum().backward()
  print(x.grad)

If grad at x == 0 is the slope rather than 1.0, fix the same way x4cx3 did: change the forward and the grad_x predicate to x > 0.0, leave any weight/slope accumulation on x < 0.0, and add a regression test with an exact zero in it. Then sweep the rest of the activation family for the same pattern (elu, celu, selu, leaky_relu, relu6, hardtanh, threshold) rather than fixing one op at a time.

Note the general lesson from x4cx3: no unit test in this repo had an exact 0.0 in a PReLU fixture, which is why the defect survived. Build any new fixture to straddle every branch boundary the op has.
close_reason:
CONFIRMED and fixed. torch 2.12.1+cpu: F.rrelu(x,0.125,1/3,training=False) on [-1,0,1] gives x.grad = [0.22916666666666666, 0.22916666666666666, 1.0] — the grad at x==0 is the SLOPE, not 1.0, so torch compares x > 0 exactly as prelu did in x4cx3. Training mode agrees: rrelu_with_noise writes a SAMPLED slope (0.19187658862549017) into the noise slot for a 0.0 input, and torch consumes an RNG draw there, so the fix does not perturb the stream.

Fixed at BOTH sites: tensor_rrelu (ft-api, forward AND backward predicate) and RReLU::forward (ft-nn, tensor_ge -> tensor_gt, which also covers eval mode). The other four entry points (functional_rrelu, rrelu_activation, rrelu_tensor, tensor_rrelu_) all delegate to tensor_rrelu.

The bead expected a grad-only defect; the FORWARD is observably wrong too, which no fixture would have caught: with a NEGATIVE slope, multiplying is not the identity on zero. torch gives rrelu(+0.0) = -0.0 and rrelu(-0.0) = +0.0 at slope -0.25, where passing the input through returns the opposite sign. The new test bit-compares both zeros.

TESTS: new rrelu_zero_input_takes_the_slope_branch_like_torch (ft-api) covering forward values, grad at zero, both signed zeros under a negative slope, and NaN; plus TWO EXISTING ft-nn tests corrected — rrelu_propagates_gradients and rrelu_training_backward_uses_realized_negative_slopes both asserted 1.0 at x==0.0, i.e. they encoded the pre-fix world and would have failed any correct implementation.

  cargo test -p ft-nn --lib rrelu             -> 7 passed / 0 failed, exit=0, rch worker vmi1153651
  cargo clippy -p ft-nn -p frankentorch-api --lib --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings -> zero lints from changed lines (3 PRE-EXISTING reds on main filed as frankentorch-0aj9z)
  cargo fmt --check -> my two files clean (2 pre-existing dirty files untouched)

title: Wire Winograd f32 3x3 conv (tolerance-accurate) — needs conv parity-policy sign-off
description:
ONE genuinely-live algorithmic target gated on a parity-policy decision (NOT engineering): wire Winograd F(2x2,3x3) for f32 3x3 stride-1 conv.

winograd_conv2d_3x3_s1_f64 (crates/ft-kernel-cpu/src/lib.rs:7279, NON-WIRED FOUNDATION, validated by winograd_conv2d_matches_direct_within_tolerance): 16 transform-domain products/tile vs 36 direct (~2.25x fewer mults). The transform-domain GEMMs run through matrixmultiply (RUNTIME AVX detection, already vectorized) so the mult-count reduction translates to real f32 speedup; f64 transform overhead eats the savings, so f32-only. Target ~1.5-2x for f32 3x3 s1 conv.

BLOCKER (policy): Winograd reassociates the conv -> ~1-2 ULP vs direct, violating the internal bit-exact conv golden. Conformance-vs-torch is ALREADY tolerance-based (within(), ~1e-12||N*scale*EPS, ft-conformance ~11696). Upstream PyTorch is itself NOT bit-exact across backends (cuDNN Winograd, MKL, varied reduction order), so torch-parity is tolerance-parity, not bit-identity. Precedent: frankentorch-esh8 (commit d9c14107) just relaxed the MHA grad golden to 1e-12 via assert_golden_within_tol because fused rayon reductions are nondeterministic at the last ULP.

DECISION NEEDED: may f32 conv return ~1-2 ULP tolerance-accurate (Winograd) results? If yes: relax the internal direct-conv bit-exact unit test to within-tolerance (NOT the external torch conformance, which is already tolerance), wire Winograd for f32 3x3 s1, prove Score>=2.0 via rch hyperfine same-worker A/B.

NOT IN SCOPE (refuted, see [[project_perf_binding_constraints]] lines 31-48): SIMD f64x4 exp/sigmoid/tanh family. wide's f64x4 lowers to SCALAR lanes on the baseline build target (no -C target-feature set), and the op is alloc/memory-bound, so it is ~1.0x default / ~1.3x even forcing avx2 -- it NEVER clears 2.0 regardless of the libm-oracle policy. Do not re-attempt as a perf lever. (A separate STASHED SIMD-exp wiring exists, blocked on the torch_exp_log_libm_subprocess_conformance bit-exact-libm oracle, but it is not worth shipping for ~1.3x.)
close_reason: Naive materialized F(2,3) Winograd wiring REFUTED by same-worker A/B (1.3-2.7x SLOWER, see comments). Parity policy sign-off was granted but the lever regresses, not a Score>=2.0 win. f32 foundation + bench harness + tolerance test landed for the real swing. Superseded by frankentorch-mvdm (fused F(4,3) transform+GEMM kernel).

title: [perf][gated] Pool/reuse large tensor buffers in-session to kill allocation churn — GATED on proving churn exists in a realistic training loop
description:
Option D of frankentorch-1ji9l, opened per operator decision. Attack the allocation churn itself — pool/reuse large tensor buffers inside the session — instead of papering over it with a process-global allocator. Fixes the mechanism rather than the symptom, and benefits users whatever allocator their binary chooses.

THIS BEAD IS GATED. Do not implement anything until STEP 0 passes. If STEP 0 fails, the correct outcome is a REJECT with evidence, not a smaller version of the work.

STEP 0 — THE GATE (criterion 1 of 1ji9l): does the churn appear in a REALISTIC workload?
Every number motivating this bead comes from pytorch_gauntlet_bench, whose lanes rebuild their input tensor inside b.iter every iteration. Real training does NOT do that: it allocates parameters and input batches once and reuses them across steps. So the synthetic rebuild may be manufacturing the entire effect.
Profile a training loop that REUSES its input tensors across steps — forward, backward, optimizer step, repeated — and measure allocation volume and time under the system allocator vs mimalloc.
  PASS (churn is real): large-buffer alloc/free traffic persists across steps and the allocator swap moves the loop measurably. Proceed to STEP 1.
  FAIL (churn vanishes): the effect is a benchmark artifact of the per-iteration rebuild. Record a NEGATIVE-EVIDENCE LEDGER ENTRY with the profile, close this bead as REJECTED, and note on 1ji9l that the answer to the allocator question is documentation only (option A/C), not engineering. REPORTING THAT IS A SUCCESS, not a failure — it saves the pooling work entirely.
Retry predicate if rejected: re-open only if a real user workload (not a bench) is shown to allocate large tensors repeatedly in steady state.

DO NOT QUOTE THESE AS USER-FACING NUMBERS — they are synthetic-rebuild figures from the gauntlet's per-iteration input rebuild and describe the harness, not a user's training loop:
  avg_pool1d grad  FT 32.283ms -> 11.560ms  (2.79x)
  BatchNorm2d f32  FT 29.357ms ->  7.408ms  (3.96x)
They are recorded here ONLY as the reason the gate exists. The honest framing is: under the system allocator these lanes overstate FT's loss by that much; that is a statement about the bench.
The conv2d lane is the counter-example that shapes the hypothesis — 4MB input, high compute per iteration, allocator swap moves it 1.27x -> 1.28x, i.e. not at all. Whatever pooling is built must be justified against workloads that look like avg_pool1d's allocation profile, not conv2d's.

STEP 1 — SCOPE, only if STEP 0 passes.
Pool or reuse large tensor buffers inside the session so a repeated workload stops returning 32MB blocks to the allocator and re-faulting them. Design constraints that are non-negotiable here:
  - Autograd correctness outranks everything (project non-regression rule). A pooled buffer must never alias a tensor still reachable from the tape, and the DAC evidence contract must be unaffected. This is the main risk of the whole idea and is where review effort belongs.
  - Determinism must hold: pooling must not make results depend on allocation history.
  - #![forbid(unsafe_code)] applies in ft-api/ft-autograd; ft-kernel-cpu allows unsafe only at documented sites.
  - Bit-exactness is free here in principle (a buffer is a buffer), so any output change means a bug, not a tolerance question.
  - Bound the pool. An unbounded cache is a memory leak wearing a costume; it must have a cap and a release path.

STEP 2 — EVIDENCE BAR. Same as every other perf bead: live incumbent arm in the SAME invocation, A/A null gate, executing-ELF SHA-256, median-CI decision, and the >=2.0 Score bar measured on the REALISTIC loop from STEP 0 — not on the gauntlet. Both arms must use the SAME allocator, or the measurement is just re-measuring mimalloc.

CONTEXT: this is the same mechanism that made three of five vs-PyTorch loss rows look catastrophic (frankentorch-ug4ep, closed — all five re-baselined, three are now wins and no remaining row is a 2x gap) and that refuted the tensor_variable lever (frankentorch-uqsit, closed). The largest real vs-PyTorch gap left anywhere on that list is avg_pool1d at 1.92x, so if STEP 0 passes this is plausibly worth more than any remaining op-level lever; if it fails, there is very little left to chase on that list at all. (QuietCondor)
close_reason:
REJECTED on measured evidence. Gate required BOTH criteria; (a) passes, (b) fails on every realistic lane.

(a) DOES CHURN SURVIVE INPUT REUSE? PASS. It does. Steady-state large blocks (>=1 MiB) per step,
counted directly by a GlobalAlloc wrapper rather than inferred from timing:
  pool_rebuild (harness-shaped)  4 alloc,  96.00 MiB
  pool_reuse   (input once)      3 alloc / 3 free,   64.00 MiB
  mlp_reuse    (params+batch once, in-place SGD)  15 alloc / 15 free,  58.12 MiB
Allocations and frees are exactly balanced in the reuse lanes, which is the definition of churn.
The harness rebuild accounts for only 1 of the pool lane's 4 large blocks.

(b) DOES THE ALLOCATOR SWAP MOVE THE LOOP? FAIL. Both binaries preserved and run INTERLEAVED,
3 reps each, alternating arms on one host, distinct self-reported ELF SHAs:
  lane            system(a0df1848)  mimalloc(0fb3fff5)  ratio   ranges
  pool_rebuild    32.466 ms         16.647 ms           1.95x   [31.955,32.644] vs [16.293,17.033] DISJOINT
  pool_reuse      22.130 ms         21.393 ms           1.03x   [21.416,22.291] vs [20.866,21.544] OVERLAP
  mlp_reuse       63.640 ms         65.398 ms           0.97x   [63.504,65.145] vs [65.100,65.400] OVERLAP
Large-block traffic is byte-identical on both arms (the control): the swap changed how the same
allocations are served, not how many. mimalloc is worth 1.95x on the lane that rebuilds its input
every iteration - the gauntlet's shape, and the shape every number motivating this bead came from -
and is worth nothing at all on the two lanes that reuse inputs the way training does.

JOINT READING: the churn is real but it is NOT COSTING ANYTHING. A pool would remove traffic that
the measurement says is already effectively free in steady state. The 2.79x/3.96x figures were real
measurements of a real effect, but the effect belongs to the harness's per-iteration input rebuild,
not to a training step's steady-state churn.

WHY REJECTING IS THE RIGHT OUTCOME: the bead itself flagged pooling's highest risk as a pooled
buffer aliasing a tensor still reachable from the tape, against the project rule that autograd
correctness outranks kernel speed. Buying that risk for a measured 0% is a bad trade - and it is now
a measured bad trade rather than an intuition.

NOTHING REPLACES IT. The allocator question is already closed by frankentorch-1ji9l option C
(landed 7f57fce3): fair-alloc opt-in for FT's own measurement binaries, never in the library, and
the gauntlet prints which allocator produced its numbers.

RETRY PREDICATE: re-open ONLY if a real user workload (not a benchmark) both (i) repeatedly
allocates large tensors in steady state AND (ii) is measurably moved by an allocator swap with
non-overlapping ranges over interleaved reps. Both halves required - the whole finding here is that
the first is satisfied by workloads where the second is not.

  rch exec -- cargo build ...
(no sh -c, no pipes) whenever you need the binary back on the local box. A pipe inside the command
also makes rch refuse it outright as a "non-compilation command" (RCH-E301), which at least fails loudly.

MODE 2 — incremental sync can race a git commit.
A subsequent bare build then failed with
  error: couldn't find file `crates/ft-api/examples/training_loop_alloc_profile.rs`
on worker vmi1152480, although the file exists locally, is git-tracked, and is not ignored. The file
had just transitioned untracked -> tracked by being committed mid-flight, and the worker's synced tree
did not have it. Retrying the same command is the workaround.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ERGONOMICS: this campaign's rule that every perf row must carry an
executing-ELF SHA-256 self-reported from inside the process is exactly what caught mode 1. Without it
I would have published a "fixed binary" re-run that was the unfixed binary. If you are running a
self-A/B through rch, print the ELF SHA from inside the process and compare the two arms' SHAs before
believing any ratio.

title: tensor_interpolate linear/bilinear/trilinear autograd via index_select + weighted sum
description:
After frankentorch-ov0v added a fail-loud guard, tensor_interpolate with mode='linear'/'bilinear'/'trilinear' is unusable in autograd flows. Each output position is a weighted sum of 2 (linear), 4 (bilinear), or 8 (trilinear) input pixels — compose via tensor_reshape + tensor_index_select (per corner) + tensor_mul (with non-grad per-position weight tensor) + tensor_add.

Bicubic uses 16 corners with cubic Hermite spline weights — defer.

Affects: crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs tensor_interpolate (line 14674) — interpolate_linear_1d, interpolate_bilinear, interpolate_trilinear paths.

title: Bilinear bias broadcast uses tensor_expand on wrong rank
description:
Bilinear::forward (line 1047) calls tensor_expand on bias (shape [out_features]) targeting [*, out_features]. tensor_expand requires the input rank to match the target — same bug pattern as ConvTranspose1d (frankentorch-ru7u). Use_bias=true would panic with ShapeMismatch.

Fix: tensor_reshape bias from [out_features] to a shape with the same rank as out_shape (1s in all leading dims, out_features in the last) before expanding.

Affects: crates/ft-nn/src/lib.rs Bilinear::forward (line 1046+).

title: Remaining ft-api ops with fail-loud autograd guards: stft, istft, affine_grid, grid_sample, complex/view_as_real/view_as_complex
description:
After closing frankentorch-1tax (statistical/special ops), 7 ops in ft-api still reject requires_grad=true inputs with hard errors instead of carrying gradients:

- stft (line 1248) — short-time Fourier transform; PyTorch's torch.stft supports backward via inverse FFT.
- istft (line 1411) — inverse short-time Fourier transform; symmetric to stft.
- stft window tensor (line 6733) — separate guard rejecting tracked window inputs.
- affine_grid (line 7774) — torch.nn.functional.affine_grid supports backward.
- grid_sample (line 7905) — torch.nn.functional.grid_sample supports backward.
- complex (line 994/1001) — torch.complex(re, im) supports backward through real and imaginary inputs (Wirtinger derivatives).
- view_as_real / view_as_complex (lines 1101, 1145) — complex view ops also support gradients in PyTorch.

These are not 'severed-autograd' — they're explicit guards that fail-loud, so users can't accidentally lose gradients silently. But they DO block training paths that would work in PyTorch (e.g., audio models using STFT, vision models using affine_grid + grid_sample for spatial transformer networks).

Each child needs its own fix bead. Children grouped by domain:
  Audio:   stft + istft + stft-window
  Vision:  affine_grid + grid_sample
  Complex: complex + view_as_real + view_as_complex (deferred — Wirtinger calculus is non-trivial; PyTorch's complex autograd took years to stabilize)

Priority for audio/vision (P2): real downstream training paths blocked. Priority for complex (P3): Wirtinger calculus is genuinely tricky and may need its own design doc first.
notes:
affine_grid slice closed in 669df96 (frankentorch-bfj5). Remaining children that still need work:
  - stft / istft / stft window — Audio. Backward via inverse FFT or windowed-overlap-add gradient. Non-trivial.
  - grid_sample (bilinear mode) — Vision. Backward via bilinear interpolation derivatives in both input and grid; nearest mode is non-differentiable in grid.
  - complex / view_as_real / view_as_complex — Wirtinger calculus. PyTorch's complex autograd took years to stabilize; needs a design doc first.

Each remaining child should get its own bead when picked up. Priorities:
  - stft + istft + stft-window: P2 (audio training paths blocked)
  - grid_sample: P2 (vision training paths blocked, e.g. spatial transformer networks)
  - complex/Wirtinger: P3 (defer until design doc)

title: [perf][no-gaps] f32 custom-op autograd infra -> f32 conv/depthwise/linear GRAD fast paths
description:
GAP: the fused GRAD fast paths for conv2d / linear (and the depthwise no-grad fast paths 7a924b10/9e53a3bb) are F64-ONLY because the tape's borrowed-inputs custom-op mechanism — tensor_apply_function_f64_borrowed_inputs (ft-api:7181 -> tape apply_function_f64_borrowed_inputs) — only exists for f64. So f32 conv2d/depthwise/linear with requires_grad FALL THROUGH to the slow COMPOSED path (unfold+permute+reshape+matmul, or the per-group narrow+im2col+cat loop). Training is overwhelmingly f32, so this is the dominant training workload running on the slow path.

ROOT CAUSE + SCOPED FIX: the tape custom-op forward returns Vec<f64> -> builds an F64 leaf; for f32 we must produce an F32 OUTPUT leaf (torch f32 conv -> f32 output; an f64 leaf breaks dtype parity, the same class of bug fixed in fk5l/b3fg). Add tensor_apply_function_f32_output_borrowed_inputs: forward closure returns (Vec<f32>, shape) -> F32 leaf; backward closure receives the f64 incoming grad (tape grad-space stays f64 for precision) + borrowed f32 inputs, returns f64 input grads (tape accumulates in f64 as today). This keeps grad precision while fixing output dtype. Requires a tape custom-op node variant that stores an f32 forward output but flows f64 grads.

THEN wire f32 grad fast paths (mirroring the existing f64 ones):
- conv2d: f32 grad fast path in functional_conv2d (mirror the f64 block ~19457) using conv2d_forward_f32 + a NEW conv2d_backward_f32 kernel.
- depthwise conv2d/3d: f32 grad custom op in functional_conv2d_grouped / functional_conv3d_dilated using depthwise_conv{2,3}d_forward_f32 + NEW depthwise_conv{2,3}d_backward_f32 kernels.
- linear: f32 grad fast path (mirror f64 ~18206).

KERNELS NEEDED (ft-kernel-cpu): conv2d_backward_f32, depthwise_conv2d_backward_f64/f32, depthwise_conv3d_backward_f64/f32 (dinput=col2im/full-correlation parallel over N*C planes; dweight=correlate input·dout per channel parallel over C; dbias=sum dout per C). Tolerance parity (conv grad is GEMM/reduction-backed; grouped path checked vs torch 1e-9).

VALUE: f32 conv/depthwise training step = multi-x (avoids unfold/permute/transpose materializations + per-group loop), the common training case. A/B vs the composed path, Score>=2.0. PARITY: tolerance (match torch 1e-9 / the existing composed path). RISK: tape custom-op f32-output node is engine work — test the infra in isolation (a trivial f32 custom op fwd+bwd) BEFORE wiring conv. See [[project_compute_bound_parallel_vein]] (depthwise forward 7a924b10/9e53a3bb) + [[project_f32_parity_vein]]. Also covers the f64 depthwise BACKWARD (lower priority — f64 training rare).
notes: f32 LINEAR grad: MEASURED + REJECTED (1.12x, reverted). Linear is GEMM-dominated; the fused fast path only avoids the weight-transpose materialization (~16MB, tiny vs the n³ GEMM), so wall-clock is 1.12x — below Score>=2.0 (the f64 linear fast path was likewise a transpose/MEMORY win, not a 2x compute win). f32 grad fast paths only clear 2.0 when the composed path is materialization-HEAVY relative to the GEMM (depthwise: no GEMM mixing; plain conv2d: unfold+permute materializations). DONE: f32 depthwise conv2d (49f1bc1e 4.5-9x) + f32 plain conv2d (de615991 11.8x). REMAINING (niche / lower-priority): f32+f64 depthwise conv3d backward. Linear excluded (GEMM-bound).
close_reason: HIGH-VALUE CASES COMPLETE. Shipped: f32-output custom-op autograd infra (fa39b198) + f32 grad fast paths for the three dominant training ops: SDPA/attention (f564fd66, 10.4x — the transformer training bottleneck), plain conv2d (de615991, 11.8x), depthwise conv2d (49f1bc1e, 4.5-9x). All via the f32-output custom op (f32 output dtype parity + f64 grad-space + f32-precision backward); f32 grads match f64 path within 1e-3. EXCLUDED: f32 linear grad (measured 1.12x — GEMM-bound, the fast path only avoids the small weight-transpose materialization; not a perf win, like the f64 linear fast path which was memory-not-compute). The f32-grad recipe (<op>_backward_f32 + f32 grad block via the f32-output custom op) is proven 3x and documented in [[project_compute_bound_parallel_vein]].

title: Add basic quantization support (torch.quantization equivalent)
description:
PyTorch's quantization allows running models with INT8 weights for faster inference and smaller model size. This is increasingly important for edge deployment.

Implementation plan (CPU quantization only):
1. Add quantized dtypes to ft-core: QInt8, QUInt8 (with scale and zero_point metadata)
2. Add QuantizedTensorMeta extending TensorMeta with quantization parameters
3. Add quantize/dequantize functions:
   - session.quantize_per_tensor(input, scale, zero_point, dtype) -> quantized tensor
   - session.dequantize(quantized) -> float tensor
4. Add quantized linear layer (QuantizedLinear) in ft-nn:
   - Stores INT8 weights + F32 bias
   - Forward: dequantize weights -> matmul -> add bias (or fused quantized matmul if we add a kernel)
5. Add basic observer (MinMaxObserver) for calibration:
   - Tracks running min/max of tensor values
   - Computes optimal scale/zero_point
6. Add post-training quantization workflow:
   - Calibrate observers on representative data
   - Convert float model to quantized model

Tests:
- Unit test: quantize then dequantize recovers original values (within quantization error)
- Unit test: quantized linear forward matches dequantize-then-matmul
- Unit test: MinMaxObserver correctly tracks min/max
- Unit test: scale/zero_point calculation is correct
- E2E test: train a float model, quantize it, verify inference output is close to float model
- Edge case: quantize with scale=0 should error, not divide by zero

title: ft-optim: Adam/AdamW lack amsgrad variant
description: Adam and AdamW have no amsgrad option (torch.optim.Adam/AdamW(amsgrad=True)). amsgrad keeps a per-element running MAX of the second moment and uses it in the denominator: max_exp_avg_sq = max(max_exp_avg_sq, exp_avg_sq); denom = sqrt(max_exp_avg_sq)/sqrt(bias_correction2) + eps. Add: amsgrad:bool field + v_max:Vec<Option<Vec<f64>>> state (lazy, only when amsgrad) + .amsgrad(bool) builder. IMPLEMENT VIA A SEPARATE CODE PATH so the perf-tuned non-amsgrad fused parallel loop stays byte-identical (it is a peer perf-tuned hot path). Test with CONTROLLED gradients (tensor_set_accumulated_gradient) where v decreases, e.g. grads [3,3] then [1,1] then [1,1], so v_max != v_hat and amsgrad diverges from Adam; golden vs torch. NOTE: sum(x^2) loss does NOT discriminate amsgrad (v monotonically grows) — verified in optimizer_trajectories_match_torch where Adam==Adam_amsgrad.
notes: Adam amsgrad SHIPPED cfb8cbff (separate code path, non-amsgrad byte-identical, verified vs torch with [10,0,0] discriminator). REMAINING: AdamW amsgrad — same pattern (add amsgrad:bool + v_max:Vec<Option<Vec<f64>>> + .amsgrad() builder + separate step path). AdamW step is at ft-optim ~664.

title: [perf][no-gaps] ft-optim AdamW workspace/layout primitive after state-buffer keep
description: Profile-backed fallback because br ready --json is empty and active perf lanes are claimed. Fresh rch Criterion baseline on vmi1227854: adamw/step_64x1024 [369.78 us 381.30 us 392.61 us], adam [316.88 us 325.14 us 336.61 us], sgd [239.49 us 246.79 us 253.63 us]. AdamW is the largest isolated row after prior state-buffer keep and beta-hoist rejection. Use /repeatedly-apply-skill over /extreme-software-optimization: one structural lever only, preferably workspace/layout or batched update primitive, preserving parameter order, state commit order, floating-point expression order, RNG absence, and golden sha256. Baseline via rch first already captured; rebench same worker; keep only Score >= 2.0.
notes:
RESOLVED — workspace primitive landed; the remaining deep lever (cross-param
parallelism) empirically REJECTED by same-worker A/B proof.

Attacked a fundamentally DIFFERENT parallelization model per the no-ceiling
directive: the per-param inner loop (1024 elems) is below the rayon threshold so
it always runs serial, but the 64 params are fully independent updates — so
parallelize ACROSS params. Built a same-worker A/B probe (adamw_probe bench,
optimizer_bench.rs) using SCOPED rayon pools so serial/1/4/8/16/32-thread all run
in ONE process on ONE worker (avoids the separate-rch-exec worker-variance trap).

Result (ovh-class worker, criterion medians, owned buffers = compute ceiling, no
session/copy overhead):
  serial            367 us
  parallel_1thread  430 us   (rayon dispatch overhead)
  parallel_4thread  345 us   (1.06x)
  parallel_8thread  341 us   (1.08x  <- peak)
  parallel_16thread 369 us   (regresses to serial)
  parallel_32thread 405 us   (worse than serial)

Diagnosis: the AdamW step is MEMORY-BANDWIDTH-BOUND, not compute-bound. Per
element it streams grad + m(rw) + v(rw) + param(rw) ≈ 7 array accesses for ~10
flops + 1 sqrt + 2 div — arithmetic intensity is far too low for either thread
parallelism or SIMD to help; cores starve on bandwidth (peak 1.08x, then negative
past 8 threads as memory contention dominates). This is exactly why the shipped
zero-clone lever (2816633d, 1.08x) WORKED — it reduced traffic, the only thing
that moves a bandwidth-bound kernel.

NOT a 'ceiling' claim — a measured physical bound with the campaign-mandated
same-worker proof. No bit-exact >=2.0 lever exists for THIS kernel on these
workers (mixed-precision m/v would cut traffic but breaks bit-exact parity =
forbidden). Closing. The probe bench is committed as a regression guard so future
agents don't re-attempt the parallel lever. Next perf target should be a
COMPUTE-bound kernel (e.g. the non-symmetric eig/geev gap l9xod), where
parallelism/blocking can actually clear 2.0.

title: multilabel_soft_margin_loss severs autograd; delegate to bce_with_logits_loss
description:
multilabel_soft_margin_loss at lib.rs:10507 implements the per-element BCE-with-logits formula manually (max(x,0) - x*t + log1p(exp(-|x|))), accumulates in plain f64, and rebuilds a requires_grad=false leaf — same severed-autograd pattern fixed across the recent ft-api cleanup.

For a 2-D input [batch, classes] the multilabel_soft_margin_loss formula reduces to mean over all (i, j) of BCE_with_logits(x[i,j], t[i,j]), which is exactly what bce_with_logits_loss computes (the latter is autograd-aware via composition through tensor_relu + tensor_abs + tensor_log1p + tensor_mean).

Fix: delegate to self.bce_with_logits_loss(input, target) with the existing 2-D shape validation. Same arithmetic, same numerical stability via log1p(exp(-|x|)), but with the autograd tape preserved.

Sister of frankentorch-ilwr (cross_entropy with smoothing severance). Surfaced during /reality-check pass.
notes:
Fixed in this commit. Replaced the manual per-element BCE accumulator with delegation to bce_with_logits_loss, which already implements the same numerically-stable formula max(x, 0) - x*t + log1p(exp(-|x|)) via composition through tensor_relu + tensor_abs + tensor_log1p + tensor_mean (all autograd-aware). For shape [batch, classes] both losses produce identical scalars (mean over all elements) and now both share gradient flow.

Added multilabel_soft_margin_loss_propagates_gradient_via_bce_with_logits regression test. Tests at x = ±1 to avoid the relu/abs corner at x=0 where FrankenTorch's sub-gradient convention differs slightly from the smooth sigmoid(x)-t form. ft-api lib tests: 1152.

title: tensor_linalg_vector_norm severs autograd via tensor_values + non-grad rebuild
description:
tensor_linalg_vector_norm in ft-api (line 12741) extracts tensor_values, computes the chosen norm in plain f64, and rebuilds via session.tensor_variable(vec![norm], vec![1], false). This silently severs autograd through every vector_norm computation — used widely in normalization, loss functions, gradient clipping, etc.

Fix: compose through autograd-aware primitives. For each ord:
- ord = inf: tensor_abs + tensor_max (max is differentiable at the strict argmax)
- ord = -inf: tensor_abs + tensor_min
- ord = 0: non-differentiable (integer count) — keep severed but add fail-loud guard for requires_grad
- ord = p (positive finite): tensor_abs + tensor_pow(p) + tensor_sum + tensor_pow(1/p)

Affects: crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs tensor_linalg_vector_norm (line 12741).

title: tensor_repeat_interleave severs autograd; sum-of-R-grad backward
description:
tensor_repeat_interleave at lib.rs:11097 takes a 1-D input and repeats each element R times consecutively. PyTorch's torch.repeat_interleave IS differentiable.

Backward: grad_input[i] = sum over j where j // R == i of grad_output[j]. Each input element gets the sum of the R consecutive output gradients that came from it.

Wrap in tensor_apply_function.

Each input element gets the sum of the R consecutive output gradients that came from it. Preserved the byte-size overflow check (output count alone can fit in usize even when out_len * 8 bytes overflows). title: [parity][threshold] serial-vs-parallel equivalence sweep across the size-gated elementwise/activation kernels
description:
FrankenTorch gates many kernels on tensor SIZE — PARALLEL_THRESHOLD=8192, SOFTMAX_PARALLEL_NUMEL_THRESHOLD=65536, SCALAR_UNARY/SIMD_UNARY_PARALLEL_THRESHOLD=524288, plus ~57 further size-gated sites in ft-api alone. Above the gate a different code path runs. Nothing systematically checks that the two paths agree.

OBSERVED DEFECT CLASS, not speculation — this exact shape has produced two real bugs recently:
  * frankentorch-fmmns (OPEN, P0, peer-owned): the max_pool1d 2x2 pair SPECIALIZATION disagrees with the generic route. Confirmed at clean HEAD. The divergent window is all-NaN: specialization reports offset=6.0, generic reports 0.0.
  * frankentorch-x4cx3 (closed): prelu's zero-convention bug had to be driven past the 65_536-element gate specifically because "the parallel branches use their own compare" — the serial fix alone would not have covered them.
So: a second implementation of the same math, selected by size, with no equivalence test between them.

THE PROOF SHAPE (from the RNG sub-stream vein, where serial==parallel bit-identical IS the certificate): for an ELEMENTWISE op, chunking is semantically the identity. So build ONE input of N >= threshold, evaluate f on the whole vector (parallel path), then evaluate f on sub-threshold slices of the SAME values and concatenate (serial path), and compare .to_bits() element-for-element. Any difference is a real defect, and the comparison needs no oracle — FT is its own oracle.

INPUTS MUST STRADDLE EVERY BRANCH BOUNDARY, which is the lesson x4cx3 paid for (no PReLU fixture had an exact 0.0, which is why a years-old grad bug survived): +0.0, -0.0, +/-1, NaN, +/-inf, exact op boundaries (0 for relu/prelu/rrelu, 6 for relu6, +/-1 hardtanh, +/-3 hardsigmoid/hardswish, +/-lambda for the shrinks, the softplus threshold 20), ties, and denormals. Pad with benign values to cross the size gate.

SCOPE: forward AND backward for the size-gated elementwise/activation surface first, since that is where the gates and the known defects are. Reductions and softmax have their own gate (65536) and are a natural second round.

NOT IN SCOPE: fixing frankentorch-fmmns. That is a peer's open bead and stays theirs; it is cited here only as the evidence that this class is real.

NEGATIVE RESULT IS A FINE OUTCOME and should be recorded as such: if every gated op already agrees across its threshold, that is worth knowing and worth pinning with a live test, exactly like frankentorch-1knqk (which found all ten suspected sites already clean and shipped the gate anyway).
close_reason:
NEGATIVE RESULT + live gate shipped. Landed c35e4478.

No serial-vs-parallel divergence found. 20 ops, forward AND backward, all bit-identical across every size gate.

METHOD (needs no oracle): for an elementwise op, chunking is the identity. The same values go through each op twice — once as ONE 600_000-element tensor (parallel side of PARALLEL_THRESHOLD 8192, SOFTMAX 65536 and SCALAR/SIMD_UNARY 524288) and once as 4_096-element chunks (serial side of all three) — compared with to_bits(). FrankenTorch is its own oracle; any difference would be a defect whatever torch does. Same certificate shape as the RNG sub-stream vein, where serial == parallel bit-identical WAS the proof.

Bit patterns, not values: -0.0 == +0.0 under ==, and the sign of zero is exactly what distinguishes 'took the multiply branch' from 'took the identity branch' — the discrimination that caught the rrelu forward bug in 3eq5b.

INPUTS straddle every boundary these ops branch on (signed zeros, 6, +/-1, +/-3, +/-0.5, 20, NaN, +/-inf, subnormals), placed at the head, across a chunk seam, mid-tensor, and inside the SHORT FINAL CHUNK. x4cx3 survived for years because no PReLU fixture contained an exact 0.0.

prelu covered with BOTH positive and negative weight — it carries an explicit xv.len() >= 65_536 gate on its backward and is the op whose parallel branch was actually wrong in x4cx3; the negative weight is the variant where the sign of zero is observable. CHUNK=4096 is not a divisor of 600_000, so the short final chunk is exercised deliberately.

The suite includes a SELF-TEST (the_comparison_actually_detects_a_difference) feeding a deliberately mismatched pair through the same comparator, so the two passing tests cannot be passing vacuously.

WHY SHIP A TEST THAT FOUND NOTHING: same reasoning as 1knqk. It costs ~8s and fails the moment a new specialization or threshold lands that does not agree with its own serial path. The hazard is structural — the gates and the second implementations are still there.

HOME: ft-conformance, not ft-api — it is cross-component (AGENTS.md) and ft-api/src/lib.rs was under an exclusive peer reservation throughout.

GATES: cargo test -p ft-conformance --test threshold_serial_parallel_equivalence -> 3 passed / 0 failed, REAL_EXIT=0, rch worker vmi1153651. cargo clippy -p ft-conformance --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings -> clean, rch worker vmi1149989. rustfmt clean. No timed rows banked.

TWO SPIN-OFF FINDINGS landed separately in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md while the fleet was slot-starved (both measured on torch 2.12.1+cpu, no rch worker):
  32de175a — torch's MISH FORWARD is vector-width dependent by 1 ULP in f64, flipping at the same n=8 boundary as the jedc6 NaN gradients. 24 of 25 ops swept are width-stable; mish is not. The VECTORISED value equals the naive x*tanh(softplus(x)) composition and torch's own SCALAR kernel is the odd one out, so FT (which composes) matches at n>=8 and is 1 ULP off at n<8. Nothing red today — the only mish check is metamorphic at 32-ULP tolerance — but a future bit-exact mish golden against torch must pin its size class.
  398a3c42 — THE BOUND: ordinary-value gradients ARE width-stable. Same 25 ops at finite non-boundary inputs across n=1..257 in f64 and f32: every gradient bit-identical. So the width hazard is confined to special values and mish, and normal-path gradient parity claims stand. Recording the bound matters as much as the hazard, or the honest reading of the first two findings would be 'any torch comparison might be size-dependent'.

NOT IN SCOPE and untouched: frankentorch-fmmns, cited as the evidence this class is real, remains a peer's open bead.

FOLLOW-ON worth a bead if anyone wants it: reductions and softmax have their own 65536 gate but are NOT chunk-invariant, so they need a different equivalence technique than this one.

Planted-asymmetry test verified to FAIL pre-fix and pass after. Reported plainly: the A/A gate went 47/48 -> 44/48 PASS, because the checksum was ballast damping the null's relative variance. Supersedes k1h8g's 2.83x avg_pool2d figure (now 1.87x); its 1.50x same-timer speedup is unaffected.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FOUND BY: RainyReef/cc while profiling frankentorch-k1h8g, 2026-08-08.

DEFECT. In crates/ft-api/examples/gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h.rs, timed_op stops its timer AFTER computing the gradient checksum:
    let started = Instant::now();
    ... build / sum / backward ...
    let checksum = report.gradient(x).expect("grad").iter().sum::<f64>();
    (started.elapsed()..., checksum)
The PyTorch arm does NOT:
    s=time.perf_counter()
    fn(x).sum().backward()
    return (time.perf_counter()-s)*1e3, x.grad.sum().item()
Python evaluates tuple elements left to right, so the elapsed term is computed BEFORE x.grad.sum().item(). Torch's grad sum is outside its measurement; ours is inside.

SIZE OF THE ERROR, measured on the avg_pool2d lane [8,64,64,64] f64: the checksum is report.gradient(x).iter().sum() over 2,097,152 f64 — a SERIAL dependent-add chain — at 1.599 ms, which was 24% of that lane's 6.562 ms session. Every lane in this harness pays a term like this, scaled by its input size, and no lane's PyTorch arm pays it. So every FrankenTorch figure in this harness is inflated by a checksum that is not op work, and the inflation is largest exactly where inputs are largest.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE LANE: this harness is the instrument the campaign quotes vs-PyTorch ratios from. An asymmetric timed region is a systematic bias in the same class as frankentorch-6atx2 (arms not interleaved) and frankentorch-8ieqm (anti-conservative null) — it does not average out with repetition, because it is present in every repetition of one arm only.

FIX OPTIONS, either is defensible but the choice should be deliberate:
  (a) move the FT checksum outside the timer, matching the PyTorch arm — smallest change, makes the two regions comparable;
  (b) time the checksum on BOTH arms — also comparable, but then both arms measure a reduction that is not the op under test.
(a) is the closer match to 'OP WORK ONLY', which is what this harness's own header claims to measure.

GATE-CHANGE PROTOCOL APPLIES. This changes every published number in the harness downward on the FT side, so it needs the before/after set and the integrity report that frankentorch-8ieqm's protocol requires: publish which lanes move and by how much, and confirm the direction is uniformly 'FT looks better' (a fix that made FT look worse somewhere would mean something else is wrong). Expected: every lane's FT time drops by its own checksum cost, ratios improve, and NO lane's standing flips from loss to win purely from this — if one does, that lane was never a real loss.

DO NOT quote a corrected ratio until this lands. On the avg_pool2d lane, deducting the checksum would move 2.83x to roughly 1.9x, but that arithmetic is not a measurement and was deliberately not quoted as the k1h8g result.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIXED AND MEASURED (RainyReef/cc, 2026-08-08). Code: c015c655.

THE FIX. The timed region is now named once — ft-api::harness_interleave::TIMED_STEPS = [forward, loss_sum, backward] — the gradient checksum is teardown on BOTH arms, and both arms DECLARE the region they timed: the Python side prints PT_TIMED_STEPS as an independent literal beside its own run(), and the harness hard-fails via timed_region_disagreement if the declarations differ. Option (a) from this bead, which matches the harness's own 'OP WORK ONLY' claim. A declaration is not an observation — no cheap way to observe what the child timed — but it makes drift loud instead of silent, and it is enforced at runtime rather than asserted in a comment.

INTEGRITY REPORT (gate-change protocol). 12 BEFORE/AFTER pairs alternating in one window, interleaved arms, A/A width-veto gate, torch 2.12.1+cpu, load median 14.59. BEFORE ELF 2af564260a7fb55d, AFTER ELF 476c6c933806201f — BEFORE already carries the k1h8g kernel fix, so the ONLY difference between arms is where the clock stops.

  lane          FT before   FT after     drop   drop ms | ratio before  ratio after
  avg_pool2d        5.130      3.418    33.4%     1.712 |       2.77x        1.87x
  max_pool1d       15.546     12.415    20.1%     3.131 |       1.98x        1.55x
  max_pool3d        5.361      4.032    24.8%     1.329 |       6.55x        4.77x
  conv3d           20.596     20.530     0.3%     0.065 |       3.38x        3.23x

Direction is UNIFORM — every lane drops, none rises. NO lane flipped loss to win; all four remain SLOWER. That was the stated check that this is a measurement fix rather than a way to manufacture wins, and it holds. Parity 48/48 match on both arms.

THE DROP TRACKS LEAF SIZE, which is the positive evidence that exactly the checksum came out and nothing else: max_pool1d 33 MiB leaf -> 3.131 ms, avg_pool2d 16 MiB -> 1.712 ms, max_pool3d 8 MiB -> 1.329 ms, conv3d 2 MiB -> 0.065 ms. conv3d's leaf is tiny, so its correction is 0.3% — a fix that had removed real op work would not track the leaf that cleanly.

REPORTED PLAINLY, not buried: the A/A gate got slightly WORSE, 47/48 PASS before to 44/48 after. Expected and arguably correct — the checksum was a large, stable additive term that damped the null's RELATIVE variance. Removing it exposes the true variability of the op work. The gate was previously flattered by ballast.

PLANTED-ASYMMETRY TEST, VERIFIED TO FAIL PRE-FIX rather than assumed to: planting the pre-fix configuration (gradient_checksum back inside TIMED_STEPS) makes the_shipped_timed_region_excludes_teardown FAIL with ' is teardown and must not be inside the timed region'; restored, all 30 harness_interleave tests pass. Seven tests total: the exact pre-fix pair rejected with the offending step named; an incumbent timing EXTRA work also caught (the check is deliberately not one-sided, since that biases the ratio the other way); reordered steps caught; an undeclared region parsed as None rather than agreement, because silence is not symmetry.

DOWNSTREAM CORRECTION: every ratio previously published from this harness was inflated on the FT side. In particular frankentorch-k1h8g's recorded 2.83x for avg_pool2d was measured under the asymmetric timer and reads 1.87x here. The 1.50x FT-vs-FT speedup that bead landed is unaffected, being a same-timer comparison. The banked lane-sweep-reps16 artifact predates all of this and its FT figures carry the same inflation; it is not re-banked here.

Gates: cargo test -p ft-api --lib = 2532 passed / 0 failed; clippy -p ft-api --all-targets --no-deps -D warnings exits 0; fmt --check exits 0.

title: [perf][groupnorm] 57% of the f32 lane is outside its kernels — separate estimator from allocation before any lever
description:
The GroupNorm f32 lane spends MORE time outside its kernels than inside them, and I cannot yet say whether that is real work or an artifact of the estimator. Resolve that before any further lever on this lane -- it is the largest remaining vs-incumbent gap (6.96-11.77x across five invocations, harness=crates/ft-api/examples/gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h.rs, same_host=thinkstation1, AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5975WX, governor powersave, 64 rayon threads, torch threads 8, mimalloc; timing local because rch workers have no PyTorch).

THE GAP. In one invocation (ELF 2cbe821a, 24 rounds):

  group_norm_f32_kernels LANE   ~2.045 ms   (median of 4 per round, balanced square)
  the same three kernels        0.851 ms    (min of 9, breakdown block)
      forward_f32                 0.173
      sum_tensor_contiguous_f32   0.145
      backward_scalar_f32         0.533

So ~57% of the lane is unaccounted for by its own kernels. The lane has NO session and NO tape -- it is three kernel calls -- so the candidates are narrow:

  (a) per-rep allocation churn. Each rep allocates a 1.6 MiB forward output and a
      1.6 MiB dx and drops them; the breakdown's warm min-of-9 loop does not pay
      what a cold-ish allocation pays.
  (b) the ESTIMATOR. The lane takes a median of 4 samples per round; the
      breakdown takes a min of 9. On a host carrying a dozen peer agents the
      median mostly measures the neighbours. This is not hypothetical here:
      frankentorch-dmpho measured the same parallel kernel at 1.819 ms under
      load ~13-20 and 0.535 ms under load ~10-12.

These have opposite consequences. If (a), there is a real lever (reuse the output
buffer across reps, or take from ft_core::buffer_pool, which already has a
generic recycle side). If (b), there is NO lever -- the lane is simply reporting
a contended host, every ratio banked from it is inflated, and the right response
is to fix the reporting rather than the code.

DESIGN. Do not add another standalone probe; that is what produced the
disagreement recorded as NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE item 11. Put both estimators over the
SAME work in ONE invocation:

  1. In the breakdown block, time the three kernels twice per rep -- once
     reported as min-of-N and once as median-of-4 -- so estimator is the only
     difference. If the median arm reproduces ~2.0 ms while the min arm stays at
     ~0.85 ms, the gap is (b) and the lane numbers need a health warning, not a
     lever.
  2. Only if a real remainder survives that: add an arm that reuses one output
     allocation across reps, to price (a) separately.

NEGATIVE CASE a naive implementation would fail: if the two estimator arms come
out within a few percent of each other, the hypothesis that estimator explains
the gap is REFUTED and (a) is implicated -- record that, do not quietly keep the
flattering arm. Either outcome is publishable; the failure mode is picking one.

PROVENANCE REQUIRED on every row: harness file + estimator, same_host= (or
RCH_WORKER= if ever run on a worker), ELF digest, observed thread count,
governor, and the observed load. A row that cannot name where it ran and with
what is not comparable to any other row (frankenlibc: two sanctioned harnesses,
one worker, 5.9459x vs 12.385414x with both A/A nulls passing; frankenscipy:
13.6x swing for one cell across two workers, both nulls passing).
close_reason: Resolved by measurement in c45d84c2: the estimator accounts for 1.512x of the 2.43x lane-vs-kernel gap (step min-of-40 0.760 ms vs the same step under the lane's median-of-4 estimator 1.149 ms, one invocation, ELF 72c80e41, same_host=thinkstation1). Per-rep allocation churn REFUTED as the explanation -- the step arm pays identical 1.6 MiB out + 1.6 MiB dx allocations every rep. Residual 1.61x recorded as OPEN (interleaving vs allocator warmth; this design cannot separate them). No lever built, because the phase it would have targeted was an artifact of subtracting two different estimators.

title: [parity][in-place] round 3: the matmul family (addmm_, baddbmm_, addbmm_, addmv_, addr_, addcmul_, addcdiv_)
description:
Third and final round of the in-place sweep begun in frankentorch-q06x9 (16 unary ops, clean) and continued in frankentorch-jvst1 (12 scalar/binary ops, which FOUND A REAL DEFECT — tensor_hardshrink_ zeroed NaN where torch and the out-of-place form keep it).

Same certificate, no oracle: after a.foo_(...), a must hold bit-for-bit what b = x.foo(...) produced. FrankenTorch is its own reference; compare on to_bits().

WHY THIS ROUND IS DIFFERENT AND NEEDS MORE CARE, which is why jvst1 deferred it: these ops take MULTIPLE TENSOR OPERANDS with shape relationships, so a sweep cannot use one flat payload. Signatures were checked and all seven have a matching out-of-place sibling with the same extra arguments (beta/alpha or value), so no signature trap of the hardtanh/leaky_relu kind applies here — that was verified before writing, not assumed.

Shapes must satisfy the op's contract:
  addmm    input [n,p], mat1 [n,m], mat2 [m,p]
  baddbmm  input [b,n,p], batch1 [b,n,m], batch2 [b,m,p]
  addbmm   input [n,p], batch1 [b,n,m], batch2 [b,m,p]   (reduces over the batch)
  addmv    input [n], mat [n,m], vec [m]
  addr     input [n,m], vec1 [n], vec2 [m]
  addcmul / addcdiv  all same shape (elementwise)

EXPECT A DIFFERENT RISK PROFILE from rounds 1-2. These route through GEMM/BLAS-like kernels with their own blocking and parallel gates, so an in-place form that re-associates differently from its out-of-place sibling would differ in the LAST BITS rather than at a special value. That is still a defect — the two forms are the same op — but it will look like a 1-ULP spread across many elements rather than the clean NaN/0.0 split hardshrink_ showed. Do not weaken the comparison to a tolerance if that happens; record it and decide deliberately, because a re-association difference between two forms of one op is exactly what a bit-exactness gate exists to surface.

Boundary values still belong in the inputs (signed zeros, NaN, infinities) but matmul propagates them across whole rows, so a single NaN makes an entire output row NaN. Keep the boundary set SMALL and positioned so a divergence is still localisable.

A NEGATIVE RESULT IS A FINE OUTCOME and ships the gate anyway, per q06x9 / jvst1 / 5237b / h37tn / 1knqk.

NOTE: rch refuses ft-conformance test jobs on 6/10 workers (frankentorch-1v8kz). Use -j2.
close_reason:
SECOND REAL DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED — and it is a vs-TORCH PARITY bug, not just an internal inconsistency. Landed 72dec3b7.

THE BUG: torch computes addcdiv as input + (value * tensor1) / tensor2. FrankenTorch's OUT-OF-PLACE form computed input + value * (tensor1 / tensor2). Different rounding.

ORACLE EVIDENCE (torch 2.12.1+cpu): over 400 random f64 cases, (value*t1)/t2 matched 400/400; value*(t1/t2) matched only 329/400. On the pinned fixture torch.addcdiv(0.5, 2.25, -1.75, value=0.75) = 0xbfddb6db6db6db6e while the old association gives 0xbfddb6db6db6db70 — 2 ULP apart.

ALL THREE out-of-place paths were wrong: the f64 no-grad fast path, its f32 sibling, and the composed fallback (div -> scale -> add, now scale -> div -> add). The IN-PLACE tensor_addcdiv_ was already CORRECT —  parses in Rust as (value*t1)/t2 — so the in-place form was right and the elaborately-optimised out-of-place form was wrong, the opposite direction from the hardshrink_ defect in jvst1.

★ WHY IT SURVIVED, and this repo has been burned by it before: the fast paths were verified BIT-EXACT AGAINST THE COMPOSED PATH, and they genuinely were. But the composed path was itself wrong versus torch, so the fused==compose lock test passed while BOTH arms were wrong. That is exactly the lerp FMA parity lesson. SELF-CONSISTENCY IS NOT PARITY, and only an oracle separates them. The source even carried a comment asserting bit-exactness, which is what made it look settled.

HOW IT WAS FOUND: by comparing the two forms of one op — the whole argument for the in-place sweep. The comparison alone said only that they disagreed, NOT which was right. torch settled it. Note the sweep would have gone green if I had 'fixed' the in-place form to match the out-of-place one, which is why the fix is pinned to torch instead.

TEST: addcdiv_scales_before_dividing_like_torch asserts torch's bit pattern directly rather than FrankenTorch against itself, and asserts the two associations are distinguishable on that fixture so it cannot go vacuous.

ROUND 3 COVERAGE: matmul family added — addmm, baddbmm, addbmm, addmv, addr, addcmul, addcdiv. The first six agree bit-for-bit. The predicted risk profile was right: the divergence was a re-association in the last bits across 5383 elements, not a special-value split, which is why the bead insisted it not be softened to a tolerance.

GATES: cargo test -j2 -p ft-conformance --test inplace_matches_out_of_place -> 6 passed / 0 failed, REAL_EXIT=0, rch worker vmi1152480. Before the fix: 4 passed / 1 failed on the same worker, naming addcdiv and 5383 divergent elements. rustfmt clean. No timed rows banked.

IN-PLACE SWEEP NOW COMPLETE across three rounds: 35 op pairs pinned (16 unary + 12 scalar/binary + 7 matmul-family) of 222 in-place ops, and it found TWO real defects — hardshrink_ zeroing NaN (jvst1) and addcdiv's association (here). Both were invisible to every existing test.

title: [parity] tensor_remainder breaks the Euclidean identity where torch does not — r=0 while floor_divide q=45 (torch r=0.529)
description:
Found by a metamorphic fuzz test that has NEVER been run in any gate (see the ungated-fuzz bead). Not yet reproduced outside the harness — but the numbers below are FrankenTorch's own output, printed by the failing assertion.

CASE: a = 24.352941176470587, b = 0.5294117647058824

  FrankenTorch  floor_divide(a,b) = 45      remainder(a,b) = 0
  torch 2.12.0  floor_divide(a,b) = 45.0    remainder(a,b) = 0.5294117647058808

FT AGREES WITH TORCH ON floor_divide AND DISAGREES ON remainder, which makes it internally inconsistent: q=45 means a = 45*b + r, and 45*b = 23.823529411764707, so r must be 0.5294... . FT's r=0 reconstructs to 23.82 against a=24.35 — the identity is off by a whole b.

torch is self-consistent on the same inputs (45 * 0.5294117647058824 + 0.5294117647058808 = 24.352941176470587 = a).

LIKELY MECHANISM, offered as a hypothesis and NOT verified — I have been wrong twice this session guessing mechanisms from numbers, so treat this as a starting point rather than a finding: a/b is EXACTLY 46.0 in f64 while torch's fmod-based div_floor_floating yields 45. If tensor_remainder computes a - (a/b).floor()*b using the NAIVE floor (46), it gets a - 46*b, which is a tiny negative that can land on 0 — while floor_divide correctly uses the div_floor_floating path. That would make this the same root cause as frankentorch-bh6bh (fixed in a70e44df for floor_divide) simply never applied to remainder, i.e. a sibling op left behind by a parity fix. The repo has hit that exact pattern before (huber_loss module vs functional; one_hot tensor_ vs session.).

WHY THIS MATTERS: the ledger currently records remainder as 'VERIFIED-CORRECT vs torch, do NOT re-probe' from the 2026-06-09 sweep. If this holds, that note is wrong for at least this input class, and a 'verified, do not re-probe' note is exactly the kind of claim that stops anyone looking again.

FIRST STEP: reproduce a2 = tensor_remainder(24.352941176470587, 0.5294117647058824) directly in a unit test and compare against torch's 0.5294117647058808. If it is 0, read tensor_remainder and check whether it shares floor_divide's div_floor_floating path.
close_reason: Fixed in bd02f26b: remainder is now fmod-based across all 6 sites, matching torch 14/14 including signed zeros. Workspace --tests 5554/0; the fuzz property passes; clippy/fmt clean.

comments.text:
CONFIRMED AND FIXED in bd02f26b. My filed hypothesis was right this time, and I checked it in source before acting rather than inferring from the numbers.

ROOT CAUSE, as suspected: every remainder path computed `a - (a / b).floor() * b`. torch derives remainder from fmod. `a / b` for the failing input is EXACTLY 46.0 in f64 while the true quotient is just below, so the naive form subtracted 46*b and returned 0 where torch returns 0.5294117647058808 — off by a whole b. bh6bh fixed floor_divide for precisely this reason (a70e44df) and never touched the sibling, so FT's own floor_divide said 45 while its remainder implied 46. The internal inconsistency was the tell.

A SECOND DEFECT I DID NOT EXPECT, found while validating the replacement across a spread rather than just the failing case: SIGN OF ZERO. torch gives -7.5 % 2.5 == -0.0 and -3.0 % 3.0 == -0.0; the naive form gave +0.0 for both. The fmod form preserves it for free, because `m != 0.0` is false for -0.0 under IEEE equality. Same property as frankentorch-dtyiz, in a different op, and it would have been missed entirely by testing only the input the fuzzer minimised to.

VERIFIED AGAINST TORCH BEFORE WRITING RUST: 14 cases across both signs, exact quotients, signed zeros and both failing fuzz inputs. fmod-based 14/14, naive 10/14.

The example — inplace_more_ab.rs — mirrors the formula as an A/B reference; left stale it would have benchmarked the new kernel against the old formula and reported a difference that was really my own edit. Fixing a subset would have left two remainder paths disagreeing, which is dtyiz's rule and also the exact defect being repaired.

GATES: --workspace --tests 39 targets / 5554 passed / 0 failed; --all-features 6 failures -> 5, this property now passing; clippy --all-targets rc=0; fmt --all clean. Nothing asserted the old values.

★ LEDGER CORRECTION OWED: the differential-parity notes record remainder as 'VERIFIED-CORRECT vs torch (don't re-probe)' from the 2026-06-09 sweep. That is wrong for this input class.
