title: [perf][revert] un3os's L3 size gate is a 4.24x kernel win but a ~15% LANE LOSS on max_pool3d — revert it
description:
REVERT frankentorch-un3os's DENSE_SCATTER_PARALLEL_MIN_BYTES gate. It is a 4.24x win on the isolated
kernel and a ~15% LOSS on the op-level lane. Evidence:
artifacts/perf/frankentorch-87sz8/gate_lane_ab_DECIDED.md

THE DECIDING MEASUREMENT (16 round-pairs, quiet host, two FT ELFs differing only in
dense_scatter_should_parallelize, ratio-of-ratios (FT/PT)_B/(FT/PT)_A over rounds where BOTH arms
passed their A/A gate):
  lane          n  ftB/A  ptB/A  rr med  effect      95pct CI     FT slower  verdict
  max_pool3d   16  1.150  1.041   1.150   0.87x  [1.036,1.198]        16/16  GATE HURTS LANE
  max_pool1d   16  1.009  1.009   1.007   0.99x  [0.943,1.031]        10/16  no effect
  avg_pool2d   14  0.979  0.964   1.037   0.96x  [0.819,1.204]         5/14  no effect
  conv3d       14  1.003  0.987   1.009   0.99x  [0.965,1.036]         8/14  no effect  <- NEGATIVE CONTROL
conv3d is the negative control (the gate touches no conv3d kernel) and it lands at 1.009 with a tight
CI, which is what makes the max_pool3d row credible. 16/16 rounds show FT slower, minimum 1.040.

WHY (hypothesis, NOT yet tested): the gate keys on BUFFER SIZE as a proxy for "fits in one core's
32 MiB L3 slice". In the isolated probe that proxy holds — the 8 MiB gradient effectively owns L3. In a
real session the AUTOGRAD TAPE HOLDS MANY OTHER LIVE TENSORS, so the same buffer is NOT L3-resident,
which puts it in the regime where the measured crossover says PARALLEL wins. The crossover measurement
was clean; the PREDICTOR is wrong. A size gate cannot see the tape.

EXACT STEPS:
 1. crates/ft-kernel-cpu/src/lib.rs — remove the `if dense_scatter_should_parallelize(...)` branch at
    all FOUR sites, restoring the plain par_chunks_mut driver:
      max_pool3d_backward_from_indices_f64, max_pool3d_backward_from_indices_scalar_f64,
      max_pool1d_backward_from_indices_f64, max_pool2d_backward_from_indices_f64
    Keep the one-body-two-drivers closure only if it stays used; otherwise inline it back.
 2. Remove DENSE_SCATTER_PARALLEL_MIN_BYTES and dense_scatter_should_parallelize once unused.
 3. Update/remove the tests that assert the gate: dense_scatter_gate_sits_at_sixteen_mib, and the
    `assert!(!dense_scatter_should_parallelize(..))` lines inside the four
    *_serial_and_parallel_drivers_are_bit_identical tests. THE BIT-IDENTITY TESTS THEMSELVES ARE STILL
    WORTH KEEPING if the two-driver shape survives anywhere; if not, drop them with the drivers.
 4. Re-run the lane A/B to confirm the revert recovers the ~15%. Do NOT skip this — the whole lesson
    here is that an isolated-kernel result did not transfer.

WHAT THE REVERT MUST NOT THROW AWAY: the measured crossover data (sibling_ab.md, avgpool_prediction.md)
and the DO-NOT-GATE notes on max_pool3d_backward_2x2s2_f64, avg_pool2d_backward_f64 and
avg_pool1d_backward_f64 are correct and hard-won. What is wrong is using BUFFER SIZE as the residency
predictor, not the finding that residency matters.

CONFIRMING RUN IS ADVISED BEFORE LANDING: this is one 16-round result, strong (16/16, CI excludes 1.0,
clean negative control) but single. A second run in a quiet window is cheap insurance against reverting
on a fluke. Driver: scratchpad sib/run_h2h_ab.sh; torch arm recipe in the 87sz8 comments.

Removed the gate branch at all four sites plus DENSE_SCATTER_PARALLEL_MIN_BYTES, the helper and the boundary test; behaviour returns to pre-un3os. WHY IT FAILED: the gate keyed on BUFFER SIZE as a proxy for L3 residency; in an isolated probe the buffer owns L3 so the proxy held, but in a real session the autograd tape holds many live tensors and the buffer is not resident — the regime where the sweep says parallel wins. title: ft-api: logcumsumexp returns NaN for leading/repeated infinities (torch returns the infinity)
description: tensor_logcumsumexp uses the max-shift streaming logsumexp: running_sum += (val - running_max).exp(). When val==running_max and both are the SAME infinity (e.g. a leading -inf, or repeated +inf), (±inf - ±inf).exp() = NaN, poisoning the cumulative result. torch keeps the cumulative logsumexp at that infinity. Fixed by short-circuiting: if val==running_max && val.is_infinite() { result=val; continue }. Verified vs torch 2.x: [-inf,0,1]->[-inf,0,1.313], [-inf,-inf]->[-inf,-inf], [inf,inf]->[inf,inf], [0,-inf,1]->[0,0,1.313], [inf,-inf,0]->[inf,inf,inf]. Real-world impact: masked positions (-inf) in log-domain ops (CTC/HMM/attention) hit this.
notes: Same max-shift NaN bug found+fixed in tensor_logsumexp too (the single-reduction sibling): all-(-inf) or any-(+inf) gave NaN where torch returns the infinity (logsumexp([-inf,-inf])=-inf, [inf,inf]=inf, [inf,-inf]=inf). Fixed with the same is_infinite() short-circuit. logsumexp_dim delegates to tensor_logsumexp so it's covered. Verified vs torch 2.x goldens for both ops. (softmax/log_softmax all-(-inf) -> NaN in torch TOO, so those already match — not a bug.)
close_reason: Shipped 8e5972ff. logsumexp + logcumsumexp now short-circuit infinite max (is_infinite check) -> return the infinity not NaN, matching torch. Was a real bug for masked (-inf) positions in log-domain ops. Verified vs torch 2.x goldens for both ops. ft-api suite 2049 pass.

title: Add metamorphic invariant tests for softmax/log_softmax/transpose/inverse equivalences
description:
Existing fuzz harness in ft-conformance covers 4 ops (abs, add, sum, matmul) with shape/finiteness assertions. There are no metamorphic equivalence tests — checking that two algebraically-equivalent paths produce the same output within ULP tolerance.

Catch-cases this would lock down:
1. exp(log_softmax(x)) ≈ softmax(x)   — composition equivalence
2. log(softmax(x)) ≈ log_softmax(x)   — direct vs explicit
3. softmax(x).sum() ≈ 1.0             — probability invariant
4. softmax(x + c) ≈ softmax(x)        — translation invariance
5. transpose(transpose(x)) ≡ x        — involution
6. matmul(I, A) ≈ A                   — identity invariance
7. matmul(A, A.inv()) ≈ I             — inverse invariance (well-conditioned A)
8. (a + b).sum() ≈ a.sum() + b.sum()  — sum linearity

Each can be a proptest with random valid inputs. The log_softmax precision bug fixed under frankentorch-ebrb would have been caught by (1) and (2) — that's the kind of bug these target.

Filed during /testing-metamorphic round of the multi-pass cycle.
notes:
Fixed in this commit. Added 4 metamorphic property tests inside the existing #[cfg(feature='fuzz')] proptest! block in ft-conformance:
  - fuzz_metamorphic_log_softmax_equals_log_of_softmax (the case that would have caught frankentorch-ebrb at random inputs)
  - fuzz_metamorphic_softmax_sums_to_one (probability-distribution invariant)
  - fuzz_metamorphic_softmax_translation_invariance (softmax(x + c) == softmax(x))
  - fuzz_metamorphic_double_transpose_is_identity (bit-exact involution)
ULP-tolerant comparators with absolute-floor fallbacks. ft-conformance lib tests with --features fuzz: 135 passing.

notes: BoldFalcon 2026-06-10. lu_solve_contiguous_f64 already has a bit-exact column-parallel path gated at n^2*num_rhs>=2^26 (inv_256=16.7M < 67M so inv_256 runs SERIAL). Findings (vmi/ovh, some contended): (1) the column-CONTIGUOUS solve loop is ~1.57x faster SERIALLY than the rhs-inner serial path (inv_256 RAYON=1 13.0ms vs old rhs-inner 20.4ms) — contention-independent, bit-exact (golden a9527abce2fc63959170fb8d563c842cb1c33df988e3529d1caf522591b6843a unchanged). (2) Parallelism saturates ~8-way then REGRESSES: inv_256 thread-sweep T1=14.5 T4=10.5 T8=10.2 T16=10.7 T32=14.2 T64=17.5ms — TRSM streams the SHARED L (n^2 f64), memory-bandwidth-bound. (3) TRAP: capping TASK count (par_chunks grouping) does NOT cap rayon's POOL thread count, so on a contended 64-core worker default still spins 64 threads and inv_256 NEW-default=21ms ~= OLD 20.4ms (no win) while RAYON=8 gives 10ms. Rigorous same-worker old-vs-new (FT_INV_OLDSERIAL env switch, one exec): inv_256 OLD 20.36 vs NEW 20.99 (no win, contended); inv_512 OLD 83.6 vs NEW 72.1 (1.16x). CONCLUSION: unlike the compute-bound SVD sweep (shipped 2.2x, scales with cores), inv-TRSM is bandwidth-bound so parallelism is contention-sensitive and does NOT ship cleanly via task-cap. REAL fix to confirm on a QUIET worker: (a) size-aware: column-order serial for L2-resident L (robust 1.57x, no parallelism), (b) custom bounded rayon ThreadPool (~8 threads) for the L2-resident case to actually limit active threads. Harness: examples/inv_golden.rs (FT_INV_GOLDEN=1).
close_reason: Bounded thread POOL (the suggested fix) CONFIRMED insufficient for a robust >=2x. Implemented trsm_bounded_pool (<=8 threads via available_parallelism, install) + gate lowered to 2^24; bit-exact (inv golden a9527abce2fc...843a unchanged). Same-worker old-vs-new A/B (FT_INV_OLDSERIAL switch, one rch exec): inv_256 OLD 23.05ms vs NEW 20.08ms = 1.15x; inv_512 OLD 86.96 vs NEW 72.26 = 1.20x. The TRSM is so memory-bandwidth-bound that on a CONTENDED shared worker even 8 threads thrash (NEW 20ms > the 13ms 1-thread column-order from last session). Robust component is only the column-order loop (~1.5x serial, contention-independent) which is <2.0 and risks regressing wide num_rhs>>n solves. REVERTED. The real >=2x for f32 inv is native-f32 kernels (half the bandwidth), see new bead. Closing: no robust bit-exact >=2x achievable for f64 inv TRSM.

title: [bug][autograd] no version check at backward — in-place mutation of a borrowed input silently changes gradients
description:
FrankenTorch has NO version check at backward. Mutating a tensor in place between the forward that needs it and the call to backward silently produces gradients computed from the MUTATED data. PyTorch raises "one of the variables needed for gradient computation has been modified by an inplace operation" for exactly this, via the version counter it already maintains -- and FrankenTorch already maintains one too (ft_core Tensor::version, bumped by every in-place op, asserted by tensor_unary_in_place_bumps_version_counter). It is simply never consulted on the backward path.

Found while wiring frankentorch-qkwsy. Searching ft-autograd for a backward-time version comparison returns nothing: no "version mismatch", no guard, no error variant. The borrowed-inputs mechanism (frankentorch-3jmy3) deliberately re-reads the live leaf at backward time instead of cloning it into the tape, which is what makes the gap observable -- the gradient is computed from whatever the leaf holds when backward runs, not from what the forward saw.

REPRODUCTION (no new machinery needed):
  x = leaf requiring grad
  y = f(x)                      // any op using apply_function_*_borrowed_inputs
  x.mul_(2.0)                   // bumps x.version(), no error
  loss = y.sum(); loss.backward()
  -> gradients silently reflect the mutated x. torch errors instead.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND PARITY: this is the class of bug that produces a model which trains to slightly wrong weights with no diagnostic anywhere. The DAC contract in AGENTS.md is explicitly about deterministic, auditable gradients; a gradient whose provenance silently depends on when a mutation happened to land is the opposite of that.

SCOPE: record the version of each borrowed/saved input at forward time and compare at backward, raising a dedicated error on mismatch. The version is already recorded per tensor, so this is a comparison plus an error variant, not new bookkeeping. Decide deliberately whether Strict mode errors and Hardened mode recovers, per the mode-split doctrine.

NEGATIVE CASE the fix must satisfy: a test that mutates a borrowed input between forward and backward and asserts an ERROR, plus a test that a mutation AFTER backward (or to an unrelated tensor) does not error -- otherwise the guard could be implemented as "always error when any version moved" and pass a single-case test.

INTERACTION with frankentorch-qkwsy, which is why this was filed rather than noted: qkwsy caches the forward's per-group statistics on the GroupNorm f32 sum shortcut and validates them against the input's version -- but it can only check at tensor_sum time, because the backward closure receives (&[f32], &[usize]) and has no access to the tape or the version. So a mutation strictly between the loss and backward would pair forward-time statistics with backward-time data. That window exists ONLY because there is no backward-time guard; closing this bead closes it for every op at once, and qkwsy's local check can then be removed rather than duplicated.
close_reason: Landed e9af8e85. Backward now refuses a borrowed input mutated after the graph was built (BorrowedInputVersionMismatch naming tensor and both versions), recorded via a side map touching only the four borrowed constructors. GATE: ft-api 2571 passed / 0 failed including both new tests; built on vmi1152480 via the build lane and executed locally because the test lane is unschedulable (see c1ct1). SCOPE CORRECTION found by the tests themselves: FT already forbids in-place mutation of a leaf that REQUIRES grad, so both tests failed their first run against their own premise; the reachable exposure is the borrowed input that does NOT require grad and is still needed for another input's gradient. Also fixes a pre-existing flake: backward_gradients_are_bit_identical_with_and_without_the_buffer_pool flipped the process-global pool switch without taking BUFFER_POOL_TEST_GUARD (1 failure in 3 parallel runs, green single-threaded).

title: [parity][quantization] quantized_linear dequant diverges from torch by ~1.16e-6 (f64 vs torch's f32 rounding)
description:
quantized_linear_packed_weight_oracle_matches_torch FAILS against the real torch oracle. It has been
reporting PASS because on a default checkout the torch probe fails first and the test returns early
-- a normal return, which cargo prints as "1 passed" (frankentorch-imtpq).

Surfaced by 8d81a433. Reproduce:
  FT_LEGACY_ORACLE_PYTHON=<repo>/.venv-oracle/bin/python \
    cargo test -p ft-conformance --lib quantized_linear_packed_weight_oracle_matches_torch

FAILURE, verbatim:
  quint8_per_tensor_clamps_unsigned_edges: output[2] = 75.80000000000001,
  expected 75.7999988436699, tolerance 0.000001

MEASURED against torch 2.12.0+cpu (this box's .venv-oracle). Note the repo ledger's rule that the
torch VERSION is part of the measurement; frankentorch-dtyiz recorded 2.12.1 elsewhere, so whoever
takes this should record the version their oracle reports.

READING OF THE NUMBERS, offered as a hypothesis and explicitly NOT verified. 75.7999988436699 is
what 75.8 looks like after a round trip through f32 (f32 has ~7 decimal digits; the value is 75.8
perturbed at the 8th). FrankenTorch's 75.80000000000001 is an f64-accurate 75.8. So the likely story
is that torch's quantized path computes the dequantization scale/zero-point arithmetic in f32 while
FrankenTorch does it in f64, leaving a ~1.16e-6 gap against a 1e-6 tolerance -- i.e. FT is MORE
precise than torch here and diverges for that reason.

THAT MAKES THE FIX A JUDGEMENT CALL, not a mechanical correction, which is why this is filed rather
than fixed:
  (a) If FT should bit-match torch's quantized arithmetic, the dequant must round through f32 the
      way torch does. That is a real behavioural change to a numeric path.
  (b) If quantization is a tolerance domain rather than a bit-exact one, the tolerance is simply too
      tight for an f32-rounded oracle and should be widened with the reason recorded.
The repo's doctrine is "preserve PyTorch-observable tensor semantics" and its parity stance is
bit-exact for elementwise ops, but the eigensolver precedent (frankentorch-eig-tolerance-policy)
shows tolerance domains are ratified case by case. Quantization has no such ratified policy that I
found. Someone should decide (a) vs (b) deliberately instead of nudging the tolerance until green,
which is the tempting and wrong move.

DO NOT simply widen the tolerance to make this pass without deciding the above. If the answer is
(a), a widened tolerance permanently hides a real divergence in a numeric path, and this test has
already spent its entire life hiding one.

NOT a regression from 8d81a433: that commit only changed the !torch_available branch, which does not
execute when torch IS available. The failure predates it and was merely invisible.
close_reason: Fixed in 0ab9059a: dequantize now computes in f32 and widens once, matching torch.Tensor.dequantize(). Workspace 5420/0; oracle test passes vs torch 2.12.0+cpu. Not a tolerance question — torch's f32 dequant rounding is observable, so this was ordinary parity.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
★ MY OWN HYPOTHESIS IN THIS BEAD'S DESCRIPTION IS REFUTED. Measured, do not inherit it (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). No code change.

I wrote in the description that torch's 75.7999988436699 'is what 75.8 looks like after a round trip through f32' and that FT is probably computing in f64 where torch rounds through f32. I flagged it as a hypothesis and not verified. It is WRONG, and checking took one probe:

  torch value          75.7999988436699
  f32(75.8)            75.80000305175781      <- NOT the torch value
  f32(379)*f32(0.2)    75.80000305175781      <- NOT the torch value
  f32(torch value)     75.79999542236328      <- torch value is NOT f32-representable
  75.8 - torch value   1.1563301001160653e-06
  torch value / 0.2    378.99999421834946     <- NOT an integer

So the torch result is a genuine f64 quantity that is neither an f32 round-trip of 75.8 nor scale × an integer. The 'f64 vs f32 rounding' story in the description is dead, and with it the (a)/(b) framing I offered — 'make FT round through f32' would NOT reproduce that number.

WHAT THE NUMBERS DO SAY: the relative error is ~1.5e-8, which is well BELOW f32 epsilon (~1.2e-7), so this is not a wholesale f32 computation. And it cannot be a differing quantized INTEGER, because one integer step at scale 0.2 would move the result by ~0.2, not by 1.2e-6. The integers therefore agree and the divergence is in the arithmetic AFTER quantization — most likely the accumulate/requantize sequence, where torch's qlinear does something FT's path does not (a different summation order, an intermediate requantization, or a bias handling step).

I did not chase it further and I am not guessing again in this bead. The next step is to have the oracle script return torch's INTERMEDIATE values (the quantized integer tensors and the accumulator) alongside the final output, and diff those against FT's — that converts this from inference to measurement, which is what the first attempt should have been.

WHY THIS CORRECTION MATTERS more than the finding: an unverified hypothesis sitting in a bead description is read as background by whoever picks it up. This whole session has been a chain of exactly that failure — frankentorch-dtyiz (four tests locking a value nobody had checked against torch), frankentorch-r2ayl (a test that had never run), frankentorch-v8f5k (my own 'one-line fix' scoping that was wrong once I opened the code). I put a plausible unchecked mechanism in a bead and it survived less than a turn. Leaving it there would have cost the next agent a wasted investigation.

The tolerance-vs-bit-exact policy question in the description still stands and is untouched by this. What changes is that nobody now has a mechanism, so the policy call cannot be made yet.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIXED in 0ab9059a. Workspace green: 13 crates, 5420 passed / 0 failed, and quantized_linear_packed_weight_oracle_matches_torch now passes against real torch 2.12.0+cpu.

THE MECHANISM WAS IN THE ORACLE SCRIPT THE WHOLE TIME:
  output = F.linear(input, qweight.dequantize().to(torch.float64), bias)
dequantize() returns FLOAT32 and .to(float64) widens afterwards. So torch's f32 rounding lives in the WEIGHTS, and the output is an f64 dot product OF f32-rounded weights -- which is precisely why the value is neither f32-representable nor scale x an integer, the two things I checked when I refuted my own first hypothesis. I had probed the output when the rounding was upstream of it.

Both my earlier readings on this bead were wrong in instructive ways: the original 'output is f32-rounded' was wrong, and my refutation's conclusion that 'this is not an f32 effect' was ALSO wrong -- it is an f32 effect, one layer up. The refutation's evidence was sound; the inference from it was too broad. Worth noting because a confident negative can mislead as badly as a confident positive.

VERIFIED BEFORE EDITING, not after: ((q - zp) as f32) * (scale as f32) is bit-equal to torch.quantize_per_tensor(...).dequantize() across the full tensor -- equality, not tolerance. Then confirmed both directions on the failing case: f32-dequant reproduces torch's four outputs exactly; f64-dequant reproduces FrankenTorch's exactly.

TWO SITES FIXED TOGETHER. ft-core DenseTensor::dequantized_values_as_f64 (what QuantizedLinear::forward actually calls) and ft-nn dequantize_i64 (used by dequantized_values). I fixed ft-nn first, re-ran, and got the IDENTICAL failing value -- which is how I learned the forward path never touches it. Fixed both rather than only the live one: two dequantizers disagreeing on rounding is frankentorch-dtyiz's hazard, and that divergence would be much harder to find than this one.

THE POLICY QUESTION IN THE DESCRIPTION IS MOOT. I framed this as bit-match-torch vs widen-the-tolerance. Neither: torch's dequantize genuinely produces f32, that rounding is PyTorch-observable, and matching it is ordinary parity rather than a tolerance decision. No policy call needed. Good thing nobody widened the tolerance to green it -- that would have permanently hidden a real divergence, which is what I warned about and also what I would have been doing.

NOTHING IN THE WORKSPACE ASSERTED THE OLD f64 VALUES -- the real risk of a value-changing fix per the ledger's standing gotcha, now measured.

title: rms_norm double-backward: f64+f32 ERR (no create_graph backward)
notes: ROOT CAUSE (cc): functional_rms_norm grad path uses tensor_apply_function_f64_borrowed_inputs / tensor_apply_function_f32_output_borrowed_inputs (lib.rs ~25339/25368) — NO create_graph backward, so 2nd order ERRs 'requires a create_graph backward'. Taken even with weight=None (unlike layer_norm whose fused path needs affine present). FIX = switch to apply_function_with_create_graph_borrowed_inputs (f64) / apply_function_f32_output_with_create_graph_borrowed_inputs (f32) — keep the fast fused 1st-order backward, add a cg backward. RMSNorm is NONLINEAR (not bilinear like conv/pool), so the cg backward is the analytic double-backward: per row N, r=(mean(x^2)+eps)^{-1/2}, c=sum_j x_j*dy_j; dx_i = r*dy_i - (r^3 x_i/N)*c (dn=dy*w if weight). Build dx from differentiable primitive nodes (square/mean+eps/rsqrt/row-sum/broadcast/mul/sub) so 2nd order composes; cast F32 inputs to F64 grad-space (gir5b). MUST verify vs torch f32+f64, weight+no-weight, input-Hessian AND full gradient-penalty before shipping (wrong 2nd-order is worse than the current honest ERR — do NOT ship unverified). torch goldens (no weight, x=[(i%5)*0.3-0.5], [2,4]): input-Hess diag=[-0.0018,0.001,0.0014,-0.0006,-0.0008,-0.0001,0.0004,0.0005]. Finder: examples/struct_hessian_probe.

title: [parity][numerics] pdist p=2 is ~34x less accurate than torch — composed path uses the cancelling Gram form torch never uses
description:
torch's pdist and cdist agree EXACTLY below cdist's 25-row mm threshold. FrankenTorch's no longer do, because pdist is the inaccurate one. Exposed by fixing cdist (frankentorch-bei5w, 7eea3021) — not caused by it.

MEASURED, two 1-D points 35/17 and 33/17 where the exact answer is 2/17:
  true 2/17     0.11764705882352941
  torch.pdist   0.11764705882352922      torch.cdist  0.11764705882352922
  FT cdist      0.11764705882352922      (bit-exact vs torch after 7eea3021)
  FT pdist      0.11764705882352276      err 6.647e-15  (~34x worse than FT cdist's 1.9e-16)

MECHANISM: tensor_pdist's COMPOSED path builds the Gram matrix — input · inputᵀ, per-row ‖·‖², then sqrt(nx_i + nx_j - 2*gram_ij). That is the same catastrophic cancellation just fixed in cdist, and torch's pdist NEVER uses it: torch pdist == torch cdist at 5 rows exactly, and diverges at 30 rows only because CDIST switches to mm while pdist stays direct. So torch's pdist is unconditionally direct.

NOTE the f64 no-grad fast path (tensor_pdist, p==2, DType::F64) routes to ft_kernel_cpu::pdist_forward_f64, which reduces per-pair directly and is fine. It is the composed fallback — taken for f32, and for any dtype the fast path declines — that carries the Gram form. So the accuracy of pdist currently depends on which path a caller happens to take, which is its own problem: two paths for one op disagreeing (frankentorch-dtyiz's rule).

FIX SHAPE: make the composed path direct — pairwise differences, square, sum, sqrt — rather than the Gram identity. Unlike cdist there is NO threshold to replicate, because torch's pdist has no mm mode at all; direct is correct at every size. Check the f32 path specifically, since that is the one most likely to be taking the composed fallback today.

CURRENT STATE: fuzz_metamorphic_pdist_cdist_consistency is RED and correctly so. It should stay red until this is fixed. Everything else in that suite passes (240/241).
close_reason: Fixed in 8ff9f151: removed tensor_pdist's two early p==2 fused matmul-identity paths; torch's pdist never uses the mm form at any size. Entire metamorphic fuzz suite now green (241/0). ft-api --lib 2544/0, clippy rc=0, fmt clean.

title: ft-api: fused single-pass im2col panel for conv2d (kill permute copy)
description:
Largest vs-upstream gap in the suite. ops_bench conv2d/hw/32 (batch=4 in_ch=64 out_ch=64 k=3x3 stride1 pad1) measured 220.58 ms p50 in committed pass frankentorch-61ds vs PyTorch 2.12 conv2d_32x32 p50 3.58 ms (benchmarks/pytorch_baseline.json) -> ~61x gap. conv2d_64x64 anchor 28.16 ms, conv2d_128x128 73.18 ms.

Root cause (functional_conv2d, crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs ~15664): im2col is built as a 4-stage tensor pipeline unfold(dim2)->unfold(dim3)->permute([0,2,3,1,4,5])->reshape, then transpose(weight)+matmul. For conv2d/hw/32 the unfolded_hw tensor is [4,64,32,32,3,3] = 2.36M f64 = ~19 MB, and tensor_permute MATERIALIZES a second ~19 MB copy purely to move the in_ch/kernel axes next to each other. Each stage also allocates a fresh autograd node (>=6 nodes/call) even though the bench tensors are requires_grad=false. The matmul itself ([4096,576]x[576,64], ~150 MFLOP) is a small fraction of the cost; the gap is memory-bound im2col + permute copy + node churn.

Lever (ONE): replace the unfold->unfold->permute->reshape->transpose chain with a single fused im2col gather that writes the [batch*out_h*out_w, in_ch*kh*kw] panel directly in patch-major, (in_ch,kh,kw)-minor order in one pass over the padded input, then one matmul against the flattened weight. Eliminates the ~19 MB permute copy and 3-4 intermediate autograd materializations. Alien-graveyard anchor: nested-data-parallel flattening / packed-panel GEMM packing (im2col is the convolution analogue of GEMM panel packing).

Constraints / proof obligations: output bit-exact to current path (same NCHW layout, same patch gather order, same accumulation order in matmul so floating-point identical); must preserve backward (scatter) semantics for the requires_grad path OR keep the composed path for grad and fast-path only no-grad — must be proven against existing conv2d gradient tests bit-exact; dtype/shape diagnostics unchanged; no RNG.

Acceptance: rch crate-scoped fresh baseline first (conv2d/hw/32,64,128 on one worker); ONE lever; deterministic bit-exact golden sha256 vs current output AND existing conv2d backward tests; rebench same worker; keep only if Score>=2.0 and a real speedup (target >=1.5x on conv2d/hw/32, ideally toward closing the 61x gap across hw/64 and hw/128).
notes: Fresh same-worker rerun captured in artifacts/optimization/2026-06-03_ft_api_conv2d_fused_panel_frankentorch-a29q.md: clean HEAD on rch ts2 hw/32 [182.32 ms 183.45 ms 184.52 ms], hw/64 [897.21 ms 900.57 ms 903.93 ms], hw/128 [3.8836 s 4.0330 s 4.2500 s]; after fused no-grad panel hw/32 [36.719 ms 36.922 ms 37.221 ms], hw/64 [141.93 ms 143.11 ms 144.12 ms], hw/128 [610.28 ms 613.29 ms 616.27 ms]. p50 speedups 4.97x/6.29x/6.58x; Score 10.0; golden sha256 fb414ed3ce5db49ddfdd26e37e647754580f18884d9417333bc4cd0468859445.

title: backward_create_graph silently swallows tensor read errors as empty gradients
description:
TensorTape::backward_create_graph (crates/ft-autograd/src/lib.rs ~12933, ~12958) calls grad_node.tensor.contiguous_values_as_f64().unwrap_or_default() in two places.

If contiguous_values_as_f64() returns an error (e.g. UnsupportedLayout for a non-contiguous result, or StorageSpanOverflow for a malformed meta), unwrap_or_default() yields an empty Vec, and the leaf's gradient silently becomes [].

Risks:
- The TensorBackwardReport reports a None/empty-but-nominally-success gradient.
- persistent_grads accumulator zip-iterates over an empty 'vals', leaving the entry untouched on second-and-later backward passes — silently breaking gradient accumulation across calls.

This violates the project's non-regression rule (autograd correctness outranks kernel speed) by hiding a DenseTensorError as a missing gradient.

Fix: propagate the error via ? into AutogradError (already has From<DenseTensorError>), so a malformed gradient tensor surfaces at the backward boundary instead of being silently dropped.
close_reason: backward_create_graph now propagates DenseTensorError via ? at both gradient-extraction sites instead of unwrap_or_default-ing tensor reads to empty Vec. Malformed grad tensors surface as AutogradError::DenseTensor at the backward boundary, restoring the 'autograd correctness outranks kernel speed' invariant. All 310 ft-autograd + 1082 ft-api tests pass; clippy + ubs clean.

title: Add compile-time exhaustiveness guard for DType match arms
description:
## Context
The stub/placeholder audit (2026-04-02) found 26 unreachable!() calls. Many exist because match arms on DType handle a subset of variants and use unreachable!() for the rest after an early validation check. This pattern is fragile: if a new DType variant is added, the early check might be updated but the match arm might not, causing a panic.

## Problem
The DType enum has 9 variants (F64, F32, F16, BF16, I64, I32, Bool, Complex64, Complex128). Functions that only handle a subset (e.g., floating-point types) use an early if-guard then unreachable!() in the catch-all. A better pattern is to use a helper that converts the subset to a sub-enum, making the match exhaustive at compile time.

## Plan
1. Create typed helper enums or use existing type-level dispatch patterns:
   - FloatingDType { F64, F32, F16, BF16 } with TryFrom<DType>
   - NumericDType { F64, F32, I64, I32 } with TryFrom<DType>
2. Convert the most dangerous unreachable!() sites (those in hot paths like dispatch and backward) to use these sub-enums
3. The match becomes exhaustive and the compiler catches missing arms on enum changes
4. Less critical sites (test helpers, edge cases) can keep unreachable!() with messages

## Acceptance Criteria
- At least the 14 unreachable!() sites in ft-dispatch are converted to exhaustive matches
- New DType variants cause compile errors (not runtime panics) in dispatch code
- All existing tests pass

## Dependencies
- Depends on: frankentorch-dwy (DenseTensor::storage panic fix) -- both touch DType handling
- Should be done AFTER the storage() refactor to avoid merge conflicts

## Reasoning
This is the highest-leverage defense-in-depth change. It converts 14 potential runtime panics into compile-time errors, which aligns with the DAC correctness doctrine and Rust's zero-cost abstraction philosophy.
close_reason: Replaced all 14 ft-dispatch DType/promotion unreachable!() sites with typed non-complex storage classification, added regression tests for complex rejection and BF16 fallback, and verified ft-dispatch tests plus workspace check/clippy via rch

title: [perf] ft-kernel-cpu: multi-threaded row-blocked GEMM (close single-thread vs ATen/MKL gap)
description: GAP: matrixmultiply is single-threaded, so a large solo matmul/bmm/conv/linear used one core while torch's BLAS (MKL/OpenBLAS) is multi-threaded. PRIMITIVE (alien-graveyard: cache-blocked GEMM + embarrassingly-parallel row partition): split the GEMM output across M-row blocks on the rayon pool, each block an independent matrixmultiply call over a contiguous row range. ISOMORPHISM: per output element the k-accumulation order is fixed by the micro-kernel independent of row count -> bit-for-bit identical (proved by gemm_row_split_matches_single_bit_exact, f64+f32). BASELINE (RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1) vs OPTIMIZED (all cores), same binary: f64 1024^3 44.28->15.31ms (2.89x), f32 1024^3 21.84->8.04ms (2.72x), f64 512^3 5.43->2.36ms (2.30x), f32 512^3 2.69->1.16ms (2.33x). Threshold: flops>=1<<20 and m>MIN_BLOCK_ROWS so small matmuls keep the single-call path. Safe Rust (rayon), no new unsafe.
close_reason: Multi-threaded row-blocked GEMM; bit-exact (gemm_row_split_matches_single_bit_exact f64+f32); f64 1024^3 2.89x, f32 1024^3 2.72x, 512^3 ~2.3x. 370 ft-kernel-cpu tests pass, clippy clean.

title: ft-optim: ASGD diverges from torch — missing (1-lambd*eta) shrinkage + eta decayed one step early
description:
ASGD.step() computed eta_t = lr/(1+lambd*lr*t)^alpha BEFORE the step (t=1 on step 0 instead of initial eta=lr), and applied plain SGD param -= eta*grad, omitting torch's (1 - lambd*eta) shrinkage. torch: param = param*(1-lambd*eta) - eta*grad with current eta (init lr), then decay eta/mu AFTER the step.

Found via new optimizer_trajectories_match_torch ASGD golden (lr=0.1, loss=sum(x^2), x=[1,2]): step0 want [0.799989997, 1.599979994], got [0.8000015, 1.6000030].

Fix: capture current eta; update = lambd*eta*p + eta*g (param -= update -> param*(1-lambd*eta) - eta*g); move eta/mu recompute to after the param loop.
close_reason: Fixed: ASGD now applies param=param*(1-lambd*eta)-eta*grad with current eta (init lr), eta/mu decayed post-step. optimizer_trajectories_match_torch ASGD golden passes; full ft-optim suite 211/211.

title: tensor_cumulative_trapezoid severs autograd; same composition as trapezoid + cumsum
description:
tensor_cumulative_trapezoid at lib.rs:15689 is the cumulative variant of trapezoid: instead of summing all weighted-avg pairs it returns the running cumulative sum. The body extracts values, computes the cumulative sum in plain f64, and rebuilds a non-grad leaf. PyTorch's torch.cumulative_trapezoid IS differentiable.

Same composition as tensor_trapezoid (frankentorch-b4ys) but with tensor_cumsum at the end instead of tensor_sum_dim:
   y0 = narrow(y, dim, 0, n-1)
   y1 = narrow(y, dim, 1, n-1)
   avg = (y0 + y1) * 0.5
   dx = (x1 - x0) if x else 1
   result = cumsum(avg * dx, dim)
notes: Fixed in this commit. Composed tensor_cumulative_trapezoid through narrow + add + mul + cumsum primitives — same recipe as tensor_trapezoid (b4ys) but with cumsum instead of sum_dim. All ops autograd-aware. Added cumulative_trapezoid_propagates_gradient_through_y regression test (y=[1,2,3,4] → cumulative=[1.5, 4.0, 7.5]; under sum loss, grad_y=[1.5, 2.5, 1.5, 0.5] computed via reverse-cumulative routing). ft-api lib tests: 1173.

title: [tooling] the ubs hook's 'timed out, unexpected' IS expected — 50k threshold is ~1.6x too generous for its 120s budget
description:
The pre-commit hook prints, on ordinary-sized files:

    ubs: TIMED OUT on files all under 50000 lines - unexpected.
    ubs: passing ... Worth reporting if it recurs, because it should not happen at this size.

It has recurred (observed twice: commits 97cf5326 and e1795860, both staging ft-autograd). Reporting as the hook asks. It is NOT unexpected -- it is arithmetic.

MEASURED, ubs --only=rust on single files, no local cargo contention:
    ft-optim      13,594 lines ->  52s
    ft-autograd   31,705 lines -> 132s   (rc=1, MODULE_TIMEOUT)
    ft-kernel-cpu 53,227 lines -> 208s
Linear fit: ~3.94 ms/line, intercept ~0. ubs scan time is essentially proportional to file size.

THE MISCALIBRATION. The hook has two budgets and one threshold:
    LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD = 50,000 lines   -- decides BOTH exclusion and which budget applies
    run_ubs_staged 300  -- extended, when a large file is staged
    run_ubs_staged 120  -- standard, otherwise
At 3.94 ms/line the STANDARD 120s budget buys about 30,900 lines. So the 50k threshold is roughly
1.6x too generous: every file between ~31k and 50k lines is admitted to the scan under a budget that
cannot finish it.

WHICH CRATES ARE IN THAT DEAD BAND (estimated from the fit):
    ft-conformance  43,318 -> ~169s   TIMES OUT
    ft-nn           37,660 -> ~147s   TIMES OUT
    ft-autograd     31,705 -> ~132s   TIMES OUT  (measured, not estimated)
    ft-optim        13,594 ->  ~52s   ok
    ft-dispatch      9,703 ->  ~37s   ok
    ft-core          6,075 ->  ~22s   ok
So three of the eight crates silently burn 120 seconds per commit and examine nothing. ft-autograd
sits at 132s against 120s -- a 10% overshoot, which is exactly why it is INTERMITTENT rather than
consistent, and why it reads as a mystery instead of a threshold error.

FIX SHAPE: set LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD from the budget rather than guessing it -- ~30,000 lines for a
120s standard budget, or raise the standard budget to ~200s and keep 50k. Note frankentorch-0o6ai:
the threshold ALSO selects the budget, so the two must be changed together or the fix inverts.

WORTH KNOWING BEFORE ANYONE INVESTS IN THIS: ft-autograd's scan reports 45 Criticals and all 45 are
false positives -- 43 are the 'Secret, signature, or token compared with ==/!=' rule firing on
ordinary equality checks, and 2 are panic! macros at lines 30047/30063, both inside the
#[cfg(test)] module that starts at line 20986, which the repo's OWN forbidden-macro guard correctly
skips. Consistent with 0o6ai: every Critical ubs has produced in this repo has been noise. Making
the gate finish faster does not make it find anything.
close_reason: Fixed in 914178d5: LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD derived from the 120s budget (50000 -> 25000) at a measured 3.94 ms/line. The three dead-band crates are now excluded+named instead of burning 120s scanning nothing. Tracked hook only, deliberately not installed; self-test 8/8.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIXED in 914178d5, tracked hook only.

LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD is now DERIVED from the 120s standard budget instead of guessed: at the
measured ~3.94 ms/line, 120s buys ~30,900 lines, so 50000 was ~1.6x the real capacity. Set to 25000,
which leaves ~20% headroom for machine load (25k * 3.94ms ~= 98s of 120s).

EFFECT, verified by re-running the classification with the new constant:
    ft-conformance  43,318  EXCLUDED + named   (was: burned 120s, examined nothing)
    ft-nn           37,660  EXCLUDED + named   (same)
    ft-autograd     31,705  EXCLUDED + named   (same; 132s measured vs a 120s budget)
    ft-optim        13,594  scannable
    ft-core          6,075  scannable

NOT A COVERAGE REGRESSION, and worth being precise about: those three crates were never actually
scanned. They consumed the full 120s and produced nothing. This changes what the gate SAYS about
them and stops it reporting a false "unexpected" — the message asked to be told if it recurred, and
the honest answer was that the threshold, not the tool, was wrong.

DELIBERATELY NOT INSTALLED. .git/hooks/pre-commit is the mcp-agent-mail chain-runner; the tracked
hook runs as a copy at pre-commit.orig. Editing the tracked source leaves the three other agents
committing through this checkout undisturbed, and the change takes effect when someone next
installs. Confirmed the installed copy still differs.

VERIFIED: hooks/pre-commit --self-test all 8 checks pass; sh -n clean; classification table above.

★ THE TRAP IS NOW DOCUMENTED AT THE DEFINITION, because it is genuinely counter-intuitive and I
nearly recommended the inverted fix myself two turns ago: this constant selects BOTH the exclusion
set AND which timeout applies, since a staged over-threshold file switches the remaining files to
the 300s extended path. So RAISING it to admit a big file would simultaneously drop that file to the
120s budget and guarantee the very timeout it was meant to cure. Anyone reading
LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD as "the size ubs can handle" gets it backwards (frankentorch-0o6ai).

AND THE THING THAT SHOULD TEMPER ANY FOLLOW-UP: making this gate finish faster does not make it find
anything. Every Critical ubs has produced in this repo is a false positive — 1432 in ft-api, 45 in
ft-autograd, dominated by a "Secret/token compared with ==/!=" rule firing on dtype equality checks,
plus panic! macros inside #[cfg(test)] that the repo's own forbidden-macro guard correctly skips.

title: tensor_trapezoid severs autograd; composable through narrow/add/mul/sum_dim
description:
tensor_trapezoid at lib.rs:15607 computes the trapezoidal-rule integral along a dim. PyTorch's torch.trapezoid IS differentiable — it's linear in y (and bilinear-ish in x via dx pre-computation).

Composable through autograd primitives:
   y0 = narrow(y, dim, 0, n-1)
   y1 = narrow(y, dim, 1, n-1)
   avg = (y0 + y1) * 0.5
   dx = if x is provided: x1 - x0 (similar narrow). else: 1.0 broadcast.
   weighted = avg * dx
   integral = sum_dim(weighted, dim)

All ops autograd-aware so gradients flow to y (and x when provided). Surfaced during /reality-check pass.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Composed tensor_trapezoid through narrow + add + mul + sum_dim primitives. Math: y0 = narrow(y, dim, 0, n-1); y1 = narrow(y, dim, 1, n-1); avg = (y0 + y1) * 0.5; dx = (x1 - x0) if x else 1; integral = sum_dim(avg * dx, dim). All ops autograd-aware. Added trapezoid_propagates_gradient_through_y regression test (y=[1,2,3,4], uniform spacing → integral=7.5, grad_y=[0.5, 1.0, 1.0, 0.5]). ft-api lib tests: 1172.

title: [perf][no-gaps] eigh reduction: attack BANDWIDTH via mixed-precision tridiagonalization (f32 tred2 + f64 eigenvalue refinement)
notes: RATIONALE: the eigh symmetric-tridiagonalization wall (gates 92yny eigh-with-vectors at 1.5x and eigvalsh) has been attacked twice and BOTH refuted: blocked-dsytrd (t0b4l, eigh_tridiag_reduce_blocked exists) measured 0.37-1.2x — memory-BANDWIDTH-bound, so halving flops via BLAS-3 blocking can't help; two-stage band (5oqum) measured 1.3-2.3x SLOWER (two O(n^3) passes). NOVEL ANGLE (this bead): cut the actual bottleneck — BANDWIDTH — with mixed precision. f32 tred2 has ~half the memory traffic of f64 -> ~2x on a bandwidth-bound reduction. But f32 eigenvalues are only ~1e-6 accurate (violates the 1e-9 eigvalsh tolerance), so follow with f64 EIGENVALUE REFINEMENT: use the f32 tridiagonal's eigenvalues as starting estimates for a few f64 bisection/Sturm-sequence steps (the tridiagonal eigenvalue problem is cheap O(n^2) vs the O(n^3) reduction). This mirrors lu_solve_mixed_refine (f32 factor + f64 refine) which beat pure-f64. PLAN: (1) f32 tred2 (reuse eigh_tred2_values_only_full_lower ported to f32, OR a packed-f32 variant for cache), (2) f64 Sturm-bisection refine of the eigenvalues, (3) A/B vs eigvalsh_f64 on a 64-thread + 10-thread worker (the reduction is worker-sensitive per t0b4l), target >=1.8x with eigenvalues within 1e-9. RISK: f32 reduction may lose small eigenvalues (cancellation) — validate on clustered/ill-conditioned spectra. ALSO consider f32 reduction in the PACKED half-triangle (best cache) since t0b4l's full-n^2 footprint lost the cache fight.
close_reason: REFUTED + PARTIAL SHIP (638d7992): the bandwidth-2x hypothesis FAILED. Built native f32 eigvalsh (eigvalsh_contiguous_f32: f32 tred2 + f32 QL) and A/B'd vs f64-upcast: only 1.03x@1024 / 1.08x@512 / 1.12x@256 — NOT the expected ~2x. The symmetric tridiagonalization is NOT bandwidth-bound enough at n<=1024 for f32's half-traffic to win 2x (consistent with t0b4l's blocked-dsytrd 0.37-1.2x). So f32 reduction is a THIRD refuted lever for the eigh wall (after blocked-dsytrd t0b4l and two-stage 5oqum). The f64-eigenvalue-refinement idea is also moot — refining eigenvalues back to f64 accuracy from an f32 tridiagonal is fundamentally hard (info lost in f32 reduction; unlike linear-solve mixed-refine you can't cheaply correct eigenvalues without the eigenvectors / O(n^4)). SHIPPED ANYWAY as f32 DTYPE PARITY (native f32 eigvalsh matches torch's f32 contract + incidental 1.1x, consistent with the b3o90 f32 linalg family); the old f64-upcast was more accurate but diverged from torch f32. eigh-with-vectors f32 still upcasts (follow-up). The f64 eigh perf wall remains genuinely unbroken across 3 attacks — needs a fundamentally different primitive (band-packed reduction or a graveyard communication-avoiding algorithm).

title: functional_embedding severs autograd via tensor_values + non-grad rebuild
description:
ft-api functional_embedding (line 5411) extracts tensor_values from both indices and weight, looks up rows in plain f64, and rebuilds via session.tensor_variable(result, out_shape, false). This silently severs autograd through the weight tensor — breaks training for any model that uses F.embedding directly (transformers using token embeddings outside the nn.Embedding wrapper, custom layers, etc.).

The corresponding nn.Embedding module impl (Module for Embedding in ft-nn) already composes via tensor_reshape + tensor_index_select; functional_embedding should do the same.

Fix: compose via tensor_reshape(input, [n_indices]) + tensor_index_select(weight, 0, flat_indices) + tensor_reshape to [*input_shape, embedding_dim].

Affects: crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs functional_embedding (line 5411).

title: tensor_autograd_grad mishandles grad_outputs (broken VJP)
description: tensor_autograd_grad ran backward with a ones seed and then elementwise-multiplied the i-th INPUT's gradient by grad_outputs[i] — conflating the output index with the input index and applying the seed in the wrong vector space. PyTorch's grad_outputs seeds the backward per-output, yielding the vector-Jacobian product Sum_k J_k^T v_k (a contraction over the output dimension). The bug was invisible for diagonal Jacobians (where J^T v == (J^T ones) elementwise* v) but wrong for any mixing Jacobian, and it corrupted the public tensor_functional_vjp which delegates here. Fix: build a scalar surrogate s = Sum_k <output_k, v_k> with v_k a non-grad constant (defaulting to ones) and run one ordinary backward; d s/d input = Sum_k J_k^T v_k exactly, no tape changes. Added matmul-based regression (non-diagonal J, v!=ones), diagonal case, VJP test, and grad_outputs length-mismatch guard. ft-api autograd_grad/vjp/hvp/create_graph tests pass.
close_reason: Rewrote tensor_autograd_grad to build a scalar surrogate s = Sum_k <output_k, v_k> (v_k non-grad, default ones) and run one backward, giving the exact VJP Sum_k J_k^T v_k. Fixes both autograd.grad(grad_outputs=...) and functional_vjp. Added matmul non-diagonal regression + diagonal + vjp + length-mismatch tests; all ft-api autograd_grad/vjp/hvp/create_graph tests pass.

title: [parity][numerics] cdist(x, x, p=2) self-distance is 5.96e-8, not 0 — expanded-form cancellation where torch uses the direct formula
description:
FrankenTorch's cdist gives a NON-ZERO distance from a point to itself. torch gives exactly 0.0.

MEASURED, torch 2.12.0+cpu vs FT:
  x = [[-30/17, 48/17]]  (single row, 2 features)
  FT     cdist(x, x, p=2)[0,0] = 0.00000005960464477539063   (5.96e-8)
  torch  cdist(x, x, p=2)      = 0.0                          (exactly)

MECHANISM, hypothesis — flagged as such, since I have guessed wrong from magnitudes before this session, though here the number is unusually diagnostic: 5.96e-8 is sqrt(~3.55e-15), i.e. the square root of a catastrophic-cancellation residue. That is the signature of the EXPANDED form ||a||^2 + ||b||^2 - 2*a.b, which for identical points subtracts two nearly-equal quantities and leaves a tiny positive value that sqrt then amplifies to ~1e-8. The direct form sum((a_i - b_i)^2) yields exactly 0 for a == b and cannot produce this.

torch has this exact tradeoff as an explicit knob: cdist's compute_mode, defaulting to use_mm_for_euclid_dist_if_necessary, which uses the matmul/expanded path ONLY when the row count exceeds 25. For a 1-row input torch takes the direct path and returns exact 0. FrankenTorch appears to take the expanded path unconditionally, or at least for small inputs.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE FUZZ FAILURE: self-distance being exactly 0 is relied on by anything that reads the diagonal of a distance matrix — knn (a point is its own nearest neighbour at distance 0), clustering, and any 'is this the same point' test. A 1e-8 floor also swamps genuinely tiny distances. And it is asymmetric with FT's own pdist/cdist p=1 paths, which have no such cancellation.

FIRST STEPS:
  1. Reproduce directly (not via the fuzz harness): cdist of a single row against itself, p=2.
  2. Read FT's cdist p=2 path and confirm whether it uses the expanded/gemm form.
  3. Decide the fix against torch's actual rule rather than inventing one: torch switches on row count (>25) via compute_mode. Matching that switch reproduces torch including its own precision behaviour at scale; always using the direct form would be MORE accurate than torch and therefore divergent in the other direction — the exact trap frankentorch-9rvxq turned out to be, where FT was more precise than torch and that was the bug.

FOUND BY: fuzz_metamorphic_cdist_self_distance_symmetry, in the never-gated fuzz feature (frankentorch-oo3pd). This is the LAST of that suite's 6 failures still red; the other 5 were 4 test bugs (fixed) and 1 real bug (frankentorch-5jwh8, fixed). The suite's failing property here is CORRECT and should stay red until this is fixed.
close_reason: Fixed in 7eea3021: expanded-form path gated on torch's >25-row rule across all 3 sites; cdist now bit-matches torch. Exposed a second pre-existing bug in pdist, filed as p2wqe.

title: affine_grid lacks autograd: linear in theta, easy backward [child of 3v6e]
description:
tensor_affine_grid currently has a fail-loud guard rejecting requires_grad=true theta. Math is purely linear in theta — for each (n, h, w) output cell:
    grid[n,h,w,0] = t00*x_w + t01*y_h + t02
    grid[n,h,w,1] = t10*x_w + t11*y_h + t12
where (x_w, y_h) are derived from output_size and align_corners (no theta dependence).

Backward (vector-Jacobian):
    grad_theta[n,0,0] = sum_{h,w} grad_grid[n,h,w,0] * x_w
    grad_theta[n,0,1] = sum_{h,w} grad_grid[n,h,w,0] * y_h
    grad_theta[n,0,2] = sum_{h,w} grad_grid[n,h,w,0]
    grad_theta[n,1,0] = sum_{h,w} grad_grid[n,h,w,1] * x_w
    grad_theta[n,1,1] = sum_{h,w} grad_grid[n,h,w,1] * y_h
    grad_theta[n,1,2] = sum_{h,w} grad_grid[n,h,w,1]

Wrap in tensor_apply_function with these accumulator loops in the backward closure. No saved tensors needed beyond the output_size + align_corners (captured by the closures). Standard PyTorch parity — torch.nn.functional.affine_grid supports backward.

Child of frankentorch-3v6e.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Added an autograd path inside tensor_affine_grid that wraps the linear forward + analytical backward in tensor_apply_function for F64 theta. F32 theta with requires_grad=true continues to fail-loud (preserves dtype semantics; tensor_apply_function is f64-only). Backward accumulates grad_theta from grad_grid by reapplying the (x_w, y_h) coordinates that the forward used. Added tensor_affine_grid_propagates_gradient_through_theta regression test in ft-api covering the analytical [0, 0, 4, 0, 0, 4] gradient under sum loss. Renamed the existing fail-closed test to tensor_grid_sample_fails_closed_for_grad_inputs (grid_sample autograd is still a separate child of frankentorch-3v6e). ft-api lib tests: 1137.

title: [perf] ft-api einsum: contraction-path order REJECTED (permute-overhead-bound); real lever = einsum_binary transposes
close_reason: REJECTED greedy contraction-path for multi-operand einsum. It was CORRECT (16 einsum tests + 1881 ft-api pass; value-matches left-to-right <1e-9, grads flow) but a PERF REGRESSION: A/B chain 'ab,bc,cd,de->ae' [2048x8,8x2048,2048x8,8x2048]: manual-matmul-left-to-right 6.22ms vs greedy einsum 70.44ms (11x SLOWER); at 256x8 it was 485us vs 1307us. ROOT CAUSE: einsum is einsum_binary-OVERHEAD-bound, NOT contraction-order-bound. einsum_binary sets up each pairwise contraction by MATERIALIZING full-tensor transposes via the op-graph tensor_permute (to feed contiguous matmul); at scale those 32MB transposes dominate, and the greedy's index orderings + the final output permute trigger large ones, swamping the ~3x flop savings. So the contraction-PATH optimization is invisible/counterproductive under the permute overhead. CONTRAST multi_dot (i3ez, 3.7x): it composes raw tensor_matmul directly (no per-step transpose materialization), so reordering wins there. comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ROOT CAUSE of the frankentorch scheduling starvation, measured 2026-08-15. It is not target-pool pressure; it is the per-command slot requirement in the SHARED rch config at ~/.config/rch/config.toml:

    build_slots = 4
    test_slots  = 8
    check_slots = 2

Against this fleet, only three workers have 8 total slots (vmi1152480, vmi1153651, vmi1227854 at 8 each; vmi1264463 and vmi1293453 have 6; ovh-a 4; hz2 3; hz1, vmi1149989, vmi1156319 at 2). So every 'cargo test' from frankentorch is admissible on at most 3 of 10 workers, and one of those is routinely removed by active_project_exclusion because a peer frankentorch job already holds it. The refusal reports it exactly: 'insufficient_total_slots=7, active_project_exclusion=1'.

Observed consequence over ~40 minutes today: EVERY 'cargo test' was refused with EXIT=103 at every scope, from --workspace down to '-p frankentorch-autograd --lib', while the fleet showed 20/49 slots free. Meanwhile 'cargo build' (4 slots) and 'cargo check' (2 slots) were admitted immediately and completed in 50s-95s. That asymmetry is the signature: builds land, tests starve.

WORKAROUND that unblocks progress without touching shared config: 'cargo check --release -p <crate> --all-targets' costs 2 slots and still type-checks test code, so a change can be compile-verified while the test lane is starved. It is NOT a substitute for running the tests, and must not be reported as a gate.

Do NOT lower test_slots unilaterally. It is global config shared by every project and agent on this box, and 8 is presumably sized for the memory a heavy test link actually needs; halving it could oversubscribe a worker and turn a scheduling problem into an OOM. If it is to change, it should be measured against a real frankentorch test link's peak RSS first, and announced, because every other franken* project inherits it.

title: [perf][no-gaps] dense SVD ~300x slower than LAPACK dgesdd — needs D&C or BLAS-3 back-transform (algorithmic)
notes:
BIGGEST perf gap in the codebase, previously untracked (only a code comment at golub_reinsch_svd ~lib.rs:11362). Profile (in-code, prior rch measurement): svd_f64_256x256 ~1.6s, ~300x slower than LAPACK dgesdd.

ROOT CAUSE: golub_reinsch_svd (NR Golub-Reinsch) diagonalizes the bidiagonal form with an implicit-shift QR sweep = a long stream of BLAS-1 Givens rotations applied to U (m rows) and V (n rows) every iteration. This O(n^3) BLAS-1 rotation stream is the dominant cost.

CLEAN LEVERS ALREADY MEASURED + REJECTED (do NOT retry; see code comment):
- Row-parallelizing the rotation loops: memory-bound (2 elems/row) -> regresses.
- Parallelizing the Householder bidiagonalization / U,V accumulation: MEASURED, REGRESSED (applies small fraction vs sweep).
- Transposing U/V for contiguous rotations: MEASURED ~1.4x REGRESS (cols j,j+1 adjacent -> already share a cache line row-major).

REAL LEVERS (algorithmic, multi-session, tolerance-parity -> update SVD golden to tolerance):
(A) BLAS-3 back-transform: accumulate each sweep's Givens cascade into a banded orthogonal block, apply to U/V via dgemm (level-3, blocked+parallel). Target ~5-20x. Lower risk.
(B) Divide-and-conquer bidiagonal SVD (dbdsdc): deflation + secular equation. Target ~50-300x. Largest effort.
(C) One-sided Jacobi SVD: naturally parallel, high rel. accuracy. Different algorithm.

svd_lowrank_contiguous_f64 is ALREADY proper randomized SVD (fine). This bead = the FULL/exact svd_contiguous_f64 path. Sibling of l9xod (eig dlaqr5) — same blocked-GEMM-back-transform family.

title: masked_scatter all-false fast path drops source zero-gradient
description: Reviewer finding in crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs. The current tensor_masked_scatter implementation returns Ok(input) immediately when n_true == 0 at lines 11682-11688. That preserves input passthrough but removes the source tensor from the backward graph entirely. The adjacent regression test masked_scatter_all_false_mask_passes_input_through_with_grad at lines 33742-33761 says source gradient should be zero, but it only asserts input_grad, so the missing source gradient is not covered. Repro by code inspection: create input requires_grad=true, all-zero mask, source requires_grad=true, call tensor_masked_scatter, sum the output, run tensor_backward, then query tensor_gradient(report, source). Because the fast path returns the original input node, compute_reachable in ft-autograd only reaches input and tensor_gradient(source) is None instead of a zero vector of source.numel(). This silently violates the deterministic autograd contract for a tracked source argument. title: functional_normalize severs autograd; composable through abs/pow/sum_dim/div
description:
functional_normalize at lib.rs:5151 computes y = x / max(||x||_p along dim, eps) but the body extracts values, divides in plain f64, and rebuilds a requires_grad=false leaf — silently severing autograd through every L2-normalization layer. PyTorch's torch.nn.functional.normalize IS differentiable.

Compose through autograd primitives:
   abs_x   = tensor_abs(input)
   pow_x   = tensor_pow(abs_x, p)
   sum_x   = tensor_sum_dim(pow_x, dim)
   norm    = tensor_pow(sum_x, 1.0 / p)
   norm_c  = tensor_clamp_min(norm, eps)
   norm_kd = tensor_unsqueeze(norm_c, dim)
   norm_b  = tensor_expand(norm_kd, original_shape)
   y       = tensor_div(input, norm_b)

All ops are autograd-aware so gradients flow back to input. Sister of frankentorch-7yvv (dropout severance) — both are critical for training paths.
notes:
Fixed in this commit. Composed functional_normalize through abs/pow/sum_dim/clamp_min/reshape/expand/div primitives — same observable y = x / max(||x||_p along dim, eps) but with the autograd tape preserved.

The norm reduction is reshaped to a keepdim=true-style broadcast shape (input's shape with dim set to 1) so the subsequent expand + div work uniformly across 1-D and higher-rank inputs.

Added functional_normalize_propagates_gradient_through_input regression test for input=[3,4] L2-normalize on dim=0:
   y = [0.6, 0.8] under sum loss → grad = [(1 - y_i * sum_y) / ||x||_2] = [0.032, -0.024]
asserts to 1e-12.

title: Add end-to-end training example and integration test
description:
FrankenTorch has e2e training loop tests buried in ft-optim's test suite, but there is no standalone, documented example showing users how to train a model. This is critical for proving the system works end-to-end and for user onboarding.

Create a comprehensive integration test (in ft-conformance or a new examples/ directory) that:

1. Defines a 2-layer MLP: Linear(784, 128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128, 10)
2. Generates synthetic MNIST-like data using the existing TensorDataset/DataLoader
3. Trains for 5 epochs using Adam optimizer with learning rate scheduling (StepLR or CosineAnnealing)
4. Tracks loss per epoch and asserts it decreases monotonically (with tolerance for noise)
5. Uses no_grad context for evaluation pass
6. Saves model state_dict to file, loads it back, verifies predictions match
7. Uses BatchNorm or LayerNorm in the architecture to exercise normalization paths
8. Logs: epoch number, batch count, loss per epoch, final accuracy estimate, elapsed time

This test exercises the full stack: ft-data (DataLoader) -> ft-nn (modules) -> ft-api (forward/backward) -> ft-autograd (gradient computation) -> ft-optim (parameter update) -> ft-serialize (save/load).

If any component fails to compose correctly, this test catches it.

Tests:
- The example IS the test: it should be a #[test] fn in ft-conformance or similar
- Assert loss decreases over 5 epochs
- Assert save/load round-trip produces identical predictions
- Assert no_grad eval context doesn't corrupt gradient state
- Log detailed per-epoch metrics for debugging

title: MaxUnpool1d/2d/3d sever autograd; scatter-then-gather backward needed
description:
MaxUnpool1d (line 6149), MaxUnpool2d (line 6237), and MaxUnpool3d (line 6337) all extract input values, scatter them via indices in plain f64, and rebuild requires_grad=false leaves. PyTorch's torch.nn.MaxUnpool* IS differentiable.

Each variant has the same forward/backward structure with different spatial indexing.
notes: Fixed in this commit. All three MaxUnpool variants (1d/2d/3d) now wrap their forward in tensor_apply_function with the analytical scatter-then-gather backward. The (input_pos → output_pos) indices mapping is captured by both forward and backward closures; backward gathers grad_output from the destination positions back to grad_input. ft-nn lib tests: 517.

title: tensor_diag_embed is severed-autograd: linear backward, easy fix
description:
tensor_diag_embed at lib.rs:3444 places a 1-D input vector onto the diagonal (or sub/super-diagonal) of a zero-initialized 2-D matrix. PyTorch's torch.diag_embed is differentiable. The forward is purely linear in the input:
   output[row, col] = input[i] if (row, col) is on the requested diagonal else 0
so the backward is just the diagonal-extraction:
   grad_input[i] = grad_output[row, col]
where (row, col) is the same position the forward placed input[i] in.

Wrap in tensor_apply_function with this analytical backward. Save offset and k for backward; or capture via closure. Surfaced during /reality-check pass scanning for the values-then-non-grad-leaf pattern.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Wrapped tensor_diag_embed in tensor_apply_function with diagonal-extraction backward: grad_input[i] = grad_output[row, col] for the same (row, col) the forward placed input[i]. Captured offset (positive vs negative) and abs_offset via closure (Copy-by-move). Added diag_embed_propagates_gradient_via_diagonal_extraction regression test using a weighted sum over a 3x3 main-diagonal embedding (input [1,2,3] gets gradient [1,5,9] = weights[i,i]). ft-api lib tests: 1145.

title: tensor_linalg_pinv: autograd via normal-equation formulation for full-rank A
description:

Implement an autograd-aware pinv path for full-rank A:
- m >= n (full column rank): A^+ = (A^T A)^{-1} A^T
- m <= n (full row rank): A^+ = A^T (A A^T)^{-1}

title: tensor_linalg_solve severs autograd via direct LU kernel + non-grad rebuild
description:
tensor_linalg_solve in ft-api (line 11899) directly calls the LU factorize + LU solve kernels and rebuilds the result via session.tensor_variable(_, _, false). This silently severs autograd through every linear solve — used in normalizing flows, Bayesian models, optimization layers, GP regression, etc.

Fix: compose via tensor_linalg_inv + tensor_matmul. The linalg_inv was made autograd-aware in frankentorch-frq7 (-Y^T grad Y^T backward); composing X = inv(A) @ B delivers the standard gradient:
  dL/dB = A^{-T} dL/dX
  dL/dA = -A^{-T} dL/dX X^T = -A^{-T} (dL/dX) X^T

Trade-off: forward pass uses explicit inv instead of LU solve, slightly less numerically stable for ill-conditioned A. But the inv-based formulation matches PyTorch's autograd backward path, so gradient correctness is the same.

Affects: crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs tensor_linalg_solve (line 11899).

title: perf(groupnorm): route-match the f32 phase split, then attack the term it names
description:
Ledger item 7f (frankentorch-npod3) invalidated the existing GroupNorm f32 phase split: the session lane takes the sum-loss shortcut (group_norm_f32_sum_shortcuts -> group_norm_backward_scalar_f32, no dense dy ever materialized) while the raw kernel lane in gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h took the GENERAL route AND allocated a 1.6 MiB all-ones dy inside the timed region. The split therefore measured general-route vs shortcut-route, not engine cost, so the live 8.81-10.93x GroupNorm f32 standing has no attributable phase.

Step 1 (this bead): make timed_group_norm_f32_kernels enter the SAME kernels the session enters (group_norm_forward_f32 + sum_tensor_contiguous_f32 + group_norm_backward_scalar_f32), with the output meta built outside the timer. Then one live-arm invocation yields: PT vs session (the standing), session vs kernels (engine + f64 grad-space conversions), PT vs kernels (is the kernel competitive at all).

Step 2: attack whichever term that names. The structural candidate already located: the tape's gradient space is f64 even for an f32 op, so try_group_norm_f32_sum_shortcut widens dx from f32 to f64 with a SERIAL .iter().map(f64::from).collect() over 401,408 elements (crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs:26127) — 1.6 MiB read plus a serially first-touched 3.2 MiB write. 112 such widening sites exist in ft-api. Do NOT ship that lever before the split says the engine is the term; a 3% micro-lever on a 10x loss is the failure mode Rule 5 names.

Negative case: a route-matched split must show the kernel lane taking LESS time than the general-route lane it replaces (the general backward scans a dense dy; the shortcut does not). If the new kernel lane is not faster than the old one, the routes were not actually switched and the sentinel discipline applies before any further reading.
close_reason: Route-matched split landed (5855ef66) and refuted the f64 grad-space lever; parallel-gate lever landed (e434e93a) with sentinel-proved 4.0x on group_norm_forward_f32 (0.692 serial -> 0.173 parallel, interleaved, bit-identical every rep). Lane-level paired verdict recorded as UNDECIDED, not claimed as a win.

title: tensor_linalg_cond severs autograd via tensor_values + non-grad rebuild
description:
tensor_linalg_cond in ft-api (line 12858) severs autograd in both code paths:

1. p=±2 path: extracts svdvals to f64, picks sigma_max/sigma_min by index, computes ratio in plain f64, rebuilds via tensor_variable(_, _, false). Severs gradients to the input matrix through the SVD.

2. p != ±2 path: invokes tensor_matrix_norm (autograd-aware) twice but then extracts both norms to f64 scalars and multiplies in plain f64, rebuilding a non-grad leaf. The two intermediate norm tensors carry gradients but the multiplication is done outside autograd.

Fix:
- p=±2: use tensor_narrow + tensor_reshape to extract sigma_max (first element) and sigma_min (last element) as 1-element tensors, then tensor_div them. Handle the zero-divisor case via a small epsilon clamp or fail-loud guard since gradient at sigma=0 is undefined anyway.
- p != ±2: drop the two tensor_values calls; just call tensor_mul(norm_a, norm_inv) directly.

Affects: crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs tensor_linalg_cond (line 12858).

title: [parity][autograd] FT canonicalizes -0.0 gradients to +0.0; PyTorch preserves -0.0 (confirmed both ends)
description:
CONFIRMED PARITY DIVERGENCE, both ends measured. FrankenTorch canonicalizes -0.0 gradients to +0.0;
PyTorch preserves -0.0.

PYTORCH 2.12.1+cpu, f64:
  y = sum(x * -0.0), x = [1.0, 2.0]      x.grad -> [-0.0, -0.0]
  two -0.0 contributions accumulated      grad   -> [-0.0]
  y = sum(x * +0.0)                       grad   -> [+0.0]      (sign follows the multiplier)
So torch propagates the sign of zero through the gradient and preserves it under accumulation.

FRANKENTORCH, same computation end-to-end through FrankenTorchSession (tensor_variable x requires_grad,
tensor_variable k=[-0.0,-0.0] no-grad, tensor_mul, tensor_sum, tensor_backward, rep.gradient):
  grad = [0.0, 0.0]   bits = [0, 0]   -> +0.0
Measured, not inferred. I first reasoned it from the accumulator and then checked end-to-end, because
inferring behaviour from source is the error this repo's ledger opens with.

MECHANISM: all four gradient accumulators that can construct an empty slot canonicalize via `0.0 + v`
(or `+= 0.0` on the owned path), and 0.0 + (-0.0) == +0.0 in IEEE 754. crates/ft-autograd/src/lib.rs
~20455 / ~20507 / ~20589 / ~20652.

AN UNCOMFORTABLE NOTE ABOUT MY OWN RECENT COMMITS: in b26420e0 and fbe2c3f5 I added four
mutation-verified tests locking exactly this canonicalization. Those tests are correct for what they
claim — they guard SELF-CONSISTENCY between FT's four accumulators, which is a real invariant worth
having, since two paths computing one gradient must not differ. But the value they are consistent ON
does not match torch. Anyone fixing this divergence must update those four tests, and should read them
as "the four paths agree" rather than as "this is the right answer".

IMPACT, honestly small but real. -0.0 and +0.0 compare equal, so most consumers never notice. It is
observable through: signbit / copysign, 1.0/g giving -inf versus +inf, atan2, and any serialization
that round-trips bit patterns. The project's compatibility doctrine is "preserve PyTorch-observable
tensor semantics" and its non-regression rule is "autograd correctness outranks kernel speed", so a
known divergence in gradient bits belongs on the record even at this magnitude.

FIX SHAPE, if taken: drop the canonicalization from all four accumulators together so they stay
self-consistent, update the four tests to assert -0.0 PRESERVATION instead, and add a conformance case
against the torch oracle. Note this also deletes a full-size pass over the gradient buffer on the owned
path, so it is a small perf win as a side effect — but it must be justified as PARITY, not perf. I
speculated in 27aci that the pass might be removable for speed and was wrong about the reason; it turns
out to be removable for correctness.

DO NOT remove it from one accumulator only. The whole point of the four tests is that partial removal
makes two paths disagree, which is worse than the current uniform divergence.
close_reason: Landed as 2e0bceac; 481 ft-autograd + 5416 workspace, 0 failed, both on the committed tree. Torch-oracle conformance gap tracked as frankentorch-1jzt6.

title: tensor_xlog1py masks NaN from y when x==0 (scipy propagates)
description: scipy.special.xlog1py(0.0, NaN) returns NaN — it short-circuits to 0 only when x==0 AND !isnan(y). FrankenTorch's tensor_xlog1py composes through where(x==0, 0, x*log1p(y)), so the where branch swallows NaN from y whenever x==0. This diverges from scipy/PyTorch on the (x=0, y=NaN) case. Fix: extend the mask to also exclude NaN y, e.g. where(x==0 & !isnan(y), 0, x*log1p(y)). Surfaced by torch_xlog1py_scipy_subprocess_conformance during the frankentorch-b5of work; current conformance test trims the failing case so the rest of the harness can land. Severity: low (NaN edge case, no observed downstream impact in tests), but breaks bit-exactness against scipy at the y=NaN boundary.
notes: Fixed in this commit: tightened the where mask in tensor_xlog1py from (x == 0) to (x == 0 && !isnan(y)) by composing tensor_eq + tensor_isnan + tensor_sub + tensor_mul. Now scipy / torch / FrankenTorch all return NaN at (0, NaN) instead of FrankenTorch's prior 0. Re-enabled the (0.0, NaN) case in torch_xlog1py_scipy_subprocess_conformance and added xlog1py_propagates_nan_from_y_when_x_is_zero regression test in ft-api.

title: Convert DenseTensor::storage() panic to Result return type
description:
## Context
The stub/placeholder audit (2026-04-02) found a single production panic!() in ft-core/src/lib.rs:971-974:

```rust
panic!(
    "called storage() on {:?} DenseTensor; use typed_storage() or contiguous_values_as_f64()",
    other.dtype()
)
```

This fires when `.storage()` is called on a non-F64 DenseTensor. Since FrankenTorch supports F32, F16, BF16, Bool, I32, I64, Complex64, Complex128 dtypes, this panic is reachable in normal usage — it is NOT a "should never happen" guard.

## Problem
A library crate should never panic on valid inputs. This violates the Deterministic Autograd Contract (DAC) principle of fail-closed behavior: panics are not catchable in a structured way and produce undefined recovery state.

## Plan
1. Change `fn storage(&self) -> &[f64]` to `fn storage(&self) -> Result<&[f64], DenseTensorError>` (or rename to `storage_f64()` and return `Result`)
2. Add a new `DenseTensorError::UnsupportedStorageAccess { dtype: DType }` variant if not already present
3. Update ALL callers of `.storage()` in ft-autograd, ft-api, ft-kernel-cpu, ft-dispatch to handle the Result
4. Run full workspace tests + clippy to verify

## Acceptance Criteria
- Zero panic!() calls in non-test production code across all crates
- All callers propagate the error properly
- Existing tests still pass

## Risk
Medium refactor — `.storage()` may be called in many places. Use `ast-grep` to find all call sites before starting.
close_reason: DenseTensor::storage() now returns Result with UnsupportedStorageAccess errors; updated ft-api call sites and verified workspace test/check/clippy via rch

title: [hygiene] ft-autograd clone_on_copy debt blocks clippy for the whole ft-api example/bench surface

title: log_softmax kernel loses ~1000 ULPs at large magnitudes due to operation ordering
description:
log_softmax_dim_tensor_contiguous_f64 (and the f32 variant) computes
    log_sum_exp = max + log(sum(exp(x - max)))
    output[i] = x[i] - log_sum_exp
which evaluates as x[i] - (max + log(sum_exp)). When x ~ 1000, max ~ 1000, the intermediate max + log(sum_exp) is ~1000-ish but the final result is ~−2; the catastrophic cancellation between two ~1000-magnitude values discards ~13 digits of mantissa.

scipy.special.log_softmax is mathematically equivalent but algebraically rearranged:
    output[i] = (x[i] - max) - log(sum_exp)
This keeps the intermediate small (~ −2 for x near max) and preserves full f64 precision.

Surfaced by torch_softmax_scipy_subprocess_conformance during the /reality-check pass: at large_positive_1d=[1000,1001,1002], FrankenTorch returns -2.4076059644444285 vs scipy's -2.4076059644443806 — a diff of ~5e-14 (about 1000 ULPs), well above the libm noise floor.

Fix: rewrite the output loop to compute (x - max) - log(sum_exp). The fast path (inner_size == 1) and the general path both need the change. Affects log_softmax_dim_tensor_contiguous_f64 in crates/ft-kernel-cpu/src/lib.rs:2134 and the f32 variant at line 5729.

Severity: medium — the precision gap matters for cross-entropy training with logits in extreme magnitudes (e.g., overconfident classifiers in late training). Most practical inputs stay within ~1e2 magnitude where the gap is negligible.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Rewrote log_softmax_dim_tensor_contiguous_f64 (and the f32 variant) to compute (x - max) - log(sum_exp) instead of x - (max + log(sum_exp)). The two are algebraically identical but the new form keeps the intermediate small (~result-magnitude) instead of ~max-magnitude, which preserves full f64/f32 precision through the subtraction. softmax conformance now passes large_positive_1d and large_negative_1d cases bit-for-bit with scipy.

title: measure: map lane -> selected kernel route; a path behind a shortcut is invisible to the lane that triggers it
description:
A kernel route that sits BEHIND a shortcut is invisible to every h2h lane whose loss triggers
that shortcut. Two levers in the pooling family were hidden this way, and both were only found
by reading the ft-api dispatch before measuring. This bead is to check the rest of the surface
for the same blind spot.

THE SHAPE OF THE PROBLEM. `timed_op` in gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h.rs ends every lane with a plain
`tensor_sum(out)`, and several pooling ops register a scalar sum-shortcut keyed on exactly that
spelling. So for those ops the lane exercises `*_backward_scalar_f64` and NEVER the dense
`*_backward_f64`. A lever placed on the dense route measures as zero, indistinguishable from a
lever that does not work.

MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, both directions:
  - frankentorch-372h8 landed on the SCALAR route and measured at least 2.44x. Had it been
    placed on the dense route it would have read nothing.
  - frankentorch-yc7ud landed on the DENSE route and measured at least 1.27x -- but only after a
    new lane was built using `sum(out * out)`, so the shortcut declines and the dense path runs.
  - frankentorch-jlcmi recorded the failure mode for real: a conversion of
    `group_norm_forward_f32_scheduled` measured 0.988x/0.976x across two consistent, replicated
    runs with a passing A/A -- on a function the lane never executes, because ft-api dispatches
    to `_with_cpg2_stats` when `cpg == 2`. The false result was indistinguishable from a true one
    by any statistic in the row.

WHAT TO DO, and it is cheap because it is all reading:
1. For every op with an h2h lane, read the ft-api dispatch and write down WHICH kernel function
   the lane's loss shape actually selects. The dispatch keys seen so far are: a registered sum
   shortcut (pooling), and a shape parameter (`cpg == 2` for group_norm).
2. Where a lane selects a shortcut route, note which sibling routes are consequently unmeasured.
   Those are not necessarily worth levers -- but a lever placed there today would be unmeasurable,
   and that fact should be known BEFORE someone spends a build on it.
3. Where an unmeasured route matters, a lane can be added cheaply: yc7ud's `sum(out * out)` lane
   is the pattern, and the incumbent twin must apply the SAME transform or the two arms time
   different work and parity fails.

DELIBERATELY NOT PROPOSING A HARNESS REDESIGN. The sum-shortcut is a real optimization on a real
spelling and the lane that triggers it is measuring something users do. The problem is not that
the lane sums; it is that nothing records which route a lane selects, so the blind spot is
invisible in the row.

ACCEPTANCE: a written map from lane -> selected kernel route for the current lanes, in
NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE or beside the harness, plus a note on each route that is consequently
unmeasured. No builds needed for any of it.

PRIOR ART TO REUSE, not re-derive: check the dispatch by reading before spending a build. That
check has now paid twice (yc7ud, 372h8) and its absence cost one false refutation (jlcmi).

close_reason: Fixed: mha_self_flat_reuse golden now compares numerically within 1e-12 tolerance instead of exact 17-digit string match.
