title: ft-nn PReLU and shrink activations sever autograd
description: Reviewer finding in crates/ft-nn/src/lib.rs after the recent activation-gradient repair wave. Several activation modules still read tensor values, compute in plain f64, and return session.tensor_variable(..., false), so a requires_grad=true input produces a fresh untracked output and tensor_backward cannot propagate gradients. Concrete sites: PReLU::forward lines 3576-3642 reads both input and its learnable weight via tensor_values and returns an untracked leaf, so both input gradients and the PReLU weight gradient are dropped; Softshrink lines 3918-3938, Hardshrink lines 3966-3978, Tanhshrink lines 3991-4000, Softsign lines 4014-4023, Softmin lines 4046-4057, and RReLU lines 4154-4168 have the same severed-input pattern. Existing tests for these modules are forward-only (for example prelu_default_forward/prelu_has_parameters/prelu_multichannel, softshrink_shrinks, tanhshrink_values, softsign_bounded, softmin_is_softmax_of_negated, rrelu_module_*), and the full ft-nn test suite still passes: rch exec -- cargo test -p ft-nn reported 508 passed on 2026-04-29. Repro by code inspection: create a requires_grad=true input, run PReLU::forward (or any listed activation), reduce with tensor_sum, then tensor_backward; tensor_gradient for input is absent because the forward output is a requires_grad=false leaf. For PReLU, tensor_gradient for self.weight is also absent even though parameters() exposes that learnable slope. Fix by composing each activation through existing autograd-aware primitives (e.g. PReLU via tensor_where/tensor_mul with broadcasted weight; shrink ops via tensor_where; Softmin via tensor_neg or 0-input subtraction then tensor_softmax; RReLU via leaky_relu-style composition) and add regression tests asserting input gradients, plus weight gradients for PReLU.
close_reason: Composed all 7 listed activation modules through autograd-aware primitives: PReLU via tensor_reshape+tensor_expand+tensor_mul+tensor_where (now propagates to both input and learnable weight); Softshrink/Hardshrink via nested tensor_where + tensor_abs/tensor_sub/tensor_add + tensor_gt/tensor_lt; Tanhshrink via tensor_sub(input, tanh(input)); Softsign via tensor_div(input, 1+abs); Softmin via tensor_neg + tensor_softmax; RReLU via where(x>=0, x, slope*x). Added 8 gradient regression tests asserting analytical d/dx for each module (plus PReLU weight grads, both single-slope and multichannel). All 11 existing forward tests continue to pass — forward parity preserved.

title: cdist p=2: matmul identity replaces broadcasted [P,R,M] sweep (50-62x)
description: tensor_cdist for p=2 (Euclidean, the dominant case AND torch's default compute_mode) composed through a broadcasted [P,R,M] (or [B,P,R,M]) difference tensor: unsqueeze+expand+sub+abs+pow(2)+sum_dim+pow(0.5). title: ft-api: f32 dtype-parity gaps in value-reading ops (errors or upcasts on f32 input)
description:
A probe across value-reading ops on f32 inputs found 11 broken (torch preserves f32; we error or silently upcast to f64). TWO root mechanisms.

MECHANISM A — composed op builds a CONSTANT via self.full(shape,val) which is F64, so a downstream div/mul/eq promotes the f32 result to f64 (upcast) or fails tensor_eq's matching-dtype check (hard error):
  cov, corrcoef, renorm  -> OK but dtype=F64 (silent upcast)
  xlogy, sinc            -> ERR 'tensor comparison requires matching f32 or f64 dtypes'
  (+ spherical_bessel_j0, same full+eq pattern, not in probe)
  FIX: build constants with full_like(reference,val) so they match the input dtype.

MECHANISM B — no-grad/direct path reads values via tensor_values / storage().to_vec() (F64-only) then rebuilds, so f32 hard-errors UnsupportedDType:
  pdist (p!=2), cdist (p!=2), nanmedian, kthvalue, copysign, logaddexp
  FIX: read via tensor_values_lossy_f64 + build output in the input dtype.

torch returns the input float dtype for all of these. Fix in mechanism-grouped commits with golden-value + dtype regression tests.

Tests f32_constant_ops_preserve_dtype + f32_value_read_ops_preserve_dtype (dtype + golden values + f64 no-regression); ft-api 1897 pass. title: [tooling][rch] two rch modes silently serve a STALE local binary while reporting build success
description:
Two rch behaviours that each silently produce a STALE local binary while reporting success. Both cost
real time on frankentorch-3i7c0 and both are invisible unless you check an ELF SHA.

MODE 1 - `rch exec -- sh -c "..."` does not sync artifacts back.
  env RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- sh -c "cargo clippy ... && cargo build ..."
compiles on the worker, prints `Finished`, exits 0 - and the local
target/release/examples/<name> keeps its previous mtime and bytes. Running it afterwards executes the
OLD code. Detected only because the example self-reports its ELF SHA-256 and the "before" and "after"
runs printed byte-identical SHAs. A pipe inside the command is different and better: rch refuses it
outright as a non-compilation command (RCH-E301), which fails loudly.
WORKAROUND: whenever you need the artifact locally, use a BARE `rch exec -- cargo build ...` with no
sh -c and no pipes.

MODE 2 - stale per-worker sync manifest after a file goes untracked -> tracked.
A bare build then failed repeatedly with
  error: couldn't find file `crates/ft-api/examples/training_loop_alloc_profile.rs`
on vmi1152480, for a path that exists locally, is git-tracked, and is not gitignored. The file had
just been committed (untracked -> tracked). ovh-a built the same commit fine, so it is per-worker
state, not a repo problem. Retrying does NOT clear it.
WORKAROUND: `rch sync --worker <id> --force` (14 cache entries removed) or `rch sync --all --force`.
After that the next build produced a new SHA immediately.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A BEAD: mode 1 defeats the campaign's core measurement discipline silently. A
self-A/B that rebuilds one arm through `sh -c` measures the SAME binary twice and produces a
perfectly plausible "no change" or "big win" row. The executing-ELF SHA-256 rule is what caught it -
that rule exists for exactly this and it earned its keep here.

SUGGESTED FIX (upstream rch): either sync artifacts for sh -c wrapped commands too, or refuse them
the way piped commands are already refused, so the failure is loud instead of silent. And make the
stale-manifest case self-heal or emit a diagnostic naming `rch sync --force` rather than a bare
"couldn't find file".
close_reason: Published RCH stale dependency-preflight remediation in a7a83345

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
DEFENCE HARDENED IN-REPO; UPSTREAM FIX STILL OPEN (RainyReef/cc, 2026-08-08). Code: f0873873. Not closing — the rch behaviours this bead reports are unchanged.

WHAT I COULD ACTUALLY DO HERE. The suggested fix is upstream in rch and is not mine to land. What IS in this repo is the defence that caught the failure: the executing-ELF SHA-256, which this bead rightly says "earned its keep". It was copy-pasted into SEVEN harness examples with no test anywhere. A guard living in seven unverified copies is not a guard, so it is now one tested function.

  executing_elf_sha256 — hoisted into ft-api::harness_provenance beside the other evidence-contract helpers, with the reasoning attached rather than assumed.
  identical_arm_digests — NEW, and it is this bead's trap in one check: if a rebuild never reached the binary being run, both A/B arms execute identical code, and the row reads as a clean "no change" instead of a broken experiment. The message names the digest, this bead, and the known causes (bare rch exec with no sh -c and no pipes; check where a worker-scoped target dir retrieved the artifact; rch sync --worker <id> --force for a stale manifest).

A THIRD MECHANISM, not in this bead's original write-up, hit me directly this session and is now documented in the helper: RETRIEVAL CAN LAND THE ARTIFACT SOMEWHERE OTHER THAN THE PATH YOU THEN RUN. rch rewrote CARGO_TARGET_DIR to a worker-scoped path and retrieved artifacts there; target/release/examples/<name> kept its previous bytes and mtime while the build had genuinely succeeded. Distinct from mode 1 (no sync-back at all) and mode 2 (stale per-worker manifest): here the sync-back happened, to a different directory. Detected the same way, by comparing the ELF SHA against the file I was about to run.

A FOURTH OBSERVATION, adjacent and worth recording because it wastes time the same way: an rch-built binary may not RUN locally at all. Workers are on glibc 2.43, this host is 2.42, so a retrieved release binary died with "libm.so.6: version GLIBC_2.43 not found". Not stale — unusable, and it fails at run time rather than build time. Any harness that must execute locally (anything needing the local PyTorch oracle) has to be linked locally; offloading its BUILD to rch produces an artifact that cannot be used for the measurement.

MODE 3 — a worker can link against a NEWER GLIBC than the local host, producing an artifact that

  cargo build --release -p ft-api --features fair-alloc --example pool_kernel_vs_tape_probe
  [RCH] remote hz2 (126.8s)
  Custom CARGO_TARGET_DIR artifacts retrieved: 143 files, 862809 bytes

                               (required by ./pool_kernel_vs_tape_probe)

Exit 0 from the build, artifacts genuinely retrieved, ELF present with a fresh digest — and
unrunnable. The fleet is heterogeneous, so whether you get a usable binary depends on which worker
you land on. A sibling build in the same session landed elsewhere and produced an ELF that was
byte-identical to a later LOCAL build and ran fine, which is what makes this intermittent and
therefore worth writing down.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE ANNOYANCE: this only bites work that RUNS the artifact locally, which is
exactly the perf-measurement work the campaign depends on. For cargo test / cargo clippy it is
invisible, because those execute on the worker.

WORKAROUND, and it follows from rch's own admission logic rather than any flag: `rch diagnose`
reports "Tier 1: structure_analysis — no pipes/redirects/backgrounding" as a PASS condition for
interception. So adding a redirect keeps the build LOCAL:

  cargo build --release -p ft-api --features fair-alloc --example probe > /path/build.log 2>&1

That is the same structural property mode 1 abuses (sh -c) and mode 2's pipes trip, used
deliberately. It is a side effect of the admission heuristic, not a supported switch, so it could
change; a real `--local` / RCH_FORCE_LOCAL=1 escape hatch would be the right fix upstream.

SUGGESTED UPSTREAM FIX: have rch compare worker glibc against local (it already compares node/npm/bun
versions and warns) and either refuse to route, or warn loudly, when a build produces an artifact the
local host cannot execute. The capability check already exists — it just does not cover libc.

CROSS-CHECK THAT SAVED ME: the executing-ELF SHA-256 rule again. I nearly recorded a "successful"
build whose binary could not run, and the thing that caught it was insisting the probe self-report
its own digest and actually executing it before trusting the build.

comments.text:
A FIFTH MODE, and the first one where OFFLOADING ITSELF is the defect rather than a sync bug
(YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). Not taking this bead -- it is RainyReef's and its real fix is upstream
in rch. Recording an instance, which is what this bead is for.

AN ORACLE-BACKED CONFORMANCE TEST CANNOT BE OFFLOADED, AND ITS SKIP PATH IS SILENT.

Hit while writing frankentorch-1jzt6's test (landed 3b0954d7). I reflexively ran
  rch exec -- cargo test -p ft-conformance --test pytorch_signed_zero_gradient_conformance
That compiles AND RUNS on the worker. The test's oracle is a local torch interpreter
(.venv-oracle, or FT_LEGACY_ORACLE_PYTHON). On the worker that path does not exist, so
torch_available() returns false, the test prints a one-line "torch unavailable, skipping" to stderr,
returns early, and cargo reports

    test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed

A PASS. Not a skip, not an ignore -- a pass, because the early return is a normal function return.
Every ft-conformance test with a torch_available() guard behaves this way, which is the correct
design for a machine that genuinely lacks torch and the wrong outcome entirely for a machine that
has one and was merely not asked.

WHY THIS BELONGS ON THIS BEAD RATHER THAN A NEW ONE: it is the same shape as modes 1-3 -- rch
reports success for work that did not happen -- but the mechanism is new. Modes 1 and 3 are about
the ARTIFACT not arriving where you then run it; mode 2 is a stale manifest. Here the build and the
run both succeeded exactly as designed. What went missing was the ORACLE, an environmental
dependency that does not travel with the code, and nothing in rch could detect that. The fourth
observation already on this bead (glibc 2.43 vs 2.42, retrieved binaries that will not execute
locally) is the closest relative: both say some work is not offloadable, and it fails at RUN time.
The difference is that glibc fails LOUDLY and this fails silently and green.

DETECTED THE SAME WAY THIS BEAD KEEPS RECOMMENDING -- positive execution evidence, not an exit code.
The test prints its oracle's torch version on every run, so a real run shows

    pytorch_signed_zero_gradient_conformance: oracle torch 2.12.0+cpu

and a skipped run cannot produce that line. I killed the rch invocation before it finished and re-ran
locally with FT_LEGACY_ORACLE_PYTHON set. Had I trusted "1 passed" I would have shipped a
conformance test for frankentorch-dtyiz that had never once spoken to torch -- which is precisely
the mistake dtyiz and 1jzt6 exist to correct, arrived at from a completely different direction.

RULE I would put in AGENTS.md if it is not there: anything needing the LOCAL torch oracle must be
built and run locally. That is the same conclusion as this bead's fourth observation, reached
independently, and it now covers ft-conformance's whole oracle-backed surface rather than just
harnesses that execute a retrieved binary.

WORTH CONSIDERING for whoever fixes this properly: the skip path could be made loud when the caller
plainly EXPECTED an oracle -- e.g. skip silently only when FT_LEGACY_ORACLE_PYTHON is unset, and
fail when it is set but unusable. That converts "I asked for the oracle and silently did not get it"
from a green pass into an error, without breaking genuinely torch-less machines. Not doing it here;
it touches ft-conformance's shared harness and belongs to whoever owns that surface.

title: [bug][max_pool1d] pair specialization disagrees with generic first-argmax on ties — RED on main
description:
cargo test --release -p frankentorch-kernel-cpu --lib fails at clean HEAD (verified via rch exec --base HEAD --clean-overlay --no-overlay, so it is NOT working-tree contamination): tests::max_pool1d_pair_specialization_matches_generic_first_argmax_bits.

Decoded assertion (f64 bit patterns):
  left  = [0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0, 6.0]
  right = [0, 3.0, 4.0, 0.0, 6.0]

The two paths disagree at exactly one index: one scatters a 5.0 gradient at index 3, the other leaves it 0. That is a first-argmax TIE-BREAK divergence in max_pool1d backward — the pair specialization and the generic scan choose different winning indices when the window holds equal maxima, so the gradient lands in a different input slot.

Provenance: introduced by the pre-reboot max_pool1d specialization work (frankentorch-6dvg5 f64 2x2 no-grad forward, -gdxc1 f64 2x2 first-argmax forward, -es4np pool-plus-sum scalar argmax backward, -oddz2 small index-scatter backward). All four beads were closed; this test was left red on main and the swarm died before anyone noticed.

Autograd correctness outranks kernel speed (AGENTS.md non-regression rule), so this outranks the perf queue.

Do NOT fix by relaxing the test or regenerating its expectation — the generic first-argmax scan is the reference and PyTorch's documented tie-break is the FIRST maximal index. Fix whichever path deviates from that, and add a case that pins tie-breaking explicitly rather than only comparing the two implementations against each other (a shared bug hides from a path-vs-path comparison, which is how this class of defect survived).
close_reason: Fixed in c891ba2e. 49 max-pool scan sites converted to pool_max_beats (ATen rule: NaN displaces any value, last NaN keeps the index) plus 8 arg=0 seeds corrected to the window start. Cited evidence: frankentorch-kernel-cpu --lib 619 passed/0 failed (was 618/1), full workspace suite exit 0. New test max_pool_nan_and_neg_inf_windows_match_the_torch_oracle pins values/indices against torch 2.12.0+cpu; two tests that encoded the pre-fix behaviour were re-derived from the oracle.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SCOPE CORRECTED by running the oracle (torch 2.12.0+cpu, .venv, same host thinkstation1). This is NOT a tie-break bug between two FT paths; it is a NaN-propagation parity bug against PyTorch affecting ALL max-pooling forwards, and the two FT paths merely disagree with each other as a side effect.

Input [1.0, 1.0, NaN, 4.0, 5.0, NaN, NaN, NaN, -0.0, 0.0], kernel 2 stride 2:

  torch max_pool1d values : [1.0, nan, nan, nan, -0.0]
  torch max_pool1d indices: [0, 2, 5, 7, 8]
  (torch max_pool2d with (1,2)/(1,2) returns the SAME, so the two torch routes agree)

  FT max_pool1d values : [1.0, 4.0, 5.0, -inf, -0.0]   offsets [0, 3, 4, 6, 8]
  FT max_pool2d values : [1.0, 4.0, 5.0, -inf, -0.0]   offsets [0, 3, 4, 0, 8]

FT diverges from torch on 3 of 5 windows -- every window containing a NaN:
  [NaN,4.0] torch nan@2, FT 4.0@3
  [5.0,NaN] torch nan@5, FT 5.0@4
  [NaN,NaN] torch nan@7, FT -inf@6 (max_pool1d) or -inf@0 (max_pool2d)

ROOT CAUSE. FT scans with a bare `if v > m`, seeded `m = f64::NEG_INFINITY`. `NaN > x` is false, so a NaN never wins and an all-NaN window returns NEG_INFINITY -- a value not present in the input. ATen's condition is `if ((val > maxval) || std::isnan(val))`, so NaN always wins AND, because every NaN re-triggers the assignment, the LAST NaN in the window takes the index. That is why torch reports 7 for the [NaN,NaN] window and not 6: the rule is first-argmax for ordinary ties (strict `>`) but LAST-NaN for NaNs. Any fix that reaches for "first argmax" for NaN too will reproduce 6 and still be wrong.

The correct predicate is exactly `v > m || v.is_nan()`. Note `!(v <= m)` is NOT equivalent: once m is NaN it admits any subsequent finite value, which torch does not.

BLAST RADIUS: 23 `> m` comparison sites in the pooling region of crates/ft-kernel-cpu/src/lib.rs (max_pool1d/2d/3d, f32 and f64, plain forwards, with-indices forwards, the 2x2 and 2x2x2 specializations, and the sum-fused variants). The two FT routes agreeing with each other is not sufficient -- they currently agree on being wrong for windows w1 and w2 and only diverge on w3 -- so the fix must be pinned against torch's output, not against the other FT route. That is exactly how this survived: the test is named `..._matches_generic_first_argmax_bits` and compares FT to FT.

The max_pool2d `arg = 0` initializer is a second, separate defect: for a window with no winner it reports absolute index 0 rather than anything in the window. It disappears once NaN wins, since then some element always wins, but it should be corrected rather than left load-bearing on that.

Also fixed en route: the test asserted on Vec<u64> and printed two rows of raw bit patterns on failure, which is a large part of why a red test sat unread. It now reports per-window value/bits/offset for both routes.

PERF NOTE for whoever lands it: this adds an is_nan check to the innermost loop of every max-pool forward, including the specializations that were tuned this campaign. Measure the pooling lanes after, and remember the contention finding from frankentorch-dmpho -- a parallel kernel's timing on this host moves 3.4x with peer load, so use the paired lane and name the harness.

My first sweep found only 23 because the pattern grep keyed on 'if X > m {' and half the sites spell the accumulator 'max_value' -- worth remembering for any future kernel-wide audit: grep the ACCUMULATOR, not the comparison.

Also fixed: 8 'let mut arg = 0usize;' seeds in max_pool2d/3d, which reported global index 0 for an all -inf window. torch reports the WINDOW START (verified: max_pool1d over [1.0,2.0,-inf,-inf] gives indices [1,2], not [1,0]).

Two tests were pinning the OLD behaviour and had to be re-derived from the oracle rather than regenerated:
  - max_pool3d_indexed_2x2s2_specialization_preserves_first_argmax_bits asserted values[1]==NEG_INFINITY and offsets==[0,0] for an all-NaN window. torch gives values [-0.0, nan], indices [0, 15]. Now pinned to that, with the oracle invocation in a comment.
  - max_pool3d_2x2s2_backward_matches_generic_first_tie_bits carried an inline reference implementation using the old 'v > m' rule, i.e. the test's own reference encoded the bug it was meant to catch.

New test max_pool_nan_and_neg_inf_windows_match_the_torch_oracle pins three contracts against torch 2.12.0+cpu, not against another FT route: (1) NaN displaces any value, (2) among NaNs the LAST takes the index -- window [NaN,NaN] at offsets 6,7 gives 7, so uniform 'first argmax' reasoning passes (1) and still fails, (3) an all -inf window keeps the window start.

ft-kernel-cpu lib: 619 passed, 0 failed (was 618/1 with the RED). Workspace suite running.

NOT in scope, checked and left alone: the remaining 'v > m' scans are all in cross_entropy_forward/backward, where the max is a log-sum-exp stability max rather than an argmax and a NaN logit propagates through exp() regardless. Worth its own bead if anyone wants it verified against torch rather than argued.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
AUDIT CLOSED: max_pool was the only family with this defect. Checked every other argmax-style op in ft-kernel-cpu -- argmax_dim/argmin_dim (f32 and f64) already carry explicit NaN handling ('if !acc.is_nan() { if val.is_nan() {..} else if val > acc {..} }'), and there are no adaptive_max_pool / fractional_max_pool / max_unpool kernels in the tree at all. The remaining bare '> m' scans are cross_entropy log-sum-exp stability maxima, where a NaN logit propagates through exp() regardless -- confirmed on the torch side (F.cross_entropy with a NaN logit returns nan; with a -inf logit returns a finite 0.1269).

So the reason this bug survived is specific and worth remembering: max_pool was the one family whose comparison was written as a bare '>' seeded at NEG_INFINITY, while its neighbours were written NaN-aware. A kernel-wide audit that greps for is_nan and assumes its absence is deliberate would have missed it; the tell was the SEED (NEG_INFINITY appearing in an argmax, which means 'no element has won yet' and therefore needs a rule for what wins).

title: softmax / log_softmax lack subprocess conformance against torch/numpy
description:
tensor_softmax and tensor_log_softmax are the canonical activation/output functions for classification heads, attention layers, and most loss formulations. They have unit tests in ft-api but no subprocess conformance against an authoritative reference (torch.nn.functional.softmax / scipy.special.softmax / numpy). Bit-exact agreement matters because:

- Numerical stability: log_softmax(x) = log(softmax(x)) is computed via the max-subtraction trick to avoid exp overflow; the equivalence with the naive form must hold within libm precision across all inputs.
- Gradient stability: softmax/log_softmax forward/backward are coupled (dL/dx = softmax(x) - target for cross-entropy). Drift between FrankenTorch and PyTorch here corrupts every classification training run.
- Edge cases: large positive inputs (exp overflow risk), large negative (underflow), uniform input (all equal probabilities), single-element softmax (degenerate).

Add torch_softmax_torch_subprocess_conformance covering interior, large-magnitude, near-uniform, and edge-case inputs along multiple dims; assert ULP-tolerant equality against scipy.special.softmax (or numpy formulation if scipy unavailable). Same for log_softmax.

Bias toward filing-from-/reality-check: this is a pre-existing instance test gap, not a new bug.
notes: Closed by adding torch_softmax_scipy_subprocess_conformance covering interior, uniform, scalar, large-positive / large-negative (with max-subtract numerical stability), mixed-sign, and 1-D / 2-D / 3-D shapes across multiple dims. 8-ULP tolerance with 1e-15 absolute floor. Also surfaced the log_softmax precision bug tracked under frankentorch-ebrb (now fixed in the same commit).

title: Implement tensor_linalg_inv autograd: grad_A = -A_inv^T grad_out A_inv^T [child of tw0y]
description:
Wrap tensor_linalg_inv in tensor_apply_function with the standard matrix-calculus backward:
    grad_A = -Y^T @ grad_Y @ Y^T   where Y = A^{-1}
Save Y (the forward output) for backward to avoid recomputing the inverse. Output shape is [n, n] for n×n input. F64-only autograd path; F32 input with requires_grad continues to fail-loud (consistent with the affine_grid pattern).

Add tensor_linalg_inv_propagates_gradient regression test in ft-api: for diagonal A, the inverse is reciprocal-diag and the gradient under sum loss simplifies to a clean closed-form for verification.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Wrapped tensor_linalg_inv in tensor_apply_function with the analytical backward grad_A = -Y^T @ grad_Y @ Y^T where Y = A^{-1}. Y is saved for backward to avoid recomputing the inverse; the matmul chain is implemented inline in the closure (n×n is small enough). Added linalg_inv_propagates_gradient_via_inv_transpose_outer regression test (diagonal A=[[2,0],[0,4]] under sum loss → grad = [-1/4,-1/8,-1/8,-1/16]). ft-api lib tests: 1140.

title: ft-api: 7 heavy numeric lib tests flake under full-suite parallelism (pdist/rnn/lobpcg)
description: Running the FULL ft-api --lib suite (1955 tests, default parallel) flakes ~7 tests: pdist_l2_matmul_matches_direct (lib.rs:83896), rnn_raw_forward_golden_isomorphism (108434), lobpcg_api_matches_eigh_extreme_pairs (85347), +4. They PASS in isolation and in scoped runs. Confirmed PRE-EXISTING (clean HEAD 39f75103 with no working changes also fails the same 7 under the full suite; a scoped run of the same tests passes). Likely rayon thread-pool contention / memory pressure when ~1955 tests run concurrently on the rch worker, or a numeric-tolerance test sensitive to parallel scheduling. Needs: pin these tests to a tolerance robust under contention, or mark them serial (cargo --test-threads or a serial guard), or reduce their working-set. Not blocking feature commits (verify scoped).
design: DIAGNOSIS (cc, 2026-06-07): NOT flaky/random — DETERMINISTIC test-ordering pollution. The 7 (cdist_l2_matmul_matches_direct_2d_and_batched, functional_conv2d_no_grad_fast_path_matches_composed_path_bit_exact, gru/lstm/rnn_raw_forward_golden_isomorphism, pdist_l2_matmul_matches_direct, lobpcg_api_matches_eigh_extreme_pairs) are ALL bit-exact GOLDEN-DIGEST tests (fnv/checksum of f64 output). They FAIL with a different digest but still pass their loose abs<1e-10 value checks => output drifts ~ULP. Ruled out: (1) rayon non-determinism — RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1 still fails the same 7 (ran 7.77s, serial confirmed); (2) cargo test-thread concurrency — --test-threads=1 (fully serial) STILL fails the same 7; (3) running the 7 alone as a group PASSES (0.29s), and each passes isolated. So the cause is a test EARLIER in full-suite order mutating bit-affecting GLOBAL state that leaks forward. No static mut/Atomic/OnceCell config in ft-kernel-cpu or ft-api. PRIME SUSPECT: x86 MXCSR FP control register (rounding mode or FTZ/DAZ denormal flush) toggled by some test's SIMD/unsafe path (matrixmultiply or a transcendental approx) and not restored — per-thread, so with serial execution it persists to the 7 and changes denormal/rounding behavior => digest drift. NEXT STEP: bisect the ~1948 preceding tests (binary search by name prefix or insert a MXCSR read/assert before each of the 7) to find the polluter; then restore FP state after it (or stop the global mutation). Alternatively relax these 7 to tolerance digests, but that weakens the perf-isomorphism guarantee. NOT my change (clean HEAD reproduces). Validate ft-api edits via SCOPED runs.
notes: SESSION-4: DETERMINISTIC confirmed — two full-suite runs produced BYTE-IDENTICAL computed (wrong) digests (cdist left=3018070494873948101, gru=14497563193174927436, etc. both runs). So it is deterministic state pollution, NOT a race. Op-FP-state theory ALSO REFUTED: in-process repro running 3000 iters of exp/log/tanh/sqrt/pow/div/neg/abs/clamp on denormal-prone (~1e-160) inputs between two pdist digests => NO drift. Second-ingredient bisection: base+transcendentals=366 PASS, +div=380 PASS, +abs PASS; base+both(448) FAIL — so the trigger is a narrow COMBINATION, not a single op class. CUMULATIVE REFUTED LIST: rayon (RAYON=1 fails), cargo concurrency (--test-threads=1 fails), single polluter, ID counter + allocator churn (40k allocs no drift), backward (467 grad tests pass), op computations (3000 transcendental+arith no drift). EVERY in-process repro passes; only the real multi-#[test] suite at ~448+ tests fails. ONLY remaining decisive experiment: instrument MXCSR (needs unsafe -> gemm module or test-only crate), read+assert ==0x1F80 before each golden in a full-suite run, to catch WHICH test leaves it dirty. The computed-digest drift is real (forward output depends on accumulated suite state) — a genuine determinism bug, just elusive. DO NOT retry: count/alloc/backward/single-op-FP repros (all refuted).
close_reason: ROOT CAUSE FOUND + FIXED: matrixmultiply SIMD micro-kernel sets x86 MXCSR FTZ/DAZ and does not restore it, leaking flush-to-zero into later FP ops on the same (libtest-reused) thread, so GEMM-heavy golden digests drifted ~1 ULP depending on whether a GEMM ran earlier. Fix: dgemm_mm/sgemm_mm wrappers restore MXCSR 0x1F80 after each matrixmultiply call (matmul output unchanged). Full ft-api 1960/0 parallel AND --test-threads=1 (was 7 failing). Guard: kernels_do_not_dirty_mxcsr.

title: [parity] heaviside(nan, values) returns nan, torch returns 0.0

title: Own deterministic mul_add GEMM for bit-identical matmul across CPUs (replace matrixmultiply runtime FMA dispatch)
description: matrixmultiply selects its AVX2/AVX512/FMA microkernel by runtime CPU detection, so matmul output is not bit-identical across heterogeneous workers (root cause of the now-fixed qb1g2 test flake). NO-GAPS swing: build our own cache-blocked, register-tiled safe-Rust dgemm/sgemm whose inner accumulation uses f64::mul_add / f32::mul_add EXCLUSIVELY. f64::mul_add is IEEE single-rounding and bit-identical on every CPU (hardware vfmadd where present, correct soft-fma fallback otherwise) AND matches torch's FMA-BLAS rounding -> simultaneously cross-worker-deterministic and torch-bit-exact. Constraint: must stay perf-competitive with matrixmultiply on FMA hardware (register-blocked microkernel; mul_add lowers to vfmadd so FMA throughput is preserved). Verify: re-pin bit-exact matmul goldens, run on >=3 heterogeneous workers, same-worker GEMM bench A/B vs matrixmultiply (no regression). Once shipped, the cdist/pdist/lobpcg/lstm/gru/rnn goldens could be restored to bit-exact.

This is the 5th attempt in the streak (scalar mul_add 0.036x, packed, std::simd, row-parallel 0.0, now Kulisch); per the NO-CEILING addendum a rejected-lever streak is a TRIGGER to STOP iterating this loop. title: [regression][conformance] I put a panic! in production code and my --lib gates never ran the guard that forbids it
description:
In 05bdf9ca I added `oracle_required_or_skip` to ft-conformance's production source with a `panic!` in it. The repo forbids that: `production_code_contains_no_forbidden_stub_or_panic_macros` (ft-conformance/tests/smoke.rs) scans crates/**/src for panic!/todo!/unimplemented!, skipping #[cfg(test)] blocks.

It was red for SIX commits (05bdf9ca, e8cbe568, 8d81a433, 6387fd5f, and everything after) and I did not know, because every gate I ran all session was `cargo test ... --lib`, and that guard is an INTEGRATION test. `--lib` never builds crates/*/tests/*.rs at all.

MEASURED: cargo test --workspace --tests -> 39 test targets, 5554 passed. My --lib gates covered 13 targets and 5420 tests. So 15 integration test files and ~134 tests were outside every 'workspace green' claim I made — including cholesky/inverse/logdet/solve/triangular_solve double-backward parity and grad_fd_audit, which are exactly the surface my dtyiz, cg_pow and dequant changes could have disturbed.

★ THIS IS THE THIRD TIME IN THREE BEADS that a gate's SCOPE was narrower than the claim it appeared to support: r76bc (--lib excludes --tests for clippy), y8lv8 (same, on tests I had just edited), and now this one — same excluded surface, but for cargo test rather than clippy, and this time it hid a real regression rather than a lint. The pattern is not 'I keep forgetting --tests'; it is that a passing command names a scope, and I kept reading it as a claim about the codebase.

FIX: the helper returns Result<bool, String> and each caller does .expect(..). Production stays panic-free, the decision stays pure and testable, and the process-ending behaviour lives with the test that wants it — which is the better factoring anyway, not just lint compliance.
close_reason: Fixed in e5a88516: helper returns Result, 32 call sites .expect(..), production panic-free. --workspace --tests 39 targets/5554 passed/0 failed; clippy --all-targets rc=0; fmt --all clean.

FULL GATES, at the widest scope I now know to ask for:
  cargo test --workspace --tests   39 targets, 5554 passed / 0 failed
  cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --no-deps -D warnings   rc=0
  cargo fmt --check --all   clean

WHAT THE WIDER GATE REVEALED beyond the regression itself: --lib was 13 targets / 5420 tests; --tests is 39 targets / 5554. Fifteen integration files and ~134 tests sat outside every 'workspace green' claim I made this session, including the cholesky / inverse+logdet / logsumexp / solve / triangular_solve double-backward parity suites and grad_fd_audit — exactly the surface my dtyiz, cg_pow and dequant changes could have disturbed. All pass. That is now measured rather than assumed, which it was not before today.

I DELIBERATELY DID NOT GAME THE GUARD. Two workarounds would have made the scan green while leaving an explicit panic in production: assert!(false, ..), and Err::<bool,String>(msg).expect(..) as a one-liner keeping the -> bool signature and requiring zero call-site edits. The second was genuinely tempting at 32 call sites. Both satisfy a textual lint while defeating its purpose, and that is the exact failure mode this bead family exists to document. title: f32 create_graph over f32 leaf params ERRs UnsupportedDType (blocks f32 weight-grad-of-grad / full f32 WGAN-GP)
description:
The f32 conv double-backward INPUT-Hessian works (conv2d/grouped f32 verified vs
torch — frankentorch-lboou), but the WEIGHT-gradient-of-gradient path (the full
WGAN-GP: grad(sum(grad(loss,x,create_graph)^2), weight)) ERRs with
DenseTensor(UnsupportedDType(F32)) for BOTH conv2d-f32 and grouped-f32.

ROOT (suspected): the create_graph backward machinery hits an f64-only DenseTensor
op (ft-core lib.rs ~1155/1161 UnsupportedDType) when processing an f32 LEAF
parameter (weight/bias) that requires grad in 2nd-order mode. NOT a bug in the
conv cg closures — their input adjoints are verified, and the dweight/dbias nodes
are correct-by-construction (same recipe as the verified f64 + f32-input paths).
Likely the same dtype-awareness class as ng1hw's backward_create_graph numel/dtype
allocation gaps.

REPRO: f32 gradient-penalty over conv2d/grouped weights (see the f32 cg closures in
functional_conv2d / functional_conv2d_grouped, frankentorch-lboou). Affects ALL f32
second-order-over-f32-parameters, not just conv.

IMPACT: f32 input-Hessian (analysis, input-only penalties) works; full f32/mixed-
precision WGAN-GP weight updates via gradient penalty do not. f64 WGAN-GP is fully
supported (j4uio).
notes:
ROOT CAUSE PINNED (cc): the UnsupportedDType(F32) is thrown by
DenseTensor::from_typed_storage (ft-core lib.rs:1154-1155) on a meta.dtype() !=
storage.dtype() MISMATCH — NOT 'f32 unsupported'. So backward_create_graph builds
a grad NODE for the f32 leaf weight using the LEAF's F32 meta but F64 grad-space
storage → mismatch. FIX = make the create_graph grad-node construction
dtype-aware: grad nodes live in F64 grad-space, so build them with an F64 meta
(mirror the leaf SHAPE but force dtype=F64), the same way the regular backward
accumulates f64 grads onto f32 leaves via the length-generic
accumulate_tensor_gradient. Locate the grad-node build in backward_create_graph
(ft-autograd) — likely where it clones the input node's meta to make the grad
leaf/accumulator. HIGH BLAST RADIUS: this path serves ALL create_graph backward
(f64 works today) — verify the full f64 double-backward suite (conv/linear/special-
fn/linalg probes) stays bit-exact after the change, plus the f32 gradient-penalty
probes (conv2d/grouped) then match torch. Related: ng1hw (same dtype-awareness
class in the complex create_graph alloc).
close_reason:
Shipped e4313739: full f32 gradient-penalty (WGAN-GP) for conv2d-f32 + grouped/
depthwise-f32 now matches torch f32 exactly (pen/gw_sum/weight+bias grads).
ROOT was NOT a deep create_graph infra gap (the original framing): the f32 conv
cg closures built grad nodes via tape.apply_function, which infers output dtype
from its inputs — feeding the F32 weight/padded made the grad NODES F32, so the
F64-only readers (tensor_values/autograd_grad) rejected them. FIX: cast the F32
weight/padded inputs to F64 (tape.to_f64 -> differentiable CastF64) before the
nested apply_function, so grad nodes live in the F64 grad-space (kernel math stays
f32-exact). Verified vs torch (conv_f32_gp_values_probe). The general f32
create_graph-over-f32-leaf path was already fine (minimal elementwise f32
gradient-penalty worked) — this was conv-cg-specific.
Residual f32 tail tracked on lboou: conv3d-f32 (ERRs UnsupportedDType even for
input-Hessian — its f32 grad path is unwired / hits an f64-only op; distinct
issue) and conv_transpose2d-f32 (silent-zero Hessian — detachment). Both niche.

The ops_bench runs 110 convs on ONE long-lived session (b.iter reuses s), so the session retains every iteration's intermediate tensors (padded input ~4.2MB + conv output ~4.2MB per call), and tensor_values gets progressively slower (allocator/cache pressure or an O(nodes) access path). NET: this dominates the conv1d 'gap' — at call#60 the ft-api WRAPPER is ~30ms (tensor_values 8.3ms + tensor_pad + reshapes, all tape-growth-sensitive) vs the conv2d_forward_f64 KERNEL only ~11.8ms (im2col 5.8 + dgemm 4.3 + transpose 1.7). The conv kernel is FINE; the gap is autograd-engine node retention. SYSTEMIC: affects ALL repeated no-grad forwards (inference loops), not conv. FIX CANDIDATES (one lever each, same-worker A/B): (1) no-grad ops should NOT register intermediate tensors on the session's retained node store (free after read / arena-per-forward / a with_no_grad scope that drops nodes); (2) make tensor_values an O(1) storage lookup if it isn't; (3) conv no-grad path: pad into a local Vec instead of a tensor_pad SESSION node (halves retained storage/iter). Profile which dominates first (allocator vs node-access).

title: tensor_renorm severs autograd; composable via permute/reshape/norm/clamp/div/mul
description:
tensor_renorm at lib.rs:15185 normalizes sub-tensors along a dim so their p-norm is bounded by maxnorm. The body extracts values, computes the per-slice norm in plain f64, conditionally scales, and rebuilds a non-grad leaf — silently severing autograd. PyTorch's torch.renorm IS differentiable (sub-gradient at the boundary norm == maxnorm).

Closed form for the scale factor:
   scale_d = maxnorm / max(norm_d, maxnorm)
which equals 1 when norm_d <= maxnorm and maxnorm/norm_d when norm_d > maxnorm.

Composable via:
   permute dim to position 0
   reshape to [dim_size, other_size]
   abs + pow + sum_dim(1) + pow(1/p)  → norm per slice
   denom = clamp_min(norm, maxnorm)
   scale = maxnorm / denom
   broadcast scale via unsqueeze + expand
   mul, reshape back, permute back

Used heavily in embedding regularization (torch.nn.Embedding(max_norm=...)). Surfaced during /reality-check pass.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Composed tensor_renorm through permute/reshape/abs/pow/sum_dim/clamp_min/div/mul/expand. The closed-form scale per slice is maxnorm / max(norm, maxnorm), which equals 1 when norm <= maxnorm and maxnorm/norm when norm > maxnorm — clamp_min(norm, maxnorm) gives exactly the denom we want. Strategy: permute dim to position 0, reshape to [dim_size, other_size], compute per-row L_p norm, scale each row, reshape + permute back. dim==0 case skips the (no-op) permutes. Added renorm_propagates_gradient_through_input regression test (mixed clamp / no-clamp rows; row 1 in identity branch gives grad=1, row 0 in scaled branch gives finite non-zero). ft-api lib tests: 1166.

title: LOBPCG: top-k symmetric eigenpairs (torch.lobpcg) — O(n^2 k) vs full eigh O(n^3)
description:
torch.lobpcg has no FrankenTorch equivalent — the only way to get the top/bottom-k eigenpairs of a large symmetric matrix is the full eigh (O(n^3)). LOBPCG (Locally Optimal Block Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient) computes them iteratively in O(n^2 k) per iteration x few iterations — the eigh analog of the randomized SVD just shipped (svd_lowrank a3fb0f54 / pca_lowrank b87c54e0), and a real torch parity gap + big algorithmic win for spectral methods (graph Laplacians, spectral clustering, covariance PCA).

ALGORITHM (reuses the SAME building blocks as randomized SVD: gemm::dgemm + qr_contiguous_f64 + the now-CORRECT eigh_contiguous_f64 for the small Rayleigh-Ritz): (1) X = random n x k, orthonormalize (QR). (2) iterate: R = A X - X (X^T A X) [residuals]; build search subspace S = [X | R | P] (P = prev conjugate direction, empty on iter 0); orthonormalize S (QR); Rayleigh-Ritz = small eigh of (S^T A S) [3k x 3k], take the k extreme eigenpairs; X_new = S Coeff; update P; check residual norms < tol. (3) eigenvalues = the k Ritz values, eigenvectors = X.

SUBTLETIES (why it needs a dedicated turn, not a rushed commit): orthogonalization stability (re-orthonormalize against converged/locked vectors), soft-locking of converged pairs, handling the empty-P first iteration, ill-conditioned S^T A S. VALIDATION GATE: lobpcg top-k eigenvalues match full eigh's top-k to tol; A v = lambda v residual < tol; on a moderate SPD matrix (n=64, k=4). Optionally support largest=true/false. ft-kernel-cpu + ft-api wiring. Use /alien-artifact-coding for the convergence/locking proof obligations.
close_reason: Shipped commit 12f5f72f: tensor_lobpcg / functional_lobpcg wired into ft-api (kernel was 31f0e5d9). torch.lobpcg parity gap closed — top-k symmetric eigenpairs O(n^2 k)/iter. Test lobpcg_api_matches_eigh_extreme_pairs passes (n=32 k=3, largest true/false, evals match eigh to 1e-6, A*v=lambda*v < 1e-5). Pushed main+master.

title: OneCycleLR phase boundary off-by-one vs torch (warmup peak lands a step late)
description: FT OneCycleLR computes phase1 = floor(pct_start*total_steps) (integer), but torch uses end_step = pct_start*total_steps - 1 (float), spanning steps [0, total_steps-1]. Result: FT's warmup peak lands one step late and the whole lr/momentum trajectory is shifted. Confirmed vs torch 2.12: max_lr=1.0,total=10,pct_start=0.3 -> torch peaks at step 2 (lr=1.0) then descends (0.857 at step3); FT peaks at step 3. Two existing tests encode the buggy values (one_cycle_lr_linear_phase_boundaries asserts peak@step3; one_cycle_lr_edge_cases asserts pct_start=0 -> 1.0 but torch=4e-6). Fix: replace integer phase_steps with torch's float end_step schedule (start/end lr+momentum per phase, progress=(step-start)/(end-start)).

title: ft-api: amax/amin backward routes full grad to first argmax instead of splitting across ties

title: porting: add tensor_broadcast_to + tensor_expand_as for torch parity
description: torch.broadcast_to(input, shape) explicitly broadcasts input to a target shape if compatible. Differs from tensor_expand in that it accepts a target shape with HIGHER rank than input — it first prepends size-1 dims on the left to match rank, then expands. tensor_expand_as is a one-line wrapper that takes a reference tensor instead of an explicit shape. Both are autograd-aware via reshape + expand composition.

title: [parity][threshold] row-chunk equivalence for the row-independent ops across the 65536 softmax gate
description:
Extends frankentorch-5237b, which pinned serial-vs-parallel equivalence for ELEMENTWISE ops by chunking the tensor. That technique stops at the boundary of the elementwise surface, and it left the SOFTMAX_PARALLEL_NUMEL_THRESHOLD = 65536 gate untested.

WHY ELEMENT-CHUNKING DOES NOT EXTEND, and why that is not the end of it:

  * A FULL reduction (tensor_sum over everything) genuinely cannot be chunked. A parallel tree reduction and a serial in-order sum associate the additions differently, so they are EXPECTED to differ in the last bits. A bit-exact serial-vs-parallel test for tensor_sum would fail by design and would be wrong to write. Do not write one.
  * But ROW-INDEPENDENT ops can be chunked BY ROW instead of by element. softmax over dim=1 of an [R, C] tensor computes each row from that row alone, so splitting [R, C] into R separate [1, C] tensors is semantically the identity — exactly the property 5237b relied on, one axis up. The gate is on NUMEL, so [R, C] with R*C >= 65536 takes the parallel path while each [1, C] slice sits far below it.

CANDIDATES (row-independent along the reduced dim):
  softmax, log_softmax, tensor_softmax_dim / log_softmax_dim
  dim-wise reductions where each output element depends on one slice: sum(dim=1), mean(dim=1), max/min(dim=1), argmax/argmin(dim=1), logsumexp(dim=1), norm(dim=1)
  layer_norm and group_norm (per-sample / per-group statistics)
  cumsum / cumprod along dim=1 (each row is an independent scan)

PER-OP THE CLAIM MUST BE CHECKED BEFORE IT IS TESTED. Row-independence is a property of the op AND the dim. A reduction over dim=0 of [R, C] is NOT row-independent and must not be chunked by row. Get this wrong and the test asserts something false and then gets 'fixed' by weakening it, which is worse than no test.

ALSO EXPECT LEGITIMATE DIFFERENCE where a row is itself reduced in parallel: if softmax's per-row sum is parallelised for wide rows, a [1, C] slice and a row inside [R, C] could associate differently. If that shows up, it is NOT automatically a bug — establish which it is before filing. The elementwise sweep had no such ambiguity, which is why it could assert bit-exactness flatly.

METHOD, unchanged otherwise: compare .to_bits(), straddle branch boundaries in the payload, include a self-test that feeds a deliberately mismatched pair through the comparator so a green result cannot be vacuous, and put it in ft-conformance next to threshold_serial_parallel_equivalence.

A NEGATIVE RESULT IS A FINE OUTCOME and should ship the gate anyway, per 5237b and 1knqk.
close_reason:
NEGATIVE RESULT + gate shipped. Landed a4147f19.

softmax, log_softmax, sum_dim, mean_dim and cumsum along dim=1 are all bit-identical between the whole-tensor arm and the per-row arm, forward AND backward. No divergence across the 65_536 SOFTMAX_PARALLEL_NUMEL_THRESHOLD.

METHOD: element-chunking (5237b) cannot reach these — a softmax row is computed from the whole row, so splitting by element changes the answer. Splitting by ROW is the identity instead, one axis up. [256, 512] = 131_072 elements takes the parallel path; each [1, 512] slice sits far below every gate. Compared on to_bits(); FrankenTorch is its own oracle.

DELIBERATELY ABSENT, and it would be a DEFECT to add it: a FULL reduction. tensor_sum over everything associates its additions differently in a parallel tree than in a serial loop, so the two are EXPECTED to differ in the last bits. A bit-exact serial-vs-parallel test for tensor_sum would fail by design and would invite someone to 'fix' a kernel that is already correct. This is written into the test's doc comment so the omission is not mistaken for an oversight.

The caveat filed with this bead did NOT materialise: no op showed a legitimate re-association difference. COLS was kept modest (512) precisely so the only difference between the arms is the numel gate — a very wide row could plausibly get its own per-row reduction parallelised, and that would have been indistinguishable from a defect. If anyone widens COLS later, that ambiguity comes back and the result must be re-interpreted, not just re-run.

Row-independence is a CLAIM PER OP AND DIM, not a convenience. A reduction over dim=0 is not row-independent and is not listed; adding one would make the test assert something false.

Payload: every row carries the boundary values in its leading positions so they appear in each independently-computed slice rather than only in row 0, and the filler varies per row so an implementation that computed one row and broadcast it would still be caught.

GATES: cargo test -p ft-conformance --test threshold_serial_parallel_equivalence -> 5 passed / 0 failed (3 from 5237b + 2 new), REAL_EXIT=0, rch worker vmi1227854. cargo clippy -p ft-conformance --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings -> clean, rch worker hz1. rustfmt clean. No timed rows banked.

COMBINED STATE of the threshold-equivalence surface after 5237b + h37tn: 25 ops (20 elementwise element-chunked, 5 row-independent row-chunked), forward and backward, across PARALLEL_THRESHOLD 8192 / SOFTMAX 65536 / SCALAR+SIMD_UNARY 524288 — zero divergences found, all pinned by a live ~10s gate with a self-test proving the comparator can fail.

description: The tensor autograd engine's elementwise binary ops (add/sub/mul/div/min/max/atan2/fmod/remainder) required EXACTLY matching shapes and errored with ShapeMismatch otherwise — a fundamental torch-parity gap that caused a whole class of latent bugs (tensor_normalize muan, 5 norm ops 3pvd, info_nce) where callers forgot to expand manually. Fixed at the root in TensorTape::binary (ft-autograd): when operand shapes differ but are NumPy-broadcast-compatible, materialise each operand to the common shape via autograd-aware reshape (prepend leading axes) + expand BEFORE the kernel. The inserted expand nodes' existing backward (cg_sum_to_shape) reduces gradients over the broadcast axes, so the op's own backward stays matching-shape and UNCHANGED. Matching-shape and non-elementwise (matmul/dot/outer/bmm) paths are bit-identical -> all 1858 ft-api + 433 ft-autograd + 708 ft-nn + 207 ft-optim tests pass unchanged. title: tensor_unfold severs autograd; gather-then-scatter backward needed
description:
tensor_unfold at lib.rs:15083 extracts sliding windows. Each output element is a copy of an input element via a deterministic mapping (flat_out → in_flat). PyTorch's torch.Tensor.unfold IS differentiable.

Backward: scatter — grad_input[in_flat] += grad_output[flat_out] for each (flat_out, in_flat) pair the forward used. The mapping is deterministic given (dimension, size, step) and the input shape, so we can recompute it inside the backward closure.

Wrap in tensor_apply_function with this gather-then-scatter pattern.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Wrapped tensor_unfold in tensor_apply_function with gather-then-scatter backward. The (flat_out -> in_flat) mapping is computed once in the outer body and captured by both forward (gather) and backward (scatter) closures so the same routing is used in both directions; overlapping windows (step < size) accumulate via += in the scatter. Added unfold_propagates_gradient_via_scatter regression test (x=[1,2,3,4], size=3, step=1 → 2 overlapping windows, grad_x = [1,2,2,1] under sum loss). ft-api lib tests: 1164.

title: tensor_matrix_norm has severed-autograd + lacks numpy subprocess conformance
description:
tensor_matrix_norm exists in ft-api/src/lib.rs:11602 supporting fro / 1 / -1 / inf / -inf orderings. It extracts tensor values and rebuilds a requires_grad=false leaf, silently severing the autograd tape (same severed-autograd pattern as the cov / corrcoef / mode / quantile family that was fixed under frankentorch-1tax). PyTorch's torch.linalg.matrix_norm IS differentiable — for 'fro' it's just sqrt of sum of squares (composable through autograd primitives), and for the operator norms it's a max/min over column/row L1 sums (also composable through tensor_abs + tensor_sum_dim + tensor_max/min).

Also missed during the c36b closure: my earlier closure note claimed matrix_norm 'has no separate API in ft-api' — that was wrong, it does. It just wasn't covered by a subprocess conformance harness.

Two fixes needed:
  1. Compose tensor_matrix_norm through autograd primitives (or wrap in tensor_apply_function) so gradients flow.
  2. Add torch_matrix_norm_numpy_subprocess_conformance harness covering all five orderings.

Surfaced during a /reality-check pass scanning for severed-autograd patterns.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Composed tensor_matrix_norm through autograd primitives: 'fro' = sqrt(sum(A*A)) via tensor_mul + tensor_sum + tensor_sqrt; '1'/'-1'/'inf'/'-inf' = max/min over (sum_dim of tensor_abs) via tensor_abs + tensor_sum_dim + tensor_max_dim/min_dim. Output shape preserved as [1] via tensor_unsqueeze when reductions yield 0-D scalars. Added matrix_norm_frobenius_propagates_gradient and matrix_norm_inf_propagates_gradient_to_max_row regression tests in ft-api (1139 passing). Added torch_matrix_norm_numpy_subprocess_conformance covering all five orderings (fro / 1 / -1 / inf / -inf) across 12 matrices. Subprocess conformance count now 32 (was 31).

title: ft-api: lu_factor returns direct-permutation pivots, not torch LAPACK IPIV format
description: tensor_lu_factor returns pivots as a 0-indexed DIRECT row permutation (pivots[i]=original row now at position i), e.g. [2,0,1] for [[2,1,1],[4,3,3],[8,7,9]]. torch.linalg.lu_factor returns 1-indexed LAPACK IPIV (sequential swap targets), e.g. [3,3,3] for the same matrix (verified torch 2.12.0+cpu). So a user porting torch code that inspects or re-uses lu_factor pivots gets divergent values. The final P/L/U are correct (tensor_lu_unpack shipped pv8k composes correctly and matches torch P/L/U bit-exactly), but the pivots OUTPUT format differs. FIX (coordinated, parity-critical — touches LU core feeding solve/inverse/det): (1) kernel lu_factor_contiguous_f64 records the per-step max_row swap sequence (IPIV) alongside/instead of the direct permutation; (2) tensor_lu_factor returns IPIV (1-indexed); (3) tensor_lu_solve + tensor_lu_unpack accept IPIV and convert IPIV->direct-perm internally (perm=identity; for k in 0..n swap(perm[k],perm[ipiv[k]-1])); (4) verify all LU-consuming ops (lu_solve/linalg_lu/det/inverse/solve) still pass + add torch-golden pivot test. Higher blast radius -> own session. torch venv: /tmp/torchvenv (probe_lu.py captures the exact IPIV/P/L/U).
close_reason: SHIPPED 598487ce. lu_factor (+ linalg_lu_factor) now return torch-compatible 1-indexed LAPACK IPIV pivots. Kernel records the per-column swap sequence as new LuFactorResult.ipiv (direct perm kept for unchanged lu_unpack/lu_solve/det/linalg_lu); API layer converts IPIV<->direct via lu_ipiv_to_permutation. Verified vs torch 2.12 (session_lu_factor_pivots_match_torch_ipiv: 4 matrices incl 4x4 [3,3,4,4] + 2x2 [2,2]); round-trip lu_solve/lu_unpack still compose. 32 ft-api + 26 kernel LU tests pass.

description:

   a. Traces a model forward pass to capture the computation graph

   c. Serializes the graph + weights to ONNX protobuf format
2. Add session.export_onnx(model, dummy_input, path) to ft-api
3. Map core ops: Linear, Conv2d, ReLU, BatchNorm, LSTM, Softmax, MatMul, Add, etc.
4. Use the onnx-pb crate for protobuf serialization (or manual protobuf encoding)

title: Add adversarial/fuzz test coverage for high-risk paths (spec Gate G4)
description:
COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENTORCH_V1.md §5 requires 'adversarial fixtures and fuzz/property suites for high-risk entry points' and §18 defines Gate G4 (adversarial + property tests) as release-blocking.

Current state: ft-serialize has 5 proptest properties. ft-core has none. ft-api, ft-autograd, ft-kernel-cpu have none. The spec's Security Threat Matrix (§16) defines 8 threat categories that need adversarial coverage.

Implementation plan:
1. Add proptest properties for ft-autograd:
   - Random computation graphs maintain gradient correctness (numerical gradient check)
   - Backward on disconnected subgraphs doesn't corrupt other gradients
   - In-place mutation version tracking prevents stale gradient reads
2. Add proptest properties for ft-kernel-cpu:
   - Broadcasting produces correct shapes for random input shapes
   - Reduction ops produce correct results for random input tensors (cross-check against naive impl)
   - Matmul associativity: (A*B)*C matches A*(B*C) within tolerance
3. Add proptest properties for ft-api:
   - Random tensor ops maintain shape consistency (output shape matches PyTorch rules)
   - save_state_dict -> load_state_dict round-trip preserves all values for random state dicts
4. Add adversarial fixture tests for ft-serialize:
   - Fuzzed JSON payloads don't cause panics (catch_unwind + verify Error returned)
   - Fuzzed binary payloads don't cause panics
   - Oversized shape dimensions don't cause OOM (our recent checked_mul fix)
5. Add adversarial tests for ft-nn:
   - NaN/Inf inputs to forward() produce NaN/Inf output (not panic)
   - Zero-sized batch inputs handled gracefully

Tests: The beads ARE the tests. Each property test should use proptest with 256+ cases.
Success criterion: cargo test --workspace --all-features passes with all new property tests.

title: Add mixed precision support (torch.amp equivalent)
description:
torch.cuda.amp (Automatic Mixed Precision) is used in virtually every modern training pipeline. Even on CPU, F16/BF16 mixed precision can be useful for inference and for testing AMP workflows before moving to GPU.

Since FrankenTorch already supports F16 and BF16 dtypes in ft-core, the infrastructure exists — what's missing is the autocast and grad scaling machinery.

Implementation plan:
1. Add an AutocastContext to ft-api that tracks whether autocast is active and the target dtype
2. Add session.autocast_enter(dtype) / session.autocast_exit() (matching no_grad pattern)
3. Add session.with_autocast(dtype, closure) panic-safe wrapper
4. When autocast is active: matmul, linear, conv operations auto-downcast inputs to the target dtype (F16/BF16), then upcast output back to F32
5. Add a GradScaler struct in ft-optim that:
   a. Scales loss by a factor before backward (prevents F16 underflow)
   b. Unscales gradients before optimizer step
   c. Checks for inf/nan in gradients, skipping the update if found
   d. Adjusts scale factor dynamically based on overflow frequency

Key: The autocast policy (which ops to cast) should match PyTorch's known-safe list — matmul, linear, conv are safe; softmax, layernorm, loss functions should stay in F32.

Tests:
- Unit test: autocast context enters/exits correctly, respects nesting
- Unit test: matmul inside autocast uses F16, outside uses F32
- Unit test: GradScaler scales loss and unscales gradients
- Unit test: GradScaler skips update on inf gradients
- E2E test: train a linear model with autocast + GradScaler, verify convergence
- Panic-safety: with_autocast restores state on unwind
close_reason: Implemented mixed precision support: (1) ft-api: autocast_enter/exit/with_autocast/maybe_autocast with stack-based RAII context, panic-safe; (2) ft-optim: GradScaler with scale_loss/step/update + dynamic backoff/growth, overflow detection, skip-on-inf semantics; (3) ft-autograd: TensorBackwardReport::tensor_gradients_iter() and scaled_clone() helpers. 8 autocast tests + 7 GradScaler tests = 15 new tests. Note: F16/BF16 conversion paths gated until ft-autograd to_dtype supports them; F32/F64 down-casting works.

title: cross_entropy_loss_with_smoothing severs autograd when label_smoothing greater than 0
description:
cross_entropy_loss_with_smoothing at lib.rs:11272 composes correctly when label_smoothing == 0 (delegates to nll_loss). But when label_smoothing > 0, it extracts the scalar values from nll and uniform_loss via tensor_values(), computes the blend (1 - s) * nll + s * uniform in plain f64, and rebuilds a requires_grad=false leaf at line 11302. This silently severs autograd for the entire label-smoothing training path.

PyTorch's torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy with label_smoothing IS differentiable. Fix: replace the tensor_values + scalar combination with tensor_lerp(nll, uniform_loss, label_smoothing), which evaluates the blend through autograd-aware primitives. Same arithmetic but with the tape edges intact.

Surfaced during /reality-check pass scanning for tensor_values + tensor_variable(false) patterns.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Replaced the severed scalar-blend body with tensor_lerp(nll, uniform_loss, label_smoothing) which evaluates the same (1 - s) * nll + s * uniform arithmetic through autograd-aware primitives. tensor_lerp is the canonical FrankenTorch primitive for lerp(start, end, w) = start * (1 - w) + end * w. Added cross_entropy_with_smoothing_propagates_gradient_through_logits regression test asserting finite + non-zero + sum-to-0 gradient on logits. ft-api lib tests: 1151.

title: [hazard][verification] piping a gate into tail/head/grep reports the PIPE's exit status — false-green gates and wrongly-chained actions
description:
A gate that pipes its tool into tail/head/grep reports the LAST stage's exit status, not the tool's.
It goes green no matter what the tool found. Fleet-wide finding; frankenmermaid hit FIVE CI gates
reporting success while executing nothing. Recording FrankenTorch's own instances so the next agent
here does not repeat them.

THE TWO FORMS, both of which bit this repo on 2026-08-06:

  1. STATUS FORM      sometool ... 2>&1 | tail -25; echo "exit=$?"
     `$?` is tail's. Always 0.
     Instance: `ubs crates/ft-api/examples/training_loop_alloc_profile.rs 2>&1 | tail -25; echo "ubs exit=$?"`
     reported "ubs exit=0". Re-verified unpiped: real exit 0, Critical 0 - the claim happened to hold,
     but the method would have reported green regardless.

  2. CHAIN FORM       somecmd ... 2>&1 | tail -1 && nextcmd
     `&&` gates on tail's status, so nextcmd runs even when somecmd FAILED. This is worse than a false
     green because it takes a WRONG ACTION.
     Instance: `git push origin main 2>&1 | tail -1 && git push origin main:master`. The main push
     failed (unstaged .beads/issues.jsonl blocked the preceding rebase) but the master push ran anyway,
     leaving origin/master on a pre-rebase commit that origin/main no longer has. Still unresolved at
     time of writing; realigning master needs a forced ref update, which is operator-approval-only.

  Demonstration: `false | tail -1; echo $?` prints 0.

WHY GREP IS NOT A WORKAROUND EITHER: `tool | grep -q PATTERN` inverts the meaning entirely - it
reports whether the pattern matched, not whether the tool succeeded.

THE FIX, use either:
  tool ... > /tmp/somewhere/out.log 2>&1; rc=$?        # redirect, $? is the tool's
  tool ... | tail -20; rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}             # if you must pipe
  set -o pipefail                                      # NOT available under GitHub Actions' default
                                                       # bash -e, which is how mermaid's went unseen

TWO CHECKS WORTH RUNNING BEYOND THE GREP, both of which came back clean here on 2026-08-06:
  - any `-p CRATE` that matches no real package silently builds/tests NOTHING while exiting 0.
    Verify names against `cargo metadata --no-deps`. All six used here (ft-api, ft-autograd,
    ft-conformance, ft-kernel-cpu, ft-nn, ft-optim) are real.
  - a clippy/test "clean" claim where a workspace run could have aborted before reaching the crate.
    Use `--no-deps` so exit 0 can only mean that crate was linted. Confirmed: `cargo clippy -p ft-api
    --all-targets --no-deps -- -D warnings` exits 0 with "Checking ft-api" present.
  - and prefer POSITIVE execution evidence over exit codes where it exists: "2486 passed" and
    "Running unittests ... ft_api-<hash>" cannot be produced by a run that executed nothing.

SPECIFIC TO UBS: **CORRECTED 2026-08-09.** This bead originally said `ubs` exits 0 even with
findings unless `--fail-on-warning`. That is FALSE — ubs exits NON-ZERO when it has findings.
The claim was inherited and repeated without checking, and acting on it shipped a commit gate
that blocked every agent on this checkout (see the 2026-08-08 comments; fixed in 17ea00aa).
Read the `Critical issues:` line rather than trusting either the exit code or this paragraph's
former advice. The correction is left in place rather than silently edited away, because a
bead that quietly rewrites its own history teaches nothing.

NO COMMITTED SCRIPT IN THIS REPO HAS THE PATTERN - `rg` over the tree for a pipe followed by a `$?`
check returned nothing. The exposure is agent shell behaviour, which is why this is a bead and not a
code fix.
close_reason: Verification-only bead; the code fix shipped in 8d81a433 (all 29 in-crate oracle tests routed through the false-green guard, after 05bdf9ca/e8cbe568 covered the helper and the three integration tests). Description's false 'ubs exits 0 with findings' claim corrected in d51a9138. Remaining content is an instance ledger with no closure criterion — closing rather than churning it.

UBS_REQUIRE_SCAN=1 opts into failing the commit, which is what a CI or release gate should set. WHETHER TO FLIP THAT DEFAULT IS AN OPERATOR CALL and is the main open question this leaves.

GATE NOW ACTUALLY SCANS — and my earlier root cause was wrong (RainyReef/cc, 2026-08-08). Code: 6dd41441.

CORRECTION FIRST. I previously wrote that ubs's --staged mode was broken. It is not. --quiet is. Isolating one variable at a time in a one-file throwaway repo:
    ubs --staged --only=rust --quiet   -> '1 detected', Files: 0   BROKEN
    ubs --staged --only=rust           -> '1 detected', Files: 1   scans
    ubs --only=rust <path> --quiet     -> Files: 0                 BROKEN
    ubs --only=rust <path>             -> Files: 1                 scans
--quiet suppresses the SCAN, not just the output, on both invocation shapes. My earlier comparison changed TWO variables at once (--staged AND --quiet) and blamed the wrong one. That is the same single-variable discipline I have been applying to perf A/Bs, and I did not apply it to my own diagnosis.

THE FIX: drop --quiet, keep --staged. --staged is kept deliberately because it scans the staged BLOB, which is what a pre-commit gate should judge; explicit paths would scan the worktree, judging a file with unstaged edits in the wrong form. Cost is a noisier commit, which is a fair price for a gate that runs.

ALSO STRENGTHENED, per this bead's own note that 'ubs exits 0 even with findings unless --fail-on-warning': the gate now reads the Critical line and fails on Critical > 0 — the always-fix class per AGENTS.md. Warnings/info still pass. UBS_SKIP=1 unchanged as the escape hatch.

SCOPED AS THE OPERATOR REQUIRED: hooks/pre-commit in this repo only. Nothing host-global, no shared config, no env left set, cannot touch another project or another agent's unrelated workflow.

WHY NOT FAIL-CLOSED BY DEFAULT (the UBS_REQUIRE_SCAN flip): the zero-file condition was UNIVERSAL, so that default would have blocked every commit by all four agents on this shared checkout for a defect none of them introduced. Fixing the scan removes the condition instead, which is strictly better. The warn path and the UBS_REQUIRE_SCAN opt-in remain as the backstop if ubs regresses.

TEST: sh hooks/pre-commit --self-test — 8 checks, no repo state, no ubs, no network, exercising the SAME helper functions the gate calls rather than reimplementations. Negatives included: an ABSENT Critical line parses as empty not zero ('absent' and 'zero findings' are different claims); an indented Critical line inside a finding body is not read as the summary; 'Files: 70' does not match the zero-file check.

BOTH VERIFIED TO FAIL WHEN THEY SHOULD: inverting the zero-file helper makes the self-test FAIL on exactly that check; relaxing the critical threshold to >= 0 makes a clean scan FAIL the commit, proving the wiring reaches return 1 and not merely that the parser works. Both restored and re-verified.

END-TO-END: against a staged Rust file in a throwaway repo the hook now reports 'Files: 1' and exits 0; before the fix it reported 'Files: 0' and its own warning.

STILL TRUE, and worth repeating: .git/hooks/pre-commit is the mcp-agent-mail chain-runner and the tracked hook runs as a COPY at pre-commit.orig. This takes effect on RE-INSTALL. Until someone re-installs, commits in this checkout are still gated by the old unscanning copy.

REMAINING UPSTREAM: --quiet suppressing the scan is a ubs bug and belongs upstream; nothing further is actionable here.

I SHIPPED A BLOCKING GATE AND IT WOULD HAVE STOPPED THE FLEET (RainyReef/cc, 2026-08-08). Fixed in 17ea00aa, same session, ~15 minutes after installing.

WHAT HAPPENED. f6ebcb46 installed a gate that actually scans. I then measured what it does to this repo — which I should have done BEFORE installing.   1. ubs exits NON-ZERO when it has findings. THIS BEAD'S OWN TEXT says it 'exits 0 even with findings unless --fail-on-warning'. I inherited that claim and repeated it without checking. That exit is what actually blocked commits — the Critical check I added lives inside the code==0 branch and therefore never sees a real finding at all. I shipped unreachable code beside the real blocking path and described it as a strengthening.

Verifying the artifact worked (which I did, three cases) is not the same as verifying what it does to the actual repo. A gate is not correct because it fires; it is correct because what it fires on is what should be stopped.

Every one of those is a match arm inside the #[cfg(test)] module (which starts at line 3032; the sites are 4716, 4743, 4768, 5457, 5566). They are idiomatic test assertions. The tool does not exclude test modules, and it reports test panics as 'panic! in library code'.

This tool's Critical is 'a panic! macro exists', counted in test code. That is a style/robustness lint, not a security finding, which is exactly why gating on it blocked most of the repo and why I was wrong to gate on it.

Of the line numbers cited inside the Critical block, nine point at lines containing no panic! at all (meta.clone(), slice indexing, bounds checks at 850, 857, 1030, 1394, 1395, 1414, 2440, 2634, 2641). Either the section boundaries in the text output are ambiguous to parse, or the citations are imprecise. I could not map all 11 findings to 11 sites, so I am reporting the category and the verbatim snippets — which are unambiguous — rather than a per-site classification I cannot stand behind.

  - Do NOT set UBS_BLOCK_CRITICAL=1 on this repo as it stands; it would block on test panics.

comments.text:
WARNING-STREAM TRIAGE — the scanner is not a bug-finder for this repo (RainyReef/cc, 2026-08-08).

My hook fix made the scanner actually run, which meant its WARNING stream (24728 findings across the crate sources) had never been examined by anyone. I said as much last turn and then went looking, because an unexamined 24k findings is either a large source of real defects or a large source of noise, and which one it is changes what the operator should do with it.

It is noise. Taking ft-core/src/lib.rs (1005 warnings) apart by category:

  445  "Potential panics via unwrap/expect"
       Every snippet the tool prints is test code — DenseTensor::from_storage(..).unwrap(),
       tensor.view(..).unwrap() — at lines inside the #[cfg(test)] module.
  465  "assert! macros present (panic surface)"
       assert! in tests. That is what a test is.
   95  "Direct indexing/slicing may panic"
       THIS is the only category in library code, e.g.
           TensorStorage::F64(v) => Ok(&v[start..end])   (dispatch_values, ~1394)

So I chased the only category that could be real, and it is a FALSE POSITIVE, for a reason worth writing down:

  dispatch_values computes  start = meta.storage_offset()
                            end   = storage_span_required_len(&meta)?
  and then slices the storage. The linter sees an unchecked slice of a Vec by
  computed indices. What it cannot see is that DenseTensor::from_typed_storage —
  the single constructor every public path funnels through — already enforces
      if storage.len() < storage_span_required_len(&meta) {
          return Err(DenseTensorError::InsufficientStorage { needed, actual });
      }
  so end <= v.len() holds by construction for every tensor that exists, and
  start <= end because `needed` is offset + span. The slice cannot be out of
  range. The bound is a CONSTRUCTION INVARIANT, and no lint that reasons
  per-function will ever see it.

RESIDUAL I AM NOT CLAIMING AWAY: that argument holds only while a constructed tensor's meta cannot be mutated in place without re-validating. Public mutation goes through TensorMeta builders (with_storage_offset and friends) and the result is re-constructed through the validating path, so it holds today. If someone later adds an in-place meta setter on DenseTensor that skips from_typed_storage, this becomes a real panic path — which is a decent argument for a debug_assert at the slice, though not for changing the code now.

NO BUG FOUND. That is the result, and I am reporting it as one rather than manufacturing a fix. What it settles:

  - The CRITICAL stream is panic!-in-tests (triaged earlier).
  - The WARNING stream is unwrap/assert-in-tests plus panic-surface lints that
    the type system and constructor invariants already discharge.
  - So this scanner is a style / panic-surface linter, not a defect finder, on
    this codebase. Mining the remaining ~24k warnings for bugs is not worth
    anyone's session.

RECOMMENDATION, unchanged in direction but now evidenced from both streams: filter by CATEGORY and exclude #[cfg(test)], or accept the gate as a code-style signal only. Do NOT set UBS_BLOCK_CRITICAL=1, and do NOT commission a triage pass over the backlog. The gate's value is that it now runs at all and would catch a NEW category appearing — not that the existing 25k findings mean anything.

THREE NEW VERIFICATION HAZARDS, ALL ABOVE THE SHELL LAYER (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). This bead has
been about shells reporting something other than what happened. Everything below is the same failure
in a different layer: a MEASUREMENT or an ANALYSIS reporting something other than what happened. All

HAZARD 4 — A HARNESS THAT PRINTS A HARD-CODED CONCLUSION ALONGSIDE ITS OWN DATA.
My create_graph probe ended with a println! that said "within the A/A null => create_graph is NOT the
term". The measured arms were 8.2 ms and 29.8 ms — a 3.5x gap, nowhere near the 8-9% null. The verdict
was right for an unrelated reason (the default has create_graph=false), but the sentence asserted
something its own numbers contradicted, and it would have been copied into a bead by anyone skimming.
  TELL: any println! containing "=>" or "therefore" whose text is a string literal rather than derived
  from the values. If the conclusion cannot change when the numbers change, it is documentation
  pretending to be a result.
  FIX: print the numbers and the DECISION RULE separately, or compute the verdict. Never both assert
  and measure in the same literal.

HAZARD 5 — A NEW HARNESS WITHOUT THE DEFENCE AN OLD HARNESS ALREADY EARNED.

  sequence. An A/A run back-to-back passes and hides it; only positional separation exposes ordering.
  FIX: the defence belongs in every new harness, not in a story about an old one. Copy the conditioner

A NEW FORM OF THIS HAZARD: A PIPED-GATE NUMBER OUTLIVES THE ABILITY TO AUDIT HOW IT WAS CAPTURED
(YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). No code change. Found while landing frankentorch-dtyiz (2e0bceac).

Every instance on this bead so far is same-session: someone writes `cmd | tail; echo $?`, and the
error is visible in the transcript right above the number. This one is not, and that is what makes
it worth adding.

WHAT HAPPENED. I ran dtyiz's final clippy gate as a background task. Its captured output was three
lines: "clippy_rc=0", then "1", then "0". My context was then cleared. On resuming I cited
"clippy rc=0" as a landing gate on the dtyiz bead and in a commit message.

I cannot audit that number. The transcript that would show whether rc came from ${PIPESTATUS[0]},
from a redirect, or from the tail of a pipe is gone, and the two trailing bare integers are output
whose meaning I can no longer reconstruct either. The number is not WRONG — it is UNFALSIFIABLE,
which for a gate is the same practical thing. This bead's whole argument is that a gate's exit code
is only as good as its capture method; the corollary is that a bare rc recorded WITHOUT its capture
method decays into an unverifiable claim the moment the transcript that produced it goes away. Beads
and commit messages outlive transcripts by design, so this is the normal case, not an edge one.

RESOLVED BY RE-MEASURING, not by reasoning about it:
  UBS_SKIP=1 rch exec -- cargo clippy -p ft-autograd --lib --no-deps -- -D warnings > <file> 2>&1
  rc=$?      # redirect, so $? is cargo's — no pipeline anywhere
  -> clippy_rc=0
and, because this bead is right that an rc is the weak half of the evidence, the POSITIVE execution
evidence from the same log:
  "Checking ft-autograd v0.1.0 (/data/projects/frankentorch/crates/ft-autograd)"
  "Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 13.73s"
  zero "warning:" lines, zero "^error" lines
With --no-deps, exit 0 can only mean that crate was linted — the check this bead itself prescribes
for the "a workspace run aborted before reaching the crate" failure. The original clippy_rc=0 was
correct. That was worth an hour's suspicion anyway: an unauditable green and a real green look
identical, and the only way to tell them apart is to re-run one of them.

WHAT I NOW THINK THE RULE IS, sharpened from "do not pipe": record the CAPTURE METHOD next to any
exit code that goes into durable storage, or record positive execution evidence instead. This bead
already recommends the latter ("prefer POSITIVE execution evidence over exit codes"), and that
recommendation is stronger than it looks — "13 test result: ok lines, 5416 passed" is
self-authenticating in a way "rc=0" can never be, because it cannot be produced by a run that
executed nothing AND it does not depend on trusting the shell plumbing that reported it. I applied
that on the dtyiz workspace gate deliberately: I piped it into grep, knew the exit code was grep's,
and quoted the thirteen per-crate result lines instead. That piped gate was fine precisely because
its exit code was never load-bearing.

CORRECTING SOMETHING ON THIS BEAD RATHER THAN LEAVING IT: RainyReef already flagged that this bead's
original text claims "ubs exits 0 even with findings unless --fail-on-warning" and that this is
FALSE — ubs exits non-zero on findings, and inheriting the wrong claim caused a gate that blocked
the fleet. That correction currently lives only in a late comment while the false claim sits in the
description where a skimming reader hits it first. Anyone editing this bead's description should fix
it there.
