title: [blocker][tooling][rch] heterogeneous worker glibc silently produces harness binaries that cannot run on the measurement host
description:
THIS BLOCKS ALL LOCAL vs-PyTorch MEASUREMENT, intermittently and silently, for every agent in the campaign.

SYMPTOM: the h2h harness, built via rch, fails to execute on thinkstation1:
  ./target/release/examples/gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libm.so.6: version 'GLIBC_2.43' not found (required by ...)

CAUSE: the rch worker fleet is heterogeneous in glibc, rch has no worker-pinning flag, and the measurement host is OLDER than some workers.
  measurement host thinkstation1 : GLIBC 2.42  (ldd (Ubuntu GLIBC 2.42-0ubuntu3.1) 2.42)
  worker hz1                     : produces binaries requiring GLIBC 2.43 -> UNRUNNABLE here
  worker vmi1149989              : produced a runnable binary earlier this session (ELF ac1156652bbd0b95 executed fine)
So whether your measurement works is decided by which worker rch happens to pick, and 'rch exec --help' exposes no --worker/--host/--pin flag to control it.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A NORMAL FLAKE — three compounding properties:
  1. IT FAILS AT RUN TIME, NOT BUILD TIME. The build reports 'Finished release profile' and REAL_EXIT=0. The failure surfaces only when you try to measure, as a confusing loader error that looks like a broken local toolchain rather than a scheduling outcome.
  2. IT SILENTLY CHANGES THE ELF UNDER YOU. target/release/examples/ is shared, so a peer's rebuild replaces the binary you measured with. I watched the harness ELF change three times in one session — ac1156652bbd0b95 (ran) -> fc53650281e8ba9a (ran, produced my certified rows) -> e7f3af08827089da -> 05b9b45c7f647196 (both unrunnable). An agent who records the ELF once and measures later can attribute a row to a binary that never executed.
  3. IT WASTES THE SCARCEST RESOURCE. Each attempt is a ~6-7 minute release build of ft-api on a fleet that already refuses ft-conformance-sized jobs on 6/10 workers for capacity (frankentorch-1v8kz). Retrying until you get a compatible worker is expensive and, per the standing orders, a seq-retry loop is banned anyway.

EVIDENCE THIS SESSION: two consecutive rebuild attempts landed on glibc-2.43 workers (hz1 confirmed; the other unidentified), both REAL_EXIT=0, both unrunnable. My certified rows (frankentorch-y4nj9, frankentorch-vhgue) were produced BEFORE this, from a binary that happened to be built on a compatible worker.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT, roughly in order of cost:
  a. A worker tag/filter so a build can request glibc <= the measurement host's, or an explicit --worker pin on rch exec.
  b. rch refusing to return an artifact whose required glibc exceeds the requesting host's, turning a silent runtime failure into a build-time refusal.
  c. Building the measurement harness with a pinned older toolchain/sysroot, or statically linking it, so worker glibc stops mattering.
  d. Failing all that, documenting which workers are measurement-safe so agents can at least recognise the failure quickly.

NOT DONE HERE: I have not attempted (a)-(d) — rch is TopazGorge's area (frankentorch-c1ct1 is an adjacent rch capacity bead) and changing fleet scheduling from a measurement pane is the wrong place for it. Filing with full reproduction so whoever owns rch can act.

WORKAROUND FOR NOW: if the harness fails with a GLIBC error, the binary is not yours and not runnable — rebuild and check 'ldd' expectations before assuming a local problem, and re-read the ELF the process self-reports rather than the one you built.
close_reason:
MITIGATED AND VERIFIED. The blocker is real and the workaround works today; the root fix stays with rch's owner.

THE MITIGATION: rch reads an RCH_WORKER environment variable. It is NOT documented in 'rch exec --help' — I found it with strings on the binary. Prefixing the normal rch exec build with RCH_WORKER=vmi1149989 pins the build to a worker whose glibc is not newer than the measurement host.

VERIFIED END TO END, not inferred:
  - the log confirms the pin: CARGO_TARGET_DIR rewritten to .rch-target-vmi1149989-pool-..., and '[RCH] remote vmi1149989 (575.9s)', 8m58s release build
  - the resulting binary EXECUTES on thinkstation1, where the two previous unpinned builds died in the loader with GLIBC_2.43 not found
  - ELF de31b539ff417d4e, and a full 14-lane h2h sweep ran to completion on it (RUN_EXIT=0)

★ IT ALSO CLOSES A PROVENANCE GAP I HAD TO RECORD AS OPEN. The frankentorch-vhgue rows were banked with an UNKNOWN build worker, because the shared target/ binary had been rebuilt by a peer between my build and my run. With RCH_WORKER the builder is chosen and therefore nameable, so a measured row can carry the worker that BUILT the binary as well as the host that RAN it — which is what rule 1 has been asking for all along. Every future row from this harness should carry its RCH_WORKER.

WORKER GLIBC MAP so far:
  vmi1149989  glibc <= 2.42  KNOWN-GOOD (runs on thinkstation1)
  hz1         emits GLIBC_2.43  KNOWN-BAD
  others      UNTESTED — 'rch workers list' does not report glibc, so the safe set has to be discovered by trying, which is itself part of the argument for fixing this properly.

WHAT IS NOT DONE, deliberately: the root fixes from the bead — a glibc-aware worker filter, an rch refusal when the artifact's required glibc exceeds the requester's, or a pinned-sysroot/static build — are untouched. Changing fleet scheduling from a measurement pane is the wrong place for it, and ~/.config/rch/config.toml is SHARED across eight projects so I did not edit it. TopazGorge has been mailed (thread frankentorch-tdpzf) since frankentorch-c1ct1 is adjacent rch work.

IMPACT: the measurement path is usable again by anyone, today, with a one-variable prefix. Landed in the ledger under the tdpzf section (swept into commit 88b6f886 by a peer's concurrent commit on the shared checkout; content verified present in HEAD).

title: tensor_cdist severs autograd; broadcastable composition for finite p > 0
description:
tensor_cdist at lib.rs:4230 computes pairwise L_p distances between two sets of vectors. For finite p > 0 the math is composable through autograd-aware primitives via broadcasted subtraction.

Strategy for shape [P, M] x [R, M]:
  x1_b = unsqueeze(x1, 1)    → [P, 1, M]
  x2_b = unsqueeze(x2, 0)    → [1, R, M]
  diff = x1_b - x2_b         → [P, R, M] (broadcast)
  d    = (sum_k |diff[k]|^p)^(1/p)

For batched [B, P, M] x [B, R, M] the same pattern works at dims 2 and 1.

Sister of frankentorch-0i8u (pdist). p == 0 / p == +inf still fail-loud on requires_grad.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Composed tensor_cdist through unsqueeze + expand + sub + abs + pow + sum_dim + pow primitives for both 2-D and 3-D batched inputs. The broadcasted subtraction handles both [P, M] x [R, M] and [B, P, M] x [B, R, M] cases. p == 0 / p == +inf still fail-loud on requires_grad to make autograd severance explicit (deferred to a follow-up — same pattern as pdist 0i8u). title: [perf][svd] second lever on the basis completion: skip the still-zero columns in the Gram-Schmidt sweep
notes:
FOLLOW-UP to frankentorch-264q0. Do NOT bundle it with the cursor fix -- one lever
per commit, and these two have DIFFERENT standards of proof.

THE OBSERVATION. svd_tall's basis completion orthogonalizes each candidate against
all u_cols columns of U, including the ones that are still ZERO. At the first
completion column of a 256x32 full_matrices SVD, 223 of the 256 columns are zero,
so ~87% of that sweep is multiplying by zeros; averaged over the completion, about
half the total work is against zero columns. Skipping them is worth roughly 2x on
top of the cursor fix.

WHY IT IS A SEPARATE BEAD AND NOT PART OF 264q0. The cursor fix is bit-exact BY
PROOF: failure is monotone, so skipping consumed seeds cannot change which seed
wins, and the winner's arithmetic is untouched. This one has no such proof. It
relies on `col[i] -= dot * u[i][prev]` with a zero column being an exact no-op,
and that is ALMOST always true but not always:

  - dot accumulates col[i] * 0.0. Each term is +0.0 or -0.0; +0.0 + -0.0 = +0.0
    under IEEE, so dot is +0.0 unless EVERY term is -0.0, which needs every col[i]
    strictly negative.
  - If dot is -0.0, the update is col[i] - (-0.0) = col[i] + 0.0, and for
    col[i] == -0.0 that yields +0.0. A sign-of-zero FLIP, and a bitwise
    difference.

So the failure mode is real, reachable in principle, and vanishingly rare.

EMPIRICAL STATUS: PASSES, which is not the same as proven. scratchpad/
verify_zeroskip.py ran it against the cursor form on five shapes (tall
full_matrices x2, wide-transposed, rank-deficient square, rank-deficient tall) and
got zeroskip-bit-identical=True on all five. That is evidence the flip does not
arise in practice; it is not the proof the cursor fix has.

WHOEVER TAKES THIS must decide explicitly which of these it is, and say so in the
commit:
  (a) bit-exact in practice, gated by a broad randomized bit-identity test, and
      accepted as such -- in which case say plainly that the proof is empirical; or
  (b) made unconditionally exact by testing the zero column with a check that
      cannot flip a sign (e.g. skip only when dot's computation is bypassed
      entirely AND the column is verified all-zero, leaving col untouched rather
      than subtracting zero from it).
Option (b) is probably straightforward and turns this into a proof-backed lever;
prefer it.

SIZE IT AGAINST 264q0's FIX, not against today's 4431 ms. After the cursor lands,
the completion is O(m^3) and the 256x32 shape should be in the tens of
milliseconds; this lever is ~2x on that remainder, so it is worth single-digit
milliseconds there. Against torch's 1.028 ms full call it still matters, but it is
a second-order lever and must not be measured against the pre-cursor baseline.
close_reason:
SHIPPED at least 1.73x, and the exactness question the bead left open is answered with a PROOF rather than the empirical pass it expected.

OPTION (b), and stronger than the bead framed it. The feared sign-of-zero flip needs dot == -0.0, which needs the sum to START at the first product. It starts at +0.0, and IEEE gives (+0.0) + (-0.0) = +0.0, so dot is exactly +0.0 for all finite col regardless of signs; the update is then col[i] - (+0.0), the identity even for col[i] == -0.0. The mask tests to_bits() == 0 rather than == 0.0, so a -0.0 column is never skipped -- against -0.0 the argument really does fail, and excluding it keeps the proof intact at a cost that in practice never arises. Scope stated: finite col, which holds because col starts as a basis vector and is only decremented by finite multiples.

GATE 30/0 on worker vmi1264463. The bitwise test runs both forms in ONE process across six shapes including interleaved rank-deficient ones, each in a normal AND a sign-flipped variant chosen so col goes negative during the sweep -- the exact configuration that would expose the flip if the accumulator argument were wrong -- plus an independent U^T U = I check.

MEASURED, interleaved arms, per-arm min-of-5, TWO WORKERS:
  m=96  k=8    1.80x (hz1)  1.76x (vmi1149989)
  m=128 k=8    1.87x        1.86x
  m=192 k=16   1.83x        1.78x
  m=256 k=32   1.74x        1.73x
CONSERVATIVE: at least 1.73x on the 256x32 headline shape, worst of the two runs.

THE BEAD'S ~2x ESTIMATE WAS RIGHT, AND MY FIRST VERSION MEASURED 1.19-1.37x. The gap was the skip-test itself: rebuilding the zero-mask per completion column costs O(m*u_cols) against a sweep of O(2*m*u_cols), so the bookkeeping ate half the lever. Hoisting the mask out of the column loop -- valid because it is MONOTONE, a column only ever goes zero to non-zero when this loop fills it -- recovered it to 1.73-1.87x. Had I banked the first version I would have recorded a real lever at half its worth and wrongly called the bead optimistic. NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE item 28.

NOT a vs-PyTorch row: no incumbent arm, FT-vs-FT maintenance on the vectors phase attributed at 44-62%.

title: Enrich Module register_parameter/register_buffer errors with module type context
description:
## Context
The stub/placeholder audit (2026-04-02) found that Module::register_parameter() and Module::register_buffer() default implementations (ft-nn/src/lib.rs) return `Err(ModuleRegistrationError::Unsupported { operation: "register_parameter" })`.

The error tells you WHAT operation failed but not WHICH module rejected it. When debugging a deep Sequential model with 50+ layers, "register_parameter unsupported" gives no clue about which layer is the problem.

## Current error type
```rust
pub enum ModuleRegistrationError {
    InvalidName { kind: &'static str },
    NameConflict { name: String },
    Unsupported { operation: &'static str },
}
```

## Design decision: How to get the module type name in a trait default

The trait default method signature is `fn register_parameter(&mut self, ...)`. We CANNOT call `std::any::type_name::<Self>()` because the default method has `Self: ?Sized` (it's on `dyn Module`).

**Solution**: Add a new required method to the Module trait:
```rust
fn module_type_name(&self) -> &'static str;
```
This is cheap (one &'static str per impl), gives correct type info even through dyn dispatch, and follows the same pattern PyTorch uses with `_get_name()`.

Each module implementation returns its name: "Linear", "Conv2d", "Sequential", etc.

The default for register_parameter/register_buffer then becomes:
```rust
fn register_parameter(...) -> Result<(), ModuleRegistrationError> {
    Err(ModuleRegistrationError::Unsupported {
        operation: "register_parameter",
        module_type: self.module_type_name(),
    })
}
```

## Plan
1. Add `module_type_name(&self) -> &'static str` to the Module trait (no default — every impl must provide it)
2. Add `module_type: &'static str` field to `ModuleRegistrationError::Unsupported`
3. Update the Display impl to print "{module_type} does not support {operation}"
4. Update default register_parameter/register_buffer to include module_type
5. Add `module_type_name()` to ALL existing Module implementations (~40+ structs):
   - Linear -> "Linear", Conv1d -> "Conv1d", Sequential -> "Sequential", etc.
6. Update any tests that construct or match ModuleRegistrationError::Unsupported

## Testing requirements

### Unit tests (in ft-nn #[cfg(test)])

#### test_unsupported_register_includes_module_type
- Call register_parameter on a module that doesn't override it (e.g., ReLU)
- Assert the error message contains "ReLU"
- Assert the error message contains "register_parameter"

#### test_unsupported_register_buffer_includes_module_type
- Same for register_buffer on a leaf module

#### test_all_modules_have_type_name
- For each major module type (Linear, Conv1d, Conv2d, LSTM, Sequential, etc.):
  - Construct an instance
  - Assert module_type_name() returns a non-empty string
  - Assert module_type_name() does NOT contain "Module" alone (should be specific)

#### test_module_type_name_matches_struct_name
- For a selection of modules, verify that module_type_name() matches the Rust struct name
- E.g., Linear::module_type_name() == "Linear"

#### test_sequential_register_parameter_succeeds
- Verify that Sequential (which DOES support register_parameter) still works correctly
- Construct a Sequential, register a parameter, verify it appears in named_parameter_slots_own()

### E2E validation
- Run `rch exec -- cargo test -p ft-nn` — all existing + new tests pass
- Run `rch exec -- cargo clippy -p ft-nn --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean

## Acceptance Criteria
- Error messages include the module type name (e.g., "ReLU does not support register_parameter")
- ALL Module implementations have module_type_name()
- 5+ new tests covering the enriched error paths
- Existing tests still pass
- Clippy clean

## Risk
Medium — this adds a required trait method to ~40 implementations. Use grep to find all `impl Module for` blocks. Each just needs one line added. Can be parallelized with subagents.

## Dependencies
None — isolated change within ft-nn.
close_reason: ModuleRegistrationError::Unsupported now carries module_type context, default Module registration methods report std::any::type_name::<Self>(), and ft-nn test plus workspace check/clippy passed via rch

title: tensor_interpolate bicubic mode autograd via 16-corner cubic Hermite gather
description:
After frankentorch-3t1t added linear/bilinear/trilinear autograd, bicubic still fails loud. PyTorch's bicubic interpolation uses cubic Hermite spline weights for 4 source pixels per axis (16 total in 2-D). Compose via 16 tensor_index_select calls + non-grad weight tensors + accumulating tensor_add — same partition-of-unity weighted blend as bilinear, just with 16 corners and cubic-Hermite weights.

Per-axis cubic Hermite weights (PyTorch's bicubic_convolution variant, A=-0.75):
  w0 = A*t*(t-1)^2
  w1 = (A+2)*t^3 - (A+3)*t^2 + 1
  w2 = -(A+2)*t^3 + (2A+3)*t^2 - A*t
  w3 = -A*t^2*(t-1)
where t = frac(src). Source pixels are at floor(src) - 1, floor(src), floor(src)+1, floor(src)+2 (clamped).

Affects: crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs tensor_interpolate (line 14674).

title: renorm omits torch's 1e-7 epsilon in the scale denominator
description: tensor_renorm (ft-api ~54094) computes scale = maxnorm / max(norm, maxnorm), i.e. maxnorm/norm when norm>maxnorm with NO epsilon. torch's aten renorm uses factor = (norm > maxnorm) ? maxnorm/(norm + 1e-7) : 1. title: pack_padded_sequence and pad_packed_sequence sever autograd
description:
Both pack_padded_sequence and pad_packed_sequence in ft-nn extract tensor_values from input, manually permute/copy to a new layout, and rebuild via session.tensor_variable(_, _, false). This silently severs autograd through every RNN/LSTM/GRU training pipeline that uses torch.nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence or pad_packed_sequence (which is most of them).

Fix:
- pack_padded_sequence: reshape input to [T*B, F], compute the flat index list (for each timestep t with batch_size bs[t], emit t*B + sorted_indices[s] for s in 0..bs[t]), then call tensor_index_select to gather the rows. Shape back if needed.
- pad_packed_sequence: invert the operation. The packed data has shape [total_elements/F, F]; build a [B*T, F] output by scatter-then-pad. Where each packed row k corresponds to (t, sorted_indices[s]), set output row at orig_batch * T + t. Use tensor_scatter (autograd-aware) and a non-grad fill tensor for padding_value.

Affects: crates/ft-nn/src/lib.rs pack_padded_sequence (line 13364), pad_packed_sequence (line 13490).

title: soft_margin_loss severs autograd; composable through neg/mul/relu/abs/log1p/exp
description:
soft_margin_loss at lib.rs:10423 computes log(1 + exp(-t*x)) per element in plain f64, builds the per-element loss as a requires_grad=false leaf, then takes tensor_mean — but the gradient can no longer reach input or target because the leaf has severed the tape.

Math: with z = -t*x,
   log1p(exp(z)) = max(0, z) + log1p(exp(-|z|))
                 = relu(z) + log1p(exp(-abs(z)))

Composable through autograd-aware primitives:
  z = tensor_mul(tensor_neg(target), input)
  loss_per_elem = tensor_add(tensor_relu(z), tensor_log1p(tensor_exp(tensor_neg(tensor_abs(z)))))
  loss = tensor_mean(loss_per_elem)

Same numerical-stability form, same per-element math, but with the autograd tape preserved.

Sister of frankentorch-ilwr / 4liu (other severed loss functions). Surfaced during /reality-check pass.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Composed soft_margin_loss through neg/mul/relu/abs/log1p/exp/add/mean primitives — same numerical-stability form (relu(z) + log1p(exp(-|z|)) where z = -t*x) but with the autograd tape preserved. Added soft_margin_loss_propagates_gradient_through_input regression test (input=[1,-1], target=[1,-1] under mean loss → analytical [-1/(2(1+e)), 1/(2(1+e))]). ft-api lib tests: 1153.

title: [perf][no-gaps] Direct depthwise conv1d + conv3d kernels (extend 7a924b10 pattern)
description:
EXTEND the conv2d depthwise win (7a924b10, 5.7-8.7x) to conv1d and conv3d, which have the SAME grouped anti-pattern: functional_conv1d_dilated (ft-api ~18938) and functional_conv3d_dilated (~20283) loop over `groups` doing per-group narrow+im2col+GEMM+cat. For depthwise (groups==channels, multiplier 1) that is C tiny per-channel convs. conv1d depthwise = audio/Conformer/WaveNet-style temporal models; conv3d depthwise = video/3D-CNN (more niche, lower priority).

RECIPE (proven on conv2d, copy exactly):
1. ft-kernel-cpu: depthwise_conv1d_forward_f64/f32(padded:[N,C,pL], weight:[C,1,K], bias:[C], batch, channels, pl, k, ol, stride, DILATION) — output[c,ol]=sum_k padded[c, ol*stride + k*dilation]*weight[c,k]+bias[c]; par_chunks_mut over N*C planes. NOTE conv1d goes through the DILATED path so the kernel MUST take a dilation param (tap spacing = dilation; dilation=1 common). conv3d analog: depthwise_conv3d_forward with kd*kh*kw triple loop + 3 dilations.
2. ft-api: no-grad depthwise fast path in functional_conv1d_dilated / functional_conv3d_dilated (detect groups==in_channels && in_per_group==out_per_group==1 && !requires_grad; apply padding via the existing pad helper; call kernel; return non-grad variable). Grad path unchanged.
3. Tests: kernel bit-exact vs naive reference (incl dilation>1, stride>1, bias); the existing functional_conv1d_grouped_matches_torch / conv3d_grouped_matches_torch (tolerance 1e-9) must still pass through the new path.
4. A/B: direct vs per-group-im2col, Score>=2.0 (conv2d got 5.7-8.7x; conv1d/3d similar, scales with channel count).

PARITY: tolerance-disciplined (grouped tests assert .abs()<1e-9 vs torch) — direct kernel valid, no bit-exact-vs-im2col needed. ft-api SHARED-INDEX: isolate dispatch hunk via filtered git apply --cached; rebase --autostash on peer pushes. See [[project_compute_bound_parallel_vein]] GROUPED/DEPTHWISE CONV note + the conv2d commit 7a924b10. ALSO optional: depthwise conv2d BACKWARD kernel (grad path still grouped loop).

title: Severed-autograd in linalg ops: cholesky_solve, linalg_inv, triangular_solve, slogdet, det
description:
After closing matrix_norm (frankentorch-i4rd), several other linalg ops in ft-api still extract values, run a kernel, and rebuild a requires_grad=false leaf — same severed-autograd pattern fixed under frankentorch-1tax for cov / corrcoef / mode etc.

Affected ops:
  - tensor_linalg_inv (lib.rs:11485) — d(A^{-1})/dA: grad_A = -A^{-T} grad_out A^{-T}. Composable via matmul + transpose + neg, with A^{-1} saved.
  - tensor_triangular_solve (lib.rs:11500) — d X / dB = A^{-T}, dX/dA contracted with grad gives an outer-product term masked to the triangular pattern.
  - tensor_cholesky_solve (lib.rs:11453) — chains through cholesky factor; gradient flows through the factor's triangular_solve calls.
  - tensor_linalg_det / tensor_linalg_slogdet — Jacobi formula: d log|det A| / dA = A^{-T}; det case: d det A / dA = det(A) * A^{-T}.

PyTorch's torch.linalg.{inv,solve_triangular,cholesky_solve,det,slogdet} are all differentiable. Surfaced during a /reality-check pass scanning for  and  patterns in linalg op bodies.

Each op gets its own child bead. Priority order based on usage frequency: linalg_inv → triangular_solve → cholesky_solve → det/slogdet.
notes:
All TensorNodeId-returning linalg ops now have autograd:
  - tensor_linalg_inv         frq7 (d364f8e)  — Y^T grad Y^T backward
  - tensor_triangular_solve   skpl (163365f)  — substitution backward
  - tensor_cholesky_solve     this commit     — composes through triangular_solve
  
The det / slogdet ops were originally listed as children but they currently return raw f64 (not TensorNodeId), so they're outside the autograd graph entirely. Adding autograd to them requires an API change (return TensorNodeId), which is a separate concern from the severed-autograd fix this umbrella tracked. Filed as a separate concern if needed.

title: ft-api: f16/bf16 dtype gaps across movement/select ops (upcast or error)
description:
Half-precision (f16/bf16) sweep found many ops that error or upcast (torch supports f16 for all):
UPCAST (wrong dtype): masked_select -> F64; cat -> F32; stack -> F32.
HARD-ERROR ('requires f32 or f64' / UnsupportedDType): gather, where, diagonal, tril, triu, nan_to_num, scatter_add, index_add (and cummax transitively via index_select).
roll/flip/repeat_interleave/unfold/clamp/norm/dist/logsumexp/sort/topk/quantile already preserve f16. Fix in classes: (1) upcast group = dtype preservation (no kernel math needed); (2) error group = relax dtype guard / upcast-compute-narrow per op (many are pure select/copy so dtype-agnostic). Probe: probe_f16_op_gaps.
close_reason: All MOVEMENT/SELECT/PREDICATE f16/bf16 dtype gaps fixed across 8 bit-exact commits: cat/stack 3f7f7bc7, index_select+take+cummax a5332e3c, diagonal/tril/triu f2046f93, masked_select+gather 0bea119a, where 0d2bb62b, comparisons+isnan/isinf 452f41c0, nan_to_num c2c839b3. Each upcasts to f64/f32 (lossless for half), computes, narrows the mask/gathered result back to the input half dtype; all bit-exact (pure copy/select/predicate, no accumulation) + grad-preserving + f32/f64 no-regression, with per-op golden-value tests. REMAINING scatter_add/index_add (arithmetic accumulation) split out to a new P3 bead — they need a torch-CPU f16-accumulation parity decision before implementing (deferred, not mechanical).

title: [parity] masked_select requires same numel; torch broadcasts mask+input
description: tensor_masked_select errors unless input.numel()==mask.numel(); torch.masked_select broadcasts input and mask to a common shape then selects (e.g. input [2,3], mask [2,1] -> selects rows where per-row mask true). Common pattern (select rows by per-row condition). Fix: broadcast both to broadcast_shape(input,mask) via tensor_broadcast_to (autograd-aware) before the existing flatten+index_select; grad flows through broadcast (sums repeats). masked_fill already broadcasts correctly. NOTE separate gap: repeat_interleave only takes usize, not a per-element repeats tensor.

comments.author: QuietCondor
comments.text:
RE-BASELINE DONE for 4 of 5 rows — ledger at artifacts/perf/frankentorch-ug4ep/loss_list_rebaseline_ledger.md.

Harness: cargo bench -p ft-api --bench pytorch_gauntlet_bench (the canonical one — runs the FT and PyTorch arms inside the SAME Criterion group vs pytorch_2_12_cpu), local host, PyTorch CPU sidecar.

  avg_pool1d grad       listed 4-7x slower    -> FT 32.283ms vs PT 6.515ms  = 4.96x SLOWER   CONFIRMED
  BatchNorm2d f32 grad  listed 10x slower     -> FT 29.357ms vs PT 7.831ms  = 3.75x SLOWER   CONFIRMED, smaller
  linear hidden 2048    listed 10.6-12.3x     -> FT  7.131ms vs PT 16.328ms = 2.29x FASTER   STALE, now a WIN
  GroupNorm f32         listed 19x slower     -> FT  3.677ms vs PT 10.821ms = 2.94x FASTER   STALE, now a WIN
  conv2d                listed 4-6x slower    -> NO HARNESS EXISTS          UNVERIFIABLE

EVERY VERDICT IS STATED AGAINST THE WORST CASE FOR FT, because Criterion ran only 10 samples and the PyTorch arms are wide:
  avg_pool1d PT ci [5.628, 7.749] — even at PT's SLOWEST bound FT is 4.2x slower. Real across the whole interval.
  BatchNorm2d PT ci [6.750, 8.914] — even at PT's SLOWEST bound FT is 3.3x slower. Real across the whole interval.
  linear PT ci [12.072, 20.270], the noisiest arm — even at PT's FASTEST bound FT is still 1.69x faster. That is the only reason the win is claimed.
  GroupNorm was measured on a calibrated h2h instead (A/A gate PASS 1.0186 ci95 [0.9489,1.0605], landed-win anchor reading its known 4.13x, executing-ELF SHA recorded).

WHICH ARM YOU QUOTE MATTERS: the BatchNorm2d group has TWO FT arms — kgs4_114 at 50.137ms and kgs4_136_scalar_sum at 29.357ms. Quoting the wrong one turns 3.75x into 6.4x. The listed "10x" predates both.

CONV2D HAS NO EVIDENCE IN THE TREE. pytorch_gauntlet_bench has groups for avg_pool1d, avg_pool2d, batch_norm2d_f32, conv3d, linear, max_pool1d, max_pool3d, sdpa — but NOT conv2d. crates/ft-api/examples/ has only intra-repo conv2d probes (conv2d_f32_grad_ab, conv2d_f32_hessian_probe, conv2d_gradpenalty_probe), which compare FT against FT and say nothing about a PyTorch gap. The "conv2d 4-6x" row should not drive priority until a gauntlet_conv2d_grad group exists. THAT IS THE REMAINING SCOPE OF THIS BEAD — leaving it in_progress for that reason, the other four rows are settled.

CONSEQUENCE FOR PRIORITY: the top perf target is no longer GroupNorm or linear. It is avg_pool1d grad at ~5.0x slower, the only row that reproduced at roughly its listed size. FT arm is frankentorch_kgs4_134_fused_sum_loss; crates/ft-api/examples/avgpool1d_phase_timing.rs already exists to start from.

Three of five rows would have sent an agent to optimize something already FASTER than PyTorch or already largely fixed. Combined with the 189x SVD row earlier this session, that is 3 stale rows out of 6 checked. A loss row is a measurement and measurements expire — re-measure before choosing a lever, and quote the arm and the CI bound rather than the headline. (QuietCondor)

comments.author: QuietCondor
comments.text:
FINAL TABLE — corrected for the allocator. Supersedes the numbers in my previous comment for the two "CONFIRMED" rows.

Those two rows were measured under the DEFAULT allocator, where the harness's per-iteration 32MB input rebuild is served by glibc mmap/munmap and re-faults 8192 pages every iteration. PyTorch's caching allocator never pays that. pytorch_gauntlet_bench already ships a `fair-alloc` feature (mimalloc) documented "for allocator-sensitive FT/PyTorch comparisons"; I had not used it. Re-running under it:

  row                    listed          default alloc        fair-alloc            verdict
  GroupNorm f32          19x slower      2.94x FASTER         (calibrated h2h)      WIN
  linear hidden 2048     10.6-12.3x      2.29x FASTER         -                     WIN
  BatchNorm2d f32 grad   10x slower      3.75x SLOWER         1.21x SLOWER          near parity
  avg_pool1d grad        4-7x slower     4.96x SLOWER         1.92x SLOWER          small real gap
  conv2d                 4-6x slower     NO HARNESS           NO HARNESS            unverifiable

CONTROL that makes the allocator explanation believable rather than convenient: both PyTorch arms are unchanged within noise across the swap (avg_pool1d 6.515->6.025, BatchNorm2d 7.831->6.117). The allocator change moved the FT side and left PyTorch alone, exactly as the mechanism predicts. If the swap had merely been a quiet-machine effect, both arms would have moved.

NOT ONE OF THE FIVE ROWS IS A LARGE REAL LOSS. Two are wins, two are within 2x under a fair allocator, one has no evidence at all. Remaining headroom on this list is ~2x on a single op, not 5-19x across five. Anyone quoting these rows must quote the fair-alloc number, or state plainly that the default-allocator number includes per-iteration mmap/munmap churn PyTorch avoids.

REMAINING SCOPE OF THIS BEAD, unchanged: conv2d still has no vs-PyTorch harness. pytorch_gauntlet_bench covers avg_pool1d, avg_pool2d, batch_norm2d_f32, conv3d, linear, max_pool1d, max_pool3d, sdpa — not conv2d — and crates/ft-api/examples/ has only intra-repo conv2d probes. Staying in_progress for that.

RELATED, recorded not actioned (needs a human decision): should FrankenTorch ship a caching allocator by DEFAULT? PyTorch effectively does. fair-alloc is opt-in and off in normal builds, so real users get the slow path on any workload that repeatedly allocates large buffers — the gauntlet is only unusual in making it visible. Product decision about default behaviour, not a kernel optimization. See the closing comment on frankentorch-uqsit. (QuietCondor)

comments.author: QuietCondor
comments.text:
CONV2D HARNESS BUILT — the last row is resolved, and it is stale too. Closing this bead.

WHAT WAS BUILT: gauntlet_conv2d_grad in crates/ft-api/benches/pytorch_gauntlet_bench.rs + benches/pytorch_conv2d_grad.py. Input 8x64x32x32 against a 64x64x3x3 kernel, stride 1, padding 1, grads on BOTH input and weight, sum() loss. Sized into the same per-iteration cost band as the existing conv3d lane so the group fits Criterion's 3s measurement window (~300 MFLOP forward). Registered in criterion_group! and documented in the file header usage list.

PARITY VERIFIED FIRST, because a timing lane is worthless if the two sides compute different things and the gauntlet groups do NOT assert that themselves. crates/ft-api/examples/conv2d_gauntlet_parity.rs reproduces the lane's exact workload and agrees with the PyTorch script to all 12 printed digits: out shape [8,64,32,32], loss -1.142627639693, x.grad[0] 0.591702728516, w.grad[0] 7.440962005517. Identical on both sides. A padding-convention or shape mismatch would have shown up here as a wrong number instead of as a flattering timing.

RESULT:
  default allocator   FT 23.519ms vs PT 29.814ms  = FT 1.27x FASTER
  fair-alloc          FT 24.148ms vs PT 30.988ms  = FT 1.28x FASTER
Listed as "4-6x SLOWER". It is FASTER. The call holds at the bound that flatters PyTorch most: FT's slowest (23.779) vs PT's fastest (27.734) is still 1.17x in FT's favour.

CONSISTENCY CHECK ON THE ALLOCATOR FINDING: the allocator barely moves this lane (1.27x -> 1.28x), unlike avg_pool1d and BatchNorm2d where it moved 4.96x->1.92x and 3.75x->1.21x. That is not a contradiction, it is the mechanism behaving as predicted: conv2d's input here is 4MB vs those lanes' 32MB, and its compute per iteration is much higher, so per-iteration mmap/munmap churn is a small share of the number. The allocator effect shows up exactly where it should and is absent exactly where it should be.

FINAL TABLE FOR THIS BEAD:
  GroupNorm f32        19x slower      -> 2.94x FASTER
  linear hidden 2048   10.6-12.3x      -> 2.29x FASTER
  conv2d               4-6x slower     -> 1.27x FASTER
  BatchNorm2d f32 grad 10x slower      -> 1.21x slower (parity)
  avg_pool1d grad      4-7x slower     -> 1.92x slower
THREE OF FIVE ROWS ARE WINS, AND NEITHER REMAINING ROW IS A 2x GAP. The loss list as written described a codebase that no longer exists. The largest real vs-PyTorch gap on it is avg_pool1d at 1.92x.

title: [test] GradScaler scale-schedule dynamics via real step()+update() calls (growth timing + overflow backoff/counter-reset)
description: Existing GradScaler tests: grad_scaler_update_grows_after_interval MANUALLY sets steps_since_growth then calls update() (doesn't exercise step()'s counter increment); grad_scaler_skips_step_on_inf_gradient only asserts scale<initial (not the exact backoff factor or that overflow resets the growth counter). Gap: no test drives the torch mixed-precision scale schedule end-to-end through REAL step()+update() calls. Add (1) growth-via-real-steps: with growth_interval=3, the scale stays put for 2 clean steps then doubles on the 3rd, again on the 6th — verifying step() increments steps_since_growth and update() grows at the right cadence; (2) overflow backs off by exactly backoff_factor AND resets a pending growth counter (steps_since_growth->0), matching torch's growth-tracker-reset-on-inf contract.

title: measure(group_norm): h2h lane fails its FT-side A/A null one-sided in 11 of 11 runs — blocks sizing 68pwz
description:
The GroupNorm h2h lanes fail their FrankenTorch-side A/A null in ONE DIRECTION, across
every run of a single binary. Until that is fixed, no GroupNorm-vs-PyTorch ratio from this
harness can be gated, which is what blocks frankentorch-68pwz from being sized.

EVIDENCE — eleven invocations, ONE binary (ELF 1fa33e62b39e125e, build worker vmi1152480),
one host (thinkstation1), harness crates/ft-api/examples/gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h.rs,
balanced-square ABBAABBA 32 rounds, incumbent PyTorch 2.12.1+cpu.

FT-side A/A null for group_norm_f32_kernels, all eleven runs:

    1.159  1.181  1.166  1.178  1.204  1.137  1.185  1.015  1.307  1.158  1.073

Eleven of eleven above 1.0; ten of eleven outside the +/-0.02 band, all on the same side.
group_norm_f32_kernels_serialfwd shows the same shape (ten of eleven above 1.0).

CONTROL, same eleven invocations, prelu_noshortcut:

    1.028  0.950  1.040  1.036  0.980  1.076  1.029  0.996  1.000  1.003  1.031

Straddles 1.0 (four below, seven above) — ordinary host noise. So the bias is not the host
and not the harness as a whole; it is specific to the group_norm lanes.

WHY THIS IS NOT FIXABLE BY RE-RUNNING. A null that fails in random directions averages out
over runs. A null that fails in one direction does not. Under a fair-coin null, eleven
same-side results is p = 2^-11. The single run that DID pass (1.015) is therefore the tail
of a biased distribution, not a clean gate — it is the run you must not trust, and two
GroupNorm candidates taken from it have been withdrawn (NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE item 24b).

WHAT THE SIGN MEANS. FT null > 1 means the FrankenTorch arm's later in-round samples are
slower than its earlier ones — a within-arm ramp. The balanced square cancels a stable
offset BETWEEN arms; it does not cancel a ramp WITHIN one (frankentorch-6atx2). The measured
ratio is therefore biased by an unknown amount in an unknown direction. This is not a
"the true number is probably slightly better" caveat; the lane is unusable in both
directions.

FIRST THINGS TO CHECK, cheapest first:
  - Lane size. The group_norm lanes have the smallest incumbent arm in the sweep by an order
    of magnitude (PT 0.199-0.310 ms, against 1.0 ms for max_pool3d and 10.5 ms for
    max_pool1d). A 0.2 ms torch call is dominated by dispatch overhead. Sizing the lane up
    into the 8-20 ms band where max_pool1d and prelu null cleanly is the obvious first move.
  - Per-round allocation. The GroupNorm lanes allocate f32 statistic buffers per sample;
    if allocator state warms across a round, the later samples of an arm are not comparable
    to the earlier ones.
  - Lane ordering. Confirm whether the ramp tracks position-within-round rather than
    identity-of-arm, by running the lane alone.

NOT CLAIMED: which of these it is. This bead reports a measured defect and its diagnosis as
one-sided, not its cause.

ACCEPTANCE: group_norm_f32_kernels produces an FT-side A/A null that straddles 1.0 across at
least five runs, with at least two runs inside +/-0.02. Only then can 68pwz be sized.
notes:
WARM-UP HYPOTHESIS REFUTED BY ITS OWN KNOB. Item 26e diagnosed the resized lane's failing incumbent null (0.867-0.900, second half faster) as torch still warming inside the measurement, and named raising the warm-up count as the fix. I added FT_H2H_WARMUP (matched on BOTH arms from one variable, default 4, so nothing already banked moves) and tested it.

At 16 iterations -- four times the default -- the null is unchanged: PT null 0.874 FAIL, PT arm 6.561 ms, drift gate PASS. Against 0.867-0.900 at four iterations. Sixteen iterations of the identical work do not absorb it, so it is not a fixed warm-up cost.

WHAT REMAINS, none of which this row separates: the interleaving itself is the cause (our 64-thread bursts between the incumbent's samples -- MossyOtter's item 27 mechanism, which NO amount of warm-up would fix because the perturbation recurs every round); or torch has per-invocation state that resets; or it is frequency/thermal tracking the round structure.

NEXT ACTION, cheap and decisive: run the incumbent arm ALONE at this size with no FrankenTorch lanes in the process. If its null goes clean, the cause is interleaving and this lane needs ISOLATING, not warming -- which would be a harness-shape conclusion, not a group_norm one, and would bear on every short lane in the sweep. NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE item 27c. frankentorch-68pwz stays blocked behind this.
close_reason:
DECIDED, and the answer is that the lane is not the problem. NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE items 26e, 27c, 29e.

The bead was filed because group_norm's FT-side A/A null failed one-sided in 11 of 11 runs. Three things were tried and the diagnosis is now complete:

1. RESIZING (item 26e) fixed OUR arm. 16x larger, incumbent at 6.3-7.5 ms instead of 0.199-0.310, and the FT null went from 1.07-1.31 to 1.024/1.010/1.023. But the INCUMBENT null then began failing one-sided at 0.867-0.900, its second half faster than its first.
2. WARM-UP (item 27c) REFUTED. FT_H2H_WARMUP was added for it, matched on both arms. At 16 iterations -- four times the default -- the null was unchanged at 0.874. Not a fixed prologue cost.
3. ISOLATION (item 29e) DECIDES IT. Running the incumbent arm ALONE at the same shape, no FrankenTorch in the process, no Rust build: null 0.9675 / 1.0369 / 1.0517 across three 64-round runs. STRADDLES 1.0. In-harness it is one-sided at 0.867-0.900 every time.

Same sign test that found the original defect: one-sided means the setup, straddling means noise. Alone torch is clean; interleaved it degrades. CAUSE = the interleaving itself, MossyOtter's item 27 mechanism -- our 64-thread bursts between the incumbent's samples. That explains why warm-up cannot help (the perturbation recurs every round) and why more rounds makes it worse.

CLOSING rather than leaving open because the bead's question -- why does this lane fail its null and what fixes it -- is answered. What remains is NOT a group_norm task: the fix is to measure this lane with arms ISOLATED rather than interleaved, which reintroduces the drift problem interleaving exists to solve (frankentorch-6atx2). That is a harness-shape decision with real costs both ways and belongs to the harness owner. frankentorch-68pwz stays blocked and its blocker is now correctly named.

The standalone probe is kept at crates/ft-api/examples/gn_alone.py so the check is repeatable without a build.

title: [perf] avg_pool1d grad 1.92x slower vs PyTorch (fair-alloc) — the last real loss on the re-baselined list
description:
The ONLY genuine vs-PyTorch loss left on the re-baselined loss list. Everything else on that list
is now a win or parity - see the canonical table in
artifacts/perf/frankentorch-ug4ep/loss_list_rebaseline_ledger.md:

  GroupNorm f32   2.97x FASTER  (listed 19x slower; independently replicated 2026-08-06)
  linear h2048    2.29x FASTER  (listed 10.6-12.3x slower)
  conv2d          1.27x FASTER  (listed 4-6x slower; parity verified to 12 digits)
  BatchNorm2d f32 1.21x slower  (listed 10x; parity under fair-alloc)
  avg_pool1d grad 1.92x slower  <- THIS BEAD

QUOTE THE FAIR-ALLOC NUMBER. Under the default allocator this row reads 4.96x slower, but that
figure includes per-iteration mmap/munmap churn on the harness's own input rebuild, which PyTorch's
caching allocator does not pay. 1.92x is the honest standing (FT 11.560 ms vs PT 6.025 ms).

WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN, so nobody re-derives it:
  - Root-causing via crates/ft-api/examples/avgpool1d_phase_timing.rs put ~43% of the default-alloc
    number in input materialisation and only ~30% in pooling. Splitting PyTorch the same way at
    34 MB gave: materialise 22677us vs 6022us (~3.8x slower), pool fwd+sum+bwd ~9600us vs 6960us
    (~1.4x slower). So the KERNEL is close to parity and the gap is mostly around it.
  - That materialisation term was then shown NOT to be a tensor_variable defect: tensor_variable is
    Arc::new(storage), a move with no copy. It was the probe's own base.clone() re-faulting 8192
    pages under glibc mmap/munmap.
  - frankentorch-3i7c0 STEP 0 criterion (a) measured that a REALISTIC reuse loop still allocates
    64 MiB/step of >=1 MiB blocks, so per-step large-buffer traffic is real and not a bench artifact
    (artifacts/perf/frankentorch-3i7c0/step0_gate_ledger.md).

SO THE LEVER IS PROBABLY NOT THE POOLING KERNEL. Read the ~1.4x kernel figure before optimizing
avg_pool1d itself; a lever aimed at the kernel is chasing the smaller half of a 1.92x gap.

CONTRACT: live PyTorch arm in the SAME invocation, A/A null gate, executing-ELF SHA-256,
median-CI decision, quoted under --features fair-alloc. A rejected lever gets ONE negative-evidence
ledger entry with a retry predicate.
close_reason:
RE-CHARACTERIZED AND CLOSED: this is NOT an avg_pool1d op loss. Landed ae14c0b0.

Splitting BOTH sides like-for-like, input built outside the timed region on both arms. Medians of

decision was option C: the library must not impose a process-global allocator on its consumers.

nothing, and costs 5 MICROSECONDS. The copy is the caller's (here the harness's base.to_vec(),
mirroring the torch script's base.detach().clone()).

title: [perf] max_pool3d dense-gradient scatter: the ~1.2 ms is NOT first-touch faults — attribute it before any lever
description:
frankentorch-zoqws established what this cost is NOT, and reverted the lever built on the wrong
model. This bead is the replacement question, filed rather than guessed at.

THE TERM: max_pool3d_backward_from_indices_f64 on [2,32,16,32,32] f64 (8 MiB dense gradient) spends
~1.35 ms, of which the par_chunks_mut scatter pass is the overwhelming majority. 87sz8 attributed
84 pct of the backward to "materialising the dense gradient" and modelled that as contended
first-touch page faults on fresh alloc_zeroed mmap pages.

THAT MODEL IS NOW REFUTED AT THIS CALL SITE (artifacts/perf/frankentorch-zoqws/in_situ_ab.md).
Inserting a serial fill(0.0) to pay the first touch cheaply made the kernel 1.118x SLOWER
(95 pct CI [1.050, 1.183], 11/12 rounds, +0.152 ms) and reduced the parallel pass by NOTHING. The
added cost was almost exactly one serial 8 MiB write. If the pass were fault-bound, a preceding
serial touch would have absorbed it.

SO: where does the ~1.2 ms go? Unknown. Candidates worth separating, none of them established:
  - genuine DRAM traffic for an 8 MiB read-modify-write scatter, in which case this is bandwidth-
    bound and the honest answer is a ledgered bound, not a lever (compare the memory ledger's
    "bandwidth-bound frontier" entry, which says remaining serial ops are DRAM-bound at <2x)
  - the scatter's ACCESS PATTERN: drow[arg] += with arg read from an f64 offsets array is a
    dependent load plus a random-ish write per output element; that is not the same cost as a
    streaming write even at identical byte counts
  - the f64-to-usize conversion per element (arg_offsets is f64, one cast per scattered value)
  - rayon task granularity at 64 planes over 64 threads

FIRST STEP, and it should be attribution rather than a lever: instrument the pass to separate
(a) touching every page with no scatter, (b) the scatter with the offsets pre-converted to usize,
(c) the full pass. That partitions bandwidth vs access pattern vs conversion. Only then choose.

METHOD CONSTRAINTS, learned the hard way on zoqws and not optional here:
  - measure IN SITU. A standalone-buffer ladder gave the opposite answer to the real call site,
    because the standalone arms differed in ALLOCATOR WARMTH and a kernel called in a loop gets a
    recycled block.
  - interleave arms and carry at least one control lane compiled identically into both binaries.
    Flat controls with a moving primary is the only thing that distinguished signal from a load
    swing here.
  - be suspicious of any measurement of a redundant write: a fill(0.0) over alloc_zeroed memory may
    be elided by LLVM entirely, which would make the row measure nothing. Step 0's 36.70 GiB/s
    serial-fill row is unverified in exactly this way.

WHY IT MATTERS: max_pool3d is the largest remaining confirmed vs-PyTorch gap (re-measured 4.66x on
2026-08-08, down from the 9.39x in 87sz8's title), and avg_pool2d (2.01x) pays the same term. But
note the possibility this bead has to stay honest about: the answer may be that the term is a real
memory-bandwidth floor and the correct outcome is a documented bound with no code change.
close_reason: Attributed and fixed. The ~1.2 ms is the PARALLELISM itself, not first-touch faults, not the RMW read, not the f64->usize cast (both of the latter came back NEGATIVE, inside the A/A null). Mechanism is the per-CCD L3 slice (32 MiB on this Threadripper), not NUMA (single node here - checked). Landed a 16 MiB size gate on max_pool3d_backward_from_indices_f64, placed inside the 24-32 MiB crossover because the risk is asymmetric (serial wins 1.35x at 24, loses 5.9x at 32). In-kernel two-ELF A/B: raw_bwd 1.389 -> 0.321 ms, paired median 4.24x faster, CI [0.214,0.255], 12/12 rounds, three identical-in-both-ELFs controls flat. Bit-exact and mutation-verified. Commits 115fb4c2 + 5d95c23d. NO vs-PyTorch ratio claimed - the lane must be re-measured against torch, which belongs to 87sz8. Sibling call sites deliberately untouched.

THE ANSWER: the cost is the PARALLELISM itself. All three candidates this bead listed are settled:
  - DRAM traffic / access pattern   -> not the story on its own
  - the RMW read ('=' vs '+=')      -> NEGATIVE, within the A/A null

MECHANISM, and it is a CACHE boundary, not the NUMA one I first guessed (this host reports a single
NUMA node; I checked rather than shipping the guess). Size sweep of the same 1-in-8 shape:

32 MiB (Threadripper PRO 5975WX), so one thread effectively has 32 MiB. Below it the buffer is
L3-resident and spreading it over four CCDs only adds cross-CCD traffic.

LANDED: a 16 MiB size gate on max_pool3d_backward_from_indices_f64. NOT at the 24-32 crossover, because
the risk is ASYMMETRIC — serial wins 1.35x at 24 MiB but LOSES 5.9x at 32.

IN-KERNEL A/B (two ELFs differing only in the gate, 12 paired rounds, interleaved, lead arm alternating):
  A 090f0cbc always-parallel  raw_bwd 1.389 ms
  B 3a748f13 gated -> serial  raw_bwd 0.321 ms
  paired median 0.236 = 4.24x FASTER, bootstrap 95pct CI [0.214, 0.255], 12/12 rounds faster,
  lead-arm split 0.236/0.235, three identical-in-both-ELFs controls flat (0.958, 0.980, 1.044).

 1. The probe predicted ~2x; in situ is 4.24x. The difference is allocator conditioning — the

    way a training step does, and the parallel arm suffers more from that. 4.24x is the realistic

    conditioner plus a rotating start lane; A/A then read 12.0% / 0.3% / 15.6%. GENERALISES: any probe

plain store in place of the accumulate made it fail exactly there (left 9223372036854775808 = 0x8000...,

title: [perf] tensor_variable input materialization ~3.8x slower than torch clone — dominates several gauntlet 'op' losses
description:
ROOT CAUSE found while scoping the avg_pool1d row (frankentorch-ug4ep). The avg_pool1d gauntlet gap is mostly NOT avg_pool1d.

Phase split of the [8,64,8192] f64 avg_pool1d train step (crates/ft-api/examples/avgpool1d_phase_timing.rs):
  tensor_variable  22677 us  43%   <-- largest phase
  forward          13247 us  25%
  backward          9566 us  18%
  sum                474 us   1%
  TOTAL            53081 us
For the fused arm the gauntlet actually times (32.283ms), tensor_variable is ~70% of the number.

The gauntlet builds its input INSIDE b.iter (values.clone() + session.tensor_variable(...)). That is not automatically unfair — the PyTorch script rebuilds its input inside its loop too (base.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)). What differs is the COST. Same 34 MB, torch.set_num_threads(8):
  materialise input:      FT 22677us  vs  torch 6022us  = ~3.8x SLOWER
  pool fwd+sum+bwd:       FT ~9600us  vs  torch 6960us  = ~1.4x SLOWER
CAVEAT bounding the claim: torch was pinned to 8 threads while the FT probe used the box default, and the gauntlet gives torch 32 threads (FT_TORCH_THREADS defaults to 32). Indicative shares, not certified ratios. The conclusion survives it comfortably.

WHY THIS IS THE HIGHER-LEVERAGE TARGET: tensor_variable is not an avg_pool1d cost. Every gauntlet lane that builds its input inside b.iter pays it — avg_pool2d and batch_norm2d are written the same way — so it sits inside several 'op losses', including the BatchNorm2d 3.75x row confirmed in ug4ep. Optimizing avg_pool1d moves ~30% of that row; optimizing tensor_variable moves ~70% of it AND part of the others. It also means the remaining confirmed op-level gaps are SMALLER than the gauntlet headlines suggest.

LEVER HYPOTHESIS (unverified, read the code before trusting it): 34 MB in 22.7 ms is ~1.5 GB/s, far below memcpy speed for a copy that size. That smells like an extra copy and/or a SERIAL FIRST-TOUCH fill — the same anti-pattern already fixed once in expand/broadcast_to, where vec![v; numel] serial first-touch was the wall and the fix was an uninit buffer whose PARALLEL fill does the first touch (see the expand-uninit-first-touch work). Check whether tensor_variable copies values twice (caller clone -> session storage) and whether its allocation is zero-filled serially before being overwritten.

SCOPE: profile tensor_variable directly, find the copies, remove the dead ones, make the surviving fill parallel/first-touch-correct. Bit-exactness is trivially preserved (it is a copy). Verify with the avgpool1d phase probe (tensor_var phase should drop) and re-run the avg_pool1d + batch_norm2d gauntlet lanes.

Ledger: artifacts/perf/frankentorch-ug4ep/loss_list_rebaseline_ledger.md (QuietCondor)
close_reason: Premise refuted by reading the code: tensor_variable is an Arc move with no copy. The cost was the harness's own 32MB Vec::clone re-faulting 8192 pages under glibc malloc, which the in-tree fair-alloc (mimalloc) feature already addresses — avg_pool1d 4.96x->1.92x, BatchNorm2d 3.75x->1.21x, PyTorch arms unchanged as control. No code change warranted.

comments.author: QuietCondor
comments.text:
PREMISE REFUTED — closing. I filed this bead on a hypothesis and reading the code disproves it. No code change was made because none is warranted.

THE HYPOTHESIS WAS WRONG. tensor_variable -> tape.leaf -> DenseTensor::from_contiguous_values -> from_storage -> TensorStorage::F64(Arc::new(storage)). That is a MOVE into an Arc. It performs no copy, has no fill, no first-touch, and nothing to optimize. The "extra copy and/or serial first-touch fill" I predicted does not exist on this path.

WHAT THE 22677us ACTUALLY WAS. The phase probe times `base.clone()` and `tensor_variable(...)` in ONE region and labels it tensor_var. The cost is entirely the clone: a fresh 32MB Vec<f64> allocation plus memcpy. Under glibc malloc an allocation that size is served by mmap and released by munmap on drop, so EVERY ITERATION RE-FAULTS ALL 8192 PAGES. That is the ~1.5 GB/s. PyTorch never pays it because its caching allocator returns the same warm block each iteration. Real asymmetry, but first-touch page-fault churn in the harness's input rebuild — not a tensor-code defect.

ALREADY SOLVED IN-TREE. pytorch_gauntlet_bench documents a `fair-alloc` feature (mimalloc) "for allocator-sensitive FT/PyTorch comparisons". I had not used it. Re-running the two confirmed rows:
  avg_pool1d grad      default: FT 32.283 vs PT 6.515 = 4.96x SLOWER  ->  fair-alloc: FT 11.560 vs PT 6.025 = 1.92x SLOWER
  BatchNorm2d f32 grad default: FT 29.357 vs PT 7.831 = 3.75x SLOWER  ->  fair-alloc: FT  7.408 vs PT 6.117 = 1.21x SLOWER
CONTROL: both PyTorch arms are unchanged within noise (6.5->6.0, 7.8->6.1). The allocator swap moved the FT side and left PyTorch alone, which is exactly what the mechanism predicts and is the reason I believe it.

CONSEQUENCE FOR ug4ep's TABLE: not one of the five loss rows is a large real loss. GroupNorm 2.94x FASTER, linear 2.29x FASTER, BatchNorm2d 1.21x slower (near parity), avg_pool1d 1.92x slower, conv2d unverifiable. Remaining headroom on that list is ~2x on one op, not 5-19x across five.

WHAT I GOT WRONG AND THE GENERALIZABLE LESSON: I inferred a lever from a phase-timing label without reading what the phase contained, then filed a P1 bead on it. The label said tensor_variable; the region also held a 32MB clone. READ WHAT A TIMED REGION ACTUALLY CONTAINS BEFORE ATTRIBUTING ITS COST TO THE NAMED CALL — a phase name is a comment, not evidence. The correct order was: read the callee, THEN believe the phase split.

LEFT FOR A HUMAN, recorded not actioned: should FrankenTorch ship a caching allocator by default? PyTorch effectively does. fair-alloc is opt-in and off in normal builds, so real users get the slow path on any workload that repeatedly allocates large buffers — the gauntlet is only unusual in making it visible. That is a product decision about default behaviour, not a kernel optimization.

Ledger: artifacts/perf/frankentorch-ug4ep/loss_list_rebaseline_ledger.md (QuietCondor)

title: [latent][autograd] cg_pow takes a TENSOR exponent but records only element 0 — silent wrong gradients for any non-uniform caller
description:
`TensorTape::cg_pow(base, exponent: TensorNodeId)` (ft-autograd, create_graph helper) computes the forward per-element correctly:

    let result = base_data.iter().zip(exp_data.iter()).map(|(&b, &e)| b.powf(e)).collect();

but then records the tape node as a SCALAR-exponent op:

    let exp_val = exp_data[0];
    ...
    op: TensorNodeOp::Pow { input: base, exponent: exp_val },

So for a non-uniform exponent tensor the FORWARD is right and the recorded op is wrong, and the backward would differentiate every element as if its exponent were element 0's. Silently — no shape error, no dtype error, just wrong gradients.

NOT CURRENTLY TRIGGERED. All three call sites pass a uniform-fill constant leaf and are safe:
  16039  cg_pow(input, exp_m1_node)   exp_m1_node = leaf(vec![exponent - 1.0; numel])   [Pow cg backward]
  16539  cg_pow(one_minus, half)      half = leaf(vec![0.5; numel])                     [asin cg backward]
  16557  cg_pow(one_minus, half)      same                                              [acos cg backward]
Verified by reading each site, not assumed from the fill pattern.

WHY IT IS WORTH CLOSING NOW RATHER THAN LEAVING AS A CURIOSITY: frankentorch-v8f5k needs a real tensor-exponent pow, and cg_pow is exactly the function its implementer will find and reach for — it is already named 'pow', already takes a tensor exponent, and already does the correct elementwise powf. Reusing it with a genuinely non-uniform exponent is the natural next step and is silently wrong. The trap is aimed squarely at the next person to work in this file.

FIX SHAPE: make the signature honest by taking `exponent: f64`. Every caller constructs a uniform leaf solely to pass it, so this removes the collapse entirely, deletes three numel-sized leaf allocations, and makes the recorded TensorNodeOp::Pow accurate by construction rather than by caller discipline. A tensor-exponent pow should then be a genuinely separate op (that is v8f5k), not this one bent into the role.

Found while sizing v8f5k.
close_reason: Fixed in 51f4b175: cg_pow takes a scalar f64; the recorded Pow op can no longer disagree with a non-uniform exponent tensor. Workspace 5420/0, create_graph 96/0, clippy rc=0.

All three call sites rewritten to pass the scalar directly (exponent - 1.0 in the Pow arm; 0.5 in the asin and acos arms), which also deletes three numel-sized uniform-fill leaves that existed only to carry one value. Incidental, and I make no perf claim about it.

title: [perf] split avg_pool2d/max_pool3d 'tape_overhead' into its four parts before choosing a lever
description:
frankentorch-k1h8g established that avg_pool2d's gap is NOT in its kernels (62-93% of the lane sits
outside them; artifacts/perf/frankentorch-k1h8g/kernels_are_not_the_gap.md). But "tape_overhead" is
currently ONE number covering at least four different costs, and attacking it as a unit would repeat
the mistake frankentorch-8obhh just made with "the dense write".

WHAT tape_overhead CURRENTLY CONFLATES, for the [8,64,64,64] f64 avg_pool2d lane (16 MiB input):
  1. FrankenTorchSession construction (a fresh session per timed iteration in the probe)
  2. leaf materialisation — tensor_variable copies the 16 MiB input
  3. the autograd tape itself — node recording, DAC evidence, gradient slot allocation
  4. the gradient reduction — rep.gradient(x) plus a 16 MiB .iter().sum()

Only (3) is "the tape" in the sense the campaign cares about. (1), (2) and (4) are harness framing and
would not appear in a real training step that reuses a session and does not sum the gradient.

THE TASK: extend crates/ft-api/examples/pool_kernel_vs_tape_probe.rs with lanes that time these
separately — e.g. session-construction-only, leaf-build-only, forward-only-with-tape, backward-only,
gradient-fetch-and-sum-only — so the residual attributable to the tape proper is isolated. Then decide
a lever, if any.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS LANE: max_pool3d shows the same shape (62-69% outside the kernels), and
frankentorch-8obhh's post-mortem concluded the tape's live working set is what invalidated a
buffer-size cache predictor. If the tape is both the dominant cost AND the thing that breaks kernel
heuristics, it is the highest-value target left on these lanes — but only once it is split.

ALREADY-KNOWN RELATED ISSUE, check before assuming a new discovery: the ledger's
project_gmuml_tape_retention records that the session tape never frees nodes, so no-grad forwards
degrade linearly. If that retention affects this path it could explain a large constant per-session
cost, and it is separately tracked rather than new.

METHOD CONSTRAINTS (from zoqws / un3os / o5t00 / 8obhh, all learned the hard way):
 - FT-vs-FT attribution needs no torch arm; keep it that way so it is cheap to re-run.
 - condition the allocator before each timed region and carry an A/A pair at different positions in
   the interleave, or the probe measures its own lane order (that veto fired at 83% once).
 - any LEVER that comes out of this must be A/B'd at the LANE (two ELFs vs one upstream arm, plus a
   lane the change cannot touch as a negative control), NOT only in isolation. 8obhh is the cautionary
   case: 4.24x in the kernel, 1.13x SLOWER at the lane.
close_reason: RE-MEASURED WITH CONDITIONING: the conclusion survives, the number was 2x inflated (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). Artifact: artifacts/perf/frankentorch-uufyp/conditioned_decomposition.md. Three runs with condition_allocator() before every timed rep plus an A/A null lane (1.5%/13.7%/13.2%, versus 83% unconditioned; the bare-clone control is now 61-105% of its container instead of 164-234%, i.e. physical). Stages: session_new 0.001/0.000/0.001 (free) | leaf_build 0.828/0.976/0.783 (bare clone 0.659/0.597/0.826) | forward 1.234/1.048/1.440 | BACKWARD 5.620/6.024/5.063 | sum 0.510/0.618/1.243 | grad_fetch_sum 1.102/0.769/1.255 | total 9.294/9.434/9.785. CORRECTED: session 16.3-17.1 -> 9.3-9.8 ms; backward 10.9-11.8 -> 5.1-6.0 ms; backward/kernel ~34x -> ~18x; backward share ~65-70% -> ~55-60%. Roughly HALF the original 11 ms was allocator first-touch, not engine work; the 34x is withdrawn and replaced with ~18x. WHAT HOLDS: tensor_backward is still the dominant stage (more than the other five combined) and still ~18x the kernel it dispatches, which is the fact that redirected k1h8g away from ft-kernel-cpu — an 18x gap redirects exactly as well as a 34x one. session_new free and leaf_build = clone are unchanged (both were already same-size comparisons). Nothing downstream needs revisiting; no lever was built on the 34x. CAVEAT: host load 82-143 during these runs; the three agree within ~16% with sane A/A nulls, which argues the conditioning made it robust, but absolute ms should be re-taken quiet — the ~18x RATIO is the durable claim. Where the 5.6 ms goes INSIDE the backward remains open in 27aci, now from a trustworthy baseline.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: REOPENED — MY HEADLINE NUMBER HERE IS NOT DEFENSIBLE (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08). See artifacts/perf/frankentorch-27aci/spike_is_a_harness_artifact.md. The follow-up sweep (27aci) shows the backward-stage cost tracks WHETHER A SIZE IS THE LARGEST YET ALLOCATED IN THE PROCESS, not the shape: N=8 reads 11.9 ms ascending and 1.8 ms descending, a 6.5x swing on identical work. This decomposition has NO allocator conditioning and no A/A null lane, and its backward lane is the first in the cumulative chain to allocate the 16 MiB gradient buffer — so an unknown, possibly dominant share of the '11 ms / 34x' is first-touch for a not-yet-seen allocation size rather than autograd engine work. NOT disproven: the backward may still be the largest term once conditioned. But the 34x is withdrawn as a quotable figure until the lanes carry condition_allocator() plus an A/A pair at different chain positions. The other results here stand — session_new is free and leaf_build is a bare clone are both same-size comparisons, not absolute first-touch costs.

title: ft-api: scatter_add/index_add f16/bf16 (arithmetic accumulation — needs parity decision)
description: scatter_add and index_add reject f16/bf16 ('requires f32 or f64 tensors'). Unlike the movement/select ops (closed under u78p), these ACCUMULATE (out[idx] += src), so the upcast-to-f64-accumulate-then-narrow approach used for gather/index_select is NOT necessarily bit-exact to torch: torch's f16 scatter_add rounds per-add (or uses an fp32 acc_type internally). REQUIRED FIRST: determine torch CPU's exact f16 scatter_add accumulation semantics (per-add half rounding vs fp32 accumulate), then implement to match. Until that parity decision is made this stays deferred — do NOT ship a rounding-divergent accumulation. Probe: probe_f16_op_gaps (in earlier u78p worktrees).
notes: RESOLVED the parity question (219ba55c). Installed torch 2.12.0+cpu, probed CPU half accumulation over 200 random trials/dtype: scatter_add = fp32-accumulate-then-narrow (acc_type<Half>=float); index_add & index_put(accumulate=true) = per-add HALF rounding (DIFFERENT). Discriminator: 1.0 + 10*f16(0.0003) -> scatter_add 1.0029, index_add 1.0. scatter_add f16/bf16 SHIPPED (upcast->f32, f32 kernel, narrow; bit-exact golden test vs torch). index_add/index_put-accumulate split to follow-up bead (per-add-half kernel) — they keep their own gates so they stay correctly rejected for now.

description:
Two simple activations missing from the functional ft-api:
  - tanhshrink(x) = x - tanh(x). Compose via tensor_tanh + tensor_sub.
  - softsign(x) = x / (1 + |x|). Compose via tensor_abs + tensor_add + tensor_div.

title: tensor_scatter_reduce mean mode autograd via scatter_add + count + div
description:
After frankentorch-dhm4 added autograd to scatter_reduce sum mode, the mean mode still fails loud. Compose mean via two scatter_adds:
1. count_tensor = scatter_add(zeros, dim, index, ones_like_src) — number of hits per output position
2. sum_tensor = scatter_add(input, dim, index, src) — input + sum of mapped src
3. divisor = count_tensor + 1 (the +1 accounts for the original input)
4. output = sum_tensor / divisor

For positions not hit (count=0), divisor=1 → output = input/1 = input, matching include_self=True semantics.

Affects: crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs tensor_scatter_reduce (line 16249).

title: ft-api: modified Bessel I-family upgraded to Cephes f64 precision
description: i0/i0e/i1/i1e used single-precision Abramowitz-Stegun polynomials (~1.6e-7 rel) — an ~8-orders regression vs torch (Cephes f64). title: [perf][svd] square full_matrices=true is gated OUT of both square fast paths, though square full == reduced
notes:
SHIPPED in cb9c7cc7. The gate was real and it cost 1.52-1.60x.

MEASURED, same process, both arms, min of 3, rch worker vmi1227854, harness
crates/ft-kernel-cpu/examples/svd_scale_probe.rs:

       n      reduced ns         full ns  full/reduced  fast paths eligible
      48          701780          666339         0.95x  neither (control)
      64          565868          904545         1.60x  reduced only
      96         1431886         2234549         1.56x  reduced only
     128         2778443         4233284         1.52x  reduced only

The n=48 control is what makes this readable: below the n>=64 threshold neither
call is eligible and the ratio is 0.95x, so "full is inherently slower for square"
is excluded by measurement, not argument. Paired within-process ratio, so it
survives worker heterogeneity.

ANSWERING THIS BEAD'S OWN THREE QUESTIONS:
1. Correct for square full_matrices? YES, and proved structurally rather than
   argued: svd_square_full_matrices_matches_reduced_bitwise_across_the_fast_path_gate
   asserts bit-for-bit agreement at n=48/64/96, and that test WOULD HAVE FAILED
   before the change since the two paths ran different algorithms.
2. Actually faster? Yes, 1.52-1.60x, with a control.
3. Parity standard? The bead predicted this would need the ratified tolerance
   policy because the algorithm changes. IT DOES NOT. For square inputs the fast
   path is now what BOTH calls take, so full and reduced are bit-identical to each
   other. Only the full call's output moves relative to its own past, and it moves
   onto the reduced path's values, which were already the shipped answer for the
   same decomposition. No tolerance relaxation was needed or taken.

The after-timing is deliberately NOT banked: the post-change probe ran on a
contended worker (725s vs 191s) and read 0.91/1.15/1.42x, which cannot be right
when the outputs are bit-identical from one code path. Noise.

GATE WITH ITS HOLE STATED: 633/0 on the full kernel-cpu lib; 4/0 on ft-api's
narrow linalg_svd filter (hz2); the wider ft-api svd filter (25 tests) hit the
1800s SSH limit and was not re-obtained, so consumer-side coverage is PARTIAL.

title: Autograd tensor tape grows unbounded — no node free/clear (memory leak)
description: TensorTape (crates/ft-autograd/src/lib.rs:4165) pushes a TensorNode for EVERY op and never frees them. Each node owns a DenseTensor (the full tensor data). There is NO clear/truncate/reset/free API and the only handling is a / flag set after backward(!retain_graph) at ~3980 that does NOT free nodes. Consequences: (1) INFERENCE/forward-only loops leak forever — under no_grad the push still happens (only requires_grad is gated, line ~1569/1577), nodes accumulate with the tensor data; (2) TRAINING leaks across steps unless the whole session is dropped (no per-step graph free). Affects every long-running workload. Verified: grep finds zero nodes.clear/truncate/drain; node access is via 382 scattered self.nodes[id.0] sites (no central accessor). FIX (multi-turn, architectural): NodeId is a flat-arena index, so a naive clear() reuses index 0 and ALIASES stale handles -> use offset/generational indexing: add base_offset (vec_idx = id.0 - base; id.0 < base => StaleHandle error), route the 382 accesses through a single checked accessor, then clear() does base += len; nodes.clear() (also truncate the parallel gradients/gradient_nodes Vecs + drop retains_grad entries >= boundary). That enables a SAFE session.clear_autograd_graph() (inference, between requests) and truncate_to(boundary) (training, keep param leaves at low indices, free per-step graph after optimizer.step()). Mirrors the EvidenceLedger leak fix (2f820623) but harder due to live handles. Interim mitigation shipped: session-level node-count observability so consumers can monitor growth + recreate the session before OOM.
close_reason: Fixed in d831f0e0: added TensorTape::truncate_graph_to(boundary)/clear_graph() + session truncate_autograd_graph/clear_autograd_graph. Reclaims the append-only arena (nodes + persistent_grads/tensor_hooks/retains_grad) without touching the 382 access sites; purely additive (default behavior unchanged, all tests pass). Callers capture node_count() after model init then truncate after each step/request. Mechanism shipped; fully-automatic free-after-backward could be a future enhancement but the API is the correct primitive (mirrors PyTorch graph-freed-after-backward).

title: [parity-gap] ft-nn Embedding missing padding_idx and max_norm
description: EmeraldPine audit (2026-05-20). nn.Embedding (crates/ft-nn/src/lib.rs:2396-2443) has no padding_idx (PyTorch zeroes that weight row and returns the zero vector + zero gradient for it) and no max_norm (PyTorch renormalizes any embedding row whose L2 norm exceeds max_norm, in-place, on forward).
