title: [parity][rrelu][f32] tensor_rrelu has no dtype guard and its helper hardcodes F64 output
close_reason:
CONFIRMED and fixed in ee021c22. The bead's suspicion was right and the failure was the HARDER of the two it predicted.

VERIFIED BY PROBE, not by reading the helper (rch worker vmi1293453, exit=101):
  s.tensor_rrelu(f32_tensor, 0.125, 1.0/3.0) -> Err(DenseTensor(UnsupportedDType(F32)))
It does NOT silently return f64 — it errors outright, while torch's F.rrelu accepts float32 and returns float32.

Mechanism confirmed as filed: tensor_apply_function_f64_borrowed_inputs reads inputs via contiguous_values() (the f64 accessor) and builds output meta as TensorMeta::from_shape(shape, DType::F64, device), so the dtype is hardcoded. relu6 and selu both carry an explicit upcast-compute-narrow guard for exactly this reason (frankentorch-x9yuq); rrelu had none.

FIX: the same guard at the top of tensor_rrelu — upcast to F64, recurse, narrow back to the input dtype. The F64 path is byte-identical (the guard is dt != F64), and the x > 0 convention from frankentorch-3eq5b survives the recursion.

TEST: rrelu_preserves_f32_dtype asserts output dtype == F32, the forward values (x > 0 keeps, else multiplies), and that the gradient survives the same route with x == 0 still taking the slope branch.

GATES: cargo test -p frankentorch-api --lib rrelu -> 3 passed / 0 failed (vmi1153651); full cargo test -p frankentorch-api --lib -> 2566 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored, REAL_EXIT=0 (vmi1153651). fmt clean. No timed rows banked.

STILL OPEN — the bead's last paragraph is NOT done and is worth its own sweep: every OTHER caller of tensor_apply_function_f64_borrowed_inputs that lacks a dtype guard has this same latent defect. I fixed rrelu only. Grep for the helper and check each call site rather than assuming rrelu was the only one; the helper's hardcoded DType::F64 output meta makes this a systematic hazard, not a one-off.

title: EvidenceLedger.entries grows unbounded — inference memory leak
description: ft-runtime EvidenceLedger.record() (crates/ft-runtime/src/lib.rs:39) pushes one heap-allocated EvidenceEntry{ts_unix_ms, kind, summary:String} per op into an unbounded Vec, via all 203 record_tensor_* callers in ft-api. title: [parity][prelu] backward and forward use x>=0 where torch uses x>0; gradients wrong at exactly zero
description:
Found by the new gauntlet prelu lane (frankentorch-k1hto), which reported parity MISMATCH on BOTH the shortcut and the materialized control arms — i.e. the defect predates the deforest lever and lives in the shared convention.

torch computes prelu as where(input > 0, input, weight*input), and its backward gives grad_x = weight_c at input == 0. FrankenTorch uses x >= 0.0 in prelu_forward_values, prelu_forward_values_f32, the tensor_prelu grad-path backward (both the parallel and serial branches) and the PreluSumShortcut backward, so it returns grad_x = upstream at input == 0.

Measured on the lane's own input ([32,512,256], seq() = ((i%251) as f64)*0.001-0.12, which lands on exactly 0.0 once every 251 elements): 16710 exact zeros, sum|grad_x| 2289801.5457 under the FrankenTorch convention vs 2273931.45 under torch's, a difference of 15870 against a 2.27 parity tolerance. Verified against torch 2.12.1+cpu: F.prelu grad_x at [-1,0,1] with w=0.25 is [0.25,0.25,1.0].

The forward differs too, but only in the sign of zero and only for a negative weight: torch prelu(+0.0) with w=-0.25 is -0.0 and prelu(-0.0) is +0.0, while FrankenTorch passes the input through unchanged.

grad_w is already correct — both sides accumulate only where x < 0, and an x == 0 element contributes upstream*0 either way.

Fix: use x > 0.0 in every prelu forward and backward path (f64 and f32, session op, functional, in-place, nn module route), then re-run the gauntlet prelu lane and expect parity match.
close_reason:
Fixed: prelu now compares x > 0 everywhere, matching torch's where(input > 0, input, weight*input).

Sites changed (crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs): prelu_forward_values, prelu_forward_values_f32, the tensor_prelu grad-path backward (parallel AND serial grad_x branches), and the PreluSumShortcut backward. The serial branch was split into two predicates so grad_x turns on x > 0 while grad_w still accumulates only on x < 0, keeping it bit-identical to the parallel branch. crates/ft-nn/src/lib.rs PReLU::forward composed the op independently through tensor_ge; that is now tensor_gt.

New regression test prelu_zero_input_takes_the_weight_branch_like_torch pins the scalar, per-channel, signed-zero-forward, and both >=65_536-element parallel branches (with and without the sum shortcut) against values read from torch 2.12.1+cpu.

title: multi_margin_loss severs autograd; composable through gather/relu/pow/mask
description:
multi_margin_loss at lib.rs:10450 computes per-sample sum_{j != y} relu(margin - input[i,y] + input[i,j])^p / classes, accumulates in plain f64, and rebuilds a requires_grad=false leaf — silently severing autograd for multi-class margin training paths.

PyTorch's torch.nn.functional.multi_margin_loss IS differentiable (sub-gradient at the relu hinge). Compose through autograd primitives:
  mask_y = one_hot(target, classes)                                  # [batch, classes]
  mask_others = 1 - mask_y
  score_y = sum(input * mask_y, dim=1, keepdim=True)                 # [batch, 1]
  score_y_b = expand to [batch, classes]
  diff = (margin scalar) + input - score_y_b
  per_elem = relu(diff) * mask_others                                # zero at j == y
  per_elem_p = per_elem^p
  loss = mean(sum(per_elem_p, dim=1)) / classes

Sister of the recent loss-severance cluster (ilwr / 4liu / tr2a). Surfaced during /reality-check pass.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Composed multi_margin_loss through one_hot + relu + pow + sum_dim + mean primitives. The mask_others = 1 - one_hot(target) handles the j != y exclusion via element-wise multiplication. score_y is gathered via input * mask_y then summed (instead of integer indexing). The forward shape contract is preserved; existing value tests continue to pass. Added multi_margin_loss_propagates_gradient_through_input regression test (input=[[0,3]], target=[0], p=1, margin=1 → analytical [-0.5, 0.5]). ft-api lib tests: 1154.

title: Add fail-loud guards for FFT ops with requires_grad
description:
tensor_fft, tensor_ifft, tensor_rfft, tensor_irfft all extract tensor_values from input, compute the DFT in plain f64, and rebuild non-grad real/imag leaves before tensor_complex. While tensor_complex itself fails loud when its inputs have requires_grad=true, the silent severance happens upstream: with requires_grad input, the tensor_values extraction strips the autograd tape, then re/im non-grad rebuilds satisfy the tensor_complex check, and the user gets a complex output with no gradient back to input.

Add fail-loud guards on all four FFT ops when input requires_grad. This matches the pattern used for stft (frankentorch-3v6e), where Wirtinger calculus would be needed for proper backward.

Affects (all in crates/ft-api/src/lib.rs):
- tensor_fft (line 15064)
- tensor_ifft (line 15105)
- tensor_rfft (line 15161)
- tensor_irfft (line 15200)

★ THE METHODOLOGICAL FINDING, which generalises beyond this row: WHAT CERTIFIES A RUN IS LOAD STABILITY, NOT LOAD LEVEL. Three invocations of the SAME binary on the same host the same day:

  load 8.42 -> 17.24 (+105%) -> 0 of 14 quotable
The certifying run did NOT have the lowest load; it had the FLATTEST. A balanced square cancels a stable offset but not a ramp, so the A/A null breaks when the host CHANGES during the run. Practical rule: sample /proc/loadavg for ~30s and start when it is flat. That is cheaper and far more effective than waiting for an idle machine, which on this box never arrives — and it is why the previous certification attempts failed.

title: EmbeddingBag.forward_with_offsets severs autograd
description:
EmbeddingBag::forward_with_offsets in ft-nn (line 2366) extracts tensor_values from indices, offsets, weight, and per_sample_weights, computes the bag aggregation in plain f64, and rebuilds via session.tensor_variable(output, vec![num_bags, dim], false). This silently severs autograd through the embedding weight AND through per_sample_weights — breaking training for any model using nn.EmbeddingBag (NLP classification, recommendation systems, fastText-style models).

Fix: compose via tensor_index_select + tensor_scatter_add (or matmul with a precomputed indicator matrix). Strategy:
1. Look up rows: emb = tensor_index_select(weight, 0, indices) → [N, D]
2. If per_sample_weights: emb = emb * psw_broadcast (autograd-aware)
3. Per-bag aggregation:
   - Build a [N] non-grad bag_assignment tensor: bag_assignment[i] = which bag i belongs to
   - For Sum: scatter_add into [num_bags, D] zeros. Mean: divide by bag_size after.
   - For Max: needs different routing (gather max per bag) — defer or composed via softmax-based approximation.
4. Handle padding_idx by zeroing out those rows pre-aggregation via mask.

Affects: crates/ft-nn/src/lib.rs EmbeddingBag::forward_with_offsets (line 2366).

title: perf(avg_pool1d): the DENSE backward still has the dead zeroing the scalar route just shed
description:
frankentorch-372h8 removed a 100%-dead zeroing from avg_pool1d_backward_SCALAR_f64 and measured
at least 2.44x FASTER (replicated, five readable paired runs). The DENSE sibling,
avg_pool1d_backward_f64, still has the same dead zeroing under the same condition and has NOT
been touched.

WRITTEN UP NOW BECAUSE A BUILD FREEZE IS IN EFFECT (/data at its 58G floor). Nothing here has
been compiled or gated. Do not land it without the gate below.

THE SITE, crates/ft-kernel-cpu/src/lib.rs, avg_pool1d_backward_f64:

    let mut din = ft_core::buffer_pool::take_zeroed(batch * ch * len);
    ...
    for ox in 0..output_len {
        let g = dout[dbase + ox] / div;
        let start = ox * stride;
        for kx in 0..kernel { drow[start + kx] += g; }
    }

THE ARGUMENT, identical in form to the scalar lever and to the avg_pool2d sibling. When
`stride == kernel` AND `output_len * kernel == len`, the windows tile the input exactly, so each
element is touched by exactly ONE window and the `+=` reads a cell that is still the initial
+0.0. `x += g` on a +0.0 cell is `0.0 + g`, so a direct store of `0.0 + g` into an
UNINITIALIZED buffer is bit-identical -- including for negative-zero and NaN `g`, which is
exactly why the store must be `0.0 + g` and NOT a bare `g` (`-0.0` differs; LLVM cannot fold the
add away for that reason, so the exactness is not wishful).

`covered_len == len` must be STRICT, not `<=`. With `<=` a trailing run is never written, and
against an uninitialized buffer that run is garbage rather than the zeros the gradient requires.
Overlap (`stride < kernel`), gaps (`stride > kernel`), and partial coverage all keep the
existing accumulating route unchanged.

DIFFERENCE FROM THE SCALAR CASE, and the only reason this is a separate bead: `g` varies per
output window here (it is `dout[ox] / kernel`, not one scalar), so the fill is a strided store
rather than a `fill()`. The coverage argument is unchanged; the write pattern is not, so the
measured value may well differ from the scalar route's 2.44x.

IMPLEMENTATION: gate on `!pool_output_zeroed()` so the existing A/B toggle drives it, then
`try_take_exact(numel)` with a `build_uninit` fallback -- NOT a zeroed allocation on the miss
path, which is the correction recorded at the avg_pool2d site.

GATE BEFORE LANDING, mirroring avg_pool1d_scalar_backward_total_coverage_matches_the_zeroed_route_bitwise:
bit-identity between toggle-on and toggle-off over exact tiling, trailing-run, gap and overlap
geometry, with NaN / infinity / +0.0 / -0.0 in `dout`, plus an assertion that everything outside
the covered run is exactly +0.0 in the partial-coverage cases.

MEASURE BEFORE CLAIMING. The route is NOT exercised by the current h2h lane: `timed_op` sums, so
the lane takes the scalar route. A lane that does not sum is needed, or this stays unmeasured --
and per item 29 an unmeasured conversion must be landed as bit-exact dead-work removal only,
never as a win. Two of the vein's four measured sites were worth nothing.
close_reason:
SHIPPED AND MEASURED. REPLICATED STANDING at least 1.27x FASTER. NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE item 36.

The total-coverage argument from 372h8 carried into avg_pool1d_backward_f64, the dense route taken whenever the loss is not a plain sum. Exact tiling means each element is touched by exactly one window, so the += reads a still-zero cell and 0.0 + g stored directly into an uninit buffer is bit-identical -- including for negative-zero and NaN g, which is why the store is 0.0 + g and not a bare g. covered_len == len is strict; overlap, gaps and partial coverage keep the accumulating route.

GATE 6/0 on worker vmi1293453, with dout carrying negative zero, NaN and infinity, across exact-tiling, trailing-run, overlap and gap geometry.

MEASURED, ELF 79ee86ea22be3015, build worker vmi1293453, paired arms adjacent in one round:
  d1  1.332x [1.271,1.398]  32/32  PT control 1.032
  d3  1.364x [1.301,1.405]  32/32  PT control 1.047
  d4  1.357x [1.326,1.399]  32/32  PT control 1.007
  (d2 discarded, PT control 1.079)
  A/A both arms zeroed: 0.986x [0.936,1.028] PT control 1.030 UNDECIDED
CONSERVATIVE: at least 1.27x FASTER, worst bound 1.271, not the 1.36x headline.

THE A/A TOOK TWO ATTEMPTS. The first read 0.986 with a PT control of 1.064 -- past threshold, so unreadable, and NOT used despite its point estimate being exactly what the lever's absence predicts. A control that says what you want but fails its own gate is not a control.

THE BEAD'S PREDICTION WAS CORRECT, which is new for this vein. It said the dense route's value may differ from the scalar's because g varies per window, making this a strided store rather than a fill(). Measured: 2.44x scalar, 1.27x dense -- roughly half the value from the same zeroing removed. The two predictions before this one were both wrong (prelu had no dead init; group_norm had it and gained nothing), so one correct call is weak evidence the model is right in general -- it is better understood for pooling backwards specifically.

A LANE HAD TO BE BUILT: no existing lane exercised this route, because timed_op sums and the sum-shortcut intercepts. The new lane uses sum(out*out) so the shortcut declines; the incumbent twin squares too, and parity reports match.

title: [code-review] ConvTranspose2d/3d output-shape arithmetic rejects valid padding or underflows
description: [HIGH] Review of recent ConvTranspose1d bias work exposed the same output-length surface in adjacent transposed-conv implementations. In crates/ft-nn/src/lib.rs, ConvTranspose2d computes h_span/w_span, rejects whenever span < 2*padding, then adds kernel/output_padding. That over-rejects valid PyTorch-style cases such as H_in=1, kernel=3, padding=1, output_padding=0 where output size should be 1. ConvTranspose3d still computes (dim-1)*stride - 2*padding + kernel + output_padding directly with usize arithmetic, so padding-erased outputs can panic/underflow instead of returning AutogradError. Fix should use checked arithmetic in mathematical order: span + kernel + output_padding, then subtract 2*padding only if the result stays positive, with focused tests for valid padding-preserved and invalid padding-erased shapes.
close_reason: Fixed ConvTranspose2d/3d output-shape arithmetic and singleton padded-output regressions

title: ft-nn Bilinear severs autograd; composable through outer + reshape + matmul
description:
Bilinear at lib.rs:987 (forward_bilinear) computes y[b, k] = sum_{i,j} x1[b, i] * W[k, i, j] * x2[b, j] manually in plain f64, then rebuilds requires_grad=false leaf and adds optional bias on top. Severs autograd through x1/x2/W.

Composable via outer-product + matmul:
   x1_3d = unsqueeze(x1, 2)             # [batch, in1, 1]
   x2_3d = unsqueeze(x2, 1)             # [batch, 1, in2]
   outer = x1_3d * x2_3d                # [batch, in1, in2]
   flat  = reshape(outer, [batch, in1*in2])
   W_flat_t = transpose(reshape(W, [out, in1*in2]), 0, 1)
   y = matmul(flat, W_flat_t)           # [batch, out]
   reshape to original output shape, then add bias.

All ops autograd-aware so gradients flow to x1 / x2 / W / bias.
notes: Fixed in this commit. Composed Bilinear through reshape + unsqueeze + expand + mul + reshape + transpose + matmul + add (bias). The bilinear formula y_k = x1^T W_k x2 + b_k is reformulated as y = vec(x1 outer x2) @ vec(W).T + b, which composes through autograd-aware primitives. ft-nn lib tests: 517.

title: tensor_kron generic path allocates a Vec per inner iteration (perf regression)
description:
fa1cf3d generalized tensor_kron to arbitrary ranks but the new generic path calls decode_coords inside the doubly-nested loop over a_vals x b_vals, allocating a fresh Vec<usize> of length rank for EACH iteration. For a 2D x 2D kron of 100x100 inputs that is 100M Vec allocations replacing what was a constant-time inner loop in the previous specialized 2D path.

Fix sketch: precompute strides for a_aligned, b_aligned, and out_shape ONCE before the loop. Inside the inner loop iterate over a_linear and b_linear directly, accumulating out_linear via stride math without intermediate coordinate Vecs. The stride for out at dim d is product(out_shape[d+1..]); a_aligned coordinate d contributes a_coord*b_aligned[d]*stride_out[d]+b_coord*stride_out[d] which can be precomputed as a per-(a_linear,b_linear) table.

Severity: MEDIUM. Functionality is correct; this is a hot-loop allocation regression that did not exist in the prior specialized 2D path. Stalls a primary tensor algebra op for any non-trivial input size.

Reproduction: cargo bench (or a hand-rolled timing harness) on tensor_kron of two 64x64 inputs vs the pre-fa1cf3d code.
close_reason: Hoisted decode_coords Vec allocation out of the doubly-nested kron loop by precomputing a_strides and b_strides via contiguous_strides() ONCE before the outer loop. Per-iteration heap allocation eliminated; output coordinates derived in-place from a_linear/b_linear via integer division/modulo. Existing 5 kron tests still pass; new kron_4d_matches_explicit_index_decomposition regression added to lock the stride-based output layout against future drift. ft-api 1087 tests pass; clippy + ubs clean.

title: ft-kernel-cpu: Golub-Kahan bidiagonal SVD to replace one-sided Jacobi
description: svd_tall uses one-sided Jacobi (up-to-100 O(m n^2) sweeps). Baseline bench: 256x128 1.169s, 256x256 ~16s/iter. Two eigensolver-shortcut levers tried and REJECTED: (1) bare Gram A^TA + eigh = 67x but FAILS U orthonormality (U^TU off by 1.8e-2 at 40x24) — condition-number squaring corrupts small-sigma U directions; (2) Gram-warm-started Jacobi = accurate but only 2.1x tall / ~1.4x square (sub-2.0, convergence checks dominate). The correct accurate-and-fast lever is Golub-Kahan-Reinsch: Householder bidiagonalization A->B (upper bidiagonal, accumulate U,V) + implicit-shift QR sweep on the bidiagonal with Givens rotations (no A^TA, no condition squaring). Target >=5x at 256x256 with full accuracy. Parity = structural (U^TU=I, VV^T=I, U diag(s) V^T = A) per the new svd_tall_orthonormal_and_reconstructs_40x24 test. Reuse the Householder machinery from eigh_tred2 + qr_contiguous_f64.

title: tensor_inner is severed-autograd: composable through dot/matmul
description:
tensor_inner at lib.rs:15480 contracts the last dim of two tensors:
   c[..a, j_a, ..b, j_b] = sum_l a[..a, l] * b[..b, l]
where a has shape [a_outer..., a_last] and b has shape [b_outer..., b_last] with a_last == b_last. The forward extracts values, computes the contraction in plain f64, and rebuilds a requires_grad=false leaf. PyTorch's torch.inner is differentiable.

Compose through autograd primitives:
- 1-D case: delegate to tensor_dot (already autograd-aware).
- Higher-D: reshape both inputs to 2-D (a_outer, a_last) and (b_outer, b_last), compute matmul(a_flat, b_flat.T), reshape to the inner output shape. matmul + transpose + reshape are all autograd-aware.

Surfaced during /reality-check pass continuing from sirh fix.
notes:
Fixed in this commit. Composed tensor_inner through autograd primitives:
  - 1-D × 1-D: delegates to tensor_dot (autograd-aware via tape).
  - Higher-D: reshape both inputs to 2-D (outer, last), transpose b, matmul, reshape to inner output shape. matmul + transpose + reshape are all autograd-aware.
The output shape contract ([1] for 1-D inputs that previously returned shape [1]) is preserved via tensor_unsqueeze on the 0-D scalar tensor_dot returns. Added inner_1d_propagates_gradient_via_dot regression test ([1,2,3] · [4,5,6] = 32 → grad_a = b, grad_b = a). ft-api lib tests: 1150.

title: measure(max_pool1d): same-binary A/B toggle for the uninit lever — cross-binary rows cannot decide it
description:
The uninit first-touch lever (frankentorch-3ja43) has been measured against PyTorch on
max_pool1d and shows NO GAIN, with a hint of a 2-3.5% regression in the FrankenTorch arm. The
comparison is cross-binary and therefore cannot decide whether the lever caused that. A
same-binary A/B would decide it, and it is the only thing that will.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT SHOWED (NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE item 25):

  max_pool1d_nopool  pre-lever  at least 1.76x SLOWER (worst bound 0.569, ELF 1fa33e62b39e125e)
                     post-lever at least 1.75x SLOWER (worst bound 0.570, ELF 0164585567e3661d
                                built on vmi1227854), two certifying runs, nulls PASS, drift PASS

  FT arm absolute:   nopool 18.435-18.459 ms (4 old runs) -> 19.078 / 19.195 ms (2 new)
                     pooled 16.866-17.034 ms (4 old runs) -> 17.271-17.343 ms (3 new)
  PT arm control:    10.615 / 10.360 / 10.373 ms in the new runs, at or BELOW the old minimum

Two independent lanes moved the same way while the incumbent did not move with them. But peer
commits landed between the two binaries, and code layout alone shifts timings at this
magnitude, so causation is not available from these rows.

WHAT TO BUILD: one binary, a runtime toggle selecting the zeroed vs uninit output path in
max_pool1d_forward_f64 and max_pool1d_forward_with_indices_f64, with both arms sampled in ONE
invocation and paired per round — the same shape as the existing "PAIRED max_pool1d: buffer
pool ON vs OFF" lane in gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h.rs, which settled the buffer-pool question on
this exact lane. Carry the PyTorch arm as the incumbent control so the row is not FT-vs-FT
maintenance.

WHY A TOGGLE AND NOT TWO BUILDS: two builds is what was just done, and it is what cannot
answer the question. The toggle removes the binary as a variable.

OUTCOMES AND WHAT EACH LICENSES:
  - uninit neutral or faster  -> keep the lever; unblock frankentorch-lu3ht and apply its saved
                                 patch (five sibling forwards, already written and gated-ready)
  - uninit slower             -> revert 3ja43, and record why an allocation-removal lever can
                                 COST time, which would be a genuinely new result for this
                                 ledger and would bear on the 75 other vec![0.0...] sites

SIZE HONESTLY: the effect under test is ~2-3.5%, which is close to what this harness can
resolve on a 17-19 ms lane. A paired same-invocation design is what makes an effect that small
readable at all; do not attempt it as a cross-run comparison.

title: [test][perf] nine fuzz properties still generate-then-filter for equal lengths — ~93% of draws wasted, same abort class as q37ra
description:
frankentorch-q37ra fixed ONE property that drew three independent vectors and prop_filter'd for equal lengths; three free lengths agree ~1 in 225, so it exhausted proptest's reject budget and aborted at random.

NINE SIBLINGS in the same file share the anti-pattern with TWO vectors:
    .prop_filter("same length", |(a, b)| a.len() == b.len())
Two free lengths from 1..N agree about 1 time in N-1, so these reject ~93% of draws (1..24 ranges). That is ~15x more headroom than the three-vector case, which is why none has aborted yet -- but it is the same failure class, and it is only ever one unlucky seed away.

MEASURED ON THE ONE ALREADY FIXED: converting from filter to construction took that property from 0.9s to 0.03s, a ~25x speedup, with the SAME number of cases executed. The time was entirely wasted draws. Nine more at ~93% reject are paying a similar tax on every run of the suite.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: this suite went green for the first time on 2026-08-08 (frankentorch-oo3pd) after hiding two real parity bugs (remainder, 5jwh8; pdist, a1nz2). It is now a load-bearing gate. A load-bearing gate that is both slow and occasionally aborts for a non-reason gets ignored, and the next real finding goes with it.

FIX SHAPE, proven on q37ra: draw ONE length, then build each vector at it --
    (1usize..24).prop_flat_map(|n| (vec(RANGE, n), vec(RANGE, n)))
so the reject path is never taken. Raising the reject budget only moves the threshold.

Deliberately filed separately rather than folded into q37ra: those nine currently WORK, and rewriting working generators under a bead about a broken one would have been scope creep.

title: Fix poisson_nll_loss autograd via tensor primitives [child of 2med]
description:
poisson_nll_loss at lib.rs:10357 computes elementwise:
  log_input=True:  loss_i = exp(inp_i) - tgt_i * inp_i
  log_input=False: loss_i = inp_i - tgt_i * log(inp_i + eps)
plus optional Stirling correction tgt*log(tgt) - tgt + 0.5*log(2*pi*tgt) for full=true.

Composable through autograd primitives — the Stirling correction is a function of target only (no input gradient) and can be precomputed as a non-grad scalar tensor and added back in.
notes:
Fixed in this commit. Composed poisson_nll_loss through autograd primitives:
  log_input=true:  exp(input) - target * input → mean
  log_input=false: input - target * log(input + eps) → mean
The Stirling correction (full=true) depends only on target, so we precompute its mean as a non-grad scalar and add via tensor_add. Added poisson_nll_loss_propagates_gradient_through_input regression test (input=[1,2], target=[1,1] → analytical [(e-1)/2, (e^2-1)/2]). ft-api lib tests: 1157.

title: porting: add tensor_sinc with safe-zero handling for torch.sinc parity
description: torch.sinc(x) = sin(pi*x) / (pi*x) for x != 0, 1 at x = 0. Compose via tensor_sin + tensor_div with safe-zero handling: build a mask = (x == 0), use a safe denominator that's pi*x except where x=0 (use 1 to avoid 0/0), then where(mask, ones, sin_term / safe_denom). Gradient at x=0 is 0 (correct limit) since the where routes to the ones constant which has no requires_grad. Useful for signal processing / interpolation.
close_reason: Added tensor_sinc with safe-zero handling matching torch.sinc. Composes through tensor_mul (pi*x) + tensor_sin + tensor_div with a safe-denominator guard (where x=0 the denominator becomes 1 to avoid 0/0; the result is then masked back to 1 via tensor_where). Gradient at x=0 is correctly 0 since the final where routes that position to a no-grad ones constant. 3 unit tests cover known values (0/0.5/1/2), zero-input no-NaN (the safe-denom guard), and analytic gradient regression (0 at x=0, -4/π at x=0.5). ft-api now at 1286 lib tests.

title: [perf] dense-gradient write: alloc_zeroed forces cold-page faults — serial fill is 5.7x faster than 64-thread parallel
description:
NOT A POOLING BUG. Every op whose backward returns a dense gradient the size of its input pays this,
so it is filed separately from frankentorch-87sz8 rather than inside it.

MEASURED (artifacts/perf/frankentorch-87sz8/backward_attribution.md, ELF 62b59932, mimalloc, 15-rep
medians, max_pool3d [2,32,16,32,32] f64 => 8 MiB gradient):
  alloc_only                        0.096 ms   ( 6% of the backward)
  alloc + touch every element       1.269 ms   (84%)  <- THE WALL
  scatter work above that floor     0.242 ms   (16%)
  raw backward                      1.511 ms

8 MiB written in 1.269 ms is ~6.3 GB/s. PyTorch's WHOLE forward+backward for the same op moves roughly
17 MiB (8 read + 1 write + 8 write) in 0.660 ms, ~26 GB/s on the same machine. FrankenTorch's
large-buffer write path is therefore roughly 4x off the bandwidth PyTorch achieves.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN ANY POOLING LEVER: even with a FREE scatter and a FREE forward,
max_pool3d would sit at 1.269 ms against PyTorch's 0.660 ms for the entire op. The dense-gradient
write alone is ~2x PyTorch's whole op. No amount of kernel-logic work in pooling can reach parity
while this term stands.

CAVEAT THAT BOUNDS THE CLAIM AND IS THE FIRST STEP OF THE WORK: the 1.269 ms figure is the floor for
*a* dense-write implementation — `par_chunks_mut` over 64 planes with scalar f64 stores — not a
proven-optimal one. 64 rayon tasks over 128 KiB chunks writing one f64 at a time is not obviously the
best way to fill 8 MiB. Part of the 4x may be the write pattern rather than an inherent limit.
ESTABLISH THE TRUE FLOOR FIRST (wider/vector stores, different chunk sizing, non-temporal stores,
possibly avoiding the zero-then-overwrite entirely where the op fully covers its output) and measure it
before writing a lever. Do not assume 6.3 GB/s is fixed, and do not assume it is improvable either.

SUGGESTED FIRST PROBE: a standalone bandwidth ladder — fill 8 MiB of f64 by (a) vec![0.0; n],
(b) par_chunks_mut scalar stores, (c) par_chunks_mut with chunk sizes swept 16 KiB..1 MiB,
(d) wide/SIMD stores, (e) alloc_zeroed with no touch as the lower bound — on this host, reporting
GB/s for each. That tells you the achievable number before any kernel is touched.

RELATED: the same term is why avg_pool2d's backward (1.795 ms) dwarfs its forward (0.898 ms), so a fix
here likely moves frankentorch-k1h8g too.
close_reason: REFUTED AND REVERTED, with evidence (YellowBrook/cc, 2026-08-08, commit 910d9a3a). The bead's hypothesis — that this kernel pays contended first-touch page faults on fresh alloc_zeroed mmap pages, so a serial fill would be ~5.7x cheaper — is FALSE at the call site. Interleaved two-ELF A/B (A 405b1d4d vs B 27f3e72e, arms differing by exactly the two landed fill statements, digests read from the running process): paired median 1.118x SLOWER, bootstrap 95pct CI [1.050,1.183], 11/12 rounds slower, +0.152 ms. Two controls compiled identically into both ELFs stayed flat (0.992, 1.008), so it is the lever and not host drift; lead-arm split (1.074 / 1.145) rules out a slot penalty. The added cost equals one serial 8 MiB write, meaning the fill reduced the parallel pass by nothing — a fault-bound pass would have been absorbed by it. Both fill sites reverted, DO-NOT-RE-LAND notes with the numbers left at the call sites, evidence in artifacts/perf/frankentorch-zoqws/in_situ_ab.md. Gates: 594 passed/0 failed, clippy 0 errors with positive checking evidence, fmt clean, ubs Critical 0. No vs-PyTorch number moves — 5f471b62 correctly claimed no speedup — but max_pool3d backward is ~10pct faster than it was at HEAD before the revert. The replacement question (where the ~1.2 ms actually goes) is filed as frankentorch-un3os rather than guessed at.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
STEP 0 DONE — BANDWIDTH LADDER (CyanAnchor/cc, 2026-08-06).
Artifact: artifacts/perf/frankentorch-zoqws/bandwidth_ladder.md
Probe: crates/ft-api/examples/dense_write_bandwidth_ladder.rs
ELF be00e0a403d876e99062ac973ebbb369813b5df4d1bf48bed8bfd9a363f65c4e, mimalloc, 8 MiB f64, 21-rep
medians, 64 threads.

THE HEADLINE INVERTS THIS BEAD'S FRAMING: parallelism is not the fix, it is the problem.
  par_chunks_mut scalar [CURRENT KERNEL]      6.39 GiB/s
  par_chunks_mut + fill, 16KiB..2MiB chunks   6.01 - 7.87 GiB/s   (chunk size buys <=1.2x)
  par_chunks_mut + wide f64x4 stores          6.52 GiB/s          (store width buys nothing)
  SERIAL slice::fill, ONE thread             36.70 GiB/s          <- 5.7x FASTER THAN ALL OF THEM
  vec![1.0; N] warm construction             63.34 GiB/s
  1-in-8 scatter (the kernel's real shape)    6.28 GiB/s          <- same as writing EVERY element

MECHANISM the numbers point at: `vec![0.0f64; N]` is alloc_zeroed; at 8 MiB that is fresh mmap zero
pages, so every call faults in the whole buffer, and 64 threads faulting one fresh mapping contend on
kernel page-table locks. Serial fill faults the same pages uncontended. vec![1.0; N] is faster still
because a non-zero init takes allocate-then-fill and can reuse a RECYCLED already-faulted block.
The 1-in-8 row is the tell: scattering into 1/8 of the buffer costs the same as filling all of it, so
the kernel is not paying for stores — it is paying for first-touch faults.

THE LEVER THIS NAMES: stop asking the allocator for zeroed memory on this path. Allocate uninitialised
and zero deliberately, so the buffer can come from a recycled warm block rather than a fresh mapping.
ft-kernel-cpu already has `build_uninit` and the reviewed precedent (expand/broadcast_to replaced
`vec![v; numel]` serial first-touch with an uninit buffer whose fill does the first touch, 2.2-5.03x,
bit-exact); frankentorch-1zrvy consolidated the crate's uninit sites onto that helper.

TWO CAVEATS THAT BOUND IT — do not quote 9.91x:
 (1) the fast arms benefit from allocator WARMTH, not just write pattern, because a zeroing allocator
     cannot hand back a dirty block. 9.91x is an upper bound on an idealised change; treat 5.7x
     (serial-fill vs current) as the honest ceiling and expect less in situ.
 (2) host load average was 22 during the run, which inflates the PARALLEL rows specifically since they
     compete for cores and the serial row does not. Direction survives (5.7x is far outside contention)
     but re-measure quiet before quoting exact ratios.

NOT SHOWN, and it is the next step rather than a conclusion: that replacing vec![0.0f64; ..] inside
max_pool3d_backward_from_indices_f64 delivers this in situ. The kernel still needs zeros in the 7-of-8
elements it does not scatter into, so it must still zero; the claim is only that zeroing a recycled
block beats being handed a fresh zeroed mapping. Requires same-binary A/B, bit-exact, in the kernel.

COMPATIBLE WITH 3i7c0, does not reopen it: 3i7c0 rejected in-session buffer POOLING because swapping
the ALLOCATOR did not move realistic reuse lanes. This is sharper and code-side — the cost is asking
for zeroed pages at all, which defeats recycling in any allocator.

title: tensor_linalg_svd doesn't complete orthonormal basis for zero singular vectors
description: On rank-deficient matrices, FrankenTorch's tensor_linalg_svd returns U columns corresponding to zero singular values as all-zeros instead of orthonormal vectors completing the basis. numpy.linalg.svd (and torch.linalg.svd) always produce a fully orthonormal U with U^T U = I_k, regardless of rank. Repro: 3x3 matrix [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]] (rank 2). numpy returns U[:,2] as a unit vector orthogonal to col([1,2,3],[4,5,6]); FrankenTorch returns U[:,2] = 0. Surfaced by torch_linalg_svd_numpy_subprocess_conformance during the frankentorch-c36b work; current conformance test trims the rank-deficient case to land. Severity: medium — breaks the U^T U = I invariant that downstream code (e.g., least-squares via SVD) may rely on; doesn't affect the U @ diag(S) @ Vh reconstruction.
notes: Fixed in this commit: unified the orthonormal-basis completion in svd_tall to handle both (a) rank-deficient inputs (zero singular values) and (b) full_matrices mode with m > k. Any column of U that ends up with norm <= tol now gets a unit vector orthogonal to all previously-set columns via Gram-Schmidt against e_0..e_{m-1}, retrying basis vectors as needed. Restored the rank_deficient_3x3 case in both torch_linalg_svd_numpy_subprocess_conformance and torch_linalg_pinv_numpy_subprocess_conformance — both pass.

title: Add metamorphic property tests for index_select identity, relu decomposition, cumsum/diff round-trip
description:
Extend the testing-metamorphic pass with four additional property tests in ft-conformance::tests under #[cfg(feature=fuzz)]:

1. fuzz_metamorphic_index_select_sequential_is_identity — for any 1-D x of length n, index_select(x, dim=0, [0, 1, ..., n-1]) must equal x bit-exactly.

title: [perf][groupnorm] price a multi-accumulator reduction before asking for the tolerance policy call
description:
GroupNorm f32 is still the worst standing after the parallel-gate and stats-reuse levers: 6.77x slower than PyTorch (harness=crates/ft-api/examples/gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h.rs, same_host=thinkstation1, ELF 5c5647cc, build worker vmi1264463, 48 rounds, parity match). Its three kernels total 0.812 ms (min of 9) against a torch arm that does the whole forward+sum+backward in ~0.20 ms, and the remaining structural difference is now narrow enough to name.

THE TERM. Every per-group statistic is a SCALAR accumulation over group_numel = cpg*spatial = 1568 elements:

    for &v in xb { sum += v }            // and the vsum pass, and sum0/sum1

Float addition is not associative, so LLVM may neither vectorise this nor break the dependency chain. At roughly 4 cycles of f32 add latency that is ~6.3k cycles per pass per group, where 8 SIMD lanes with 4 independent accumulators would be a few hundred. Torch's reductions are vectorised. This is the plausible bulk of what is left.

WHAT THIS BEAD DELIVERS, and it deliberately stops short of the change: a MEASUREMENT of what a multi-accumulator reduction would buy on this exact shape, so the tolerance question below is decided against a number rather than a hope. Add a probe arm to the existing breakdown block in gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h (NOT a new standalone probe -- see NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE item 11 for what separate probes did to this lane) timing, interleaved rep-by-rep on the same data:
  a) the current sequential reduction over one group;
  b) the same reduction with 4 or 8 independent accumulators summed at the end.
Report both plus their ratio. If (b) is not materially faster, this whole line is closed and the bead is a recorded negative -- which is the likely-enough outcome that it must be checked before anyone writes a kernel.

THE POLICY QUESTION, only if the probe says the win is real. Multi-accumulator reduction reassociates the sum and changes the last ULP of mean, rstd and every output element. There is no bit-exact version. What makes this a policy call rather than a refusal: FrankenTorch does NOT match torch bit-for-bit on this op today -- the harness reports parity by TOLERANCE and says `match` -- so the current scalar order is not torch's order either. The choice is not "bit-exact vs not"; it is WHICH non-matching order, and the vectorised one is both faster and closer to what torch actually does. Bring the measured number and let the user decide; do not ship it unilaterally, and do not regenerate the existing bit-exact lock tests to make it pass.

CONSTRAINT the probe must respect: the two arms must read the SAME data in the same cache state, interleaved rep by rep, and be reported as min-of-N. Do not compare a min from one arm against a median from the other -- that error cost this lane a whole bead (item 12), and at 1.33-1.51x the estimator difference alone is larger than the effect being measured.

Do NOT re-probe: the f64 grad-space widening (item 10), per-rep allocation churn (item 12), the parallel forward gate (shipped, dmpho), or forward-statistics reuse (shipped, item 13).
close_reason: Priced in 87169eca (ledger item 15). Sequential 1.142 us vs 8 accumulators 0.151 us over the same 1568-element group, interleaved rep-by-rep, min of 9: 7.563x headroom on the reduction PHASE. harness=gauntlet_lane_sweep_h2h, same_host=thinkstation1, build worker vmi1264463, ELF d8e61dce. The bead deliberately stops here: reassociation moves mean/rstd/output by an ULP and there is no bit-exact version, so the tolerance decision is the user's. Bounded against misreading: the GroupNorm f32 kernels total ~0.81 ms and the reductions are a fraction, so the lane effect is well below 7.5x.

title: [parity-gap] torch math functions: frexp, gcd, lcm
description:
Missing math functions from torch:

- torch.frexp(input): Decomposes input into mantissa and exponent
- torch.gcd(input, other): Element-wise greatest common divisor
- torch.lcm(input, other): Element-wise least common multiple

frexp returns a tuple (mantissa, exponent) where input = mantissa * 2^exponent.
gcd and lcm operate on integer tensors.

Ref: https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/torch.html

title: ft-kernel-cpu: matrix_exp Taylor[12]->Pade[6/6] to cut matmul count
description: matrix_exp now uses fast dgemm (frankentorch-7bj2) but still does a 13-term Taylor series = 12 matmuls per scaling step. Pade[6/6] (Higham scaling-and-squaring) needs only ~4 matmuls (A2=A*A, A4=A2*A2, A6=A4*A2, U=A*(c1 I+c3 A2+c5 A4)) + 1 LU solve q^-1 p, q=V-U, p=V+U, V=c0 I+c2 A2+c4 A4+c6 A6. Coeffs c=[1,1/2,5/44,1/66,1/792,1/15840,1/665280]. ~2-3x fewer matmuls AND better accuracy than Taylor. Reuse lu_factor_contiguous_f64 + lu_solve_contiguous_f64 for the solve (column by column or matrix solve). Parity tolerance-based; value-parity test compares grad/non-grad (both kernel) so safe. Target additional ~2x on top of the dgemm win.
notes: REJECTED: Pade[6/6] (4 matmuls + LU solve) is SLOWER than the shipped dgemm-Taylor (12 parallel matmuls). A/B 128x128: dgemm-Taylor 1.68ms vs Pade 4.74ms; 256x256 15.0ms vs 21.9ms. Root cause: the naive single-threaded lu_solve dominates; cutting parallel dgemm matmuls does not help when the solve is serial. Real lever is parallelizing the triangular solve (see new bead).
close_reason: Rejected current Padé[6/6] dirty implementation: remote rch Criterion on vmi1227854 measured matrix_exp_f64_128x128 [4.1882 ms 4.7257 ms 5.1411 ms] and matrix_exp_f64_256x256 [22.785 ms 24.146 ms 26.113 ms], regressing against the frankentorch-7bj2 dgemm baseline recorded at 128x128 1.67 ms and 256x256 13.24 ms. Source diff was not committed by BoldOx and is left untouched; next matrix_exp pass should replace the solve-heavy Pade[6/6] path with a deeper primitive or optimized solve strategy, not keep this lever.
